Anton Shilov is a contributing writer at Tom’s Hardware. Over the past couple of decades, he has covered everything from CPUs and GPUs to supercomputers and from modern process technologies and latest fab tools to high-tech industry trends.

articles.title: La guerra de Ucrania está teniendo un beneficiado inesperado: la minería ilegal de ámbar
articles.text:
Si nada cambia (y parece difícil) en febrero la guerra de Ucrania cumplirá cinco años, un lustro de enfrentamientos que se ha saldado con decenas de miles de fallecidos en ambos bandos, un gasto millonario en armamento y ayuda humanitaria y, en general, un tensionamiento en la geopolítica mundial que parece lejos de aflojarse. Hay sin embargo un negocio al que el conflicto parece estar sentándole bastante bien: el comercio ilegal de ámbar ‘made in Ucrania’.
La guerra ha hecho que el esfuerzo regulador activado por Kiev en 2019 pasase a un segundo plano. Hoy la prioridad no es el ámbar, sino el frente.
El negocio del ámbar. China es un mercado de 1.400 millones de potenciales clientes, lo que explica que no haya sector que no sueñe con abrirse camino allí. Si hablamos de ámbar los negocios cuentan además con un aliciente extra: el gigante asiático muestra un interés especial por esta resina fosilizada y preciada en joyería. Tanto, que los exportadores polacos (referencia en el sector) estiman que alrededor del 40% de la producción acaba en China y el Sudeste Asiático.
Los compradores de Pekín, Shanghái, Shenzhen o el resto de metrópolis chinas también despertaron el interés de otros exportadores de ámbar, como Rusia o Ucrania. Y es lógico. AFP recuerda que el aumento de demanda generado en Asia hizo que el sector viviese su particular ‘fiebre del oro’, con valores que se dispararon un 1000% entre 2010 y 2015.
La ‘cara B’ del negocio. Al calor de ese porcentaje, hubo quien decidió lanzarse a la extracción de ámbar sin reparar en los daños que pudiera causar al medioambiente o las líneas rojas que establece la ley. El resultado fue una “mafia del ámbar” que, lamenta Olena Belichenko, de la Asociación Internacional del Ámbar (IAA), causó un “verdadero caos” y una “catástrofe” ecológica.
“La minería se realizaba ilegalmente, el medio ambiente sufría graves daños y nuestros recursos fueron saqueados durante 30 años”, concuerda Oleg Bogelsky, de Amber Galbin, una empresa minera que opera en Rivne, al oeste del país.
La hemeroteca demuestra que tienen motivos para quejarse. En 2017 National Geographic publicó una amplia crónica en la que alertaba de la “minería ilegal” de ámbar en “el salvaje oeste de Ucrania”. Más allá de su impacto en el terreno, con “miles de hectáreas de bosques de pinos y abedules devastados”, su reportero John Wendle hablaba también de bandas que recurrían a las armas para disputarse los mejores yacimientos y “rumores sobre funcionarios corruptos”.
Y llegó 2019. El panorama cambió en 2019, cuando el Gobierno de Ucrania impulsó nuevas normas para “regular” la extracción de ámbar. La idea era promover la extracción legal y, de paso, frenar el mercado negro.
Resulta difícil saber hasta qué punto se alcanzó ese último objetivo, pero los datos de Aduanas sugieren que como mínimo el cambio de 2019 ayudó a desviar mercancía al cauce legal: las exportaciones oficiales de resina sin procesar se dispararon en cinco años, pasando de 0,6 toneladas en 2020 a 88,8 en 2025.
Nuevas prioridades. Por más preocupante que fuese el mercado ilegal de ámbar y su impacto económico, medioambiental y social, el 24 de febrero de 2022 el asunto pasó a un segundo (o tercer) lugar en la lista de prioridades de Kiev. Ese día las tropas rusas avanzaron hacia Ucrania, iniciando una guerra que sigue enquistada casi un lustro después y acumula decenas y decenas de miles de muertos en ambos bandos. Esa situación ha llevado al Parlamento ucraniano a ir prorrogando desde entonces la ley marcial para centrarse en la guerra.
¿Qué tiene que ver con el ámbar? Que según la agencia AFP ese cambio de prioridades ha afectado al celo regulador que se activó con las nuevas normas de 2019. No se trata de que se hayan derogado, sino de si en plena guerra se siguen realizando inspecciones y auditorías que permitan a las autoridades controlar el negocio. Y dada la situación actual en Rivne hay motivos para ser escépticos.
El problema lo reconoce Mykola Kotniuk, de la Asociación de Empresas de Ámbar de Ucrania, quien asume la posibilidad de que a día de hoy haya gente extrayendo resina cuando solo tiene permiso para trabajos piloto o sondeos.
La lógica es muy sencilla: tras más de cuatro años de guerra, toca priorizar recursos. Y la industria minera no parece estar en primer lugar. “Algunos explotadores del subsuelo abusan de su posición y, tal vez, algunos extraen recursos de forma ilegal”, añade el responsable de la patronal del sector.
Más que sospechas. Durante su investigación AFP charló con un directivo de la industria ucraniana que asegura que entre el 60 y 70% del ámbar del país es de origen ilícito. Sea o no cierto, la misma agencia cita un dato oficial: desde 2024 Ucrania ha abierto 360 investigaciones por la extracción y posesión ilegal de ámbar, según datos de la Fiscalía Ambiental.
Entre ellas se cuenta una red minera descubierta en junio. El negocio estaba liderado por un funcionario y se le achaca un daño ambiental valorado en ocho millones de dólares. Con todo, desde el sector hay quien matiza también que las infracciones flagrantes representan casos “aislados”.

articles.title: Talkdesk's life sciences play shows why industry depth beats AI cost-cutting - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Talkdesk’s life sciences play shows why industry depth beats AI cost-cutting
The customer experience arena, specifically the contact center, has been the low-hanging fruit for artificial intelligence deployments, with much of the focus on cost-cutting. The goals include fewer agents, shorter calls, higher containment and lower cost per interaction.
Those are legitimate goals, but they lead every vendor to the same pitch. When everyone sells the same savings, the market becomes a price war that favors the companies with the deepest pockets.
Talkdesk Inc. is taking a different path, and today’s announcement reinforces that. This week, the company introduced Talkdesk Life Sciences Experience Cloud, a platform designed for biopharmaceutical companies’ patient services operations. The goal is not to make calls cheaper. It is to move patients from a written prescription to therapy faster and keep them there.
That outcome is one a pharma executive will pay for, and one a generic contact-center-as-a-service platform is poorly equipped to deliver. This adds to Talkdesk’s portfolio of industry clouds, including financial services, government, retail, travel and others.
The news
The new offering connects AI agents, human specialists, systems, and workflows across the specialty care journey, which typically includes enrollment, prior authorizations and specialty pharmacy handoffs. Talkdesk cites IQVIA research showing that nearly one in three commercially insured patients cannot access a prescribed therapy within 30 days, and Boston Consulting Group data indicating that 90% of biopharma leaders view fragmented platforms as their primary bottleneck.
The platform analyzes patient service conversations to pinpoint where patients get stuck, assists specialists in real time, and coordinates tasks among hubs, providers, payers, specialty pharmacies and safety teams. It supports the U.S. Food and Drug Administration’s 21 CFR Part 11 requirements for electronic records and signatures and integrates with existing customer relationship management, hub, pharmacy and safety systems.
One of the world’s five largest pharmaceutical companies has already deployed it. That customer uses AI to classify and route inbound calls and to monitor live conversations for potential reportable events, or PREs, which are adverse event signals that must be captured and sent to pharmacovigilance systems. When the system detects a PRE, it guides the frontline agent to collect the required details, preserves the source conversation and triggers approved workflows to document and route the information.
“A prescription should mark the start of healing, not the beginning of an administrative maze,” said Patty Hayward, general manager of healthcare and life sciences at Talkdesk. “We are focusing first on Therapy Access because quickly getting patients onto prescribed treatments is one of the most urgent, measurable challenges in healthcare today.”
Hayward’s choice of the word “measurable” is the key point. Time to therapy is a metric that appears on a drug maker’s revenue line and in patient outcomes, not just on a contact center dashboard.
Industry focus is how a smaller vendor wins
Talkdesk competes in a crowded market against much larger companies. NiCE Ltd. and Genesys Cloud Services Inc. have scale in the contact center, while Microsoft Corp., Salesforce Inc., and Amazon Web Services Inc. can bundle customer service capabilities into platforms that customers already own. A smaller company cannot outspend those rivals on horizontal features, and it should not try.
What it can do is go deeper into specific industries than the giants are willing to go. Talkdesk has been building industry-specific clouds for several years, and life sciences is a logical next step from its healthcare work. Pharmacovigilance workflows, Part 11 compliance, hub services and specialty pharmacy coordination are not features a horizontal vendor casually adds to its roadmap. They require domain expertise, regulatory knowledge and integrations that take time to build, and that time becomes a competitive moat.
The industry approach also changes the sales conversation. A generic platform is evaluated on price per seat and feature checklists, usually by the information technology department and the contact center leader. An industry platform is evaluated on whether it solves a business problem the executive team already worries about.
In pharma, patient abandonment between prescription and first fill represents lost revenue and a failed treatment. That conversation happens with the head of patient services, which is a much better place for a smaller vendor to be.
The industry approach has helped channel partners sell Talkdesk. I asked Joe Rittenhouse, co-CEO of Converged Technology Professionals Inc., one of the premier communications resellers, about it.
“We’re no longer leading with features or price per seat,” he said. “We’re leading with the customer’s workflows, their compliance requirements and the outcomes they’re measured on. That industry approach is a key differentiator for us. It lets us skip the generic AI conversation and get straight to the problems that keep the business up at night, shortening the sales cycle and making the deployment stick.”
CXA needs industry context to work
The bigger story is how this fits into Talkdesk’s customer experience automation or CXA strategy, which is not a typical contact center-as-a-service sell. The idea is to coordinate AI agents, people, knowledge and enterprise systems to resolve a customer need from start to finish, rather than simply answering or routing an interaction faster. Resolving issues across systems is a far bigger value proposition than call deflection, but it is also much harder to deliver in the abstract.
That is where industry depth becomes critical. End-to-end automation is only possible when the platform understands what “end” means. In a retail return, the end might be a refund. In specialty pharma, the end is a patient who has completed benefits verification, obtained prior authorization, had the drug shipped and is still taking it six months later.
Each step involves different systems, organizations and regulatory obligations. A horizontal AI agent cannot orchestrate that journey without someone first mapping it. Talkdesk is effectively packaging that work into the product.
This is also why the industry approach shifts AI from a cost story to a transformation story. Using AI to reduce handle time on patient service calls might save a few dollars per interaction, and identifying that patients in each program repeatedly stall at prior authorization, then fixing that bottleneck, can change how many patients start therapy. The first is an efficiency gain. The second changes the economics of the business.
The pharmacovigilance use case makes the same point. Missing a reportable adverse event carries regulatory consequences. AI that detects those signals and routes them correctly reduces risk and improves quality, rather than reducing headcount, a value proposition that is far easier to justify to a board.
What this means for buyers
For life sciences leaders, the lesson is to stop evaluating customer engagement technology based solely on contact center metrics. Start with the patient journey, identify where patients drop off and measure vendors on their ability to shorten time to therapy and improve adherence. Insist on proof of regulatory readiness, particularly for Part 11 and adverse event handling, and validate integration with the hub, CRM and safety systems already in place.
For buyers in other industries, the broader point still holds. AI that only cuts costs will eventually commoditize. AI that understands your business’s specific workflows, regulations and outcomes can transform it. Ask CX vendors how well they understand your industry, not just how good their models are.
For Talkdesk, life sciences is a smart focus area. It will not win every horizontal deal against larger rivals, but it does not need to. By targeting industries with complex, regulated journeys tied to clear outcomes, it can make CXA tangible and give customers a reason to buy that has nothing to do with price.

articles.title: Estos son los 4 cambios que tendría el iPhone Duo de Apple en el año 2027
articles.text:
Apple ya estaría trabajando en cuatro cambios para la segunda generación del iPhone Duo, el teléfono plegable que llegó al mercado hace apenas unas semanas. Pese a lo reciente de su lanzamiento, la compañía necesita definir pronto las características del sucesor si quiere cumplir con su calendario habitual de presentación en septiembre.
Así lo detalló Mark Gurman en Bloomberg, donde señaló que la empresa ya cuenta con prototipos del dispositivo, identificado internamente con el nombre en clave V78, y que trabaja en paralelo en cuatro frentes de mejora.
Cuáles son los cambios que tendría el iPhone Duo
- Face ID
El primer cambio, y el más urgente para Apple, es la incorporación de Face ID al iPhone Duo 2. El modelo actual utiliza Touch ID, un sistema que funciona de forma correcta pero que resulta menos cómodo que el reconocimiento facial para buena parte de los usuarios.
Según Gurman, la compañía ya desarrolló prototipos del dispositivo con Face ID integrado en la pantalla exterior. Los ingenieros continúan trabajando en esa integración, aunque todavía no está confirmado si la tecnología también llegará a la pantalla interior del plegable.
El reconocimiento facial seguro requiere Face ID, un sistema que proyecta e interpreta un mapa de puntos infrarrojos para identificar el rostro del usuario. Su llegada al iPhone Duo 2 depende de si Apple logra ubicar los componentes necesarios dentro de un chasis plegable con espacio limitado.
El tiempo juega en contra de este objetivo. Si el lanzamiento se mantiene en septiembre del año próximo, la compañía debe cerrar las definiciones de hardware en las próximas semanas, lo que convierte a Face ID en un desarrollo todavía incierto para la versión final que llegue al público.
- Un botón de acción compartido con la cámara
El segundo cambio contemplado es la incorporación de un botón de acción, ausente en el primer iPhone Duo. Se trata del único modelo de iPhone sin ese conmutador o botón dedicado a silenciar el equipo o ejecutar funciones rápidas, una omisión que, según Gurman, respondería a limitaciones de espacio dentro de un chasis compacto.
Para resolverlo sin sacrificar superficie interna, Apple evalúa combinar esa función con el botón de control de cámara, de manera que un mismo componente cumpla ambas tareas. La medida resulta coherente con reportes de usuarios que señalan un uso poco frecuente del botón de cámara en su formato actual.
- Cámara teleobjetivo
El tercer punto de la hoja de ruta apunta al sistema de cámaras. Pese a que los resultados fotográficos del iPhone Duo actual resultan convincentes, el dispositivo carece de una cámara teleobjetivo pese a tratarse de un modelo más caro que los iPhone Pro.
Apple estudiaría sumar una tercera cámara principal con esa función, aunque el desafío vuelve a ser el espacio disponible: en un cuerpo plegable donde la mayor parte del volumen interno se destina a la batería y al sistema de bisagras, cualquier cámara adicional implica rediseñar buena parte de la placa.
- Diseño más delgado
El cuarto objetivo es el más exigente en términos de ingeniería: un diseño más delgado y liviano que el actual, sin reducir el tamaño de pantalla ni las prestaciones. Apple buscaría lograrlo mientras suma, al mismo tiempo, Face ID, un botón adicional y una cámara extra, aunque Gurman no precisó en qué magnitud se reduciría el grosor del equipo.
Plazos ajustados y margen de cambios
Gurman advirtió que el desarrollo del iPhone Duo 2 se encuentra en una etapa temprana. Apple suele finalizar sus prototipos definitivos hacia febrero, para luego someterlos a pruebas de fábrica antes de iniciar la producción en julio, con vistas a un lanzamiento entre septiembre y octubre.
Esa ventana implica que alguno de los cuatro objetivos podría quedar descartado si los plazos se ajustan antes de lo previsto. El periodista remarcó que la información disponible retrata el estado actual del desarrollo, sin garantizar que todas las funciones lleguen al modelo final.
Según Gurman, los compradores del primer iPhone Duo no deben esperar que sus comentarios o encuestas de satisfacción influyan en el diseño del Duo 2. El cronograma de la segunda generación ya estaba definido antes del lanzamiento del modelo original, por lo que cualquier ajuste basado en la opinión de los usuarios recién podría incorporarse en una eventual tercera versión.

articles.title: Sonos Ace à -56% avant même le Black Friday : isolation, autonomie, Dolby Atmos
articles.text:
Amazon n’attend pas le Black Friday pour faire passer le Sonos Ace sous la barre des 200 €. Le casque est affiché à 199 € au lieu de 449 €, prix conseillé indiqué par Amazon, et notre test lui avait attribué 9/10 en juin 2024, avec trois réserves : des aigus inégaux, des voix en retrait et un poids élevé.
Premier casque de la marque, le Sonos Ace réunit une réduction de bruit active, le Bluetooth multipoint et un audio spatial Dolby avec suivi dynamique des mouvements de la tête. Amazon le vend 199 € au lieu de 449 € dans sa version noire, soit 56 % de remise au titre de son offre Pré-Black Friday.
Sonos a depuis lancé l’Ace Ultra, un modèle plus récent, et notre test de l’Ace date de juin 2024. Voyons si ce casque, que nous avions jugé « presque parfait », vaut ce prix selon votre usage.
Le casque Bluetooth Sonos Ace à réduction de bruit est affiché à 199 € au lieu de 449 € sur Amazon, dans sa version noire.
Pourquoi choisir le Sonos Ace ?
- Une isolation qui compte en déplacement : notre test juge l’isolation phonique excellente, notamment dans les basses fréquences. Dans un train ou un open space, c’est ce qui sépare un fond sonore subi d’un fond sonore oublié.
- Trente heures sans chercher la prise : Sonos annonce 30 heures d’autonomie avec la réduction de bruit, et nous avons mesuré 30 h 30 en aptX HD. Cela représente un mois de trajets d’une heure par jour avant de recharger.
- Le cinéma à la maison : relié à une barre de son Sonos compatible, le casque reçoit un flux Dolby Atmos avec un suivi de la tête que notre test juge presque aussi réussi que celui d’Apple. La fonction reste réservée aux foyers déjà équipés Sonos.
Du trajet quotidien au film du soir
Le Sonos Ace se montre d’abord à l’aise en mobilité. Il se connecte à deux appareils en multipoint, accepte l’AAC, l’aptX, l’aptX HD et l’aptX Adaptive, et offre un kit mains libres que notre test du Sonos Ace juge très bon, avec une voix claire et détaillée. À la maison, le suivi de la tête rend l’audio spatial plus naturel devant un film, à condition de posséder une barre de son Sonos compatible. Sans elle, vous profitez d’un casque Bluetooth classique, mais bien isolé.
Le son plaira à ceux qui aiment des basses légèrement mises en avant et une scène large. Les aigus restent inégaux et les voix en retrait, un point à écouter avant d’acheter si vous écoutez surtout de la musique vocale. Le poids compte aussi : 312 g, contre 254 g pour le Sony WH-1000XM5 et 252 g pour le Bose QC Ultra Headphones, ce qui rend le casque moins confortable sur les très longues sessions d’écoute.
Face aux casques Bluetooth plus récents
Notre test date de juin 2024 et Sonos a depuis lancé l’Ace Ultra : l’Ace est donc plus ancien que le casque actuel de la marque. Pour le situer face aux références du moment, comme le Sony WH-1000XM6 qui figure dans notre comparatif des meilleurs casques Bluetooth, mieux vaut regarder ce que vous en attendez. Sans produit Sonos, l’atout du suivi de la tête devant la télévision disparaît, et le choix se joue sur l’isolation, l’autonomie et le prix. Avec une barre de son Sonos compatible, il se justifie davantage.
✅ Les points forts
- Isolation phonique jugée excellente par notre test
- Autonomie annoncée à 30 heures avec réduction de bruit, 30 h 30 mesurées en aptX HD
- Immersion Dolby Atmos avec suivi de la tête, depuis une barre de son Sonos compatible
- Très bon kit mains libres et bonne qualité de fabrication
❌ Les limites
- Poids de 312 g, supérieur à la moyenne
- Aigus peu linéaires et voix en retrait
- Casque non pliable, application aux réglages limités (égaliseur à trois bandes)
- Modèle plus ancien que l’Ace Ultra
Le tarif de 199 € concerne la version noire du Sonos Ace, dans le cadre de l’offre Pré-Black Friday : vérifiez-le sur la fiche Amazon avant de commander.
À 199 €, le Sonos Ace coûte 250 € de moins que son prix conseillé de 449 €, soit 56 % de remise. Notre note de 9/10 repose sur une isolation, une autonomie et une construction solides, nuancées par un son que nous avions trouvé inégal dans les aigus. Le casque convient bien aux trajets, aux appels et aux films devant une barre de son Sonos.
Passez votre chemin si vous cherchez le modèle le plus récent de la marque, si 312 g vous gênent en écoute prolongée ou si vous écoutez surtout des voix. Si vous possédez déjà une barre de son Sonos compatible, c’est là que ce casque prend tout son sens ; sans elle, comparez-le d’abord aux autres modèles de la catégorie.
Comment profiter des offres exclusives du Black Friday ?

Retrouvez tous les bons plans du Black Friday 2026 sur la page dédiée à l'événement.
Pour les aficionados de X, n'hésitez pas à suivre notre compte Clubic Bons Plans pour être au courant en direct des meilleures offres.

articles.title: New US rules aim to close loophole, restrict Chinese firms’ remote access to AI servers and infrastructure — seeks to combat cloud rental workarounds to export controls
articles.text:
New US rules aim to close loophole, restrict Chinese firms’ remote access to AI servers and infrastructure — seeks to combat cloud rental workarounds to export controls
The Bureau of Industry and Security has released an interim final rule to ensure physical restrictions cannot be bypassed by using cloud-based infrastructure.
New steps have been taken to ensure that countries and companies that are not on whitelists that would allow them to import advanced AI hardware cannot use cloud-based workarounds. The U.S. Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) has today unveiled an interim final rule, or IFR, in collaboration with the Department of Treasury and the National Security Council, aimed at backing up existing limitations on the export of hardware built by companies like Nvidia to non-whitelisted companies based in countries such as China. "The rule is designed to ensure that existing restrictions on access to sensitive American technology cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements" using data centers in third-party countries, a statement explains.
Nvidia, for example, is only allowed to export its high-performance AI chips to companies that are on a whitelist. But amid ongoing claims of black market GPU sales and a recent crackdown on overseas AI GPU rentals from China, it has become clear that these restrictions perhaps aren't as robust as they were intended to be. Nvidia Blackwell Ultra B300 GPUs were even recently discovered in a data center used by China Telecom.
But while blocking the sale of physical goods is one thing, the cloud-based workaround is another entirely. Nvidia itself told data center operators earlier this month that they must limit remote access to their services — 51% of their business must come from non-Chinese companies. But, again, it's unclear how effective that approach has been in ensuring access to powerful AI capabilities doesn't fall into the wrong hands, even if they're accessed remotely rather than in person.
The new BIS rule means that overseas data centers will be required to do more to limit access to their services where U.S-based technology is being used. Restrictions will also be placed on data centers that supply remote access to companies whose headquarters are deemed to be in higher-risk countries, such as China, Russia, and Iran. A license will also be required for anyone trying to export advanced chips to companies with headquarters in Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, or Brazil. The new requirements will officially go into effect in 90 days.
This latest rule comes against a backdrop of ongoing uncertainty over America's AI crown jewel, Nvidia. Jensen Huang, the company's CEO, resigned after confirming an affair, but is now potentially in line for a quick-fire comeback, despite the fact that the woman involved in the affair is an alleged Chinese spy.

articles.title: Slow Horses : Apple TV offre un renouvellement exceptionnel à son hit d'espionnage
articles.text:
Slow Horses : Apple TV offre un renouvellement exceptionnel à son hit d'espionnage
La plateforme de streaming Apple TV vient de reconduire la série Slow Horses pour deux saisons supplémentaires.
Plus rien n'arrête Slow Horses sur Apple TV. Le service de streaming vient en effet d'accorder un renouvellement de plus à la série avec Gary Oldman, annonçant qu'elle aura droit à des saisons 9 et 10 alors que la saison 6 vient récemment de se conclure. La série d'espionnage a donc encore de beaux jours devant elle.
Jackson Lamb en a encore sous le capot
La saison 8 ne sera pas la dernière de Slow Horses, loin de là, même si elle adaptera le dernier livre de Mick Herron dont la série s'inspire. Apple TV compte en effet continuer de surfer sur le succès de cette fiction d'espionnage portée par Gary Oldman, Jack Lowden et Kristin Scott Thomas.
Le service de streaming a dorénavant annoncé que la série aura droit à des saisons 9 et 10, même si cela pourrait donc vouloir dire que le show ira au-delà des écrits littéraires d'Herron.
Il est bien trop tôt pour savoir de quoi retourneront ces futures saisons, mais on sait cependant que la saison 7 a quant à elle déjà été tournée et que la production est maintenant occupée avec la saison 8. Ces deux saisons s'inspirent du roman Clown Town de la saga "Slough House" d'Herron.
Quoi qu'il en soit, Slow Horses est la série la plus longue d'Apple TV et continue d'être un grand succès sur le service de SVOD, dont les programmes sont disponibles via le site officiel, Prime Video Channels, et sont inclus dans l'offre Ciné Séries de Canal+.
Pour rappel, Slow Horses suit une équipe d’agents secrets britanniques mis au placard par le MI5 suite aux erreurs qu’ils ont commises en mission. Placés sous les ordres d’un chef aussi brillant qu’irascible, le célèbre Jackson Lamb (Oldman), ils naviguent dans le monde de l’espionnage, où règnent les faux-semblants, pour défendre la Grande-Bretagne contre les forces ennemies.

articles.title: 'I think current pricing is already signalling the end of GeForce': some PC gamers remain skeptical as Nvidia's GeForce Evangelist assures us that 'nope', it isn't the end for its gaming GPUs
articles.text:
If you thought Jensen Huang's exit meant the worst for Nvidia's gaming graphics cards, think again — GeForce Evangelist assures us it isn't the end for these GPUs
GeForce Evangelist does what he's paid to do and makes it clear that Nvidia's gaming GPUs aren't on life support
- Following Jensen Huang's resignation, Nvidia's GeForce Evangelist, Jacob Freeman, was asked whether "this is the end of GeForce"
- Freeman said "Nope" in a brief but very clear response
- PC gamers still have doubts over the future of Nvidia's gaming GPUs, and for good reasons
If you were at all worried that the departure of CEO Jensen Huang last week means that GeForce GPUs will be even less of a priority for Nvidia, apparently any such concerns are unfounded.
Wccftech spotted that Jacob Freeman, GeForce Evangelist at Nvidia, made it clear that the CEO's exit will not affect consumer GPUs in a reply to a post on X.
Someone asked: "Hey Jacob, lots of people are saying this is the end of GeForce. Thoughts?" To which Freeman replied: "Nope."
It's a short and sweet response to say the least, but unwaveringly clear. As you can imagine, there was a veritable slew of follow-up comments and questions, but Freeman wouldn't be drawn to say anything further on the matter.
Analysis: a GeForce reckoning
When the news broke of Huang's resignation, I discussed the potential ramifications for Nvidia's gaming GPUs at length. My broad conclusion was (and still is) that I think this is yet another blow for PC gamers and graphics cards, with the market already in a dire state thanks to Nvidia (and AMD) prioritizing chips for AI boards (against the backdrop of the memory crisis, of course).
My reasoning is that the next CEO has one big leather jacket to fill, and that in an effort to keep Nvidia stable and live up to what Huang has achieved in terms of market value, there will inevitably be an even greater focus on AI and profits for shareholders.
On top of that, Huang was involved in the creation of the GeForce brand, and while priorities have clearly changed greatly for Nvidia during this current decade, I'd argue that without him, these gaming GPUs are even more likely to be sidelined as the new CEO won't have any such fond sentiments.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
Remember that earlier this year, at GTC 2026, Huang observed that "GeForce is Nvidia's greatest marketing campaign" and that "We attract future customers starting long before you could afford to pay for it yourself. Your parents paid for you to be Nvidia customers." The argument being that eventually when you became a developer or computer scientist, Nvidia would be in your bones, as it were. While that's exaggerated for effect, no doubt, there's a belief here that any replacement chief executive isn't likely to share.
However, all that said, I get where gamers are coming from when they shrug their shoulders about Huang's exit and argue that GeForce GPUs were in the process of being canned anyway. It's difficult to disagree with that in some respects given what has happened with Nvidia's gaming line-up of late — pricing is through the roof, and high-end GPUs in particular are effectively vanishing (with rumored refreshes cancelled to boot). As a commenter on X replying to the above thread put it: "Unfortunately I think current pricing is already signalling the end of GeForce."
Nvidia doesn't seem particularly keen to come to the rescue of gamers, and with video RAM more expensive than ever — and the demands of AI seemingly unrelenting — it's clear we're moving into more difficult territory for desktop GPUs next year.
Freeman may be adamant that it isn't the end for GeForce graphics cards, and of course, that's his job as the official Evangelist for the GPU range. I fully expect there will indeed be another generation of GeForce GPUs, of course — the RTX 6000 series in 2028 theoretically — but beyond that, the future feels distinctly shaky, and it'll take some sort of major event to change that picture. What we see with RTX 6000 may be much less focused on higher-end GPUs, too, in an AMD style — as a kind of compromise in terms of keeping the heavyweight chips for the data centers.
The big hope for some gamers is the AI bubble popping, but how any such seismic shift might occur is so far up in the air, it is — ironically — in the clouds. Short of a full-on rebellion against AI technology given some huge faux pas therein, it's difficult to envisage that the nearer future is going to be anything but more of the same from the RAM crisis — probably much worse for a time, too, and certainly nothing good for PC gamers.
Meanwhile, rumors that Huang could make a comeback are circulating, following a petition to bring the ex-CEO back. A lot of what's happening in the PC sphere may be rather depressing to say the least, but you can't accuse it of lacking drama and interest.

articles.title: Xbox Confirms Project Helix Is Not a PC, But It's Closer Than Ever
articles.text:
Monday, November 16th 2026
Xbox Confirms Project Helix Is Not a PC, But It's Closer Than Ever
It's basically a running joke at this point that gaming consoles are just PCs with extra steps, and Xbox previously confirmed that the upcoming Project Helix would be a PC-console hybrid, capable of playing both PC and console games. This led to speculation and even rumors that Xbox would finally treat the Helix as if it were a proper PC, similarly to the Steam Machine. In the recent Xbox 25th Anniversary Magazine, Xbox Vice President of Next Gen, Jason Ronald, has confirmed that this will not be the case, although he also suggested that the way the Xbox Helix games will work is more akin to a PC than a console.
Jason Ronald, VP of Next Gen at XboxWe're very clear on the design goal: Helix is designed to be a console capable of playing PC games from your PC. It is not a PC that can also play console games. The goal is making it easy, intuitive, and instant to access my games. But if you're a hardcore gamer or a power user who wants to have that deeper level of customizability across settings and performance options, you can absolutely go for it.
The implication with Ronald's comments appear to be that Xbox games will open up more customization options for players, likely exposing more granular quality settings so that players can tune their game's visual fidelity and frame rates. Although it's unclear exactly where those customization options will fit into the traditional dichotomy between PC and consoles. The executive goes on to explain that the reason for removing some of the constraints came from talking to developers at Xbox Game Studios.
The very first next-generation conversations we had were with all of our first-party studios. That was absolutely foundational to the design of what we've done with Project Helix—talking about where they saw the future of their franchises going, and what was constraining their creative ambition.
Source:
				Xbox 25th Anniversary Magazine

articles.title: At KubeCon 2026, the illusion of AI control meets the reality of implementation - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
At KubeCon 2026, the illusion of AI control meets the reality of implementation
I revisited Salt Lake City for KubeCon/CloudNativeCon NA 2026 hoping to find practical approaches to delivering customer value amidst a rapidly shifting kaleidoscope of artificial intelligence-driven solutions that are making it increasingly difficult to trust our own eyes and ears.
This year, the host Cloud Native Computing Foundation set its theme as “Cloud Native Without Limits,” and judging by the record-shattering pace of new community developments with more than 230 active projects, and the increasing adoption rate of AI for building and consuming applications, the momentum will only grow.
“If you look back at last year’s KubeCon in Atlanta, OpenClaw was not released yet, MCP was less than a year old, and inference in cloud native was just getting started,” Chris Anzyzcyk, chief technical officer of CNCF, said in the opening remarks.
“We knew we were moving out of a phase where most of the AI compute was used for training and we were going to massively ramp up inference,” said Jonathan Bryce, executive director of CNCF. “Just in the last eight months, we’ve seen a 4X increase in inference traffic across the industry. That’s really an incredible increase in the AI footprint. Inference is no longer just an opportunity, it’s now a cloud-native production workload.”
With more than 350K CNCF contributors and 21.2 million cloud-native developers worldwide, fully three-quarters of them are already using AI coding agents, according to the latest State of Cloud Native Development Q3 2026 report, and a show of hands in the room hinted at a much higher presence of AI tooling on the engineer’s desktop.
Likewise, two-thirds of self-described AI-driven organizations are standardizing on Kubernetes and related open-source technologies.
There’s a clear connection here, but AI is not the whole story. Enterprises still need to modernize their application fleets, and deploy, scale, secure and observe their most critical systems, in order to get beyond the AI hype and realize business value.
With an open mind and a skeptical eye, here were some of the interesting new perspectives and vendor solutions I encountered at the show.
Building open paths to Kubernetes and AI productivity
With the rapid enterprise rollout of agentic AI, every developer is being challenged to apply human decision insight while working at agent speed, one of the major themes of the show.
Getting there will take more than new technologies, it will also require a lot of collaboration and understanding. The Kubernetes AI Conformance Program launched at KubeCon NA 2025 now has 42 major participating vendors agreeing to consistent standards, and this year there are new Kubernetes AI Certifications for upskilling engineers, whether they are just starting out, or if they are “Golden Kubestronauts” who already passed every course CNCF offers.
“Kubernetes has become the standard API for deploying a workload to a computer, including AI,” said Dan Ciruli, vice president and general manager for cloud native at Nutanix Inc. “The reason, in my opinion, is because the CNCF gave a safe haven for anyone from the smallest startup of two people to the largest companies on Earth to feel safe in donating labor, and code, and IP, and agreeing on things. And that, in turn, gave everybody, from governments to financial services to hot startups, the confidence that they could consume it.”
The firm recently introduced their Nutanix Agent Gateway and an NKP Metal solution that allows Kubernetes clusters and workloads to run on bare metal as well as virtual machines in EKS, AKS or GKE for what they call a “dual-native” experience.
“How are you going to safely and sustainably connect thousands of agents to the systems of record that actually run the business such as customer loyalty or inventory?” asked Matt DeBergalis, CEO, Apollo Graph Inc., doing business as Apollo GraphQL, which supports the popular open source GraphQL query language, presenting a new semantic domain model for deterministically interpreting AI prompts and controls for each record.
Eliminating resource constraints, both digital and human
Last year CNCF announced a Dynamic Resource Allocation or DRA capability, which unlocked new possibilities for the community to optimize AI workloads running in Kubernetes. This year, sandboxing, or running agents in secure instances to prevent escapes, hijacking and overprovisioning, was the watchword.
Development has moved fast in this area, with two new projects: a Agent Substrate layer contributed by Google that optimizes resource consumption of thousands of agent sandboxes, and OpenShell, an Nvidia Corp.-contributed project for secure sandboxed runtimes.
Startup Apelogic Inc. doing business as HyperShell built an operational agent envelope based on OpenShell that defines guardrails what systems an autonomous agent can access, and what actions it can take, based on the business or system intent the agent was intended to serve.
Cast AI started out as a cloud cost optimization layer for rightsizing clusters on major hyperscalers, but as cloud native infrastructure started taking over enterprise environments, it now finds itself automating and optimizing more AI workloads across CPUs and GPUs, memory and storage. New at KubeCon, their Kimchi code agent governs and deploys application infrastructures from a prompt, which allows developers shift left agentic reviews before production tuning.
Floxdev Inc., which I covered as a startup with their Nix-based lean containerized environment deployments in 2025, put its Flox platform directly in the AI delivery path, giving agents skills to stamp out identical complete environments that include all dependencies, without reproducing any element of the software supply chain inventory that wasn’t intended to change. This moves agentic loops faster with lower compute costs, but the real value is when human engineers can reduce future maintenance and security remediation costs.
Observability isn’t just for SREs anymore
This year’s CNCF graduation of the OpenTelemetry project couldn’t come at a better moment, making OTel the lingua franca of application performance, scalability and reliability.
While observability was traditionally considered the domain of engineers and operators, now everyone from data analysts to business executives may be using an LLM or an agent to interact with enterprise applications, potentially changing software, or delivering more agents, in the process.
Splunk, a division of Cisco Systems Inc. has added to its agent observability suite with a specialized language model called Eval-G1 that can run prompt-and-response evals in sub-second times at sub-cent costs, giving engineers the ability to interrupt a faulty response in real time, before it reaches customers. A new Evaluation Studio helps teams generate guardrails in a low-code graphical environment. Also cool, a tokenomics feature (from the recent acquisition of Galileo, which we just covered) that analyzes token spend versus system and business performance metrics.
“It’s been exciting to see how OpenTelemetry, which started out as tens of thousands of adaptors for every application and client, has transitioned with the AI revolution so that now, we have frameworks that just emit OTel natively,” said Morgan McLean, senior director of product management at Splunk and OpenTelemetry co-creator. “So Splunk, and our competitors, can just launch new observability features without putting 30 people on writing new integrations.”
Since a lot of AI projects start out as experiments, observability stalwart Dynatrace LLC has made several moves to meet smaller teams where they are in validating each feature for performance and reliability before enterprise-scale rollouts. It recently acquired Bindplane for OTel-native telemetry pipelines, BlueBox, which gives developers a custom agent for debugging and checks within a coding IDE, and Arize, which maintains the popular Phoenix open-source tool for AI evaluations.
New Relic Inc. released a new Autopilot Kubernetes Agent, a virtual SRE that users can interact with via natural language to look across telemetry and APM data to assess the health of the cluster and application, triage issues with a complete stack trace, and recommend resolutions.
“Especially when you bring agents into your environment, you can’t just take your telemetry and throw it over to a general-purpose LLM, because there are known deterministic patterns and historical insights about Kubernetes we’ve been working to resolve for years,” said Jemiah Sius, vice president of market strategy and developer relations at New Relic.
Making agent deployments safer, by making them easier to sustain
A lot of the governance difficulty with agents and sandboxes and policies isn’t a technical problem; it is about user experience. Human engineers don’t like being “in the loop” for AI, aka “Meat Proxies,” that continuously pass along approvals. Humans need to be in control, with less toil and more focus on what customers want out of AI applications.
“You can try to create a secure agent sandbox with a policy where everything is disabled by default until a human approves it, but eventually, someone gets tired of being in that approval loop,” said Simone Morellato, senior director of product marketing, Rafay Systems Inc., an AI infrastructure delivery platform used by leading neoclouds. “So you give an agent access to one thing, and eventually you end up giving them access to everything. And at that point, you are back at square one.”
Since I covered Edera Inc. last year, this hardened runtime container vendor is finding new traction in this agentic age by continuing to strengthen the stack from the bottom up, with an agent runtime and OCAP bounded authority that acts as a switchboard for discretely defined agent capabilities, rather than assigning agents credentials or access to MCP servers or APIs or other agents that can be expanded or exploited for another HuggingFace-type incident.
“You can consume capabilities in our system and publish capabilities,” said Edera founder and Chief Technology Officer Alex Zenla. So, for example, for an MCP server, we publish each tool call as a capability. And then when you spin up your agent, you ask for the tool calls that you want. And then it consumes just those capabilities. And we’re able to enforce policies because we have one central pathway for everything to go through, so we can know exactly which agents are using which capabilities.”
“I love the focus on reliability that I’ve seen in the talks and on the floor here at KubeCon,” said Kolton Andrus, CEO of Gremlin Inc., which was there demonstrating their new Foresight AI solution that proactively injects failure conditions in order to identify and remediate failure risks. “You can no longer wait for things to fall apart before taking action. “Everyone’s moving 100 miles an hour trying to keep up with AI, and waking up to the fact that reliability can’t be an afterthought anymore. You can no longer wait for things to fall apart before taking action.”
The Intellyx take
This being my eighth KubeCon, I keep coming back because the community atmosphere here is unparalleled. There’s a real sense of camaraderie among developers and engineers from wildly different backgrounds, as they build new fundamentals and enjoy the journey toward a cloud native future.
We’ve come a long way over the last eleven years since Kubernetes was introduced. Interoperability, portability, control planes, observability, networking, identity, security and many more mature capabilities are there for the taking. Now AI is being layered on top. But that’s not the story here.
What really impresses me is how much this open source community gives back for the benefit of everyone. All of these people have real jobs to do, and yet they invest their own time, as much as the software industry invests in them.
Indeed, as CNCF’s own Jonathan Bryce said: “Some problems can only be solved in the open.”
Jason English is a principal analyst and chief marketing officer at Intellyx. He wrote this article for SiliconANGLE. At the time of writing, Gremlin and Rafay are current Intellyx customers, Dynatrace, New Relic, Nutanix and Splunk are former customers, and none of the other companies mentioned here is an Intellyx customer. articles.title: SpaceX ha hecho historia con el vuelo 14 y 15 de Starship: ahora espera repetir la hazaña con el vuelo 16
articles.text:
El vuelo 14 de Starship fue un éxito, con su inserción en órbita por primera vez para depositar una carga útil. Solo la mitad del vuelo 15 ha sido exitoso, pero ha sido justamente la mitad más importante, así que hay un gran revuelo al respecto. Ahora toca pensar en qué será lo siguiente. ¿Habrá un vuelo 16? ¿Qué hará SpaceX con la nave que han recuperado? ¿Cómo se investigará lo sucedido con la primera etapa? Vayamos por partes.
Vuelo 16 a la vista (pero no mucho). Lógicamente, habrá un vuelo 16. Sin embargo, de momento no hay información oficial al respecto. Algunos medios de comunicación hablan de una fecha tentativa en torno al mes que viene (diciembre de 2026). No obstante, se trata de datos citados en prensa a partir de material de planificación de la Administración Federal de Aviación de Estados Unidos, por lo que no proceden directamente de SpaceX.
Tampoco hay mucha información sobre el desarrollo de dicho vuelo. Se ha mencionado que podría ir cargado con el lote 30-1 de Starlink y que sería el primer vuelo de Starship en lanzarse desde Florida, aunque se seguirán haciendo lanzamientos desde Starbase (Texas). Sea como sea, hay que tener en cuenta que, incluso si SpaceX contaba de verdad con lanzar en diciembre, esta fecha podría experimentar retrasos, ya que debe quedar claro qué es lo que falló con la recuperación de la primera etapa en el vuelo 15 antes de programar definitivamente el siguiente.
Después del vuelo 15. Tras el vuelo 15 ha llegado el momento de que SpaceX demuestre que puede reutilizar de forma rápida cualquiera de las dos etapas. El propulsor Super Heavy se ha reutilizado en dos ocasiones, pero con meses de diferencia, y la segunda etapa nunca ha volado dos veces. No se pudo recuperar el Super Heavy con el vuelo 15, pero sí la Ship que compone la segunda etapa, por lo que la siguiente fase será prepararla para su reutilización. Aunque en un principio se habló de usarla en el vuelo 16, desde NASA Space Flight señalan que lo más probable es que dicha prueba se lleve a cabo sin esperar a que la Ship del vuelo 15 esté lista.
Más reutilización, más vuelos. Elon Musk ha manifestado en varias ocasiones que su objetivo es llevar a cabo 10.000 lanzamientos por año de Starship en 2030. Eso sería más de un lanzamiento por hora. Lógicamente, para que sea viable económicamente y, de paso, no abarrote aún más la órbita terrestre de basura espacial, lo ideal sería reutilizar tanto la primera como la segunda etapa de la misma. Lo logrado con el vuelo 15 demuestra que es una posibilidad. Ahora hay que trabajar en ella.
Destino: la Luna. Si todo va bien, la Ship de Starship, esa segunda etapa que se ha logrado recuperar, se convertirá en uno de los módulos de aterrizaje de los que dispondrá la NASA para alunizar durante las misiones Artemis. Por eso, además de seguir demostrando su viabilidad para colocar cargas útiles en órbita, se debe seguir trabajando en la instalación de una cabina y un sistema de soporte vital. Así, podrá albergar a los tripulantes elegidos para alunizar, mientras el resto siguen en la cápsula Orión de la NASA.
SpaceX ya está trabajando en un prototipo de tierra, llamado Cabin 1, que debe estar listo para finales de 2026. Además, para que la Ship pueda llegar a la Luna necesita más combustible del que puede acarrear desde la Tierra, por lo que tendrá que repostar directamente en órbita. Esto se hará gracias a dos tipos de Ship: una que actuará como camión cisterna y otra que hará de depósito y permanecerá siempre en órbita. El objetivo es que las Ships cisterna viajen regularmente a llenar el depósito, al que se tendrá que acoplar la Ship que debe repostar para el alunizaje. Todo esto también se debe perfeccionar para que Starship esté lista para Artemis IV, cuando finalmente, si todo va bien, los humanos vuelvan a caminar sobre la Luna. No es poco todo lo que le queda por delante a SpaceX después del gran logro de su décimo quinto vuelo.

articles.title: Researchers ‘recognize that AI will never replace HPC,’ says AMD executive — high-precision workloads will ‘exist for a very long time’ even as AI usage expands
articles.text:
Researchers ‘recognize that AI will never replace HPC,’ says AMD executive — high-precision workloads will ‘exist for a very long time’ even as AI usage expands
When FP64, AI, and quantum collide
While AI continues to reshape industries across science and mathematics, traditional supercomputing has seemingly taken a back seat. However, AMD's Scott Tease told Tom's Hardware Premium that most HPC sites “recognize that AI will never replace HPC,” and suggests that building a heterogeneous compute stack is the best path forward to tackle bleeding-edge research, despite Nvidia pushing performance on lower-precision data types higher for AI workloads at the cost of native performance for the important double-precision FP64 format that’s critical for HPC workloads.
A heterogeneous compute stack brings together quantum, HPC, and AI under one roof, a fleet that AMD is helping pilot at Oak Ridge National Laboratory alongside IBM. Tease is AMD’s corporate vice president of HPC and sovereign AI, who joined the company earlier this year after more than a decade at Lenovo (and, before that, another 13 years at IBM). We spoke with Tease ahead of SC26 to get a read on the state of HPC, how it intersects with AI, and what’s actually driving the research community in a time when computer chips are driving headlines about international espionage plots.
An awful lot of numbers
FP64 is important for HPC workloads because of its precision. FP64 is a hot-button issue, largely due to how Nvidia’s GPUs have progressed over the past two generations. Or rather, how they haven't progressed. Nvidia’s latest Rubin GPU has 33 TFLOPs of FP64 compute, which is lower than the four-year-old H100’s 34 TFLOPs of FP64. For context, AMD’s year-old Instinct MI355X peaks at 78.6 TFLOPs of FP64 compute, while its upcoming HPC-angled MI430X peaks at 288 TFLOPs.
Nvidia has leaned on emulation to drive FP64 performance higher, a tactic that AMD is now pushing back on, but regardless, it’s easy to see why the HPC world could feel left behind in this new AI era. AI is defined by fuzzy, low-precision data formats, which is diametrically opposed to the accuracy of high-precision FP64. And, over the last generations of hardware from the big green giant that is Nvidia, FP64 performance has seemingly stalled in favor of driving low-precision data formats for AI workloads.
“Maybe a few years ago, people in HPC might have felt a little threatened by AI because it was taking some of the limelight,” Tease told Tom’s Hardware Premium. “But I think now they’ve come to realize that AI is an essential part of scientific discovery today. It’s just, how are you going to deploy it?”
That central question recontextualizes the apparent conflict between AI compute and HPC compute. Tease pointed to researchers spawning dozens of agents to explore viable paths for a given intent, while still leaving the complex simulations for a traditional FP64-driven HPC fleet. “...to try to do that with old approaches where you have islands of CPUs or islands of GPUs or something like that, and they're very different. They're not interconnected. It's just not going to be able to keep up,” Tease said.
Enter quantum
One of the challenges right now is actually connecting those systems, which is an area AMD is exploring with its recent collaboration with IBM and Oak Ridge National Laboratory to deploy AMD’s “classical” computing stack in the Umbra HPC system alongside IBM’s 129-qubit Quantum Nighthawk quantum computer. The systems will connect to the Oak Ridge Leadership Computing Facility, allowing researchers to “explore how integrated quantum, AI, and scientific computing can accelerate scientific discoveries and national security.”
If the HPC crowd felt slighted by AI, you can imagine how quantum researchers probably feel.
Regardless, Tease says the future of scientific computing looks like a unified fleet that brings together AI, HPC, and quantum. “There [are] going to be a lot of problems where quantum will not be the be-all, end-all. There are some problems like human health, chemistry, where quantum’s going to allow us to do things we really can’t do with classical computing today. So having those things coexist, having them in a single workload, is where we want to get to.”
Scheduling workloads for HPC is a solved game, with open-source schedulers like Slurm driving much of the TOP500 to properly schedule workloads on supercomputers. Tease described something that goes deeper to connect these systems. “What we want to be able to do is not only do those kinds of ‘where should it go, here or there’ for HPC, we want to figure out when AI could be applied to it, when [GPU acceleration is] appropriate… and also when is it best to go in a quantum environment?”
The Oak Ridge Leadership Computing Facility is a test bed for figuring out how to hook these systems together properly. The press release explicitly states that it’s a “shared environment to evaluate the architectures, software, and workflows that future hybrid quantum systems will require.” The system is a co-design initiative with IBM, bringing together quantum and classical computing into one system.
With the system, researchers are exploring how to accelerate quantum error correction with classical systems, a critical step in quantum computing to weed out environmental influences. The goal is ultimately to accelerate quantum systems in the Quantum Genesis Q competition, an initiative launched by the U.S. Department of Energy that will provide up to $215 million in funding for quantum research.
By late 2028, the competition calls for quantum computers “with at least 100 logical qubits that are capable of performing hundreds of millions [of] fault-tolerant operations.” IBM describes the error correction research that will be performed at Oak Ridge as a “key component” in driving toward that goal. Separately, AMD announced last week an investment in quantum outfit PsiQuantum to provide CPUs, GPUs, and FPGAs to drive the company’s first fault-tolerant quantum system.
Jake Roach is the Senior CPU Analyst at Tom’s Hardware, writing reviews, news, and features about the latest consumer and workstation processors.
- Jame5 “with at least 100 logical qubits that are capable of performing hundreds of millions fault-tolerant operations.” 
Time frame? seconds? hours? days? years?
On a long enough timeline, current quantum computers easily hit hundreds of millions of operations. Reply

articles.title: Utilisateurs de Fitbit Sensa et Versa, attention à vos cadres et apps tierces après le 28 novembre
articles.text:
Google enterre toujours plus les montres connectées Fitbit avec la fin des applications tierces
Si vous possédez une Fitbit Versa ou Sense et utilisez des applications ou cadrans tiers, attention, Google va bientôt couper le robinet.
Google Pixel Watch 5
Rachetée par Google en 2019, la marque de montres connectées Fitbit poursuit sa lente et inexorable agonie au fil des mois et des suppressions de fonctionnalités, et du remplacement de la gamme par les Pixel Watch sous Wear OS. En cette fin novembre 2026, ce sont plusieurs modèles de Fitbit Versa et Sense de ces dernières années qui vont très bientôt perdre un élément central.
Adieu applications et cadres tiers sur Fitbit
Dans une courte annonce, Google dévoile ainsi que dès le 28 novembre prochain, la Fitbit App Gallery de certaines montres Fitbit n'affichera que des applications et cadres créés par Google et Fitbit. En d'autres termes, cette galerie proposant jusqu'ici des cadrans et applications développés par des tiers, va leur fermer ses portes.
Ainsi, il ne sera non seulement plus possible d'en télécharger, mais surtout les cadres et applications installés ne pourront plus recevoir de mises à jour ou être récupérés après une éventuelle suppression de la montre ou une réinitialisation de cette dernière. Si vous souhaitez récupérer une application ou un cadre tiers, c'est donc le moment ou jamais, puisque les éléments installés devraient malgré tout continuer à fonctionner.
Sont concernées par cette suppression les montres commercialisées entre 2018 et 2022 que sont les Versa, Versa 2, Versa 3 et Versa 4, ainsi que les Sense et Sense 2.
On relèvera que cette suppression des éléments tiers de la Fitbit App Gallery avait déjà été appliquée dans l'Union Européenne à l'été 2024, alors pour des "exigences réglementaires". Mais la suppression de cette ouverture de la gallerie, cette fois à l'échelle mondiale, vient définitivement prouver que Google a décidé de tourner la page de Fitbit comme marque de montre connectée pour se concentrer sur les bracelets connectés.

articles.title: Google quietly purged 362 shady Russian Chrome VPN extensions following TechRadar investigation — but the Chrome Web Store’s ‘whack-a-mole’ continues
articles.text:
Google quietly purged 362 shady Russian Chrome VPN extensions following TechRadar investigation — but the Chrome Web Store’s ‘whack-a-mole’ continues
Copycats are still slipping past Chrome's defenses
Last month, TechRadar published an investigation highlighting 369 suspicious VPN extensions targeting Russian users. Since then, Google has removed all but seven of them.
Many of the purged extensions used throwaway, personal developer emails, had inadequate privacy policies and mimicked well-known brands, including ExpressVPN and Windscribe. Several had even been flagged in threat intelligence reports months before.
While the removal of these apps is a positive step, a quick look through the Web Store shows that there’s still work to be done.
Hundreds of shady VPN extensions removed
Our initial investigation flagged more than 350 extensions targeting Russian civilians, which had over 200,000 users combined.
VPNs have become a critical tool in Russia owing to heightened internet censorship and surveillance. Unfortunately, this also means they have become a prime target for groups looking to turn a quick profit.
We shared details of all the extensions included in our investigation with Google ahead of publication and, less than one month later, almost all of them have been removed from the Chrome Web Store.
Google did not respond to requests for comment to confirm whether the extensions were removed as a result of our investigation or as part of routine maintenance of the store.
Ongoing enforcement issues
Looking at the VPN and proxy Chrome extensions still live today, it's clear that many apps bearing all the same hallmarks of an untrustworthy operation remain.
These include a Russian extension using the Nord brand name, extensions with thousands of downloads managed from personal email addresses, and others hosting privacy policies on anonymous sites.google.com domains.
We also found three active VPN extensions linked to an email address previously flagged as belonging to a threat actor. We inspected the source code of one of these apps and found comments suggesting it is deliberately avoiding standard permissions to slip past Google’s Manifest V3 security rules.
In the extension's source code, the developer explicitly notes that they “intentionally avoid” requesting host_permissions, webRequest, and other standard functions to maintain a "safe MV3 install flow".
While a proxy or VPN extension doesn’t necessarily need those permissions, notes on its compliance in its source code suggest it may have been structured in a way to immediately pass Google’s automated checks.
Either way, it’s clear that cleaning up the Chrome Web Store is no easy feat. As Rebecca Rosenberg, Head of Growth at Windscribe, previously told TechRadar: “It’s pretty much a game of whack-a-mole now, [a] copycat is pulled and two more pop up.”
We’ve shared details of some of the live extensions referenced in this article with Google and asked for more details on how the company is protecting users of its extension store. The company did not respond by the time of publication.
Are VPN extensions really worth it?
Even as Google removes hundreds of shady VPN extensions, the Web Store still contains apps that you would be better off avoiding. And the issue runs deeper than bad actors.
In fact, VPN extensions are, by their very nature, not the best tool if you’re looking to protect your privacy online.
Speaking to TechRadar, a senior technical expert at Russian digital security group RKS Global said: “A Chrome extension is not a VPN in the technical sense. It does not create a tunnel; it uses the browser's API to configure a proxy: HTTP, HTTPS or SOCKS. That is why it has limitations.”
This means that any other internet-connected activity on your device runs unencrypted and unprotected — including messaging apps, email apps, and anything else running outside your browser.
The RKS Global spokesperson also noted that “reliable anti-censorship protocols such as AmneziaWG, VLESS with Reality, or Shadowsocks cannot be implemented inside an extension”. So, choosing an extension to evade internet censorship in a highly monitored location such as Russia is rarely the best option.
That’s made worse by the fact that many of these shady extensions were, of course, never designed for censorship circumvention in the first place. Instead, they were built to turn a profit, with some actively harming your privacy rather than improving it.
The RKS Global spokesperson highlighted proxyware as one such example, where “a free ‘VPN’ extension turns the user's browser into an exit node of a residential proxy network”. In this scenario, a user’s home IP and bandwidth may be sold off to third parties for ad verification, web scraping and other unauthorized uses.
Open-source anti-censorship VPN provider AmneziaVPN told TechRadar that the number of extensions with “malicious functionality” had grown recently. The company said extensions that “steal VPN keys from various services” are “released every day” and that there are also “plugins that carry malicious code for surveillance or for stealing data”.
While it’s unclear whether the extensions recently purged by Google were capable of this, experts warn that aggressive censorship in Russia is pushing users directly into the path of scams.
“State policy in Russia, under which the genuine clients of circumvention apps have been purged from the stores and blocked while demand has remained, has provided the ground for the growth of fakes in the stores and of the murky schemes through which people have to install anti-censorship solutions,” RKS Global concluded.
For anyone looking to protect their traffic, the safest approach is to use a full, system-wide VPN. Or, if you need a standalone browser extension, avoid Chrome Web Store search results and download it via a direct link on a trusted provider's website.
While Google's latest purge shows it is willing to remove the worst offenders, sticking to verified sources is well worth the extra click.
Sam is VPN Managing Editor at TechRadar. He has worked in the VPN industry since 2018 and has previously written for CNN, Al Jazeera, WIRED, and Deutsche Welle as a freelance journalist. He focuses on VPNs and digital privacy, cybersecurity and internet freedom.
Before joining TechRadar, Sam carried out research on global digital rights issues at Top10VPN. His research has been cited by the United Nations and UK Parliament, as well as publications such as The Guardian, Washington Post and BBC.

articles.title: Surveiller entrée et jardin sans câble : le pack Blink à -83% pour le Black Friday
articles.text:
Le pack de surveillance Blink repasse à 24,99 € chez Amazon en plein Black Friday, soit le tarif que nous avions déjà relevé le 29 septembre. La caméra Outdoor 4, la sonnette vidéo 2K+ et le module de synchronisation sont affichés au lieu de 149,98 €, mais sans abonnement, aucune vidéo n’est enregistrée.
Blink, la marque de sécurité connectée d’Amazon, réunit ici deux appareils sans fil : la caméra extérieure Outdoor 4 et une sonnette vidéo 2K+, reliées par un module de synchronisation fourni. Amazon propose ce pack à 24,99 € au lieu de 149,98 €, soit 124,99 € d’économie et 83 % de remise sur le plus bas prix des 30 derniers jours affiché sur sa fiche.
Ce n’est pas un prix inédit : nous relayions déjà ce pack à 24,99 € le 29 septembre, après un passage à 39,99 € en août. L’offre parle surtout aux occupants d’une maison qui veulent équiper leur entrée et leur jardin sans faire venir d’électricien.
Le pack Blink Outdoor 4 et sonnette vidéo 2K+ est à 24,99 € au lieu de 149,98 € chez Amazon.
Pourquoi choisir le pack Blink Outdoor 4 et sonnette 2K+ ?
- Aucun câble à tirer : La caméra fonctionne avec deux piles AA lithium et la sonnette avec trois, pour une autonomie annoncée jusqu’à deux ans. Les kits de montage sont fournis, et vous posez le tout là où il n’y a pas de prise.
- Une sonnette qui voit jusqu’au sol : Son image carrée cadre le visiteur de la tête aux pieds, colis posé devant la porte compris. L’audio bidirectionnel permet de répondre sans ouvrir, et la vision infrarouge sert la nuit.
- Une seule application, avec Alexa : Caméra et sonnette se pilotent depuis l’appli Blink. Reliés à Alexa, ils peuvent afficher le direct, accueillir vos visiteurs ou s’activer à la voix.
De l’entrée au fond du jardin, ce que le pack surveille vraiment
La caméra Outdoor 4 filme en 1080p avec un champ de vision de 143°, contre 110° pour la génération précédente, comme nous le relevions dans notre article sur son arrivée en France. Un seul appareil suffit donc pour couvrir une allée ou une terrasse. Sa détection de mouvement à deux zones vous alerte quand quelqu’un remonte l’allée ou s’approche d’une fenêtre, tandis que la sonnette s’occupe de la porte, de jour comme de nuit.
Le pack convient aux foyers qui veulent s’équiper sans chantier, et à ceux qui possèdent déjà des enceintes Echo. Le module de synchronisation accepte jusqu’à dix caméras, ce qui laisse de la marge pour surveiller un garage plus tard. En appartement, l’intérêt baisse nettement, puisque l’ensemble vise une porte d’entrée et un extérieur. Vérifiez aussi votre box : les deux appareils ne se connectent qu’au Wi-Fi 2,4 GHz.
Blink face aux caméras sans abonnement
Le vrai point de comparaison n’est pas le prix de départ, mais le coût d’usage. Dans notre comparatif des meilleures caméras de surveillance, la Xiaomi CW300, une caméra extérieure filaire autour de 50 €, enregistre sur carte microSD sans abonnement obligatoire, et la Ring Spotlight Cam Pro, retenue pour l’écosystème Amazon, en réclame un pour l’historique. À notre dernier relevé, Blink facturait 3 € par mois et par appareil avec Blink Basic, ou 10 € par mois avec Blink Plus. Le pack coûte donc moins cher que la Xiaomi à l’achat, mais ses vidéos enregistrées ont un coût mensuel.
✅ Les points forts
- Caméra, sonnette et module de synchronisation pour 24,99 €

articles.title: Cómo crear imágenes de los Saja Boys de Las Guerreras K-pop como personajes de Phineas y Ferb
articles.text:
Los Saja Boys, la banda rival de Las Guerreras K-pop, pueden adaptarse a una estética de animación televisiva similar a la de Phineas y Ferb con herramientas de inteligencia artificial (IA).
La clave consiste en describir qué elementos deben conservar los personajes y cuáles deben cambiar para llevarlos a otro universo gráfico.
Elegir bien las imágenes de referencia, usar una plataforma de generación, redactar un prompt detallado, revisar los errores y preparar una versión para colorear permite obtener un resultado que combine los dos universos.
Qué imágenes se deben descargar antes de empezar
El primer paso es reunir imágenes oficiales o capturas nítidas de los Saja Boys. Conviene buscar retratos individuales y una imagen grupal para identificar el peinado, el color de cabello, las prendas, los accesorios y la expresión habitual de cada integrante. Esto ayuda a que la herramienta diferencie a los personajes y evite mezclar sus rasgos.
Asimismo, se necesita una referencia visual del tipo de caricatura que se busca. En este caso, se pueden tomar como guía las formas simples, los contornos negros, los colores planos, las expresiones marcadas y los paisajes suburbanos que suelen asociarse con Phineas y Ferb.
Cuál herramienta sirve para generar la ilustración
Con las referencias seleccionadas, el siguiente paso es abrir una aplicación de generación de imágenes, como Gemini, y adjuntar los archivos en la conversación.
La plataforma de Google puede tomar esos materiales como orientación para conservar la cantidad de integrantes, los tonos principales del vestuario y algunos rasgos reconocibles del grupo.
Antes de pedir la ilustración, es clave decidir la orientación. Un formato horizontal ofrece espacio para mostrar a los cinco personajes en una misma escena, mientras que uno vertical puede servir para un retrato o una imagen centrada en uno de ellos. Se debe definir si la imagen será a color, en blanco y negro o si tendrá un fondo detallado.
Cómo redactar un prompt que dé instrucciones claras a la IA
Un prompt funciona mejor cuando organiza la información en bloques. Primero debe indicar quiénes aparecerán y cuántos serán. Luego puede describir la pose, el vestuario, el escenario y el tipo de dibujo. La precisión es importante para evitar que la aplicación agregue personajes, cambie posiciones o modifique atributos centrales.
Una opción de prompt es: “Crear una ilustración original de cinco integrantes inspirados en los Saja Boys de Las Guerreras K-pop, con una estética de animación 2D similar a Phineas y Ferb. Deben estar de pie en una calle residencial, con casas, árboles y cielo azul. Usar líneas negras definidas, colores planos, proporciones estilizadas y expresiones juveniles. Cada personaje debe tener un peinado y una ropa diferente”.
El pedido puede sumar detalles concretos, como la ubicación de cada integrante dentro de la escena, una paleta de colores o determinados gestos. Por ejemplo, se puede pedir que uno salude, otro cruce los brazos y otro adopte una pose pensativa.
Cómo generar una lámina para colorear
Una vez obtenida una versión a color, la misma composición puede convertirse en una lámina para colorear. Para lograrlo, hay que pedir una segunda versión con una instrucción específica: “Transformar esta imagen en una página para colorear, con fondo blanco, contornos negros uniformes, sin colores, sombras, degradados ni texturas”.
El resultado debe conservar los rasgos principales de los personajes, aunque conviene simplificar algunos elementos del fondo. Las áreas amplias en la ropa, el cielo, la calle o las fachadas facilitan el uso de lápices, fibras y marcadores.
Qué hacer luego de que el resultado sea el esperado
Después de seleccionar la versión definitiva, hay que descargarla en la mayor resolución disponible. El formato PNG es el adecuado para conservar contornos definidos y colores planos. Si se quiere imprimir la lámina, puede guardarse una copia en PDF para evitar cambios de tamaño al enviarla o abrirla desde otro dispositivo.
Antes de cerrar el proceso, es clave comprobar que los personajes no queden cortados por los bordes, que no haya textos agregados y que el fondo mantenga la coherencia con el estilo elegido.

articles.title: Xbox Puts Preservation at the Core of Project Helix
articles.text:
Monday, November 16th 2026
Xbox Puts Preservation at the Core of Project Helix
Xbox's VP of Next Generation, Jason Ronald, says keeping older games playable is one of the key goals for Project Helix. Xbox recently put out a 25th Anniversary Magazine, which shows off Xbox's journey through the years and also hints at what is to come, including details on Project Helix. We covered earlier that Helix might focus on Neural Rendering to keep costs down, also according to Jason Ronald. Here's what he said about preservation.
Jason Ronald, Xbox VP of Next GenerationGame preservation is core to XBOX. Not only do we feel like it's the right thing for the industry, we feel a deep responsibility as one of its biggest platforms and publishers...[Compatibility is] really informing how we design the platform and how we work with our partners to make sure that these games can not only be played, but they can also be played better than ever before in the future. Not only are we preserving those games from the past, but it's actually informing how we're designing and building the platform and games today - so that they can be preserved 20 years, 30 years in the future.
Ronald pointed to Xbox Backward Compatibility on PC as an early example of its game preservation efforts. It launched in July with four original Xbox games on PC and handhelds, and Microsoft expanded that catalog to 25 games last week. However, game preservation doesn't only cover older games. Future games also fall under that umbrella, and Xbox has been quite tight-lipped about the future of physical games on Project Helix. It did launch a disc-to-digital program, but that only covers Xbox One and Xbox Series X discs, with no support for older consoles. The next-gen "Project Helix" console from Xbox is reportedly due in holiday 2028.
Sources:
