articles.title: Beyond payments: Where venture capital will flow across Indian fintech over the next 24 months
articles.text:
Beyond payments: Where venture capital will flow across Indian fintech over the next 24 months
India's fintech decade was built on distribution. The next one will be built on infrastructure, advice and intelligence—and capital is already repricing accordingly.
India spent the last ten years solving for reach. UPI, Aadhaar-based onboarding, and the Jan Dhan push put a payment instrument in almost every adult hand, and a generation of companies was built on that distribution. That problem is now largely solved. The harder question—how to serve those hundreds of millions of customers profitably, with products that measurably improve their financial lives—is where the next cycle of venture capital will go.
The funding data already reflects the shift. Indian fintech attracted $3.5 billion across 216 disclosed deals in 2024, and $2.9 billion across 156 deals in 2025 roughly 10% less capital across 27% fewer transactions, according to Fintech Global. This fits fewer, larger cheques into a narrower set of theses. Yet fintech remained the largest sector by funding in 2025 at 22% of all Indian startup capital, and close to 26% in the first half of 2026. Capital is not leaving the sector; it is becoming far more selective about where to park itself.
Three themes stand out as most likely to absorb that capital over the next 24 months.
Financial infrastructure: Rebuilding the core
India's financial institutions are running a modern distribution business on decades-old plumbing. Core banking, lending and policy administration systems at most banks, NBFCs and insurers were built for a branch-led world of batch processing and overnight reconciliation—not for real-time payments at population scale, continuous underwriting, or products assembled on the fly from a dozen data sources. Every new capability gets bolted onto that base, and each addition costs more than the last as the architecture ages.
India’s financial institutions need to upgrade their technology, creating one of the largest infrastructure opportunities in the sector. Most legacy systems were not built for the speed and flexibility institutions now need. The next generation of technology will be cloud-based, modular and API-first, making it easier for different systems to work together. Banks and financial institutions want to launch products in weeks, adjust pricing quickly, and add new data sources or distribution partners without rebuilding their core systems. Much of their existing technology cannot support this.
The opportunity extends beyond core banking systems. Financial institutions also need better tools for compliance, managing AI models and their risks, preventing fraud and money laundering, and protecting against cyber threats. They also need infrastructure that allows non-financial businesses to offer financial products, such as loans, cards and escrow accounts. These capabilities are essential to delivering new financial products while meeting regulatory requirements.
Regulation is making these investments more urgent. Since February 2025, Sebi has held regulated intermediaries responsible for the outputs of AI and machine learning tools they use, including those provided by third parties. In August 2025, the RBI’s FREE-AI committee issued 26 recommendations, followed by draft guidance on model risk management and data governance. Meanwhile, the substantive obligations under India’s Digital Personal Data Protection Act, covering consent, notices and individuals’ data rights, are scheduled to take effect in May 2027. Financial institutions will need to demonstrate that their AI systems and data practices meet these requirements. For many, buying proven technology will be more practical than building it themselves.
For venture investors, this creates an attractive opportunity: businesses can generate recurring revenue from financial institutions, with customer relationships that become harder to replace as their software becomes embedded in day-to-day operations. Investors can also benefit from the growth of financial services technology without needing to predict which consumer-facing brand will win.
A less obvious opportunity lies in India’s Account Aggregator ecosystem. Between March 2025 and May 2026, the number of institutions consuming financial data grew by roughly 66%, crossing 1,000, while the number supplying data remained broadly flat at around 176. Demand for consent-based financial data is growing much faster than supply. Building the infrastructure needed to close this gap could become an important opportunity in its own right.
Wealthtech: The distribution is built, the advice is not
The structural tailwinds are no longer in question.
Mutual fund AUM reached Rs 85.76 lakh crore in July 2026, up from Rs 46.4 lakh crore three years earlier, according to ICRA Analytics.
Sebi’s annual report unique notes that mutual fund investors crossed 6.1 crore, growing 13% in a single financial year, with Tier III cities now accounting for more than half the investor base. Unique demat accounts stand at 12.18 crore, against 3.3 crore in April 2020. Households are visibly rotating: net financial savings rose from 27% of household savings in FY23 to 33% in FY25, and household flows into securities markets more than doubled as a share of GDP, from 0.99% to 2.17%.
But the gap between having an investment account and receiving investment advice is stark, and that is where the opportunity lies. In FY2025-26, 7.2 crore new SIPs were registered and 6.8 crore were discontinued or matured, as per Sebi data.
That is near-total churn. It is not a distribution failure because distribution worked. Rather, it is an advice failure.
The supply side explains why. India has roughly 1,042 Sebi-registered investment adviser entities against nearly 1.99 lakh AMFI-registered mutual fund distributors—about 191 commission-earning distributors for every fee-based adviser, and one adviser for every 58,500 mutual fund investors. Human advice at this ratio cannot reach the mass market, because the unit economics of servicing a Rs 5 lakh portfolio with a human adviser have never worked anywhere.
This is where the account aggregator (AA) framework and AI intersect to make something newly plausible. India’s AA rails had cumulatively fulfilled 493.5 million consents across 314.5 million linked accounts by June 2026, roughly tripling in fifteen months, and now span 16 categories of financial information, including deposits, mutual funds, equities, insurance, pension and GST filings. For the first time, a platform can obtain a consented, machine-readable, near-complete picture of a household's finances. Layer AI over that, and the marginal cost of producing a genuinely personalised recommendation—the kind previously reserved for private banking clients—falls by an order of magnitude.
AI: From feature to franchise
The third theme is the broadest, and the one where discipline matters the most. Almost every fintech firm now claims AI. The distinction worth drawing is between AI as a feature—a chatbot bolted onto an existing product—and AI as the reason the business model works at all.
Three variants look durable. First, consumer financial co-pilots that consolidate saving, investing, borrowing and insurance decisions into one interface. Their viability rests entirely on the AA-plus-AI combination above; without consented data, a co-pilot is a search engine with a friendly tone.
Second, enterprise workflow redesign inside financial institutions. Underwriting, collections, KYC remediation, claims processing, and internal audit are high-volume, rules-dense functions where agentic automation has clear economics and buyers have measurable cost lines to attack.
Third, and perhaps the most underrated, India as a delivery centre for AI-enabled professional services to the world. The IT industry was built on labour arbitrage in software; the same institutional muscle—managed delivery, compliance discipline, client trust at scale—can be pointed at legal review, audit, fund administration and healthcare operations, with AI compressing the cost base rather than headcount expanding it. Given India's incumbent position in global services, this may prove the largest of the three.
What all this adds up to
Payments proved Indians would adopt digital finance. The next 24 months will test whether the ecosystem can make that adoption profitable, well-advised and defensible, which makes a strong case for backing the layers rather than the surfaces: better technology for financial institutions, accessible financial advice for households, and AI that makes both economically possible.
The author is Principal, Flourish Ventures.
Edited by Swetha Kannan

articles.title: The race to build AI data centers at sea faces rough waters
articles.text:
The big picture: A small group of companies is designing data centers that would float on the open ocean or sit on the seabed, powering AI servers with electricity generated from waves, tides, wind, and sunlight while dissipating their heat into the surrounding water. The concept is a computing facility that requires no connection to the electrical grid, no municipal water supply, and no nearby residents to convince of its benefits. The biggest challenge is engineering hardware that can withstand saltwater, storms, and marine life while harvesting enough energy from the ocean to keep processors running.
The push for these facilities comes as battles over land-based data centers intensify. Local opposition often centers on how much power and water data centers consume and where they are built. Developers are betting that locating facilities miles offshore, with their own power and cooling systems, will take most of those arguments off the table.
The past several months have brought a series of announcements. In May, Portland-based Panthalassa raised $140 million from investors, including Peter Thiel, to build 278-foot steel structures that would drift untethered in the Pacific and power AI computing with wave energy. The company plans to test its next-generation system before beginning commercial deployment in 2027.
In July, Scottish developer Mocean Energy said it would install AI servers on floats powered by waves and sunlight far offshore, cooled by seawater and connected to land by satellite. In October, New Jersey-based Ocean Power Technologies and Florida-based Stratum Holdings signed a nonbinding letter of intent to explore whether Ocean Power's prototype buoys, which run primarily on wave, wind and solar power, could support Stratum's AI infrastructure without a power cable to shore.
Other designs would stay closer to land. Massachusetts-based DeepGreen Holdings has applied for federal permits to study tidal-powered underwater data centers on the seabed off Eastport, Maine, and in Alaska's Cook Inlet. The facilities would harness water movement near shore as tides rise and fall. Japan's Mitsui O.S.K. Lines wants to build a new ship or convert an existing one into a data center moored in port, powered either from shore or by a separate power vessel.
Mocean offers the most detailed look at how the hardware would work. Its system grew out of a decade of work developing wave energy technology for offshore oil and gas operators. A floating body moves with the swell and directly drives a generator, minimizing the number of moving parts that can fail. During a 13-month sea trial that ended in spring 2024, the unit generated electricity in waves as high as 40 feet, though its output dropped in smaller seas.
That trial unit generated about 10 kilowatts. Mocean now wants each node to supply about 500 kilowatts of power to onboard computers by combining wave and solar energy, with batteries providing backup during calm, overcast periods. The company envisions grouping the nodes into clusters of up to 100 megawatts in high-energy wave regions such as Western Europe, the US West Coast, Chile and Western Australia.
Cameron McNatt, the company's co-founder and chief executive, has set deployment targets of one gigawatt within five years and 10 gigawatts within a decade. He says the units would be difficult to see from land. "They're really low profile, sitting close to the water," McNatt told The Wall Street Journal. "They would basically be invisible."
Power is the central engineering challenge. Bryson Robertson, who directs the Institute for Integrated Energy Systems at the University of Victoria, says the cost of laying subsea cables to shore can drain a project's budget before the technology is proven. That helps explain why most of these designs generate electricity on site. Free-drifting platforms avoid the cost of moorings, Robertson says, but storms can push them off station. The energy needed to bring them back is energy that can't be used to power the servers.
Scale is another limitation. Robertson says wave converters must be tuned to the period of local waves. Simply making a device larger won't necessarily capture more energy from the ocean; it could actually capture less. "It's like building a 500-meter-wide wind turbine, but there's never enough wind to make it spin," he says.
Then there is the water itself. Climate-technology consultant Michael Barnard says saltwater corrodes metal quickly, while barnacles, mineral deposits and microorganisms accumulate on submerged surfaces. These can clog intake filters and coat the heat exchangers used to cool the servers. "You put anything into seawater, and it starts failing immediately," Barnard says.
Barnard doubts wave machines can operate reliably enough to make the concept viable. He also notes that sending repair crews offshore adds to costs. Mocean plans to use marine-grade anti-corrosion coatings and anti-fouling paint, and to tow units back to port for scheduled maintenance.
Environmental questions add another layer of complexity. In Maine, opponents of DeepGreen's plan point out that the Bay of Fundy is habitat for some of the world's most endangered whales. Kristen Monsell, oceans program litigation director at the Center for Biological Diversity, which has sought to participate in the federal review, says moving farther offshore could bring more boat traffic, increase the risk of whale strikes, and create noise that disrupts how whales feed and find mates.
She also raised concerns about water pollution and heat discharged into the surrounding environment. Louis Wolfson, DeepGreen's managing member, says the company's multiyear preliminary study is intended to examine those issues. He says the company is considering only turbines that stay within safe acoustic limits for marine mammals and fish. It will also consult tribal leaders, fishermen, and town officials before applying for a license. DeepGreen is still evaluating equipment partners and has not put anything in the water.
Wave energy has a long history of failed ventures, many undone by harsh conditions and high costs. Robertson says deep-pocketed technology companies could give the field the financial backing it needs to keep trying. "It's nice to see industries start to spend money in the wave-energy space," he says. "No technology works the first time."

articles.title: US moves to cut China’s remote access to AI chips
articles.text:
On the heels of the Nvidia scandal, the Trump administration is preparing to crack down on foreign data centers that are fueling China’s advancements in artificial intelligence by allowing remote access to otherwise restricted high-end chips necessary for AI training.
In a summary of the rule change, the Commerce Department said it was closing a loophole that previously allowed foreign rivals like China, Russia, and Iran to bypass export curbs on certain advanced computer chips by instead renting access to those chips from data centers in Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Brazil.
US rivals could possibly use that access to train and run advanced AI models “capable of supporting military- and intelligence-related activities that could threaten US national security or foreign policy interests,” the Commerce Department said. Among threats, the US fears rivals could use advanced AI to develop “more effective weapons of mass destruction and advanced conventional weapons, coordinated cyber-espionage and targeted cyber-disruption, algorithmic theft, and weaponized disinformation.”
Now, the rules have been tightened up so much that the South China Morning Post reported that, “as a result, any advanced chips made for a Chinese firm are assumed to be restricted, and factories must ask the US government for a license before shipping them.”
The rule change takes effect 90 days after it’s posted to the Federal Register. Moving forward, companies headquartered in any of those countries deemed to “present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion” to China, Russia, and Iran must apply for a license with strict know-your-customer controls when transferring high volumes of advanced chips. If a license is granted, companies will have to “perform robust due diligence,” submitting monthly reports on transactions that thoroughly detail all parties involved, as well as their parent companies, and the final destination for chips sold.
In a press release Sunday, the Commerce Department described the rule change as “designed to ensure that existing restrictions on access to sensitive American technology cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries.” An exception was carved out for companies providing computing power “exclusively used for commercial recommender systems.” The Department said it was acting to “prevent certain foreign actors from leveraging advanced computing power based on US technology to threaten US national security and foreign policy interests.”
Without the intervention, officials fear that China could develop a military or economic edge, The New York Times reported.
Trump officials clash on new rule
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned after admitting to an affair with a woman, Alice Huang, suspected of serving as a Chinese spy. Congress is probing if Alice Huang used her personal relationship with Jensen Huang to help her former company, Megaspeed, become one of Nvidia’s biggest customers, then used that position to smuggle Nvidia’s restricted AI chips into China. China has denied that Alice Huang was a spy, and Megaspeed has denied that smuggling occurred, while launching its own internal probe.
Megaspeed is a Singaporean data center firm whose primary business is cloud computing and AI infrastructure. Prior to the rule change, selling remote access to AI servers to customers in China was perfectly legal, NYT noted. But now, the Commerce Department has given firms like Megaspeed 90 days to either obtain licenses or face future export restrictions.
Whether or not to add more chip curbs has been a polarizing debate in the Trump administration. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent reportedly butted heads with Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. When the Megaspeed news broke, Bessent pushed for curbs, but Lutnick reportedly appeared “too cozy” with Nvidia to move. Instead, Lutnick initially favored looser controls that Nvidia claimed would ensure global dominance of US technology. (A Commerce Department spokesperson told NYT that Bessent has never confronted Lutnick over his handling of Megaspeed.)
Any companies found violating the rules could face a “range of consequences,” the Commerce Department said after reportedly bending to Bessent’s pressure campaign. Those include possibly facing new import restrictions, stricter license requirements, downgrading their status in the US export control regime, or other changes to their company’s or their base country’s entity-list designations.
New rule may not be aggressively enforced
Although the summary of the rule change said that “Commerce will be actively monitoring for countries that tolerate evasion” of the anti-diversion policy, it’s unclear how aggressively the Commerce Department might enforce the rule, NYT noted.
Bessent has publicly criticized Lutnick for failing to sanction Megaspeed, and NYT reported that ultimately, enforcement of the stricter rules—which Bessent helped draft—“would be up to the Commerce Department.”
“The real story here should be: Did Nvidia know their client, and was there a robust effort at Nvidia to make sure that there was no leakage and that they were selling to what were obviously pass-through shell companies?” Bessent said on a CNBC appearance. “I think it’s important that anyone at the company there be held accountable for that.”
There’s even a push to oust Lutnick over his position on chips, but The Guardian reported that Donald Trump confirmed he has no plans to replace the AI industry-friendly commerce secretary. On Monday, Trump told reporters that Lutnick was right to delay blacklisting Megaspeed, because “if you didn’t delay it… you could have a blow-up with China.”
At the press gaggle, Trump aligned with China in saying that there’s no evidence yet that Alice Huang was a spy. He also joined a band of prominent tech leaders calling for Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia, saying that it wasn’t a “bad idea.”
“Nobody’s proven that she’s a spy,” Trump said. “She may not be a spy.”
However, US investigators have alleged that they found “Alice Huang used industry contacts and a series of shell companies to access 240,000 chips banned for export into China,” CBS News reported.
Trump thinks China won’t react to rule change
China is unlikely to welcome the new rules, as it has consistently accused the US of fabricating the spying claims to justify imposing additional chip restrictions.
However, a senior Trump official, granted anonymity to discuss sensitive policy matters, told the NYT that Trump “did not expect countermeasures from China in response.”
Trump will be in China for an economic summit this week, including a meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping. The new curbs could potentially disrupt those talks, according to Hong Yuan, a researcher and secretary-general of the Center for American Military Studies at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences. Hong told the People’s Daily that China will likely view the rule change as politically motivated.
“Before any judicial causality was established, Washington handed down a political conviction, substituting suspicion for proof, espionage for personal contact, and an industrial embargo for private conduct,” Hong said. “The issue is not the cause of tighter controls, but a political catalyst.”
The new policy could hurt the US, experts told the Chinese outlets. Analysts told the South China Morning Post that the policy could “accelerate Chinese companies’ shift to domestic AI chips.” Other experts told the People’s Daily—which is the official newspaper of the Chinese Communist Party—that “the cost of switching back to US platforms will rise” over time. If that happened, it could potentially lock in Chinese technology over America’s in “the world’s largest single consumer market for chips,” experts said.
Sun Chenghao, senior fellow at the Center for International Security and Strategy at Tsinghua University in Beijing, told the People’s Daily that “what US companies stand to lose could be customers and technological influence for years to come.”
Ashley is a senior policy reporter for Ars Technica, dedicated to tracking social impacts of emerging policies and new technologies. She is a Chicago-based journalist with 20 years of experience.

articles.title: Rockstar se está convirtiendo en una “discográfica” porque la música de 'GTA VI' es ya tan rentable como el propio juego
articles.text:
Rockstar venderá su juego más esperado sin disco y, al mismo tiempo, pondrá su música en CD, en vinilo y en una edición limitada que cuesta más que el propio juego. La aparente contradicción tiene toda la lógica (aunque sea la del mercado): la saga nació dentro de una discográfica, y ahora Rockstar vuelve a funcionar como si fuera una. La presencia del audio en la franquicia es mucho más relevante de lo que parece.
Guest stars. Rockstar empezó detallando las seis primeras emisoras de 'GTA VI' y anunció que también habría un podcast bajo demanda disponible, algo inédito en la saga (y muy apropiado para reforzar su humor), además emisoras conversacionales cuando los personajes vayan a pie, gracias a auriculares conectados al móvil. Además, hay invitados especiales: Cocoteo FM, que Rockstar define como "la fiesta que nunca se apaga", y que en el juego presentan El Martillo y La Gata, que tiene detrás, según varios medios, a Bad Bunny y RaiNao. También Lana Del Rey podría estar tras la emisora de country Back Country Radio.
Como una discográfica. Alrededor de las emisoras, Rockstar ha montado un calendario de lanzamientos propio de un sello. 'Grand Theft Auto VI: The Album', con 34 temas originales, llega a las plataformas de streaming el 19 de noviembre, como el juego. Sus seis primeros sencillos reúnen a Travis Scott, Keith Richards, Morgan Wallen, Rauw Alejandro o el dúo argentino CA7RIEL & Paco Amoroso. A ellos se suman Lana Del Rey, Dua Lipa, Zara Larsson, Jennie, Arca o Justice. El álbum con la partitura de Justice, de 30 cortes más varios extras digitales, llega el 11 de diciembre. Es una decisión inesperada para una franquicia que casi siempre se ha limitado a licenciar canciones previas.
Historia de una partitura. Sam Houser, fundador de Rockstar, empezó su carrera en 1990 clasificando el correo en la sede londinense de la discográfica BMG. Era un trabajo de verano, pero en 1996 ya dirigía BMG Interactive, la rama de videojuegos de la empresa, y que en 1998 vendió a Take-Two la división con todos los derechos de 'GTA'. Antes, el primer 'GTA' de DMA Design cambiaba de emisora al cambiar de coche, con música compuesta en el propio estudio. Unos años después, en 2013, 'GTA V' incluyó la primera música ambiental dinámica original de la serie, y Rockstar publicó un volumen entero de canciones nuevas de Wavves, Twin Shadow o Tyler, The Creator.
El problema de alquilar canciones. El grueso de la radio de 'GTA' se ha ido construyendo a lo largo de los años con catálogos licenciados, un alquiler que tiene fecha de caducidad. Por ejemplo, en abril de 2018 Rockstar tuvo que retirar canciones de 'GTA IV' porque vencían licencias firmadas a diez años. Según la propia compañía, el recorte afectaba sobre todo a Vladivostok FM, la emisora de pop ruso, donde hubo que meter temas nuevos a modo de parche.
El poder prescriptivo de GTA. Es la cara que más interesa a las discográficas. Tras el primer tráiler de 'GTA VI', en diciembre de 2023, las escuchas de 'Love Is a Long Road', de Tom Petty, subieron un 36,97 % en Spotify respecto a la semana anterior. Era la canción del tráiler, y su tirón recuerda al que las canciones de 'FIFA' disfrutaron durante años. Por eso, la friolera de 34 temas encargados en exclusiva para esta nueva entrega es, más que un escaparate musical, un negocio redondo.
Cosas de discográficas. De un tiempo a esta parte, y con la limitadísima cantidad de lanzamientos en materia de videojuegos que tiene Rockstar, su actividad se ha centrado más en la música que en lo que los hizo famosos. En mayo de 2021, presentó CircoLoco Records, un sello creado junto a la marca de fiestas de Ibiza, con una frase que reconocía que "la música siempre ha sido una parte fundamental" de Rockstar Games. Ese mismo diciembre, 'GTA Online' estrenó MOTOMAMI Los Santos, una emisora presentada por Rosalía y Arca (que ahora firma un tema del álbum de 'GTA VI') y que adelantaba el primer sencillo del siguiente álbum de la catalana. Era parte de una trama que giraba alrededor a un móvil robado a Dr. Dre, cargado de temas inéditos que el jugador debía recuperar antes de que se filtraran.
El 21 de noviembre, dos días después de la salida del juego, Rockstar y PlayStation celebrarán en Miami, Grand Theft Auto VI: The Festival, dos escenarios con Travis Scott, Cardi B, Metro Boomin, Rauw & Friends, CA7RIEL & Paco Amoroso y una sesión de Justice. Y es que uno de los principales socios de 'GTA VI' es una major discográfica. Atlantic Records forma parte de Atlantic Music Group, propiedad de Warner Music Group, que en enero creó dentro del grupo de sellos una presidencia para Kevin Weaver con competencias sobre bandas sonoras, sincronizaciones e iniciativas de videojuegos. Su historial incluye 'Barbie The Album' y 'F1 The Album', y sus proyectos suman más de 65.000 millones de reproducciones.
Un recordatorio más de que GTA VI puede ser un fenómeno pop, pero también un negocio cuyos tentáculos hacen palidecer a cualquier gran empresa tecnológica actual.

articles.title: PSA: Canada to run emergency alert test on Wednesday
articles.text:
Canada will run a test of its national emergency alert system, Alert Ready, on Wednesday, November 18.
The test will run in all provinces and territories across 5G and LTE wireless devices, TV and radio. Alert Ready says this will be clearly indicated as a test that requires no action on the part of Canadians.
See below for the alert schedule by province and territory:

- British Columbia — 1:55 p.m. PCT
- Manitoba — 1:55 p.m. MBT
- New Brunswick — 10:55 a.m. AST
- Newfoundland & Labrador — 9:55 a.m. NST
- Northwest Territories — 1:55 p.m. NTT
- Nova Scotia — 1:55 p.m. AST
- Nunavut — 1:55 p.m. EST
- Ontario — 12:55 p.m. EST
- Prince Edward Island — 12:55 p.m. AST
- Quebec — 1:55 p.m. EST
- Saskatchewan — 1:55 p.m. CST

articles.title: Governed Autonomous Intelligence for Mission-Critical Utility
articles.text:
Key Takeaways
- In a regulated utility environment, an agentic operations platform keeps reasoning separate from execution: agents correlate signals, assess business impact, and propose remediation, but every production action crosses a deterministic policy boundary that the model cannot override.
- That boundary is defined outside the model. Each proposed action maps to a risk class and approval requirement in a predefined, versioned action catalog, which keeps approval decisions predictable, testable, and reviewable before deployment.
- A governed tool gateway enforces the boundary as the only path from an agent proposal to a production change, with least privilege, independent authorization, approval verification, and complete action evidence attached to that single door.
- Because every action passes through one governed path, the platform produces the evidence needed to support the regulatory and governance requirements of each system, without claiming that the platform itself creates compliance.
- Autonomy is earned rather than assumed: the platform starts read-only and expands one action class at a time, guided by recommendation quality, operator acceptance, execution outcomes, and rollback safety, and that autonomy can be revoked as easily as it is granted.
Introduction
Utility operations teams - the IT and platform teams responsible for supporting enterprise applications, integrations, and infrastructure already have more monitoring data than they can comfortably consume.
Application logs, infrastructure metrics, API telemetry, security events, job failures, service-management tickets, and business alerts all describe pieces of the same operating environment. The hard problem is not collecting another signal. It is connecting those signals quickly enough to understand what is happening, what it may affect, and what should happen next.
Agentic AI is attractive because it can reason across that fragmented evidence, retrieve operational knowledge, call tools, and coordinate multi-step work. But a utility organization cannot treat an agent the same way it treats a conversational assistant. A wrong summary is inconvenient. A wrong production action can affect a customer-facing service, a safety-related workflow, regulatory reporting, or a system that participates in reliable energy delivery.
This article describes the architecture pattern we used for an agentic operations platform in a regulated utility environment. The reference implementation uses Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, Amazon Bedrock, retrieval over enterprise runbooks and incident history, and Model Context Protocol (MCP) tool interfaces.
The model can propose anything. It can execute only what the policy gate authorizes, through the governed tool path, with human approval wherever policy requires it. Authority never lives inside the model.
Some capabilities, especially prediction and autonomous remediation, are intentionally enabled incrementally rather than all at once. That is not a limitation to hide. In a regulated environment, the ability to expand autonomy gradually and revoke it quickly is part of the architecture.
Why Utility Operations Need a Different Agentic Pattern
A large utility estate spans custom applications, SaaS products, cloud platforms, integration layers, databases, observability tools, field and operational systems, and third-party services. Each domain can be monitored well in isolation while the end-to-end service remains difficult to reason about.
The recurring operational gaps are familiar. Related signals appear in separate tools and are correlated manually. Technical severity is visible, but the business consequence is not. Runbooks and lessons learned exist, but they are spread across wikis, ticket histories, shared drives, and the memory of experienced engineers. Thresholds tell teams when a known condition has already occurred; weaker precursors across dependent systems are easy to miss. When action is finally taken, the evidence tying the change to its rationale, authorization, approver, and outcome may be assembled after the fact.
This is especially important in utilities because the governing context is not uniform. Regulatory requirements vary across utility sectors, operational environments, and jurisdictions. For example, North American Electric Reliability Corporation (NERC) Critical Infrastructure Protection (CIP) requirements apply to the Bulk Electric System (BES) and defined in-scope BES Cyber Systems. At the same time, customer-facing services, billing, field operations, and other utility programs may be subject to applicable industry-specific, federal, state, or local regulatory requirements.
The architecture therefore has to do more than produce a better dashboard. It must correlate across domains, reason with trusted operational knowledge, map technical events to business impact, support prediction without pretending prediction is certain, and preserve an execution model that security, compliance, operators, and auditors can understand.
Figure 1. Fragmented observability leaves operations teams to correlate application, infrastructure, integration, security, and service-management signals manually (Image source: created by the author)
The Control-Plane Pattern: Separate Reasoning from Execution
The organizing idea is an AI control plane. The term is borrowed deliberately from networking and cloud infrastructure, where the control plane decides what should happen and a separate plane carries it out. The separation is useful here for the same reasons: safety, auditability, and blast-radius containment.
Figure 2. The AI control plane separates reasoning authority from execution authority. The model can propose broadly; only policy-authorized actions can cross into the execution plane. (Image source: created by the author)
In the reasoning plane, the orchestrator and domain agents can analyze events, retrieve context, compare an incident with historical patterns, estimate business impact, predict likely failure modes, and propose remediation. None of those components holds authority to change a production system directly.
A proposed action crosses into the execution plane only through a deterministic policy gate and a governed tool gateway. The gate decides whether the action is permitted and what approval is required. The gateway enforces the final authorization, obtains narrowly scoped credentials, invokes the target system, records the result, and performs or requests post-action validation.
This distinction matters when the model is wrong. A hallucinated root cause in a conventional autonomous design can become a bad action. In this design, it becomes a bad proposal. Policy can reject the proposal, a human can review it, or the gateway can deny authorization. The model’s error still matters, but its cost is limited by construction.
Reference Implementation on AWS
The reference implementation runs on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. AgentCore supplies managed agent runtime, memory, gateway, identity, and observability integrations with Amazon Bedrock for model access and Bedrock Knowledge Bases for retrieval over enterprise knowledge. AgentCore Policy, generally available since March 2026, covers the boundary this pattern relies on: rules authored in natural language or policy-as-code are compiled to Cedar, AWS’s open-source authorization policy language, and attached to an AgentCore Gateway, which evaluates every agent-tool request before allowing or denying it. That is deterministic, action-level authorization enforced at the gateway rather than inside agent logic, and teams starting today should evaluate it before building an equivalent. In this design, AgentCore Gateway is the AWS implementation of the tool gateway. AgentCore Evaluations supports continuous and on-demand evaluation of agent behavior.
MCP is used at the tool boundary to standardize how tools are described and invoked. A schema-defined tool boundary gives the platform one place to constrain operations, validate arguments, enforce policy, and record evidence.
The "one place" property is important. A tool gateway is only a governance boundary if agents cannot bypass it. In our design, that means no target-system credentials in the reasoning runtime, deny-by-default identity policies, tightly restricted network paths, and credentials exposed only to the tool implementation that needs them. The principle is simple: one door to production, with every control attached to that door.
Figure 3. The pattern mapped onto AWS services. Everything in the reasoning plane can only propose; requests cross the dashed boundary solely through the policy gate and AgentCore Gateway, the AWS implementation of the tool gateway. (Image source: created by the author)
Equivalent Services on Other Platforms
The pattern is not tied to AWS. It needs a managed agent runtime, a retrieval layer, and a policy-enforcing tool gateway that agents cannot bypass. On Microsoft Azure, Microsoft Foundry Agent Service provides the runtime, Microsoft Entra supplies agent identities, and Azure AI Search handles retrieval, with Azure API Management serving as the tool gateway and an AI gateway for model and MCP traffic (some of these governance features are still in preview). On Google Cloud, the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform provides Agent Runtime and Agent Identity, with Agent Gateway as the tool gateway, enforcing IAM access policies and Model Armor screening for prompt injection.
End-to-End Responsibilities
The boundary that matters sits between the agentic layer and the tool gateway; everything above it reasons, and nothing above it can act.
| Layer | Responsibility | 
| Source | Alerts, logs, events, and telemetry from applications, infrastructure, cloud, monitoring, and security systems. | 
| Integration | Ingests and normalizes signals through APIs, webhooks, and streaming into a common schema. | 
| Queue | Buffers events for asynchronous processing and absorbs spikes without loss. | 
| Orchestrator | Receives events, determines analysis needs, routes to domain agents, and assembles findings. | 
| Agentic layer | Bounded agents for correlation, root-cause analysis, business impact, prediction, and remediation proposals. | 
| Knowledge base | Runbooks, SOPs, architecture documents, incident history, and dependency maps for trusted context. | 
| Model access | Reasoning, interpretation, and recommendations grounded in enterprise knowledge. | 
| Policy gate | Maps proposed actions to risk classes and approval requirements outside the model. | 
| Tool gateway (MCP; AgentCore Gateway on AWS) | Single governed production path enforcing authorization, approvals, scoped credentials, schema validation, and evidence capture. | 
| Target systems | Applications, cloud services, databases, networks, ITSM, and observability platforms receiving remediation. | 
| Human approval | Operator or owner review with recorded decision, identity, and timestamp. | 
| Operations view | Health, predictions, business impact, approvals, remediation status, and validated outcomes. | 
Table 1. End-to-end responsibilities across the governed pipeline, from signal ingestion to the operations view
Multi-Agent Reasoning Grounded in Operational Knowledge
The reasoning plane uses a hierarchical multi-agent structure rather than one large agent with broad access. A narrow agent with a bounded responsibility is easier to test, constrain, evaluate, and explain than a monolithic agent that knows every domain and can call every tool.
The Orchestrator Agent is the entry point for normalized operational events. It determines the analysis required, routes work to the appropriate domain agents, and assembles their findings. It coordinates but does not execute.
The Application Reliability Agent analyzes application failures and degradations against known patterns and recent history. The Platform Intelligence Agent looks at API and interface failures, latency, partial degradation, and upstream/downstream dependencies. The Business Impact Agent translates technical state into business consequences — for example, a risk to customer service, billing, a safety-related program, a reliability commitment, or a reporting deadline. The Remediation Agent is the only reasoning component allowed to propose a production-touching action, and its proposal still has no authority until it passes the policy and approval path.
Figure 4. The orchestrator decomposes each event and routes analysis to bounded domain agents; only the Remediation Agent proposes production actions, and those proposals still pass through policy and the tool gateway (Image source: created by the author)
All agents use shared operational context retrieved from enterprise knowledge. The useful corpus is the organization’s runbooks, SOPs, architecture documentation, incident history, business rules, dependency maps, and known recovery procedures. Grounding a recommendation in the documented procedure for this environment produces a very different artifact from a plausible answer based only on general model training.
The quality of this layer depends heavily on knowledge hygiene. If a runbook is outdated, contradictory, or missing a rollback step, RAG will faithfully retrieve an outdated, contradictory, or incomplete instruction. Curation, ownership, versioning, and source traceability are therefore part of the operational design, not a content-management side project.
In practice, every runbook carries a named owner and a last-review date, and retrieval returns both with each passage. Runbooks past their review interval are flagged to the owner, and operator rejections citing a faulty runbook are routed to the runbook’s owner for correction.
A common event contract is just as important as the knowledge base. We normalize incoming signals into a small operational schema that includes the affected service or component, environment, event type, timestamp, source, technical severity, dependency identifiers, correlation keys, business-service mapping, and a reference back to the original evidence. The raw payload is preserved, but deterministic parsing and source adapters, not the LLM, establish basic facts such as which system emitted the event and whether two identifiers refer to the same service. A model can help interpret an unfamiliar log message, but those foundational facts are too important to leave to probabilistic extraction.
The simplified example below shows a normalized event from the walkthrough scenario. The business-service mapping is looked up from the service catalog, not inferred by the model.
{
  "event_id": "evt-000193",
  "timestamp": "2026-04-12T14:03:27Z",
  "source": "apm",
  "source_event_ref": "apm://alerts/88213",
  "service": "customer-payments-api",
  "environment": "prod",
  "event_type": "latency_degradation",
  "technical_severity": "warning",
  "dependency_ids": ["billing-integration", "payments-queue"],
  "correlation_keys": ["chain:bill-payment-flow"],
  "business_service": {
    "name": "Customer bill payment",
    "criticality": "high",
    "mapping_source": "service-catalog"
  }
}
Walking Through a Governed Event
Consider a common integration-operations pattern. An API has not failed, but its latency begins to rise. At roughly the same time, a downstream integration starts retrying more frequently, and a processing queue grows. Each signal on its own may still be below a page-worthy threshold. Together they suggest that a customer-facing workflow could degrade if the pattern continues.
The ingestion layer normalizes the three signals and preserves their source evidence. The orchestrator recognizes that the affected components share a dependency chain and asks the Platform Intelligence Agent to analyze the interface behavior. The Application Reliability Agent checks whether the application has shown a similar resource or connection pattern in prior incidents. The Business Impact Agent maps the dependency to the business service that relies on it.
Retrieval then pulls the current runbook for this failure class and the most relevant historical incidents. The agents don't merely summarize alerts; they produce a structured operational hypothesis: the likely failure mode, supporting evidence, dependent services that may be affected, and documented remediation options. If the evidence is weak or contradictory, that uncertainty is carried forward rather than hidden.
Suppose the runbook permits two next steps: gather additional diagnostics and, if a specific condition is confirmed, restart a stateless component. The action catalog may classify the diagnostic tool as low risk and allow it to run automatically. In this deployment, the catalog maps the restart to a human-approval rule. The Remediation Agent can propose it, but it cannot decide to downgrade its risk because the model is confident.
When an operator approves the restart, the tool gateway verifies the approval reference and policy, obtains the scoped execution identity, invokes only the permitted operation, and captures the response. The workflow then checks the signals that motivated the action: latency, retry behavior, queue trend, and service health. If those conditions do not recover, the workflow does not mark the remediation successful simply because the restart command completed.
The architecture removes manual correlation and runbook hunting from a familiar operational problem while preserving the same controls an experienced engineer would expect before touching production.
Prediction Without Granting Prediction Authority
Prediction is where the platform moves beyond faster incident summarization. The goal is to identify combinations of weak signals that historically precede a failure: rising latency, queue growth, retry behavior, resource saturation, repeated warning patterns, or anomalies that become meaningful only when correlated across a dependency chain.
The prediction layer can use historical incidents, time-series trends, dependency information, and semantic analysis of unstructured logs to produce a forward-looking statement: what may fail, on what horizon, through which mechanism, with what confidence, and with what likely business consequence.
The important design decision is what prediction is not allowed to do. A confidence score is not an authorization token. Predictions enter the same governed path as observed incidents. They carry evidence, confidence, and business-weighted risk so operators can decide how to respond.
False positives are expected. They should be measured, reviewed, and reduced over time. Overselling prediction is one of the fastest ways to lose operator trust.
Governed Remediation: Deterministic Risk and Human Approval
Human control should not be a sentence in a governance document. It should sit directly on the execution path.
The platform maps every candidate action to a predefined risk class outside the model. An approved action catalog drives that classification, not the model deciding whether its own proposal is dangerous. The catalog can consider the operation, target environment, blast radius, reversibility, data impact, and dependency sensitivity, but the resulting policy is fixed, versioned, testable, and reviewable.
| Risk class | Examples | Governance | 
| Low | Read-only diagnostics, health checks, additional telemetry | May auto-execute; fully logged | 
| Medium | Reversible changes, such as approved stateless service restarts or scaling within limits | Approval per policy | 
| High | Production configuration changes, failover, sensitive data operations, or broad-impact changes | Explicit approval; dual control where policy requires it | 
Table 2. Action risk classification and governance requirements
This is intentionally conservative. In the early stages of deployment, even some low-risk actions may remain approval-only until the team has enough evidence to allow automatic execution.
The policy record should be concrete enough to test without an LLM. For each permitted operation, we keep the tool identifier, target environment, allowed scope, risk class, required approval type, execution timeout, key preconditions, and expected postconditions, plus a link to the rollback procedure where rollback is meaningful. The agent may supply parameters such as a service name or requested capacity, but policy decides whether they fall inside the authorized envelope. The risk-driving facts should come from controlled configuration, inventory, or independently verified context, because asking the model to label its own proposal low, medium, or high leaves the authority decision with the model.
Figure 5. Deterministic policy maps each proposed action to a risk class and approval requirement before the governed tool gateway can execute it (Image source: created by the author)
Post-action validation is easy to underestimate. "API returned 200" is not the same as "the system is healthy," so a remediation workflow should validate the outcome it was meant to produce and escalate if the expected state is not restored.
The gateway also provides defense in depth. It scopes least-privilege credentials to specific tools, authorizes each agent-and-action combination independently, and rechecks required approvals at execution time instead of trusting an upstream component’s claim that they happened. It also validates tool arguments against their schemas. Every invocation records the requesting identity, policy decision, approval reference, inputs, result, and post-action health status.
Typed tools constrain what a manipulated agent can request, but they do not make prompt injection disappear, because an agent can still misuse an operation within its allowed scope. The control therefore comes from layers: treating ingested content as untrusted data, narrow tools, argument validation, least privilege, policy enforcement, approval requirements, network constraints, and post-action validation.
Content inspection adds one more layer at the same boundary; since June 2026, AgentCore Policy can evaluate Bedrock Guardrails to screen tool gateway inputs and outputs for prompt injection and sensitive-data exposure (initially in a subset of AWS Regions). Treat that as one more control on the door rather than a solution to injection, and keep the bounded-authority layers regardless of how good the detection gets.
Security, Auditability, and Compliance
For regulated operations, governance is not a section added after the architecture. It is why the architecture has this shape.
Teams should manage model and agent changes with the same discipline as other production software: version-controlled prompts and agent definitions, reviewed changes, evaluation before promotion, and rollback capability. Historical incidents and adversarial cases provide useful regression tests. Teams should sample production traces and evaluate them for task completion, tool selection, groundedness, safety, and policy adherence. They should also monitor confidence and recommendation quality for drift after deployment.
Teams should also minimize operational data. Logs and tickets can contain customer, employee, or security-sensitive information irrelevant to the reasoning task. Before broad ingestion, teams should establish data classification, domain isolation, encryption in transit and at rest, and retention rules. OWASP’s Top 10 for LLM Applications identifies prompt injection and excessive agency as distinct risks, and its agentic security guidance extends that thinking to goal hijacking, tool misuse, identity and privilege abuse, and multi-agent interactions.
Audit evidence should answer more than "what did the system do?" For every consequential action, the organization should be able to reconstruct the originating signal, retrieved evidence, recommendation, applicable policy, human decision if required, executed operation, identity used, and validated result. Whether you can call that record immutable depends on the actual storage control; at minimum, it should be durable, access-controlled, tamper-evident, or otherwise protected according to enterprise evidence requirements.
The compliance mapping must be equally precise. NERC CIP does not apply to every application operated by an electric utility. For in-scope BES Cyber Systems, CIP-010-4 addresses configuration change management and vulnerability assessments; CIP-004-7 includes personnel and access-management requirements; CIP-011-3 addresses protection of BES Cyber System Information; and CIP-008-6 covers cyber-security incident reporting and response planning. An agentic platform can support the evidence needed for applicable requirements, but the platform itself does not create compliance.
For customer-facing and regulated programs, evidence and reporting obligations may vary based on applicable jurisdictional requirements. Corporate applications outside CIP scope may instead fall under internal change controls, privacy requirements, or financial controls. The practical rule is to map evidence to the regime governing the specific system rather than labeling the entire utility estate "CIP compliant".
Frameworks such as NIST AI Risk Management Framework (Govern, Map, Measure, Manage) and ISO/IEC 42001:2023 can organize the broader AI governance program, but they complement rather than replace industry-specific requirements.
Measure Value and Earn Autonomy
In regulated environments, organizations should measure agentic AI value against operational baselines, not unsupported improvement percentages. The signals we tracked included detection time from the earliest useful signal to an actionable alert; response time to validated resolution; prediction precision, false-positive rate, lead time, and operator-rated usefulness; engineering effort spent on manual correlation, after-hours paging, and repeated analysis; and governance measures such as approval latency, policy denials, blocked unauthorized actions, evidence completeness, and audit reconstruction time.
We expanded autonomy in phases, one action class at a time. No action class moved forward on model confidence alone. Each step required agreement from the system owner and change-management reviewers, based on the evidence below.
| Phase | Action class | Execution mode | Evidence required to move on | 
| 1 | All actions | Read-only: observe, correlate, retrieve, predict, and recommend | Operators consistently accepted recommendations, and rejection reasons were reviewed and addressed | 
| 2 | Read-only diagnostics and health checks | Approval-only → automatic | No diagnostic ran outside its authorized scope; evidence records were complete | 
| 3 | Reversible changes, such as stateless service restarts | Introduced as approval-only | Post-action validation confirmed recovery; rollback procedures were tested | 
| 4 | Selected low-impact reversible changes, such as restarting an approved stateless service or scaling within predefined limits | Approval-only → automatic, within defined scope and time windows | Approved consistently without modification; post-action validation confirmed recovery; rollback succeeded when tested; no policy denials or out-of-scope requests | 
| 5 | High-risk changes, such as configuration changes and failover | Always explicit approval | Not eligible for automatic execution | 
Table 3. Phased autonomy progression and evidence requirements
Conclusion: Lessons for Teams Adopting This Pattern
Agentic AI can correlate operational signals, assess business impact, and recommend remediation, but in mission-critical environments its value depends on how well its authority is governed. For teams adopting this pattern, a few recommendations stand out:
- Establish governance first: Build the governed execution path, enforce least privilege, and define the action catalog before introducing agents.
- Enforce deterministic policies: Manage risk classification and approval requirements through versioned configuration, not model prompts.
- Validate outcomes: Confirm service recovery rather than relying on successful command execution.
- Earn autonomy gradually: Enable one action class at a time, with the ability to revoke authorization when needed.
The goal is not maximum autonomy, but evidence-based autonomy that can be safely governed and revoked.

articles.title: Fiido M1 Pro : ce fat bike électrique pliant, à l'aise en ville comme en pleine nature, fonce sous les 1 000 € pendant le Black Friday — Frandroid
articles.text:
Sur le marché des vélos électriques, les fat bikes ont le vent en poupe. Si vous ne connaissez pas encore cette catégorie de biclou, sachez qu’ils se distinguent par leurs pneus surdimensionnés, qui apportent plus de stabilité sur différents types de terrains. Leurs gros pneus absorbent aussi mieux les chocs et les vibrations, ce qui améliore nettement le confort. Parmi les modèles les plus intéressants du moment, on a le Fiido M1 Pro, un fat bike électrique pliant qui ne dépasse pas les 1 000 euros pendant le pré-Black Friday.
Les points forts du Fiido M1 Pro
- Un format pliant
- Des pneus de 20 x 4 pouces
- Jusqu’à 88 km d’autonomie annoncés (mode Eco)
Initialement affiché à 1 499 euros, le Fiido M1 Pro est aujourd’hui disponible en promotion à 999 euros sur le site officiel de Fiido.
Du 10 au 30 novembre, le YUKA mini 2 500 passe à 599 € au lieu de 799 € ! Plug & Play, sans fil périmétrique à enterrer, zéro installation prise de tête. Bref, déballez, lancez, et dites adieu à la tonte !
Un VAE pliant soutenu par deux gros pneus
Le Fiido M1 Pro mise d’abord sur son format pliant, pratique pour le ranger ou le glisser dans un coffre ou un train. Mais attention, ce fat bike affiche tout de même 26,8 kg sur la balance, on est donc très loin du poids plume. Il est par ailleurs certifié IP54 : il résiste aux projections d’eau et à la poussière, de quoi rouler sous la pluie sans stress.
Ce VAE dispose par ailleurs d’un cadre en alliage d’aluminium fermé, donc un peu plus difficile à enjamber qu’un cadre ouvert. Il repose surtout sur deux larges pneus CST de 20 pouces de diamètre et 4 pouces de largeur, qui lui assurent une bonne adhérence sur différents types de terrains. Leur important volume d’air agit aussi comme une suspension naturelle. Les chocs, vibrations et petites irrégularités de la route sont ainsi mieux absorbés.
En plus de ses gros pneus, le M1 Pro a une fourche suspendue à l’avant, avec 80 mm de débattement, et un amortisseur à l’arrière.
Un capteur de couple pour une assistance en douceur
Côté performances, le Fiido M1 Pro intègre un moteur brushless de 250 W (le maximum autorisé pour un VAE), logé dans le moyeu, qui délivre un couple de 50 Nm. Associé à un capteur de couple Mivice S200, il fournit une assistance progressive et réactive, ce qui est bien appréciable dans les montées. Le VAE peut donc, en théorie, gravir des pentes assez raides et franchir des passages difficiles lors de randonnées. Il est également doté d’un dérailleur arrière Shimano TY300D associé à une transmission à sept vitesses.
Côté freinage, Fiido a opté pour des freins à disque hydrauliques à double piston, qui coupent l’assistance dès qu’on actionne les leviers. Enfin, grâce à sa batterie amovible de 556,8 Wh, le Fiido M1 Pro peut parcourir jusqu’à 88 km selon la marque. Ce chiffre vaut en mode Eco ; en mode Normal, Fiido annonce 73 km, et 62 km en mode Sport. Évidemment, tout dépendra de l’état de la route, des conditions météo ou encore du poids de l’utilisateur.

articles.title: Startup news and updates: daily roundup (November 16, 2026)
articles.text:
Startup news and updates: daily roundup (November 16, 2026)
YourStory presents the daily news roundup from the Indian startup ecosystem and beyond. Here's the roundup for Monday, November 16, 2026.
From Ola Electric making a major change to its retailing business, to India and US-based semiconductor company Bharat Semi raising $24 million in seed funding to develop programmable smart sensors, here are the latest developments across sectors.
Featured Stories
Ola Electric hands the keys to dealers. What led to this shift in gears?
On November 1, Ola Electric stopped taking orders at its own outlets. Most of them will be shut by December, as Ola moves away from the direct-to-consumer model that defined the company and turns to a dealer-led business.
Ola has recorded this in its investor presentation filed with the NSE and BSE on November 12 under Regulation 30 of the SEBI Listing Regulations. The document covers the unaudited standalone and consolidated results for the second quarter and half-year ended September 30, 2026.
In its Q2 FY27 shareholders' letter, dated November 12, the company calls the move towards a dealer-led model a "reset". What prompted this 'reset'?
Latest News
Oister Global launches Rs 600 Cr deeptech fund
Oister Global, an India-focused multi-strategy private markets asset manager, has announced the launch of a Rs 600 crore deeptech fund to back revenue generating Indian startups.
The Oister Deep Tech Fund aims to raise Rs 400 crore with a Rs 200 crore greenshoe, taking the potential corpus to Rs 600 crore.
A statement from Oister Global said this deeptech fund will build a concentrated portfolio of 8 to 10 mature companies in the frontier tech ecosystem. The fund will focus in sectors such as space technology, defence and aerospace, semiconductors and electronics, quantum technologies, advanced mobility, advanced materials and energy storage.
Funding News
Bharat Semi raises $24M to develop AI-enabled sensors
India- and US-based semiconductor company Bharat Semi has raised $24 million in seed funding to develop programmable smart sensors for Physical AI, where machines use artificial intelligence to perceive and act in the real world.
The round was led by Info Edge, the internet group behind Naukri; South Park Commons, a founder community and early-stage investor; and IndusBridge Ventures, which backs deeptech sector.
Micromax, an electronics group; Valour Capital, a deeptech investor; New York-based venture syndicate Gaingels and angel investors Mukul Agarwal and Kartik Iyer also participated.
Other News
Equity Intelligence invests Rs 2.5 crore in 90+ My Tuition App to launch Future+ Foundery
Equity Intelligence, the investment firm led by Porinju Veliyath, has invested Rs 2.5 crore in 90+ My Tuition App, owned by Daskalos Virtual Academy, at a Rs 50 crore valuation. The funds will launch Future+ Foundery, a separate brand offering school-integrated future-skills programmes. Its 15 learning areas include artificial intelligence, space technology, entrepreneurship, digital marketing, defence careers and leadership.
Students begin with a Discovery Programme, then progress through Foundation, Advanced Learning and Real Industry Learning, each a one-year pathway. Proceeds will fund curriculum, school partnerships, technology and national expansion through a Future+ Integrated School Network, while Daskalos develops an AI Teacher Programme.
Arborum Labs raises pre-seed funding to build world models for complex networks
Bengaluru-based Arborum Labs has raised an undisclosed pre-seed round co-led by Speciale Invest and Ideaspring Capital to build AI world models for complex infrastructure networks. Other participants include BCG's Neeraj Aggarwal and Pranay Mehrotra and Sriram Rajamani, while ARTPARK and FSID are also supporters.
Founded by IISc's Himanshu Tyagi and former BCG AI leader Pooja Rajdev, the startup models how power and telecom systems behave, supporting forecasting, trading, battery optimisation and outage detection. It already works with several Indian networks. The funds will accelerate development and expansion in India and the US, with a public version planned within a year.
Brighter Mind Category III AIF crosses Rs 50 crore in investor commitments
Brighter Mind Asset Management has crossed Rs 50 crore in investor commitments for its Category III AIF, Brighter Mind Inevitable Fortune Fund, launched in April 2025. The long-only fund focuses on listed Indian equities and the pre-IPO space, and uses no derivatives.
Its investment approach rests on a proprietary 3M framework: Megatrend, Management and Margin of Safety. Led by founder, managing director and CEO CA Rajeev Ranjan and co-founder and CIO Manoj Bandre, the firm says the milestone reflects investor trust. It plans to stay disciplined in portfolio construction and remain committed to high-conviction, research-driven value investing as the fund grows.
mistEO raises Rs 18 crore seed round led by MGF-Kavachh to scale climate risk intelligence
Thiruvananthapuram-based climate intelligence company mistEO has raised Rs 18 crore in a seed round led by MGF-Kavachh, with Seafund and others participating. Announced at Huddle Global 2026, the funds will scale its Climate Decision Intelligence platform for banks, insurers and agri-value chains across India and Asia, deepen its forecasting models and grow its team.
The platform fuses physics-based weather modelling with AI, using satellite, radar and sensor data to show how weather affects specific farms, assets or loans. Its Indra model forecasts at 3 km spatial resolution. mistEO already works with NABARD, UNDP, the Indian Air Force and Australian livestock farmers.
Consint.ai and Pramana HealthTech partner to drive connected health ecosystem across Asia-Pacific
Consint.ai, an Indian deep-tech company building foundational health AI models with IndiaAI Mission support, has signed a strategic partnership with Pramana HealthTech to explore opportunities across Asia-Pacific. The collaboration combines Consint.ai's generative and agentic AI capabilities with Pramana's ecosystem orchestration approach, aiming to connect financial, administrative, operational and clinical processes across payers, providers, pharmacies and laboratories.
It will examine six areas, including financing models, claims and payer coordination, programme economics and outcome-based models, aligned with Pramana's Financial Orchestration for Healthcare Sustainability domain. Both firms intend to engage regional stakeholders, focusing on claims intelligence, financial integrity and process automation across programmes.""
Arborum Labs raises pre-seed round co-led by Speciale Invest and Ideaspring Capital
Arborum Labs, a Bengaluru-based AI startup building world models for complex networks, has raised an undisclosed pre-seed round co-led by Speciale Invest and Ideaspring Capital. Backers include BCG's Neeraj Aggarwal and Pranay Mehrotra, Sriram Rajamani, ARTPARK and early supporter FSID.
Co-founded by IISc's Himanshu Tyagi and former BCG generative AI leader Pooja Rajdev, the company's models learn how infrastructure components interact, helping operators simulate scenarios. In power, they support forecasting, trading and battery optimisation; in telecom, they detect impending outages. Arborum already works with several nationwide Indian networks and will use the funds to expand in India and the US.
Zoho Desk marks 10 years from Tenkasi and unveils Blended Agents for customer service
Zoho Desk, built in Tenkasi, Tamil Nadu, marks 10 years serving more than 125,000 businesses across 155 countries, growing roughly 35% annually between 2017 and 2025. To mark the anniversary, Zoho has launched Blended Agents, powered by Zia Agents, which retrieve information, execute tasks across connected applications and hand over to humans when judgement is needed.
Businesses can build and deploy AI agents at no extra cost, paying only for LLM usage. The release also adds Automation Studio, a customisable Workstation and WhatsApp calling and payments. Zoho's Tenkasi campus houses around 1,100 employees, about half of them local.
Uber partners with Mahindra Last Mile Mobility to support 5,000 electric autos
Uber has signed a memorandum of understanding with Mahindra Last Mile Mobility to support the adoption of 5,000 electric three-wheelers over the next 12 months. The EV Auto Advantage programme will offer drivers financing, trade-in incentives and support, focusing on markets where electric vehicle penetration remains low.
Announced in Mumbai on the sidelines of Earthshot Week, the partnership aims to make electric mobility a better economic choice for drivers. Uber also showcased Connected Journeys, a feature rolling out progressively from Delhi that combines autos or two-wheelers with metro travel in a single journey plan, with route options, timings and pricing visible in the app.
Medi Assist appoints Aruna Vaidyanathan as Chief Growth and Culture Officer
Medi Assist Healthcare Services has appointed Aruna Vaidyanathan, formerly Global Head of Growth Marketing at TCS, as Chief Growth and Culture Officer, reporting to CEO Satish Gidugu. She will build a unified go-to-market engine across its three businesses: Medi Assist Insurance TPA, India's largest third party administrator; its technology platforms; and Mayfair We Care, which administers international health benefits across 185 countries.
Her remit covers brand, market messaging and stakeholder communications, with each business given its own identity under one brand. She will also build a single culture across teams brought together through acquisitions and countries. She began her career as a business journalist.
Visage Lines launches rE, a recovery brand built around 10-minute daily resets
Visage Lines Personal Care, parent company of Bombay Shaving Company, has launched rE, a recovery brand built around 10-minute daily resets. The range has 14 products across three categories: Reset, Rewind and Recover, including a massage gun, foam roller, eye massager and calf sleeve.
Short routines target areas, such as three minutes for the neck and shoulders, five for the lower back and seven for the scalp and eyes. Routines were developed with orthopaedic surgeon Dr Manan Vora and physiotherapist Dr Yamini Burkule. The brand is pursuing partnerships with marathons, gyms and workplaces, and is available online from 16 November.
Quest Global acquires Tests Assured to strengthen wearables engineering and testing
Quest Global Engineering Services has acquired Tests Assured, a San Jose-based company specialising in quality assurance and technology-enabled testing for immersive products, smart devices and wearables. Founded in 2018, Tests Assured brings expertise in AR/VR/XR and smart-glasses testing, biometric validation, human-interaction modelling and computer-vision data collection, along with a strong presence among global wearable-device companies.
The acquisition aims to strengthen Quest Global's ability to deliver engineering solutions for wearables in the high-tech consumer space and support customers across the product lifecycle. The two companies will also pursue new opportunities in the hi-tech and semiconductor industries.
Recode Studios reports 24% revenue growth in H1 FY27
Beauty and personal care brand Recode Studios reported a 24% year-on-year growth in revenue from operations to Rs 45.82 crore for the first half of FY27, compared with Rs 36.91 crore in the corresponding period last year. Profit after tax increased 27% to Rs 4.92 crore, while EBITDA rose 9% to Rs 6.45 crore. The company attributed the performance to deeper market penetration and an expanding omnichannel distribution network.
Recode has expanded its retail presence to 25 franchise outlets, two company-owned stores and seven premium kiosks across more than 20 cities. It has also increased its portfolio to over 400 SKUs. The company expects to deliver more than 50% growth in FY27.
Scalar Field records $60 million in trading activity through AI agents
Y Combinator-backed fintech startup Scalar Field has recorded $60 million in cumulative trading activity through its AI trading agents, approximately four months after launching the platform in July 2026. The figure includes both simulated and live trading activity. The platform enables investors to develop trading strategies, test them against historical market data and deploy them through supported accounts.
Its AI capabilities assist with research and strategy development, while a separate execution system applies user-defined rules and monitors positions. Ramakant Yadav, Co-founder of Scalar Field, said the platform enables investors to translate market ideas into testable strategies without requiring dedicated research and engineering teams. The startup's next priority is improving transparency and helping users understand their agents' trading decisions.
Pensionbazaar partners Zypp Electric to offer NPS to gig workers
Pensionbazaar, a brand under Paisabazaar, has partnered with electric mobility platform Zypp Electric to offer National Pension System (NPS) solutions to its gig delivery partners. Zypp operates a fleet of more than 30,000 electric vehicles across eight cities and has impacted over 2.8 lakh gig workers. Under the partnership, eligible delivery partners can enrol in NPS through a digital, consent-based process and make contributions using UPI, net banking or cards.
Zypp aims to bring 60-70% of eligible delivery partners into the pension ecosystem within the first six to 12 months. The initiative seeks to address the limited access gig workers have to formal retirement benefits and encourage long-term savings through flexible contributions.
Fireflies.ai expands platform with AI teammate Fred
Fireflies.ai has expanded its product portfolio with the launch of Fred, an AI teammate designed to help organisations manage tasks across workplace applications. The platform brings together meeting notes, email, Slack, scheduling, screen recording and enterprise search. The company said Fred completed nearly 100 million tasks over the past six months, while usage beyond meeting notes grew 140%.
The expanded offering includes AI-powered meeting preparation, voice typing, email assistance, scheduling and voice agents. Fireflies also introduced Fireflies Fly, a hardware device designed to capture notes from phone calls and in-person conversations. The platform connects with over 240 tools. Fireflies said its new experience would roll out progressively, with paid plans starting at $10 per user per month.
Embark launches location analytics tool for GCC expansion in India
Embark has launched a Location Analytics Tool to help global companies identify suitable cities and micro-markets for establishing Global Capability Centres (GCCs) in India. The platform evaluates locations across seven parameters and more than 35 sub-parameters, covering talent availability, real estate, regulatory conditions, connectivity, infrastructure and liveability.
Companies can customise criteria based on their sector, proposed workforce and business functions. The tool also provides insights into peer GCCs, role-level talent availability and office rental costs. According to Embark, its database draws on research covering approximately 2,100 GCCs in India. The platform aims to simplify location selection, which traditionally involves extensive consultant-led studies, and enable companies to make faster, data-backed expansion decisions.
Kotak Mahindra Bank, NSRCEL onboard 90 women entrepreneurs under startup programme
Kotak Mahindra Bank, through its CSR initiative Kotak BizLabs, has onboarded 90 women entrepreneurs for the sixth cohort of its Women Startup Program (WSP 6), implemented in partnership with NSRCEL at IIM Bangalore. The seven-month hybrid incubation programme, running from September 2026 to April 2027, will help founders strengthen business models, improve customer acquisition, build brands and prepare for fundraising.
The programme is aimed at women founders who have developed a minimum viable product and begun engaging with customers or generating revenue. It combines online sessions with workshops, bootcamps and exhibitions. The initiative also provides mentorship, market access and investor-readiness support to help women-led businesses build sustainable enterprises.
Unstop launches AI bootcamp for students
Unstop has launched a Student AI Bootcamp, sponsored by Amazon Web Services (AWS), to provide students with opportunities to understand and explore artificial intelligence. The initiative aims to bridge the gap between classroom learning and practical exposure to emerging technologies.
Through its platform, Unstop will help students discover and participate in programmes focused on AI and its applications across sectors such as banking, healthcare, education and manufacturing.
NIELIT Hyderabad trains over 200 students in quantum technology
More than 200 students from nine educational institutions participated in a three-day workshop on quantum communications and applications in quantum technology organised by NIELIT Hyderabad under the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology.
Conducted from November 11 to 13 in partnership with QClairvoyance Quantum Labs, the workshop covered quantum mechanics, entanglement, quantum algorithms, quantum key distribution and post-quantum cryptography.
