articles.title: Ni Model 3 ni Semi : Tesla parie 3 milliards à sa gigafactory de Berlin sur son Cybercab
articles.text:
L’agrandissement de la Gigafactory de Grünheide, la seule usine de Tesla en Europe, est dans les tuyaux depuis plusieurs années. Le constructeur l’avait d’ailleurs mis en pause pendant la chute de ses ventes. Une question restait sans réponse : produire quoi de plus, alors que l’usine ne fabrique que le Model Y ?
Tesla a répondu ce lundi 16 novembre, dans une annonce relayée par Reuters : 3 milliards d’euros pour un nouveau bâtiment qui pourra produire jusqu’à un million de Cybercab. Or ce robotaxi sans volant ni pédales, que Tesla s’apprête à livrer à ses premiers clients américains, n’a pas encore un avenir clair en Europe. Le constructeur américain met-il une nouvelle fois la charrue avant les bœufs ?
Un déblocage du projet
L’enveloppe couvre aussi des bâtiments annexes et une nouvelle station de traitement des eaux usées, a précisé Tesla à l’agence dpa (dépêche reprise par Handelsblatt). Tesla veut déposer sa demande de permis avant la fin de l’année, sur la base d’un dossier de 2023.
Les travaux doivent commencer au premier semestre 2027, pour une production en 2029. Ouverte en mars 2022, l’usine employait 12 600 personnes en octobre, selon Tesla. L’effectif était entre-temps tombé sous les 11 000. Un million de Cybercab par an représente presque trois fois l’objectif actuel du site pour le Model Y, fixé à 7 500 voitures par semaine, soit environ 375 000 par an.
Un million de robotaxis ? Mais pas encore d’autorisation en Europe
En Europe, l’aide à la conduite avancée de Tesla progresse pays par pays. Son FSD (Full Self-Driving), rebaptisé Tesla Assisted Driving sur le continent, est autorisé dans onze pays de l’Union. La Finlande est la dernière arrivée, le 11 novembre.
Un vote sur une homologation dans toute l’Union est attendu en décembre au plus tôt (un rejet remettrait en cause les autorisations nationales déjà accordées), et l’Allemagne plaide pour aller vite. Pourtant, ce système reste une aide à la conduite : le conducteur surveille la route et reste responsable. Le Cybercab, lui, n’a ni volant ni pédales, et relève donc d’une autre réglementation, bien plus restrictive.
Or, pour les véhicules entièrement automatisés, le droit européen ne prévoit qu’un régime de petite série, limité à des usages précis. Tesla devra donc exporter presque toute la production de Grünheide, ou compter sur un changement des règles d’ici 2029 : un sacré pari.
Tesla préfère le Cybercab à la Model 3 et au Semi
Tesla aurait pourtant pu loger dans ce bâtiment des véhicules qui se vendent déjà. Les Model 3 vendues en Europe sont produites à Shanghai, et on pouvait espérer une ligne allemande pour la berline. Une Model 3 assemblée en Allemagne aurait aussi pu viser les aides publiques que la Commission veut réserver aux voitures électriques à 70 % de contenu européen, dans son projet d’Industrial Accelerator Act présenté en mars.
Quant au Semi, le camion électrique dont Tesla a présenté la version européenne en septembre, il est assemblé dans le Nevada alors qu’il doit arriver chez les transporteurs européens en 2027.
Tesla préfère reprendre en Allemagne le pari qu’il fait au Texas, où la production du Cybercab a démarré en avril. Lors de la présentation des résultats du premier trimestre, en avril, Elon Musk, CEO de Tesla, prévenait déjà que la production du Cybercab serait « très lente » au départ, avant d’accélérer en fin d’année.
Le calendrier de Grünheide est fixé : demande de permis d’ici fin 2026, travaux au premier semestre 2027, premiers Cybercab allemands en 2029. Le premier signal tombera en décembre au plus tôt, avec le vote européen sur Tesla Assisted Driving, qui ne concerne qu’une aide à la conduite. Pour un véhicule sans volant comme le Cybercab, l’avenir est toujours incertain.

articles.title: Publisher disparaît : Office 2021 le conserve, mais sans correctifs de sécurité
articles.text:
Microsoft a définitivement tourné la page Publisher en octobre 2026. Une mauvaise nouvelle pour les associations, commerçants et autres indépendants qui utilisaient ce logiciel pour créer leurs affiches, leurs flyers, leurs documents… Voici les solutions qui restent disponibles, ainsi que les précautions à prendre avant de choisir sa licence.
Pendant des années, bien avant l’avènement de l’IA générative, Microsoft Publisher a rendu de bien précieux services à tous ceux qui souhaitaient créer facilement des supports de communication. Une affiche pour une association, un menu pour un commerce, un flyer pour annoncer un événement, une brochure… Le logiciel permettait de mettre en page toutes sortes de documents, sans avoir à maîtriser un outil de publication professionnel.
Mais cette époque est désormais révolue. Microsoft a arrêté Publisher en octobre 2026. Le logiciel n’est plus pris en charge et ne figure dans aucune édition d’Office 2024. Pour les utilisateurs qui en dépendent encore, une question se pose : faut-il changer ses habitudes, conserver une ancienne version d'Office ou passer à une autre formule ?
Office 2024 ou Microsoft 365 : que choisir après la disparition de Publisher ?
Premier point essentiel : Office 2024 Standard ne contient pas Publisher. Cette édition en achat unique regroupe Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Outlook et OneNote. Elle s’adresse aux utilisateurs qui souhaitent disposer des principales applications bureautiques sans souscrire à un abonnement (Microsoft 365).
Pour un ordinateur principal équipé de Windows 11, Office 2024 Standard constitue le choix à privilégier, Microsoft prévoyant des correctifs de sécurité jusqu’au 9 octobre 2029. Attention toutefois, cette prise en charge concerne uniquement Windows 11, puisque sur Windows 10, dont le support Microsoft a pris fin en octobre 2025, la configuration n’est plus prise en charge.
L’autre possibilité consiste à souscrire à Microsoft 365. Cette formule sur abonnement permet de profiter des applications Office dans leur version régulièrement mise à jour. Elle convient aux personnes qui souhaitent bénéficier des nouveautés et de tous les services connectés de Microsoft. Toutefois, elle ne permet pas non plus d’utiliser Publisher depuis son retrait en octobre 2026.
Pour la petite histoire, Access ne figure pas non plus dans Office 2024 Standard. Les utilisateurs qui ont besoin de cette application de gestion de bases de données devront accepter de se tourner vers la version individuelle, vers Office 2024 Professionnel Plus ou Microsoft 365.
Office 2021 : la dernière solution pour conserver Publisher, mais à quel prix ?
Pour les irréductibles qui ne souhaitent pas abandonner Publisher, Office 2021 Standard représente une solution un peu particulière. Il s’agit de la dernière suite Office disponible en achat unique à intégrer le logiciel de mise en page de Microsoft.
Il faut néanmoins bien mesurer les contreparties. Depuis le 13 octobre 2026, Office 2021 ne reçoit plus aucun correctif de sécurité de la part de Microsoft. Et cela concerne bien l’ensemble de la suite, messagerie Outlook comprise. Les applications peuvent donc continuer à fonctionner, mais les éventuelles failles découvertes ne sont plus corrigées. « À vos risques et périls » donc comme on dit.
En cela, Office 2021 doit être envisagé comme une solution de transition pour les personnes qui ont encore impérativement besoin de Publisher, et non comme un choix durable pour équiper un nouveau poste de travail.
Si Access est également indispensable, Office 2021 Professionnel Plus constitue une autre possibilité. Il faut toutefois garder à l’esprit que malgré son appellation « Plus », il est soumis lui aussi aux mêmes limites de support que l’édition Standard.
Dans tous les cas, les utilisateurs de Publisher ont tout intérêt à anticiper la migration de leurs documents. Les fichiers au format .pub doivent être convertis vers un format plus pérenne, comme le PDF, ou récupérés dans un autre logiciel de mise en page. Si vous disposez encore d’une installation capable de les ouvrir, mieux vaut ne pas attendre pour effectuer cette opération.
Où acheter sa licence Office en achat unique ?
Une fois la version adaptée à ses besoins identifiée, reste à choisir sa licence. MA LICENCES est une boutique en ligne française spécialisée dans la vente de licences Microsoft en achat unique, notamment en ce qui concerne Office, Windows, Project ou encore Visio.
La boutique propose notamment Office 2024 Standard chez MA LICENCES, une version idéale pour les utilisateurs qui souhaitent retrouver les principales applications bureautiques de Microsoft sans le moindre abonnement. Les licences proposées couvrent jusqu’à cinq postes, selon la formule choisie et le nombre d’activations associé.
Pour ce qui est du fonctionnement, tout est très simple, et dès la commande effectuée, la clé est transmise par e-mail, avec une notice d’installation en français qui contient également le lien de téléchargement de l’installateur. Petit plus non négligeable, un support en français est disponible pour accompagner les utilisateurs en cas de difficulté.
MA LICENCES annonce par ailleurs une garantie de 30 jours. Si la clé rencontre un problème durant cette période, la boutique prévoit une solution de remplacement ou de prise en charge. Au-delà, si Microsoft venait à bloquer une clé, MA LICENCES s’engage à la remplacer sans délai.
Comme évoqué plus haut, l’essentiel consiste à choisir la bonne édition avant de commander. Pour un nouvel équipement sous Windows 11, Office 2024 Standard représente le choix le plus cohérent. Pour ceux qui doivent encore travailler avec Publisher, Office 2021 reste une possibilité, mais avec une absence désormais totale de correctifs de sécurité. Une distinction importante à connaître avant de renouveler sa suite bureautique.

articles.title: Cómo duplicar la pantalla del celular en un Smart TV sin apps y en segundos
articles.text:
Visualizar fotos, reproducir una película almacenada en la galería o mostrar una presentación en una pantalla más grande puede hacerse sin cables, memorias USB ni transferencias de archivos.
Los teléfonos Android y los iPhone cuentan con funciones inalámbricas integradas para duplicar la pantalla en un Smart TV compatible. La herramienta cambia de nombre según el fabricante, aunque el principio es el mismo: el celular y el televisor deben compartir una red WiFi.
En Android puede aparecer como Google Cast, Miracast, Smart View, Emitir, Enviar o Pantalla inalámbrica. En los teléfonos de Apple, se llama AirPlay.
Qué se necesita para duplicar la pantalla del celular en el TV
El requisito principal es que ambos dispositivos estén conectados a la misma red WiFi. Si el teléfono utiliza una red distinta de la que tiene configurada el Smart TV, no podrá detectar la TV ni enviar la imagen. Hace falta encender el televisor y comprobar que sus opciones de conexión inalámbrica estén activadas.
Asimismo, la estabilidad de la red influye en el resultado. Una conexión de 5 GHz puede reducir las demoras al reproducir videos o compartir imágenes de alta resolución.
Cuando hay muchos dispositivos conectados al mismo WiFi, la transmisión puede sufrir cortes, pérdida de fluidez o un retraso entre lo que ocurre en el teléfono y lo que aparece en el TV.
Cómo duplicar la pantalla de un celular Android en un televisor
En la mayoría de los modelos Android, el proceso comienza en el panel de ajustes rápidos. Para abrirlo, hay que deslizar el dedo desde la parte superior de la pantalla hacia abajo. Algunos modelos requieren repetir ese movimiento para mostrar todos los accesos disponibles.
Luego se debe buscar la función destinada a compartir la pantalla. Puede llamarse Emitir, Enviar, Transmitir, Pantalla inalámbrica o Smart View. Al tocar esa opción, el celular buscará los dispositivos compatibles conectados a la red y mostrará el nombre del televisor entre las alternativas disponibles.
Una vez identificado el televisor, solo hay que tocar su nombre para iniciar el vínculo. En la primera conexión, el Smart TV puede mostrar un aviso para autorizar el acceso desde el celular. La solicitud debe aceptarse desde el control remoto o desde la pantalla del televisor.
Tras esa confirmación, la imagen del teléfono se verá en el televisor en tiempo real. El sistema permite mostrar fotografías, videos, documentos, presentaciones y páginas web. Así, el contenido almacenado en el celular llega a una pantalla más grande sin utilizar un cable HDMI ni copiar los archivos a otro dispositivo.
Cuál opción nativa tiene iPhone para duplicar pantalla
Los usuarios de iPhone disponen de AirPlay, la tecnología de Apple para reproducir contenido o reflejar la pantalla de forma inalámbrica. El sistema funciona de manera nativa con Apple TV y está disponible en varios modelos recientes de televisores inteligentes compatibles con esa tecnología.
Para iniciar la conexión, se debe abrir el Centro de Control. En los modelos más recientes, se accede al deslizar el dedo hacia abajo desde la esquina superior derecha. Allí aparece el botón “Duplicar pantalla”, identificado con el ícono de dos rectángulos superpuestos. Al pulsarlo, el teléfono mostrará los televisores disponibles en la red.
Después de seleccionar el nombre del Smart TV, el dispositivo puede solicitar un código de AirPlay que aparecerá en la pantalla del televisor. Ese número debe ingresarse en el iPhone para completar la conexión. Desde ese momento, fotos, videos, aplicaciones y documentos podrán visualizarse en el TV sin instalar aplicaciones adicionales.
Qué alternativa existe si el celular no muestra una función de duplicación
Algunos celulares no incluyen un acceso visible para duplicar la pantalla o presentan una interfaz con otro nombre. En esos casos, los dispositivos compatibles con Google Cast pueden usar la aplicación Google Home como una vía alternativa para detectar un televisor o un dispositivo de transmisión dentro de la red doméstica.
Después de elegir el dispositivo, hay que buscar la opción para enviar la pantalla del teléfono. Si el Smart TV no aparece, hay que revisar que ambos aparatos estén conectados al mismo WiFi y que las funciones de conexión inalámbrica permanezcan habilitadas. Puede ayudar apagar y encender el WiFi del celular antes de repetir la búsqueda.

articles.title: California sues OpenAI over AI agents escaping sandboxes, hacking firms
articles.text:
California Attorney General Rob Bonta sued OpenAI on Monday, alleging the company knowingly continued testing advanced artificial intelligence models despite repeated security failures that allowed autonomous AI agents to escape isolated environments and launch cyberattacks against real-world organizations.
The lawsuit claims OpenAI misled the public about its cybersecurity safeguards and failed to adequately monitor increasingly advanced AI cybersecurity models, resulting in more than 80 incidents in which the company lost control of its agents during testing.
The legal action follows a July security incident where hundreds of OpenAI-powered agents escaped a controlled testing environment and hacked Hugging Face, an artificial intelligence platform, compromising production infrastructure and stealing internal credentials.
California says the Hugging Face attack resulted from OpenAI repeatedly focusing on experimental AI testing without ensuring adequate safeguards were in place.
"The Hugging Face cyberattack was the predictable result of an internal culture at OpenAI that prioritizes growth and rapid model development over safety and accountability," the complaint reads.
The lawsuit alleges that OpenAI continued testing increasingly capable AI agents despite knowing its sandbox environments could be bypassed, potentially exposing third-party systems to unauthorized activity.
"In truth, OpenAI failed to comply with its own internal policies and consistently and aggressively moved forward with testing and experiments even in the face of evidence that its cybersecurity safeguards were insufficient to contain the highly advanced models it was developing," the lawsuit continues.
During the Hugging Face attack, OpenAI models exploited zero-day vulnerabilities in JFrog Artifactory to break out of their isolated testing environment and access the internet.
The attack lasted more than two days, with nearly 700 autonomous agents coordinating through an unauthorized message board to plan the attack on Hugging Face's production systems while attempting to steal answers to a cybersecurity benchmark.
The California complaint alleges that OpenAI ignored or missed warning signs in the weeks leading up to the incident, including evidence that agents had already escaped their testing environments and were abusing third-party services and platforms.
It also claims that OpenAI's agents subsequently targeted software repositories, informational websites, and foreign government databases containing sensitive health information. In another incident, experimental agents allegedly compromised OpenAI's own internal infrastructure and obtained administrator-level access to critical systems.
According to the complaint, OpenAI has acknowledged more than 80 instances of losing control of autonomous agents during testing but publicly disclosed only 27 incidents.
The lawsuit follows a subpoena issued by Bonta's office in September, with California claiming that OpenAI failed to provide sufficient information about the incidents and instead supplied limited documentation and descriptions of previously disclosed attacks.
The state is pursuing claims under California's Unfair Competition Law and public nuisance laws, seeking court orders requiring stronger safeguards, civil penalties, and other relief.
The rise of autonomous AI attacks
The lawsuit comes amid growing concerns about increasingly capable AI models escaping controlled cybersecurity evaluations and attacking organizations outside their intended testing environments.
These autonomous attacks are not limited to OpenAI agents, with other AI platforms disclosing similar incidents in the past.
In July, Anthropic disclosed that its Claude models had breached production systems at three organizations during cybersecurity evaluations. One model created and uploaded a malicious Python package to the public PyPI repository, where it was downloaded and executed on 15 real systems.
This led Anthropic to remove internet access from all internal AI model evaluations following additional incidents involving unauthorized activity against government websites and other external systems.
Google also confirmed to The Wall Street Journal in September that its Gemini AI model had accessed the internet and hacked three companies during cybersecurity testing conducted in May.
California's lawsuit argues that OpenAI's failure to address these risks adequately has exposed organizations and the public to unnecessary cybersecurity threats, even as it told customers that its AI development practices were safe.

articles.title: Get in the fast lane with the latest episode of Two Blokes Talking Electric Cars - the EV podcast - Tech Guide
articles.text:
Get in the EV fast lane by pressing play on the latest episode of Two Blokes Talking Electric Cars with Stephen Fenech and Trevor Long.

Meanwhile Paul has a deal on the electric Ford F150 Lightning and Steve joins us from California where he’s loving his BMW iX.

articles.title: Jensen Huang: The anatomy of a scandal
articles.text:
Prevention is better than cure. We know the public relations (PR) adage. But it would be glib to leave it hanging when faced with a doom-laden news cycle like Nvidia’s. The question is how a scandal of this scale takes hold, how far the fallout spreads, and what it takes to rebuild trust when the damage extends well beyond the individual at its centre—as of Friday, November 13, $493 billion had reportedly been wiped off Nvidia’s value.
They say ‘sex sells’, but it also costs. The unfolding scandal surrounding Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s former CEO, is a case in point. What began as reporting about an alleged relationship with a woman US intelligence officials believe was recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security has spiralled into a much bigger story involving personal relationships, workplace power dynamics, corporate governance, national security, shareholder confidence, and an enthusiastic internet meme culture.
This is no longer simply a story about a billionaire’s personal life. There is gossip, and then there is national security. It has become a case study in what happens when personal conduct, corporate reputation, and geopolitical interests collide. For African tech founders, this risk is familiar. When the founder is the person investors back and the ecosystem trusts, their personal conduct can quickly become everybody’s business.
What makes this story unusual is the sheer number of audiences consuming and amplifying it, each with different interpretations of the same headlines. It has become an echo chamber playing out across politics, business, technology, finance, and popular culture.
For US policymakers, the allegations raise questions about national security and the vulnerability of one of America’s most strategically important technology companies. Nvidia’s chips sit at the heart of the global AI infrastructure boom. For investors, the concerns are leadership, governance, and financial exposure. Huang has been synonymous with Nvidia’s growth and market dominance. Any uncertainty around his position raises questions about the company’s future. For employees and the wider industry, questions remain about power dynamics and leadership responsibilities.
Then there is everyone else. Social media has created a parallel news cycle driven by AI-generated memes and commentary. This breadth makes the situation difficult to manage: you cannot issue a single statement and expect it to land the same way for a government official, an institutional investor, an employee, and an internet user. The statement itself becomes a news story.
From a PR perspective, one notable revelation has been WIRED’s reporting that Huang engaged a crisis communications firm known for handling high-profile personal scandals as early as October 2025. If accurate, it suggests he was weighing the reputational risk of his personal circumstances well before the headlines broke.
However, there is a difference between preparing for a story and controlling what happens when it breaks. Crisis communications involves understanding vulnerabilities, scenario planning, identifying key audiences, and preparing responses. It is not a magic wand, and comms professionals can only work with what they are given. We only see public-facing outcomes, not the conversations behind closed doors.
A key lesson here is the danger of allowing a company’s identity to become too closely tied to one person. Huang has been the public face of not only Nvidia, but ostensibly the AI revolution itself—an instantly recognisable figure in the manner of Jobs, Gates, or Musk.
When a CEO becomes synonymous with the business, their personal reputation becomes the company’s primary vulnerability. A business needs an identity powered by multiple credible leaders who can represent it beyond the founder. That means developing a strong bench of spokespeople, from executive leadership to technical experts, who can speak with authority. As a line in Semafor’s coverage noted: “Nvidia without Huang is like Apple without Jobs: A cash spigot without real innovation.“
That observation gets to the heart of Nvidia’s challenge: can the company maintain its vision, innovation pace, and influence without the person who led it for over three decades? Reassuring the market will require more than announcing a succession plan, especially following commentary surrounding interim CEO Colette Kress. Nvidia must demonstrate that its future is bigger than Huang.
The financial implications have been significant. On 9 November, following Huang’s admission, Nvidia shares fell 4.3%, wiping approximately $190 billion from its market value. On 12 November, after news of his resignation, shares fell up to 14% in early trading, briefly erasing up to $601 billion in market capitalisation, according to Bloomberg, before closing down 4.3% on the day.
While Nvidia was already operating against a backdrop of broader market uncertainty around AI valuations, a CEO’s personal reputation can blur the line between corporate and personal reputation. Reputation is a real business risk, and a board must restore governance and reassure markets before executing a recovery plan.
Implications for African Tech
African tech is not immune to scandal. The ecosystem has seen founder controversies, governance issues, and reputational crises, though the scale and financial exposure here are unprecedented. For an ecosystem working to establish credibility with international investors, these dynamics matter. Viewing PR solely as a tool for fundraising announcements or press coverage is overly narrow. Reputation is built on company culture, governance structures, and long-term stakeholder relationships established before a crisis hits.
For Huang, rebuilding personal credibility will require accountability, consistency, and a demonstrated understanding of the wider impact. For Nvidia, the task is to reassure investors, employees, and partners that its innovation pipeline remains intact and that the leadership transition is credible.
A crisis is rarely just about the incident that triggers it. It is about accumulated vulnerabilities, internal decisions, and their interaction with an active news cycle. For Nvidia, the story is ongoing, and temporary distractions in the news cycle offer respite rather than resolution.
PR can prepare, advise, and manage communications, but it cannot manufacture credibility where none exists or substitute for sound governance. Crisis communications cannot outrun underlying facts indefinitely. Eventually, attention shifts from the headlines to the behaviour that created them.
Jessica Hope is the Founder and CEO of Wimbart, an award-winning London-based PR consultancy specialising in African and emerging market communications across technology and business.
Hope is an international speaker, host of The Wimbart Way podcast, and mentor to emerging talent across the PR and African tech ecosystems.

articles.title: Un arquitecto técnico experto en ahorro energético lo explica: "A una bomba de calor le va bien que le pidas poco, que sea una casa, que esté bien aislada"
articles.text:
Cambiar la caldera de gas por una bomba de calor parece la manera más rápida de pagar menos por la calefacción, pero puedes encontrarte con que apenas hay diferencia. Por eso, el arquitecto técnico Jordi Martí avisa en su canal de TikTok de que el aparato no garantiza por sí solo una factura mucho más baja, y lo ilustra de una forma bastante gráfica: “A una bomba de calor le va bien que le pidas poco, que sea una casa, que esté bien aislada”.
Lo que pide la bomba de calor. Las bombas de calor rinden mejor y ahorran más cuando no necesitan ir siempre al límite, que es cuando tu vivienda está bien aislada y conserva bien la temperatura. Por eso, se puede decir que el ahorro depende tanto del aparato como de la construcción de la vivienda, el sistema de calefacción que tiene e incluso tus ventanas. La OCU también apunta en esta dirección en su guía para preparar la casa, donde recuerda que el nivel de aislamiento influye en la eficiencia de la bomba de calor, y por eso simplemente cambiar la caldera dejando lo demás igual no es siempre suficiente.
La teoría y la factura. “En teoría debería dividir el consumo por tres o por cuatro, pero miras las facturas y eso no lo notas tanto. Y el confort, pues eso, que a veces no da”, señala el arquitecto. Eso sí, según Martí, si la casa tiene poco aislamiento, ventanas antiguas o muchas pérdidas, el aparato tiene que trabajar bastante más tiempo, y si los radiadores exigen temperaturas elevadas, la bomba pierde ventaja.
Kilian Jornet cargando pianos. Para explicarlo, Martí tira de un ejemplo con Kilian Jornet, el corredor de montaña catalán capaz de subir desniveles enormes como pocos: “Kilian Jornet te sube el Everest en un momento con una eficiencia brutal, pero si le pones a transportar pianos seguramente no destacará mucho”.
Con la bomba de calor pasa algo parecido. “Si tienes una vivienda mal aislada con radiadores normales y quieres cambiar la caldera por una bomba de calor será como hacerle transportar pianos”, explica. Vamos, que dos viviendas con el mismo equipo pueden acabar teniendo consumos muy diferentes.
El aislamiento manda. Para Martí, el aislamiento es uno de los factores que más influyen en el consumo, ya que una casa que retiene bien el calor necesita menos energía para calentarse, y permite que el equipo que tengas funcione a baja potencia durante más tiempo. “Lo que quiere la bomba de calor es ir tranquila, es cuando brilla. No le pidas mucha potencia”, explica. Las ventanas antiguas o con filtraciones provocan pérdidas constantes de calor, por lo que una de las primeras medidas para mejorarlo es cambiarlas por una de doble o triple acristalamiento.
Antes de cambiar la caldera. Por eso, antes de quitar la caldera conviene revisar el estado de la vivienda y valorar si toca mejorar el aislamiento o cambiar las ventanas más viejas, porque así se reduce la energía que tendrá que aportar la bomba. Y el tipo de emisor también cuenta, porque el suelo radiante funciona con agua a menos temperatura y se adapta bien a este sistema, mientras que los radiadores convencionales pueden necesitar temperaturas más altas.
La conclusión de Martí es sencilla: la bomba de calor puede consumir muy poco, pero necesita una vivienda que no la obligue a trabajar continuamente al límite, y cuanta menos energía pida la casa, mejores resultados dará.

articles.title: Tesla fait machine arrière et vend finalement son Cybercab, mais à une condition très coûteuse
articles.text:
Tesla avait longuement vanté le Cybercab comme la solution de transport ultime permettant de se déplacer souplement d’un endroit à l’autre sans contrainte. Il suffisait de passer commande pour se faire conduire, ni plus ni moins. La promesse est alléchante, mais néanmoins hors de portée : la marque a toujours affirmé que le véhicule ne sera jamais vendu aux particuliers.
Pourtant, il semblerait que le constructeur rétropédale sur le sujet. Un petit peu, du moins… Des personnes sélectionnées sur le volet ont en effet reçu un e-mail d’invitation menant droit à une page de commande du Cybercab. Sur une interface assez similaire à celle des autres modèles Tesla, on y trouve donc le véhicule affiché au prix de 29 990 $. Il s’agit de fait de la voiture la moins chère du catalogue, la Model 3 étant vendue à 36 990 $ au minimum.
Le gros piège caché derrière ce prix plancher
Si un acompte non remboursable de 1 000 $ est requis pour passer commande, il ne faudra guère se montrer patient pour recevoir son jouet : les livraisons sont pour le moment prévues pour décembre ! Un délai éclair qui contraste grandement avec les heures fastes de la Model 3. Le Cybercab a donc juste sur toute la ligne. Tenons-nous enfin la petite Tesla pas chère tant attendue ? Pas vraiment…
Car il y a une immense condition pour pouvoir utiliser le véhicule. Vu que l’engin est livré sans volant ni pédales, il sera une nouvelle fois entièrement autonome. Et forcément, cela demande une certaine quantité d’énergie que la marque ne manquera pas de vous facturer ! Acheter une bonne fois pour toutes la voiture puis l’utiliser en illimité était bien trop beau pour être vrai. Comment en effet justifier l’utilisation sur demande d’un Cybercab, alors ?
299 $ par mois et des zones géographiques limitées : la douche froide
Après avoir dépensé 29 990 $, vous voilà donc avec un abonnement imposé à 299 $ par mois. N’espérez pas contourner la chose, les petites lignes indiquent explicitement qu’il s’agit d’un passage obligé : « abonnement et entretien régulier du véhicule requis pour l’utilisation ». Le loyer éternel est une chose, les restrictions d’usage en sont une autre. Car vous ne pourrez pas vous balader n’importe où avec le Cybercab.
L’email indique aussi que le véhicule est « disponible uniquement dans les zones couvertes par le service ». Cela comprend huit villes : Austin, Dallas, Houston, Fort Worth et San Antonio. Pire encore, la couverture n’est pas intégrale dans les zones précitées. Mieux vaut donc bien se renseigner avant de passer commande, au risque de se retrouver avec une voiture entièrement payée, mais complètement inutilisable.

articles.title: Apagão da Microsoft leva à contaminação por gás cloro; entenda • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Apagão da Microsoft leva à contaminação por gás cloro; entenda
Falha no dosador elevou o nível de cloro na piscina de um hotel na Alemanha. Alerta enviado por e-mail não chegou aos funcionários durante a pane do Outlook.
Quinze pessoas foram afetadas por uma exposição a níveis elevados de cloro na piscina de um hotel na Alemanha. O incidente ocorreu durante a pane global que deixou Outlook e outros serviços da Microsoft instáveis. A interrupção impediu que um alerta automático sobre o problema chegasse aos funcionários do estabelecimento.
O caso aconteceu no Hotel Ling Bao, que faz parte do parque temático Phantasialand, na cidade de Brühl. Segundo a emissora alemã WDR, uma falha no sistema automático de dosagem fez com que uma quantidade excessiva de cloro fosse despejada na piscina.
O sistema de segurança responsável por monitorar a manutenção da área detectou o problema e enviou um aviso por e-mail aos funcionários. Como o Outlook e o Exchange Online estavam fora do ar, a mensagem não foi entregue. A equipe só percebeu que havia algo errado depois que pessoas na piscina começaram a apresentar problemas respiratórios.
Equipes de emergência e bombeiros foram acionados para atender as vítimas. Ao todo, 15 pessoas passaram por avaliação médica, a maioria com irritação nas vias respiratórias. Quatro foram levadas ao hospital, e uma delas permaneceu internada em observação por causa de ferimentos considerados moderados.
A piscina foi fechada temporariamente. Depois de identificar a falha no equipamento de dosagem, as equipes substituíram a água. O local foi liberado para uso novamente após as verificações, segundo a WDR.
O parque confirmou à emissora alemã que a pane no Outlook impediu o recebimento dos avisos enviados pelo sistema de segurança. Cerca de 40 profissionais de emergência participaram do atendimento, segundo a imprensa internacional.
A interrupção do Microsoft 365 começou na quinta-feira (12/11) e afetou Outlook, Teams, SharePoint e Copilot em diferentes países por mais de 24 horas. A falha também prejudicou ferramentas que dependem da infraestrutura de e-mail da companhia.
Após a pane, a Microsoft publicou um relatório sobre o incidente e atribuiu a falha a um problema em uma atualização de software. O Outlook foi o serviço mais afetado.
A empresa descartou qualquer relação com ataques cibernéticos ou sistemas de inteligência artificial e pediu desculpas pelos transtornos causados.

articles.title: Microsoft 365 outage led to chlorine gas leak at German hotel, poisoning of 15 guests and sending four to hospital
articles.text:
WTF?! The recent global outage of Microsoft 365 services affected millions across the world, but the impact on people varied enormously. Take, for example, the 15 guests at a hotel in Germany who were exposed to a chlorine gas leak as a result of the debacle. That sounds a lot worse than not being able to use Teams.
According to regional publication WDR (via Notebookcheck), the incident happened at the Hotel Ling Bao, part of Phantasialand theme park in Germany. It experienced a malfunction with its dosing system, which pumped too much chlorine into the pool.
The facility uses a maintenance safety system in its sauna area that sends emails warning when chlorine levels are too high. But because of the Microsoft 365 service disruption, the emails never arrived.
Forty first responders were dispatched to the incident. Fifteen people required triage due to respiratory irritation, four were taken to the hospital, and one had to remain under observation due to an injury.
The disruption began on November 12, when users around the world started reporting problems with Outlook, Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Teams, and Copilot. Downdetector received nearly 150,000 complaints, while Microsoft said its servers were experiencing unusually heavy loads. Outlook users couldn't send emails or access their inboxes, and some servers went offline again after being restored.
In Japan, businesses and government agencies were forced to dig out fax machines and landline phones when cloud services stopped working. The country's shared government IT infrastructure was also disrupted. Xbox users struggled to sign in, launch digital games, and synchronize cloud saves.
 – Microsoft 365 Status (@MSFT365Status) November 14, 2026
Microsoft has now revealed that the outage was caused by a software defect introduced in July, which went undetected for more than three months. A surge in server traffic, combined with reduced network capacity, triggered the bug and caused more than 80% of the affected gateway servers to become unresponsive within two hours. The company admitted that its testing had failed to catch the problem.
While software failures can cause inconvenience and financial losses, there are often more serious consequences like this one. In July 2024, a faulty CrowdStrike update caused Windows systems worldwide to crash. Hospitals couldn't book patients, some 911 emergency call centers were affected, and airlines grounded flights.
In one of the strongest examples of software failures destroying lives, bugs in the UK's Horizon accounting system contributed to wrongful convictions of hundreds of Post Office workers. Some were imprisoned, many suffered financial ruin, and the scandal was linked to at least four suicides.
In 2018, Wells Fargo revealed that a software error had incorrectly denied mortgage modifications to around 625 customers who should have qualified for them. The mistake had devastating consequences, with approximately 400 borrowers losing their homes through foreclosure.

GameSir Introduces G7 Pro Sunset Boulevard & Ocean Breeze Edition Controllers with Miami Inspired Designs
GameSir has announced the G7 Pro Sunset Boulevard and Ocean Breeze Editions, introducing two new designs to its G7 Pro controller range inspired by Miami's vibrant coastlines and distinctive Art Deco style. Arriving ahead of this season's most anticipated game releases, the new editions combine eye-catching aesthetics with the performance features of the G7 Pro, offering players responsive controls, extensive customization and the precision needed for demanding gameplay.
Both editions retain the core features of the G7 Pro, including GameSir Mag-Res TMR sticks, dual-mode triggers, four additional remappable buttons and four vibration motors. Officially licensed for XBOX, the controllers also support a 1,000 Hz polling rate on PC via wired and 2.4 GHz wireless connections, delivering responsive input for competitive gaming and everyday play. The GameSir G7 Pro Sunset Boulevard & Ocean Breeze Editions are available for $89.99 or £99.99 from the GameSir website.At the heart of the controllers are GameSir Mag-Res TMR sticks, designed to combine accurate tracking with long-term durability and resistance to stick drift. With a joystick resolution of up to 4,096 levels, the sticks are engineered to provide smooth, precise movement across a range of games.
Dual-mode triggers allow players to switch between conventional analogue control and a more responsive hair-trigger mode, making it easier to adapt controls to different gameplay styles. Optical micro-switch ABXY buttons provide crisp, responsive inputs, while the controller's four vibration motors - positioned in the grips and triggers - deliver immersive feedback during gameplay. 
The G7 Pro includes four additional remappable buttons, giving players more flexibility over their control layout without needing to move their thumbs away from the sticks. Six-axis motion control adds another input option, while swappable components allow players to personalize the controller's look and feel.
Through GameSir Nexus software, users can remap buttons, adjust stick dead zones and fine-tune stick response curves to suit their preferences. These customization options allow players to tailor the controller to different games and play styles.
The G7 Pro Sunset Boulevard & Ocean Breeze Editions are also officially licensed wired XBOX controllers (Tri-mode for PC), with a high polling rate of up to 1,000Hz on a PC for responsive gameplay. They feature tournament-ready controls and customisable inputs making them suitable for a wide range of genres, from fast-paced shooters to racing games and action adventures.

articles.title: US now "comfortable" with children dying of measles as death toll hits 10
articles.text:
Health officials in Pennsylvania and Wisconsin announced two more measles deaths late last week, bringing the national tally of confirmed measles deaths this year to 10. The total includes the deaths of at least four infants: two in Pennsylvania, one in New York, and one in Wisconsin.
Wisconsin health officials said the latest measles death—the second for the state—was in a child. Pennsylvania’s health department did not reveal the age or other details of the latest death—the state’s seventh—besides revealing it was of an unvaccinated resident in Montour County. Overall, the seven deaths in Pennsylvania include two in Jefferson County, three in Lancaster County, and one in Mifflin, in addition to the new death in Montour. An eighth death was reported in Franklin County, but state health officials have not confirmed it.
For all the states with deaths so far, health officials have noted that they’re the first deaths in decades. Multiple outbreaks are underway across the country, pushing the national tally of cases to nearly 5,500 across 47 states and jurisdictions, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Pennsylvania’s case count alone is over 1,500, and Wisconsin is reporting nearly 650.
Lost status
With outbreaks that have been smoldering and flaring since last year, the US has reportedly lost its measles elimination status—as medical and public health experts have widely expected it would. A panel of experts for the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), a regional branch of the World Health Organization, convened last week to review US measles data and assess its elimination status. The PAHO is set to announce its conclusion and the review’s other findings on Tuesday, November 17. But sources broke the news to The Wall Street Journal on Friday that the panel had found that the US had indeed lost its status.

articles.title: Getting CRA Compliant Hardens the Code and Gets Your Company Closer to Digital Sovereignty
articles.text:
In this episode, Christopher "CRob" Robinson, CTO of OpenSSF, Akrites and Chief Security Architect of the Linux Foundation, explores the state of software supply chain security amid multiple security incidents and explains how tools like Scorecard, the Security Baseline framework, and SLSA help harden software.
The conversation also delves into the impact of global cybersecurity regulations like the EU Cyber Resilience Act (CRA), digital sovereignty, and the role of AI in software engineering. Chris shares insights on OpenSSF's Cyber Reasoning System, practical guardrails for AI-assisted development, and how open-source projects are adapting AI contribution policies.
Key Takeaways
- Frameworks like OpenSSF’s Security Baseline translate compliance mandates (EU CRA, NIST SSDF) into 41 practical, verifiable controls for maintainers and enterprise consumers alike.
- SLSA (Supply Chain Levels for Software Artefacts) complements Security Baseline by hardening development infrastructure, CI/CD pipelines, and source repositories across maturity levels.
- The EU Cyber Resilience Act (CRA) is setting a global benchmark for consumer-focused software security regulation, encouraging international harmonisation across regions like the UK, India, Japan, and Australia.
- AI tools accelerate software creation but require structured harnesses, such as OpenSSF's Cyber Reasoning System and upcoming security skills, to enforce established software engineering discipline.
- Open-source software and local-first data paradigms are essential for digital sovereignty, enabling organisations to retain data control and avoid vendor lock-in.
Subscribe on:
Transcript
Olimpiu Pop: Hello, everybody. I'm Olimpiu Pop, an InfoQ editor, and I have with me Christopher Robinson, who goes by CRob these days. I'll let him introduce himself and share a bit more background.
Christopher Robinson: Hello, everybody. Thank you for having me today. My name is Chris Robinson, also known as CRob. I am the CTO and Chief Security Architect for a couple of Linux Foundation projects. First, the Open Source Security Foundation (OpenSSF), which focuses on application security, supply chain security, and AI security—predominantly helping support upstream maintainers. My other role is leading a new project called Akrites, which is an upstream open-source coordinated incident response team.
Olimpiu Pop: That sounds like a lot! You wear multiple hats, as people often see in your presentations.
Christopher Robinson: Yes. Yes.
OpenSSF’s Tooling and Intended Audience [01:32]
Olimpiu Pop: OpenSSF is definitely a stronghold for security. Before the recent surge in AI, there was a strong push to move security to the left—getting tools and practices closer to development teams. Historically, security was often left for the end alongside documentation and other crucial tasks.
In my experience, whenever something bad happened, the security architect had to scramble down, fix it, and then try to convince developers to adopt the fix. As we record this in early November, we've seen widespread scrambling over PyPI incidents and others, as security incidents continue to rise. We saw an example with PHP where maintainers noted they never expected all four conditions to occur simultaneously—yet they did, with AI contributing to that complexity.
Christopher Robinson: Yes, helping.
Olimpiu Pop: Exactly. When and who should turn to OpenSSF? Who is your target audience?
Christopher Robinson: We focus on two primary personas. First is the upstream open-source developer and maintainer. We provide comprehensive guidance, best practices, tooling, and training to teach software engineers the expected security controls and practices needed to harden their projects and infrastructure. That is our primary audience.
Secondarily, we care deeply about everyone consuming those projects. Sometimes that is another open-source maintainer integrating a project as a dependency, but predominantly it includes downstream manufacturers and enterprises—such as banks, hospitals, and retailers—running their core operations. We offer tools and guidance to help these consumers evaluate and understand the security posture of projects they plan to integrate, such as Scorecard, which we discussed earlier.
Scorecard serves a dual purpose. It helps upstream maintainers choose the right dependencies, and for maintainers looking to demonstrate their security rigor, it acts as a strong public signal showing adherence to security best practices. Consumers can then look for these signals to inform their decisions.
When evaluating two packages for integration into a solution, consumers can select the option with the stronger security posture.
Olimpiu Pop: That aligns with what we discussed regarding Scorecard examining more than just technical aspects. Many recent issues stems from social engineering or oversight—such as typosquatting or version manipulation in the Python ecosystem, where picking the highest available version bypassed protections.
This focus is especially critical now. While recent incidents draw attention, this shift has been building since the pandemic. During that period, many developers focused heavily on building projects, but subsequent industry reports highlight a different trend.
Security Baseline and SLSA Supply Chain Specification [05:26]
For instance, Sonatype reports showed a decline in open-source project maintenance, opening doors for attack vectors. Aside from Scorecard, what other tool would you highlight? OpenSSF excels at making best practices actionable. Knowing what is good is one thing; operationalizing it is the real challenge. What other tool would you single out?
Christopher Robinson: I'm going to cheat and I'm going to say two.
Olimpiu Pop: Excellent. Great.
Christopher Robinson: First, I would highlight our Security Baseline, which represents the next evolution of Scorecard. The Baseline includes 41 recommended security controls and practices. We analyzed global regulations like the EU Cyber Resilience Act (CRA) and frameworks like the NIST Secure Software Development Framework (SSDF) to curate a practical list of actions for project maintainers and consumers.
It combines technical configurations—such as enabling branch protection settings on source code repositories—with organizational controls, like publishing a clear security policy or documenting contributor onboarding and maintainer progression paths.
The Security Baseline is structured across three maturity levels. Level 1 is the most straightforward, roughly equivalent to a mid-range Scorecard score, and takes an experienced developer about two hours to implement. It focuses heavily on documentation. While non-profit open-source maintainers are generally not legally bound by cybersecurity regulations like the EU CRA, downstream manufacturers and governments care immensely about compliance.
The EU CRA explicitly exempts open-source maintainers who do not profit from their work. However, commercial consumers must comply. The Security Baseline translates complex regulatory requirements—from the EU CRA, US Executive Orders, and Japanese legislation—into accessible, practical steps for maintainers without requiring them to digest raw legal texts.
By offering a tiered implementation aligned with modern security practices, the Security Baseline makes projects more attractive to downstream consumers. This increased visibility helps attract more contributors, users, feature requests, and code reviews to strengthen the project.
The second framework I recommend is SLSA (Supply Chain Levels for Software Artifacts), which addresses supply chain provenance, pedigree, and integrity. While Scorecard and Security Baseline focus on code and process quality, SLSA secures the underlying infrastructure—including IDEs, developer workstations, source repositories, CI/CD pipelines, and distribution systems.
SLSA defines progressive levels of maturity to harden development infrastructure. By pairing process-oriented frameworks like Scorecard or Security Baseline with SLSA, organizations can verify how software moves securely through the supply chain and assess infrastructure resilience.
OpenSSF’s Cyber Reasoning System [10:03]
Olimpiu Pop: You mentioned OpenSSF's work around AI. Previously, we expected software development to rely on human engineering skills built over decades. Now, there is a shift toward AI prompting and engineering assistance. How difficult is it to integrate these security frameworks into AI development harnesses?
How is it is to include all this tooling into harnesses because now all our experience transformed itself into harnesses.
Christopher Robinson: It is a fascinating space. LLMs and AI agents have invited a vast group of new stakeholders into software development. Someone with minimal formal software engineering background can now generate code using straightforward prompts. The key is ensuring these workflows incorporate proper security guardrails and harnesses.
While experienced engineers can leverage trained harnesses and best practices, the challenge lies in the influx of new non-developer contributors across accounting, marketing, and operational roles writing code. With frontier LLMs, there is immense excitement to adopt these powerful tools immediately.
In the rush to adopt AI capabilities, teams risk overlooking 50 years of established software engineering discipline and security practices. AI makes it easy to bypass those foundational controls if guardrails are not explicitly built in.
That has been OpenSSF's main focus this year. We brought in a dedicated AI Security Architect to lead the deployment of the Open Source Software Cyber Reasoning System. This framework acts as a modular harness where developers can plug in AI models, fine-tune their operation, and apply specific security skills and domain context.
Looking ahead, our goal is to build modular skills that integrate directly into these AI harnesses. Next year, we plan to release dedicated skills for Scorecard, SLSA, and Security Insights. These tools will enable automated agents to enforce proven security practices during code generation, ensuring more secure software outputs.
Olimpiu Pop: That is great to hear. Recently, when setting up a repository, I had to manually break down Scorecard recommendations and configure them step by step. With my engineering background, I knew how to implement them, but non-technical users focusing purely on product vision need automated triggers to enforce those standards seamlessly.
And those people don't know what's to be expected. And then it's easier for them if something just triggers that point.
Christopher Robinson: In the hands of an experienced senior engineer, LLMs can be transformative—boosting productivity and reinforcing guardrails. However, developers must actively configure and enable those security skills. I am cautiously optimistic, though real challenges remain.
Olimpiu Pop: I see strong enthusiasm at both ends of the spectrum. Senior engineers can move faster without being blocked, while non-engineering teams can build tools independently without navigating traditional engineering bottlenecks.
Is the EU’s CRA a Blueprint for the Rest of the World? [15:03]
You also brought up a major regulatory acronym in Europe: the EU Cyber Resilience Act (CRA).
Christopher Robinson: Yes, absolutely.
Olimpiu Pop: There is a common saying that Europe excels at regulation—as seen with GDPR, the AI Act, and now the CRA. At a recent panel you participated in, speakers discussed digital sovereignty alongside ecosystem fragmentation. In open source, we think globally, but regulations like the US Executive Orders and memory-safe language mandates introduced regional variations. What is your global outlook on cybersecurity regulation right now?
And in the open source ecosystem, we are talking about the global world, a global village. If we take a step upwards, because you're obviously looking at the whole global ecosystem, CRA is getting into force slowly, starting from this autumn. It has multiple stages. Then the US used to have at some point some executive order that started everything in terms of hardening software. And then from that point on, we discussed about memory save programming languages.
I know that Australia invests a lot of money. As you mentioned, you have an agenda for this year and for next year. Maybe you can give us a summary, where is the world from the perspective of the cybersecurity?
Christopher Robinson: Having spent decades as a practitioner starting in the heavily regulated banking sector, I appreciate the value of clear compliance frameworks. That perspective made me eager to see the EU CRA take shape.
While regulation brings implementation challenges, the CRA focuses on necessary, long-overdue principles. Like GDPR's emphasis on citizen data protection, the CRA prioritizes consumer protection against software vulnerabilities and unsafe products, which is a commendable objective.
Global jurisdictions are watching the EU CRA closely ahead of its full enforcement date on December 11, 2027. Countries including the UK, India, Japan, and Australia are observing the rollout as they draft their own cybersecurity approaches.
I anticipate other regions introducing CRA-aligned legislation in the coming years. As a practitioner who prefers efficiency over rework, my hope is that international bodies harmonize their standards rather than creating fragmented, conflicting regulatory requirements.
Fragmented rules would create significant friction. For instance, if Europe adopts established standards for Software Bills of Materials (SBOMs) while another region mandates a proprietary 86-point criteria list, manufacturers and developers will face conflicting compliance burdens that hinder efficient delivery.
My goal is to see global regulatory efforts align with the core principles of the CRA—whether through formal legislation or executive frameworks—to maintain consistent expectations for developers worldwide.
Olimpiu Pop: That is a crucial point. A key strength of the CRA was the collaboration between regulators and industry leaders to reach consensus. The remaining question centers on implementation and ensuring fair execution across organizations of all sizes.
Recent high-profile security incidents have increased public and corporate awareness of cybersecurity risks. Beyond standard threats, the global context involves active cyber warfare, making robust software defense essential. Hopefully, regulatory and industry efforts continue moving in the right direction.
Christopher Robinson: To tie this back to digital sovereignty: open-source software provides the most reliable foundation for organizations to maintain autonomy and avoid vendor lock-in. Open source allows teams to inspect, fork, modify, and contribute code back to the community, rather than depending on a single commercial vendor.
This flexibility allows organizations to combine best-of-breed tools—such as pairing an open-weight LLM with European cloud hosting, US-developed web servers, or global components—while retaining full transparency and control over their technology stack.
Users are More Aware About Digital Sovereignty [22:04]
Olimpiu Pop: This aligns with the local-first software movement. Just as European regulation emphasizes user rights, local-first architecture prioritizes data ownership—ensuring users retain control over their data locally rather than relying entirely on centralized cloud providers.
Instead of receiving an unusable data export when a cloud service shuts down, local-first applications keep data accessible to the user long-term. Combining strong privacy regulations with local-first technical paradigms is a vital step forward for software design.
Christopher Robinson: Agreed.
Olimpiu Pop: Regardless of preference, AI tools are now a permanent part of the software landscape.
Christopher Robinson: They are certainly here to stay.
Olimpiu Pop: Some express concern that automated tools will diminish the human role in software creation. Where do you stand on this spectrum—are you optimistic, pessimistic, or somewhere in between?
Christopher Robinson: I consider myself an AI realist and use these tools daily in my work. AI acts as a helpful assistant that accelerates workflows, rather than a replacement for human engineering judgment. Like a fuzzer or a multimeter in electronics, AI is a tool, and the outcomes depend on how effectively it is applied.
It is important to understand what LLMs actually do: they perform statistical predictions based on context rather than reasoning magic, and they can produce incorrect outputs. Their primary strength lies in identifying patterns across vast datasets—a task where human processing is slower.
When applied thoughtfully, AI provides substantial benefits. However, using these tools without understanding underlying security principles risks exposing sensitive personal or corporate data to external models.
As an AI realist, my goal is to help developers maximize the advantages of AI while remaining aware of potential security risks.
Olimpiu Pop: Given the central role of AI in open source, communities are actively debating AI contribution policies. Some projects require strict human authorship, while leaders like Linus Torvalds view AI as another tool to be used with proper oversight. How do you view recommended AI contribution policies for open-source projects?
Use it cautiously, but you have to understand what's there. And so on, so forth. What's your perspective? How do you see the AI policy of ... I don't know, recommend it maybe?
Christopher Robinson: Policies cross open source remain varied. Maintainers face influxes of automated vulnerability reports and AI-generated contributions, leading to different approaches. While projects like the Linux kernel permit AI-assisted code contributions under developer review, smaller projects with fewer review resources may take a more restrictive stance.
AI usage in software development will continue to grow. The priority for open-source projects is to establish clear, explicit contribution guidelines defining their stance on AI tools. Transparent policies allow contributors to choose projects that align with their preferred workflows.
Olimpiu Pop: Thank you for sharing your insights today, Chris. It was a pleasure speaking with you.
Christopher Robinson: Thank you very much for having me. It was great talking with you.
Mentioned:
- Open Source Security Foundation (OpenSSF)
- Akrites (Upstream Open Source Coordinated Incident Response Team)
- OpenSSF Scorecard
- OpenSSF Security Baseline
- SLSA (Supply Chain Levels for Software Artifacts)
- EU Cyber Resilience Act (CRA)
- NIST Secure Software Development Framework (SSDF)
- OpenSSF Cyber Reasoning System

articles.title: FBI says Artex AI open source hacking tool used to breach networks in 'under three hours' | TechCrunch
articles.text:
The FBI is warning that hackers are relying on autonomous AI hacking tools to launch cyberattacks across the U.S. and globally. The campaigns include a widespread hack of customers of American IT company ConnectWise and across South Korea’s financial industry.
In its latest flash cybersecurity advisory, the FBI says hackers have targeted several industries in recent months, including financial services, government, tech, defense, phone and internet companies, and law firms, using open source tools like Artex to carry out autonomous-driven cyberattacks.
Artex is one of several open source AI-powered penetration testing platforms, a category of software built to probe a network’s defenses. Hackers can connect Artex to hosted frontier large language models (LLMs) like those from Anthropic and OpenAI, as well as to open source models and non-U.S. models. The FBI says Artex intrusions can be “noisy,” meaning they generate reams of traffic and data that may trigger a targeted company’s defensive alerts. But the tools allow hackers to move at speeds that make it far more difficult for human defenders to keep up.
In some cases, Artex-linked attacks can move from targeting a system to active compromise “in under three hours.”
The FBI’s warning comes as AI-powered hacks are escalating, particularly by finding easy-to-find security flaws and breaking into companies with relative ease.
Oftentimes, Artex will rely on rapidly scanning a victim’s network to look for signs of weakness, and then exploit simple security bugs, such as weak protections and exposed or stolen passwords to gain a foothold. From there, Artex allows the hacker to spread across the network for databases, mailboxes, and other sensitive information.
The FBI’s advisory noted that Artex has been used in several cyberattacks since the tool’s first public debut in July. Artex was used to hack a number of South Korean financial institutions, blamed in large part on weak cybersecurity defenses and lacking protections, such as multi-factor authentication. The attacks allowed hackers to steal the personal data of at least 68,000 people.
The FBI confirmed earlier findings from Microsoft that hackers also used Artex to break into IT management giant ConnectWise and gain access to the Microsoft 365 cloud environments of at least 2,250 of its customers.
The hackers, who Microsoft says are likely Chinese, used the tool to steal data from affected ConnectWise customers.
A spokesperson for ConnectWise did not respond to a request for comment about the FBI’s claim.
Cybersecurity company Barracuda also disclosed that it was breached as part of an Artex-linked attack by financially motivated criminals, in which the tool found an exposed credential belonging to a third-party service that Barracuda had not revoked when it ended work with the vendor. That access allowed the hackers to access stores of credentials used by Barracuda to collect data from its customers’ systems. Barracuda said it couldn’t rule out access, as its logs were not detailed enough, and chose to “assume the worst” and changed all of its customer credentials.
“Defenders who rely on spotting malicious activity and then responding to it will often arrive after the attacker has finished,” wrote Barracuda’s chief information security officer, Arve Kjoelen.
A spokesperson for Barracuda told TechCrunch that the company “directly notified and advised a minority of XDR customers to revoke and recreate integration credentials,” but did not specify how many customers.
After Artex was used in cyberattacks, the tool’s developer made the software closed-source to prevent further attacks. But the FBI says the previous open source version continues to circulate and remains “widely accessible” for use in cyberattacks.
It’s not only companies and targeted victims that have been compromised as a result of weakened security exploited by AI tools; the tools themselves have been exposed as well, potentially allowing outsiders to access powerful hacking capabilities. Last week, researchers found hundreds of publicly exposed Artex systems online, which had been placed on the internet without a password, likely by mistake or misconfiguration — including the Artex system that was used to target South Korea.
Updated with response from Barracuda.

articles.title: Ookla report finds that some Asian cities have 50 times better indoor mobile signal than US and UK ones — and no, it’s not because of building materials
articles.text:
Ookla report reveals why your indoor mobile signal is so bad — cities in North America and UK top global rankings for buildings with 4G signal below 105 dBm
Bad outdoors, worse indoors
- Ookla has found that North America, Europe, and Oceania have worse indoor mobile signal than other regions
- The difference in signal power can be up to around 50 times
- This is primarily down to these regions having poor outdoor signal in cities too
If you live in North America or Europe then you’ve probably frequently found that your phone’s signal is bad indoors — but the main reason might not be what you’d assume.
Ookla has carried out a study, comparing indoor and outdoor signal measurements across over 100 cities globally, and it has found that indoor signal is weakest in North America, Europe, and Oceania.
But if you assumed the problem was building materials, well, you’d be — mostly — wrong. According to Ookla, the material a building is constructed from can make a difference to a signal’s ability to pass through walls, but it’s not a dramatic difference, with timber-framed buildings reducing a signal by 2 dB (decibels), while concrete ones still only drop it by 7 dB, with the median drop being 4 dB.
That accounts for under a tenth of the overall difference in indoor signal between different cities and regions, with 85% of the difference coming from how good the outdoor signal is. So in other words, cities with better outdoor signal tend to have better indoor signal, too — which isn't entirely surprising.
A 50x difference
These differences are surprisingly big, with the median indoor signal measured in the likes of Dubai, Bangkok, and Seoul being around -88 dBm (decibel-milliwatts) on 4G, whereas in Naples it’s -105 dBm and in Geneva and Birmingham it’s -104 dBm. Numbers closer to zero are better here, and that roughly -17 dBm gap is a difference of around 50 times in signal power.
Overall, North American cities have a median signal of -101 dBm, with European ones similarly posting a median of -100 dBm, while in for example East Asia the median is -90 dBm — making for a much better signal.
So even though your signal might not seem bad outside, it likely is if you’re getting poor indoor signal — it’s just the move to indoors decreases it ever further, making it more noticeable.

The solution is for carriers to rethink their network deployment, with for example a denser deployment of masts and other infrastructure, or the use of more or better configured spectrum.
Still, without changes at a government level, this probably won’t be addressed, with Ookla noting that cities and countries that have indoor-specific rules for coverage tend to perform better than those that don’t.

articles.title: Logitech boosts MX Master 4 mouse with stylish special editions
articles.text:
If you’ve been eyeing Logitech’s excellent MX Master 4 mouse, but aren’t thrilled by the boring colour options, the company finally has a solution.
The MX Master 4 now has two special edition options, both of which boast snazzy new visuals on top of the same excellent features. The MX Master 4 Special Edition comes in two options, ‘Creator’ and ‘Developer.’
Logitech launched the Creator variant (pictured above) alongside the Adobe Max event earlier this week, and it starts shipping today. While the Developer version launched last month alongside the GitHub Universe event last month.
The Creator Special Edition is my favourite of the two mice, sporting a wonderful red and white colourway. (Though maybe I just like it because it matches MobileSyrup…) I love all the subtle lines to popular creator software, like the keyframe graphics and calibration band.
And the timeline on the mouse sports a few easter eggs, including 4:21 (International Day of Innovation and Creativity), 4:27 (World Design Day), 8:19 (World Photography Day), and 10:27 (World Day of Audiovisual Heritage).
The Developer Special Edition mouse is also quite nice with its two-tone body and the lime-green accents. I appreciate the little details on it as well, like the ‘Hello, World’ text on the thumb rest.
Aside from style, the new Special Editions don’t add anything to the existing MX Master 4 formula. When I reviewed it earlier this year, I was a fan of the design and ergonomics, the vertical and horizontal scroll wheels, and useful software features like the Actions Ring. The support haptics are a nice addition as well, though they don’t add much to the experience.
Since the Special Editions only bring a surface-level visual upgrade, I appreciate that Logitech didn’t increase the price. Both the Creator and Developer editions cost $159.99 in Canada (though at the time of writing, the Developer edition was temporarily sold out).

A top performer, back at its lowest price
You can pick up a serious discount on an Anycubic 3D printer right now. The Anycubic Kobra X is on sale at Amazon for $299.99, back down to its lowest ever price on Amazon. This 17% discount nets you a printer that scored you one of our Editor's Choic awards, along with a four and a half star score in our Anycubic Kobra X review.

This is an entry-level printer with a lot of potential for beginners and pros. Its multi-material ACE Gen 2 system is built in, meaning you don't have to worry about pausing your printer to switch out colors. Our testing saw that, with a four-color print with 776 color swaps, the Anycubic Kobra X was 10 hours faster than the Bambu Lab A1, despite otherwise-similar printing speeds (and a very similar design). It also has a 49-point full auto leveling system, along with an RFID tag reader, which will work with Anycubic filaments to help it quickly identify what filament you're using. articles.title: 'Jensen deserves due process, not mob justice': petition to bring back Nvidia's ex-CEO gains 175,000 signatures, as Huang reportedly mulls the 'possibility of returning'
articles.text:
'Stand with Jensen' petition calling for return of Huang as Nvidia's CEO gains 175,000 signatures including Elon Musk, Tim Sweeney and other high-profile tech execs
Campaign to reinstate Huang calls for 'independent investigation' to 'establish the facts'
- 'Stand with Jensen' petition calling for the return of Huang now has over 175,000 signatures
- It asks for an immediate reinstatement of Huang as Nvidia CEO and an "independent investigation and a fair hearing" regarding the matters he resigned over
- A separate report claims that Huang may be considering the possibility of such a return
Following the exit of Nvidia's CEO last week, a petition has been put together to campaign for the reinstatement of Jensen Huang.
VideoCardz noticed the 'Stand with Jensen' website which hosts a petition and open letter that has now been signed by some 175,000 people, some of whom are high-profile names in the tech industry.
That includes Elon Musk, Tim Sweeney (of Epic Games), Tobias Lutke (CEO of Shopify), Travis Kalanick (the former CEO of Uber), Steve Chen (the former CTO of YouTube) and Julien Chaumond (current CTO at Hugging Face). It's made clear that Huang himself doesn't endorse the letter.
The demands laid out by the letter to the Nvidia board are threefold, including firstly that Huang should be reinstated as CEO immediately – to stabilize the situation – but if the board believes "his continued absence is necessary" that they should provide an explanation of why.
The second demand is to "ensure an independent investigation and a fair hearing", and the third is to deliver a timely public explanation of what's happened and how the interests of Nvidia staff and shareholders were weighed up in this matter.
The petition states: "Thirty-three years of leadership do not place anyone above accountability. But accountability requires evidence, a fair hearing, and a reasoned decision. Jensen deserves due process, not mob justice."
Meanwhile, given all this, a separate report from The Financial Times claims that Huang is mulling a comeback bid and the "possibility of returning" based on chatter from multiple sources. An ally of the ex-CEO said they were putting together a 'war room' of big tech executives to lobby for Huang's return (presumably including Musk and the other aforementioned names).
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
Analysis: strong feelings and dim views
Some strong feelings have been aired, then, and based on the stats from the Stand with Jensen campaign, nearly 9,000 Nvidia staff (known as 'Nvidians') are signatories of the open letter – which is 20% of the employee base. Of those employees, 26 are Vice Presidents (or Senior VPs), which is a good chunk of the top leadership (maybe approaching half of them, although there are no precise numbers for VPs at Team Green).
Of course, none of this can be verified, and we have to take these numbers on trust.
Looking at Reddit, there's little sympathy for Huang, particularly among PC gamers (though his exit is arguably another distinctly negative development). Even on the subreddits relating to Nvidia stock, there's a mostly dim view of this petition (just over half of the signatories are declared as shareholders). However, it is notable that a fair few major names in tech have signed the letter – I still doubt that this will spark a turnaround in sentiment for the board, of course. These kind of campaigns aren't known for producing much in the way of concrete results, shall we say.
That said, given the 'war room' rumor from the FT, maybe the petition will give Huang a bit more impetus to launch the comeback bid that is supposedly being considered behind the scenes. If it's going to happen, it will obviously need to happen quickly.
Meanwhile, the letter signatures are likely to exceed 200,000 today. In case you missed this last week (somehow), Colette Kress (who was CFO) is currently the interim CEO while Nvidia conducts a search for Huang's permanent replacement (who could come from inside or outside the company).
