articles.title: Build memory-aware AI agents with Agentic Retrieve on Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Build memory-aware AI agents with Agentic Retrieve on Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base
Users of a knowledge-grounded application expect it to remember them, not only to search well. They ask follow-up questions that make sense only in the context of the previous turn. They expect an answer about a policy or a procedure to reflect what they told the application about themselves last month. And they still expect every answer to be grounded in the documents they are allowed to read, with citations. Whether the application is a customer support assistant, a document chat inside a SaaS product, or an internal assistant over company policies, the expectation is the same.
Meeting that expectation is hard, because the context that would sharpen a search lives outside the knowledge base. A user’s location, role, or product tier was often mentioned in an unrelated conversation weeks ago. To use it, the application has to store every conversation, extract durable facts from it, decide which facts matter for the current question, and inject them into the request. When many users share the application, every one of those steps also has to be isolated per user, and so does every document.
Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore memory, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, now take over these steps: storing each conversation, extracting facts from it, and bringing the relevant facts into the search. You turn this on by adding a memoryConfiguration to the AgenticRetrieveStream request, which makes AgentCore memory a retrieval source alongside your knowledge base. Within the same call, the service restores the conversation, and the planner decides on its own when a fact about the user would help. It retrieves that fact from long-term memory and uses it to compose the sub-queries it sends to the knowledge base. After generating the answer, the service saves the turn back to memory. The same request carries a userContext, so the knowledge base returns only the documents that the user’s access control lists (ACLs) allow. The integration is opt-in and backward compatible. Your application keeps only what is genuinely yours: authenticating the user and passing who they are.
This post shows how to build such an assistant for many users who share one knowledge base and one memory resource. Each user sees only the documents they may read, and each user’s memory stays private. The running example is an internal employee assistant for AnyCompany, a fictional company. Employees sign in with Amazon Cognito and ask questions over HR policies, IT guides, engineering runbooks, and sales plans. We show how to read the user’s identity from the Cognito ID token, how to pass it to AgenticRetrieveStream for document ACLs and for memory, how to design memory namespaces for many users, and how to read the trace to see when the planner used memory. Finally, we make AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) enforce per-user memory isolation even when application code gets it wrong. If you deployed the application from Build multi-tenant agentic chat applications on enterprise data with Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base, this post replaces its “persist conversation history yourself” step.
Solution overview
AnyCompany keeps its documents in Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3). One managed knowledge base syncs them through an ACL-enabled Amazon S3 data source. A global ACL file in the same bucket says which employees may read each folder: everyone reads HR and IT, only engineers read the engineering runbooks, and only salespeople read the commission plan. One AgentCore memory resource is shared by every employee. Amazon Cognito authenticates employees, and its ID token supplies two claims: the sub (user ID) identifies the user’s memory, and the verified email identifies the user to the knowledge base’s ACL filter. Three test users sign in: two engineers, Maya and Liam, and one salesperson, Sofia. The trace excerpts in this post are taken from a run of the sample application in the GitHub repository.
- The employee signs in with Cognito and receives an ID token, a JSON Web Token (JWT) signed by the user pool.
- The application’s API validates the token — an Amazon API Gateway JWT authorizer in production, a small FastAPI service in the sample. Unauthenticated requests do not reach the handler.
- The handler reads two claims from the verified token: sub becomes the memory actorId and namespace, and email becomes the userContext.userId. The client body carries only { question, sessionId? }. The handler then assumes the application’s IAM role for this user, with the session tag userId=<sub>.
- The handler calls AgenticRetrieveStream with the knowledge base as the retriever, userContext, and a memoryConfiguration bound to this user.
- Managed Knowledge Base restores the conversation history from short-term memory (STM) in AgentCore memory for the actor and session identified by sessionBinding.
- Managed Knowledge Base retrieves from the knowledge base with ACL filtering based on userContext. It can also retrieve the user’s configured long-term memory through speculative retrieval or memory searches selected by the planner.
- Managed Knowledge Base streams a cited answer and trace events back to the handler. The handler records the traces with a correlation ID and forwards the answer and trace information to the UI.
- With persistenceMode: DEFAULT, the service saves the question and generated answer to the session. AgentCore memory then extracts long-term records asynchronously according to the configured strategies.
Figure 2: One AgenticRetrieveStream turn with userContext and memoryConfiguration. Everything between the first and last arrow is the service’s work.
Managed Knowledge Base owns ingestion, ACL filtering, indexing, ranking, planning, retrieval, and generation. With memoryConfiguration, it also owns session restore, memory search, and persistence. AgentCore memory owns storage, retention, encryption, and extraction. Your application owns authentication, the UI, and reading the user’s identity from the token. There is no conversation table: when the UI lists or reopens a conversation, it reads the same memory resource.
How identity maps to the request
Every value is derived by the application from the verified ID token. None comes from the request body.
| Request field | Derived from | What it scopes | Enforced by | 
| userContext.userId | ID token email (verified, immutable in the pool) | Which documents can be retrieved | Knowledge base ACL filtering | 
| memoryConfiguration.sessionBinding.actorId | ID token sub | Whose short-term memory is restored and written, and the {actorId} in long-term namespaces | AgentCore memory keying, plus an IAM condition | 
| memoryConfiguration.sessionBinding.sessionId | Generated by the application for a new conversation. Listed with ListSessions | Which conversation within that actor | Keyed under the actorId | 
| memoryConfiguration.retrievalConfigs[0].namespacePath | /anycompany/<sub> | Which long-term records the planner may search | IAM condition | 
Two different claims do two different jobs. The knowledge base identifies users by email, because that is what the connected data source records in its ACLs. Memory needs an actorId that never changes and is never reused. The Cognito sub is both. An email address can be changed, or reassigned to a new employee after someone leaves, and that person would then inherit the old memory. You can use another stable user ID from your own user store as the actorId. What matters is that it never moves to a different person.
Prerequisites
- This walkthrough uses a managed knowledge base and an AgentCore memory resource in the US West (Oregon) Region (us-west-2). As described in the agentic retrieval documentation, the memory resource used with this integration must be in the same AWS account as the knowledge base and in the ACTIVE state.
- Python 3.10 or later and Boto3 1.43.72 or later.
- Permission to create an S3 bucket, a Cognito user pool, IAM roles, a knowledge base, and a memory resource. The sample’s infra/setup.py creates all of these resources idempotently.
Solution walkthrough
The following steps create the knowledge base and its data source, set up the memory resource and Amazon Cognito, build the request, and read the trace to confirm the result.
Step 1: Create the knowledge base with an ACL-enabled data source
A managed knowledge base needs no vector store:
Configure the service role for your setup by following Create a service role for managed Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases, and pass its ARN in roleArn. For model access requirements, also review the prerequisites for managed and custom models.
Documents live in the bucket under docs/<folder>/. Amazon S3 has no permission system of its own to crawl, so you supply the ACLs in a global ACL file in the same bucket. Each entry maps an S3 prefix to the emails that may read it:
The sample’s file also gives everyone docs/it/. Then create the data source. For a managed knowledge base, every connector has the type MANAGED_KNOWLEDGE_BASE_CONNECTOR, and connectorParameters.type picks the source:
aclEnabled cannot be changed after the data source is created. CreateDataSource is asynchronous, so wait for the status AVAILABLE. Then call StartIngestionJob and wait for COMPLETE. The sync reads the documents and the ACL file and indexes each document with its ACL. In the sample, all 11 documents were scanned and indexed with 0 failures. A document that no ACL entry covers is not ingested, and a user whose email matches no entry receives no results from this data source.
The same model applies to connectors that crawl permissions from the source system, such as Microsoft SharePoint, Google Drive, and Atlassian Confluence. There, the permissions come from the source, groups are resolved from the source, and the knowledge base also checks each result against the source in real time. Your application code does not change: it still passes the user’s email in userContext. For the full list, see Access Control Lists awareness enablement.
Step 2: Create the memory resource and design namespaces
One memory resource serves every user. Per-user separation comes from {actorId} in the namespace templates, which AgentCore memory resolves from each event at extraction time. Two choices matter.
Strategies. The two strategies extract different things. The summary strategy summarizes each conversation, so it captures facts that a user mentions in passing, such as “I’m on a Mac in the Frankfurt office.” Those facts are what personalize a later answer about, say, PTO. The user-preference strategy extracts stated preferences into structured records (“Prefers short bullet-point answers without tables”, “Always deploys to eu-central-1 first”) and does not treat incidental mentions as preferences. Summaries give you “what we discussed.” Preferences give you “how this person wants to be answered.” Use both.
Layout. retrievalConfigs accepts one entry, so a single namespacePath must reach everything the planner should see for a user. Put {actorId} directly under the root: namespacePath: "/anycompany/<sub>" then covers the profile and every conversation summary. A layout such as /anycompany/profile/{actorId} and /anycompany/summaries/{actorId} would let one entry reach only one of them.
Wait for the memory to reach ACTIVE. Creating the memory does not need a user or actorId, so the order of Step 2 and Step 3 does not matter. Nothing is provisioned per user: a new Cognito user becomes a new actor the first time they ask a question.
Step 3: Set up Cognito and grant the application permissions
Create a user pool and an app client without a client secret. The email decides which documents a user may read, so make it required, verified, and not changeable by the user:
Mutable cannot be changed after the pool is created. With a mutable email, a signed-in user could change their email to a colleague’s address. If your users federate from Okta or Microsoft Entra ID, map the IdP’s email to this attribute so that it matches the email in your data source’s ACLs.
The sample enables USER_PASSWORD_AUTH so the local UI and tests can sign in directly. Production applications typically use Cognito managed login or AWS Amplify.
Set up an IAM role for the application. The backend assumes it once per user, with the session tag userId=<sub>, and every memory statement is conditioned on that tag. This is the complete policy the sample runs with:
ListEvents is required with sessionBinding, RetrieveMemoryRecords with retrievalConfigs, and CreateEvent when persistenceMode is DEFAULT. ListSessions and ListMemoryRecords are for the application’s own reads (conversation list and the “what memory knows about you” view), not for AgenticRetrieveStream. The role’s trust policy allows sts:AssumeRole, sts:TagSession, and sts:SetSourceIdentity from the backend’s own identity (an AWS Lambda execution role or an Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) task role in production). If the memory uses a customer managed key, add kms:Decrypt on that key.
Step 4: Read the user from the token, then build the request
Verify the ID token and read the two claims. Only the ID token carries email. The access token does not:
jwt.decode checks the signature, the issuer (your user pool), the expiry, and the audience (your app client). For details of the claims, see Understanding the identity (ID) token. With API Gateway, a JWT authorizer does the same checks and passes the claims to your handler.
Next, get the user’s AWS credentials. The backend assumes the application role for this user and caches the session until shortly before it expires:
Every call for this user, including the memory calls that agentic retrieval makes on the caller’s behalf, now runs as assumed-role/anycompany-assistant-app-role/user-<sub> and carries the tag that the policy in Step 3 checks.
Decide the sessionId. For a new conversation, the application generates one, such as "conv-" + uuid4().hex, and returns it to the client. To continue a conversation, the client sends it back. To show a user their conversations, call ListSessions with the user’s actorId:
You do not need your own table that maps users to sessions. Accepting a sessionId from the client is safe because short-term memory is keyed by (memoryId, actorId, sessionId), and the actorId comes from the token. If Liam sends Maya’s sessionId, it names a session inside Liam’s own space, which is empty. Agentic retrieval itself does not verify that the actorId, sessionId, or namespace you supply belong to the user who is asking, so they must never come from the client. Keep your own session table only if you need data that memory does not hold, such as conversation titles.
Then build the request:
Without userContext, an ACL-enabled data source returns no results at all. Compare the request with the stateless handler it replaces:
The query before the call and the write after it are gone, and messages has one element. Three rules come with sessionBinding, and each is enforced with a specific ValidationException. First, messages carries only the current question, so you choose one history source per request. Second, persistenceMode: DEFAULT (the default) writes the question and the generated answer as one event, so it requires generateResponse: true. Third, memoryId alone is invalid. persistenceMode: NONE restores history and writes nothing, for audit or replay views.
Step 5: Update the client contract and render history
The client sends { question, sessionId? }. On a new conversation, the application generates a sessionId and returns it as the first streamed frame. The client echoes it on later turns and omits it to start over.
Because the memory resource is yours, the application reads it directly to render a conversation:
Each persisted turn is exactly one event with two payloads: the user’s question and the final answer. The history therefore renders as a clean transcript and remains usable by other AgentCore memory clients.
Step 6: Verify from the trace
The trace tells you, per turn, what the knowledge base and memory did:
| Trace event | When it appears | What to look at | 
| SessionHistoryLoad | First event, whenever sessionBinding is set | _memory_event_count and _memory_message_count, both 0 on a new session | 
| SpeculativeRetrieval | Before planning | On a new session, retrievalMetadata also lists BedrockAgentCoreMemory. Memory items carry _memory_* metadata and no text. Knowledge base items carry _source_uri | 
| Planning | Each iteration | actions[].memoryRetrieve means the planner chose to search memory, with a query it composed | 
| Retrieval with retrievalType: BedrockAgentCoreMemory | Per planned memory action | _memory_record_count. A count of 0 is a normal result | 
| A memory event with status: FAILED | Memory unavailable or access denied | failures[].message. Memory is best-effort: the request continues and the answer is generated from the knowledge base | 
The following runs show the behavior. Excerpts are verbatim, trimmed for length.
Document ACLs: Maya and Sofia, same question. “What is the weekly on-call stipend?” The on-call guide is in docs/engineering/. Maya’s retrieval included docs/engineering/oncall.md, and the answer was “500 USD or 450 EUR per week.” Sofia’s speculative retrieval and the planner’s follow-up sub-query returned only HR and sales chunks:
Her answer said that no on-call stipend is documented in the sources she can access. The application made no access decision. It passed userContext.userId: "sofia@example.com", and the knowledge base did the filtering. The reverse holds for the commission plan: Sofia gets the 12% accelerator, and Maya’s retrieval does not contain docs/sales/.
Turn 1: Maya, new conversation. “How do I set up the VPN on my laptop? I’m on a Mac in the Frankfurt office.”
The answer gives the Frankfurt gateway (vpn-fra.anycompany.example) and the macOS steps. Afterwards, ListEvents on the session shows one event with two payloads.
Turn 2: Maya, same conversation. “It keeps disconnecting every few minutes. What should I try?” The request carried only that sentence:
The planner sent retrieve("VPN disconnects every few minutes troubleshooting") and retrieve("Cisco Secure Client macOS frequent disconnect fix"). The answer resolved “it” and pointed at iCloud Private Relay, the macOS-specific cause in the guide. On a continued session, SpeculativeRetrieval queries only the knowledge base. The long-term memory lookup in that step happens on new sessions.
Turn 3: Maya, a new conversation, later. “How many days of PTO do I get per year, and do unused days carry over?” Her office decides the answer, and she never mentioned it in this conversation. Speculative retrieval searched long-term memory with the raw question and found one record:
Knowledge base and memory items share one retrievalResponse. Tell them apart by sourceRetriever.identifier or by the _memory_* keys. The record was the summary of her VPN conversation. That was enough: the planner went straight to the answer, which said “Since your memory indicates you’re based in the Frankfurt office … you get 30 days of PTO per year, granted in full on January 1, and any unused days must be used by March 31 of the following year.” A fact from an IT conversation personalized an HR answer.
Turn 4: Liam, new conversation, identical question. Same handler, same memory resource, a different token. Speculative retrieval found nothing about him, so the planner decided to search memory with its own query:
Liam received the table of all three offices and a request to say which one he is in. The application chooses where the planner may look. The planner decides whether to look and what to ask: a memoryRetrieve action appears only when the planner decides that another memory search would help. Reading Maya’s sessionId through the history endpoint with Liam’s token returned an empty list.
Figure 3: The same question from two users. Maya’s trace shows a memory hit and a Frankfurt-specific answer. Liam’s trace shows zero memory records and the generic table.
Long-term extraction is asynchronous and runs after the turn is persisted. In our run, the first record appeared 81 seconds after turn 2, but the timing is not a commitment. Design for eventual availability. A fact stated in this conversation is not guaranteed to be retrievable in the next one immediately. The sample polls ListMemoryRecords before running turn 3.
Security and multi-user isolation
In this walkthrough, the application authenticates. The knowledge base filters. ACL-aware retrieval is filtering, not authorization. Take the email only from a verified ID token with email_verified: true, make it immutable in the pool, and handle email reuse: if an address is reassigned to a different person, that person gets the old owner’s document access. The knowledge base fails closed: a document with no ACL, or an ACL error, means fewer results, not extra ones. If results are missing, check that the email matches the ACL entry.
Identity comes from the token (Step 4) for memory too: actorId and namespace come from the verified sub, never from the client.
IAM condition keys, as defense in depth. AgentCore memory exposes bedrock-agentcore:actorId on ListEvents, CreateEvent, and ListSessions, and bedrock-agentcore:namespacePath on RetrieveMemoryRecords and ListMemoryRecords. The memory calls that agentic retrieval makes during a request are authorized against the calling identity. That is why the caller’s policy must grant those actions, and why the conditions in Step 3 apply to them. With the session assumed for Maya, a request bound to Maya’s actorId proceeds normally. A request that binds Liam’s actorId is the bug that this policy guards against, and it is denied at every memory operation:
Nothing was written to Liam’s memory: his session count stayed at 0. The answer was still generated from the knowledge base. Because each user has their own role session, AWS also sees which user each call is for: the caller is assumed-role/anycompany-assistant-app-role/user-<sub> with SourceIdentity=<sub>, which the session holder cannot change.
Two further points. The memory is a customer-owned resource that other systems in your account may also write to. Treat its contents as input, and attach an Amazon Bedrock guardrail to the request through policyConfiguration. And plan the data lifecycle. Raw events expire per eventExpiryDuration, but extracted records do not. A user-deletion workflow therefore covers DeleteEvent for the actor’s sessions and DeleteMemoryRecord under the actor’s namespace.
Observability and failure behavior
Log the full trace with a correlation ID per turn. The planner’s sub-queries are as worth auditing as its final results. AWS/Bedrock/KnowledgeBases reports Invocations, ClientErrors, and TotalIterationCount for Operation=AgenticRetrieveStream. AWS/Bedrock-AgentCore reports Invocations, Latency, Errors, and UserErrors per memory operation, and InputTokenUsage/OutputTokenUsage per strategy for extraction. With Amazon CloudWatch Transaction Search enabled, AgentCore Observability, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, shows a turn’s spans end to end.
Memory operations are best-effort by design. If a memory call fails or is denied, the request does not fail. The trace carries a FAILED memory event with the failure message, and the turn continues without that memory. The answer is generated from the knowledge base. Decide whether your UI surfaces that degraded state.
Considerations
- Use a stable sessionId for the life of a conversation. The API accepts a fresh ID per request, but a fresh ID silently breaks continuity and produces one summary record per turn.
- Use namespacePath to reach all of a user’s long-term records. retrievalConfigs accepts one entry with up to five metadataFilters. namespace matches by prefix and namespacePath matches by hierarchy, so namespacePath fits per-user IDs under the root. Supply namespaces fully resolved, because a template such as /anycompany/{actorId} is rejected.
- Expect only USER and ASSISTANT conversational events to be restored. Events with the TOOL or OTHER role that other systems write are skipped.
- Keep sending messages instead of sessionBinding when your application needs to control exactly which history each request carries. For example, your existing history store may be the system of record for conversations, or you may edit or redact history before sending it. With sessionBinding, the service restores and persists the conversation for you. You can’t combine the two in one request.
- A request can carry up to five knowledge bases. With more than one retriever, the planner routes each sub-query based on the knowledge base description, so write it carefully.
- Plan for latency and cost. The session restore adds on the order of 200 milliseconds. In our runs, a full turn with one knowledge base, ACLs, and memory took 4–10 seconds with the managed model. Planning iterations drive that time, not memory. These are observed figures, not service commitments. Agentic retrieval is priced per call plus underlying retrievals, and the memory operations made during the call are billed as AgentCore memory usage. For details, see Amazon Bedrock pricing and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore pricing.
Clean up
Run python infra/teardown.py in the sample to delete the knowledge base, the S3 bucket and its objects, the memory resource (including conversation history and long-term records), the Cognito user pool, and the IAM roles.
Conclusion
Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base already gave you the retrieval stack as a service. That stack covers ingestion, document ACLs, indexing, ranking, and the planning loop in AgenticRetrieveStream that turns a hard question into a cited answer. With memoryConfiguration, the same call now carries the conversation and the user’s history. For a multi-user application, that removed the conversation store, the history replay, and the extraction pipeline. What remained was a short list of responsibilities. Authenticate the user and read two claims from the ID token: pass the verified email as userContext so that the knowledge base filters documents, and use the sub as the actorId for one memory resource with {actorId}-rooted namespaces. Use IAM condition keys on a per-user role session as a second line of defense that holds through the agentic path.
To get started, deploy the sample from the GitHub repository. Then read the AgenticRetrieveStream API reference, Access Control Lists awareness enablement, and Use AgentCore memory with agentic retrieval. For the retrieval loop itself, see Agentic retrieval for Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base. For memory concepts, see Amazon Bedrock AgentCore memory: Building context-aware agents.

articles.title: Trump Administration Moves to Block China From Indirect Access to American AI Technology
articles.text:
The Trump administration on Monday issued new rules to restrict remote access to advanced U.S. computing chips and servers, marking the latest step to limit China’s abilities to use U.S. chips to train their best artificial intelligence models.
The rule also was issued days after Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang resigned as CEO amid scrutiny of his ties to a Chinese executive who used to lead Singapore-based Megaspeed International, which is suspected of diverting advanced Nvidia chips to China in violation of U.S. export controls. The company provides computing power to Chinese companies using chips housed in Southeast Asian data centers, including facilities in Malaysia.
“The rule is designed to ensure that existing restrictions on access to sensitive American technology cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries,” the Bureau of Industry and Security under the Commerce Department said in issuing the rule that took effect immediately.
Under the new rule, overseas data centers that serve companies in countries including China, Russia, Iran and Cuba are required to identify their end users. There also will be an additional, case-by-case licensing requirements for sales of chips for Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand or Brazil — countries that “present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion” to unauthorized destinations, the rule says.
The U.S. bans sales of the country’s most advanced AI chips to China, seeking to maintain an edge in its rivalry with China for predominance in artificial intelligence. However, many lawmakers and policymakers believe the country’s export control rules are not tough enough and filled with loopholes such as cloud computing that allow China to rent processing power built on American technology.
Last year, U.S. Rep. Michael Lawler, a New York Republican, introduced a bill to broaden the U.S. export controls to include remote access. He told Congress “physical export controls” under current rules do not apply to remote access, allowing China to “access our tech through the cloud” and giving it “a real tool to sidestep” U.S. export restrictions. The bill has passed the House.

articles.title: Jensen Huang allies build a "war room" to get him back at Nvidia
articles.text:
Jensen Huang is considering a comeback as Nvidia’s chief executive, as allies in Silicon Valley pressure the company’s board to reinstate him days after the tech executive resigned over reports he had affairs with a suspected Chinese spy and a subordinate.
Huang has discussed with confidants the possibility of returning, according to multiple people familiar with the matter—even as an independent probe by Nvidia’s board investigates the conduct that led to a spectacular leadership crisis at the $4 trillion chip company this week.
One Huang ally told the FT they were putting together a “war room” of Silicon Valley executives to lobby for the former Nvidia chief’s return and would try to garner support from the White House.
“Everyone that matters in tech outside the frontier labs loves Jensen,” they said. The efforts had Huang’s support, they added.
A public campaign to reinstate Huang has gathered steam over the weekend. Tesla and SpaceX chief Elon Musk and Epic Games chief executive Tim Sweeney were among executives backing a public letter demanding that its board “Bring Jensen Back.”
Huang continues to command fierce loyalty from some employees, several of whom have gone public in calling for his return in the days since he resigned and have signed the open letter.

articles.title: Redmi Watch 6 é bom? Testamos o relógio com tela AMOLED e GPS independente • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Redmi Watch 6 é bom? Testamos o relógio com tela AMOLED e GPS independente
Smartwatch da Xiaomi entrega tela AMOLED, GPS independente e boa autonomia de bateria a um custo mais acessível
O Redmi Watch 6 é um smartwatch intermediário com recursos interessantes, como tela AMOLED brilhante, GPS independente, boa autonomia de bateria e player de música que não depende de pareamento com o smartphone.
O dispositivo ainda monitora dados básicos de saúde e chega com mais de 150 modos de treino para atender a diferentes esportistas, apesar de não contar com mapas offline ou NFC para pagamentos por aproximação.
Mas será que no balanço geral ele vale a compra? Eu testei o Redmi Watch 6 por 20 dias e detalho toda minha experiência logo abaixo.
Aviso de ética
O Tecnoblog é um veículo jornalístico independente que ajuda as pessoas a tomarem sua próxima decisão de compra desde 2005.
Esta análise não têm intenção publicitária, e ressalta os pontos positivos e negativos do produto. Nenhuma empresa pagou, revisou ou teve acesso antecipado a este conteúdo.
O Redmi Watch 6 foi cedido por empréstimo pela Xiaomi e será devolvido após os testes. Para mais informações, acesse a nossa Política Editorial.
A embalagem do Redmi Watch 6 contém o relógio, um cabo para carregamento magnético e um manual de usuário que também inclui a certificação de garantia.
O único item essencial que não vem na caixa é o adaptador de tomada, o que é algo comum da indústria de relógios inteligentes.
A boa notícia é que praticamente qualquer fonte que você tenha em casa deve funcionar, devido à potência modesta exigida de 5 W (5 V e 1 A).
Talvez seja difícil perceber à primeira vista, mas o Redmi Watch 6 é ligeiramente menor e mais fino que seu antecessor, além de estar mais leve. A caixa retangular com cantos arredondados mede 46,45 mm de altura, 40,03 mm de largura e 9,94 mm de espessura, pesando 31 g (sem a pulseira).
O comparativo abaixo ajuda a mostrar as diferenças de dimensões e peso entre os modelos.
|  | Redmi Watch 6 | Redmi Watch 5 | 
|---|---|---|
| Dimensões (A x L x E) | 46,45 mm × 40,03 mm × 9,94 mm | 47,5 mm × 41,1 mm × 11,3 mm | 
| Peso | 31 g (sem a pulseira) | 33,5 g (sem a pulseira) | 
É um relógio grande, mas leve e bem confortável — caiu bem no meu pulso. As pulseiras de TPU também são macias e facilmente removíveis: um clique nos botões da traseira e elas se destacam do corpo.
Por falar em traseira, a parte interna da caixa abriga o sensor de frequência cardíaca, microfone, alto-falantes e os pontos de contato para carregamento.
A grande novidade de design, no entanto, está no botão inédito na lateral direita. Para que ele fosse incorporado, a Xiaomi precisou reposicionar a coroa giratória de aço inoxidável, agora posicionada mais acima. Isso liberou espaço para o botão, localizado logo abaixo.
O botão lateral facilita a navegação e oferece atalhos mais rápidos de uso. Um clique nele e acessamos a Central de Controle. Com três cliques, acionamos o contato de emergência — configurado no app Mi Fitness. E se pressionarmos o botão por alguns segundos, entramos no menu liga/desliga.
O modelo que recebi é a versão em preto obsidiano, que seria minha escolha natural se tivesse comprado o wearable. Mas você também pode encontrar o Redmi Watch 6 em prata cinza ou azul glacial.
Além de ser menor e mais leve que seu antecessor, o Redmi Watch 6 chega com promessa de maior resistência resistente. A caixa retangular mantém a construção em liga de alumínio, mas o material usado é 20% mais resistente e a resistência estrutural é 40% superior em relação ao Redmi Watch 5, segundo a Xiaomi.
No meu caso, foi difícil avaliar essa parte, já que o modelo que recebi havia sido testado por outras pessoas e estava com a lateral esquerda um pouco desgastada, com pequenos arranhões e notas de desbotamento.
Ainda falando de construção, o relógio tem resistência contra água de 5 ATM, equivalente a 50 metros de profundidade. Isso significa que você pode usá-lo para nadar em piscinas ou águas rasas perto da costa.
Por aqui, ele resistiu tranquilamente a algumas sessões de natação de 10 minutos na piscina do prédio. Depois de cada treino, o dispositivo expulsa a água automaticamente do relógio para evitar degradações.
E eu aproveito o espaço para falar sobre uma questão que vira e mexe recebemos no Tecnoblog. A resistência contra água não é sinal verde para usar o relógio durante banhos quentes. E a própria Xiaomi alerta contra a prática.
A resistência de 5 ATM não protege o dispositivo contra vapor e água quente, que podem oxidar componentes internos. Portanto, tire ele do pulso antes de entrar no chuveiro para não impactar sua durabilidade.
A tela AMOLED de 2,07 polegadas é um dos grandes destaques do Redmi Watch 6. É um display amplo com bordas ultrafinas de 2 mm, o que garante bom espaço para visualização de conteúdos, especialmente de caracteres menores.
E a taxa de atualização de 60 Hz proporciona a fluidez necessária de navegação e animações das watchfaces.
O pico de brilho de 2.000 nits também ajuda na visibilidade e permitiu que eu enxergasse tudo na tela, sem dificuldades, em ambientes internos ou externos. E deixo meu elogio ao brilho automático, que se adaptou bem aos diferentes níveis de luminosidade.
A tela traz o recurso de ativação ao levantar o braço e chega com o Always-on Display, que mantém a tela ativada com dados básicos mesmo que você não esteja olhando para ela, embora aumente o gasto de energia.
E lembra que eu comentei sobre a lateral desgastada no modelo recebido? Pois a tela também chegou com arranhões de usos anteriores e passou a impressão de que risca com facilidade. Por motivos de prevenção, eu recomendaria uma película para reforçar a proteção.
O smartwatch opera sob o sistema HyperOS 3 da Xiaomi, que é simples e bem intuitivo. Temos três opções de layout, widgets personalizáveis e várias watchfaces nativas. Inclusive, você pode encontrar diversos outros mostradores de relógio pelo app Mi Fitness, disponível para Android ou iPhone.
Mas o SO não conta com uma loja de apps e nem permite a instalação de apps de terceiros. Em outras palavras, você só vai conseguir usar as ferramentas que já chegam instaladas no smartwatch.
A exemplo do modelo antecessor, o Redmi Watch 6 traz apenas um sensor de frequência cardíaca com um sensor de saturação de oxigênio no sangue.
Você pode medir batimentos cardíacos, conferir o nível de oxigênio no sangue, analisar as métricas de sono e até índice de estresse.
Não tenho do que reclamar sobre os monitoramentos. Achei que o relógio fez um bom rastreamento do meu ciclo de sono e não notei nenhum dado de saúde discrepante o suficiente para eu me preocupar.
Só é importante entender as limitações de rastreamento: o monitoramento de saúde é básico e atende a usuários que não precisam de dados complexos. Funciona para o meu caso. Mas ele não cobre medições avançadas como eletrocardiograma — presente em smartwatches premium mais caros e completos.
Em compensação, o Redmi Watch oferece 161 modalidades esportivas, incluindo corrida, ciclismo, natação e até hipismo. E durante os treinos, uma olhada rápida no relógio te deixa a par da frequência cardíaca e gasto de energia em tempo real.
Uma grata surpresa é que a Xiaomi atualizou algoritmos e os dados de frequência cardíaca estão presentes nos treinos de natação.
Mas o meu destaque vai para o GPS independente, agora com antena L1 dupla. Nesta estrutura, o relógio seleciona a antena com sinal mais forte para entregar uma conexão mais estável e posicionamentos mais precisos.
Confesso que é libertador sair para caminhar sem precisar levar o celular, já que o relógio consegue, por si só, marcar meu trajeto. E os registros foram bem certeiros.
Infelizmente, não há mapas offline e nem navegação por rotas. No entanto, assim que cheguei em casa, sincronizei os dados com o Mi Fitness e pude ver todo o percurso pelo mapa do app.
Além dos monitoramentos de saúde e treino, temos uma porção de outros recursos que facilitam a vida no dia a dia.
O relógio pode receber notificações de apps, visualizar mensagens do WhatsApp, além de receber ou fazer ligações telefônicas usando o microfone e alto-falantes dele.
Também há ferramentas para localizar o celular vinculado e apps utilitários como gravador de voz, lanterna, alarme com resposta tátil e drenagem de água. Muitas das ferramentas só funcionam quando o Bluetooth 5.4 do relógio está ativado e pareado ao smartphone.
Curiosamente, uma das funções que mais gostei funciona sem pareamento: a reprodução de músicas de maneira independente. É verdade que você vai precisar do celular para passar as músicas para a memória interna de 512 MB do smartwatch. Mas depois disso, ele poderá tocar as faixas pelo alto-falante ou fones de ouvido mesmo sem estar pareado.
É uma função ótima para quem vai correr, treinar ou passear por aí apenas com o relógio no pulso. Mas o sistema não é perfeito e a transferência de músicas só funciona em smartphones Android. Se fosse minha noiva munida de seu iPhone, por exemplo, ela teria que me pedir esse favor.
Vale destacar ainda que o Redmi Watch não tem Wi-Fi e não suporta assistentes virtuais. E também não conta com NFC para pagamentos por aproximação.
O Redmi Watch 6 chega com uma bateria de 550 mAh, que é a mesma capacidade vista no Redmi Watch 5. A Xiaomi fala em uma autonomia de até 24 dias de uso leve, 12 dias de uso normal e 7 dias de uso intenso.
Nos meus testes, o relógio durou cerca de 6 dias e 21 horas. Lembro de ter tirado o smartwatch da tomada por volta das 15h de uma quarta-feira e ele só foi descarregar completamente na quarta-feira seguinte, lá pelo meio-dia.
Confesso que esperava uma autonomia maior. Até porque usei uma watchface de baixo gasto energético, mantive o AOD desligado, ativei o brilho automático e desliguei o Bluetooth na maior parte do tempo. Expectativas à parte, ele apresentou boa autonomia durando quase uma semana inteira.
Já o tempo de carregamento se manteve dentro dos padrões de smartwatches, levando aproximadamente 1 hora e 47 minutos na tomada.
O Redmi Watch 6 vale a compra se você está buscando um relógio de monitoramento básico e com ótimo custo-benefício. Atualmente, ele pode ser encontrado na faixa dos R$ 550 a R$ 590 em marketplaces. Um bom preço pelo que entrega, e bem distante dos quase R$ 1.300 cobrados na loja oficial da Xiaomi.
Mas ele não é o único modelo competitivo do segmento intermediário. O Amazfit Bip 6, por exemplo, oferece navegação por rotas e assistente de voz custando menos que R$ 500. E o Huawei Fit 5, apesar de estar mais caro, chega com 64 GB de memória interna e inclui detecção de quedas.
No fim, tudo vai depender do que você busca em um smartwatch e no orçamento disponível. Porém, digo tranquilo que o Redmi Watch 6 é uma escolha segura e com potencial para se tornar seu fiel companheiro de pulso.
Só fica a sugestão de conferir os Achados do TB antes de finalizar a compra. De repente, o Redmi Watch 6 ou algum de seus concorrentes pode surgir lá com preços melhores para dar uma aliviada no seu bolso.
No geral, eu gostei do Redmi Watch 6. Mas e o que você achou dele? Bora continuar o papo na Comunidade do Tecnoblog!

articles.title: AWS Open-Sources Emulator for Local Testing of 200+ Services by Coding Agents
articles.text:
AWS has released AWS Emulator, a local program that serves an HTTPS endpoint for the public APIs of more than 200 AWS services. AWS Emulator lets developers and coding agents create resources, hit the same errors AWS would return, and iterate without provisioning cloud resources or incurring service charges for the operations it emulates.
Teams point the AWS CLI or an AWS SDK at it with environment variables such as AWS_ENDPOINT_URL, leaving application code unchanged. On Linux it installs as an RPM or Debian package for x86_64 or aarch64; on macOS and Windows, AWS documents a short Dockerfile and does not publish a prebuilt image. Rust tests can use an embedded mode that runs the emulator inside the test process and wires its HTTP client into the AWS SDK for Rust. An aws-emulator skill can start the emulator for coding agents and check a project against published fidelity tests. Written in Rust, it is generated from more than 400 Smithy API models AWS publishes for the SDKs, according to Swaminathan Sivasubramanian.
AWS says agents wrote and tested the code. Matthew Goldberg, a senior principal engineer at AWS, describes three teams: one writes fidelity tests from the public API models and verifies them against real AWS, one replays those tests and files issues, and one implements each fix. Every change must pass a merge gate that checks compilation, coding standards, security, and fidelity regressions. The work runs on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime Instances, AWS CodePipeline, and AWS CodeCommit.
How closely the emulator matches AWS varies by service. AWS publishes versioned fidelity tests and per-service scores with each release; a test passes only when every call matches AWS, including status codes, side effects, and exact errors. Unimplemented operations return HTTP 501 with the error code NotImplemented. AWS says fidelity is closest on control-plane APIs, while data-plane behavior and support for CloudFormation, Terraform, and the AWS CDK vary by service. Documented limits include no evaluation of IAM or resource-based policies, so it must not be used to test security; a single shared account and Region per process; in-memory state that disappears when the process stops; and no testing for long-running use or load. The evaluation suite includes tests the emulator does not yet pass.
Developers already have several local AWS stand-ins, including LocalStack, Floci, and moto. AWS Emulator is generated from AWS's own API models, ships official fidelity scores, and is dedicated to the public domain, but it is not a drop-in replacement for every workflow those tools cover, especially permission testing and infrastructure-as-code pipelines.
Developer Josh Builds wrote:
AWS just released a free local emulator of its APIs, made for coding agents and written entirely by agents. I counted its published fidelity tests: S3, DynamoDB and SQS pass about 2 in 3. CloudFormation passes under 1 in 5.
Yurii Serhiichuk compared it with existing emulators and published a container image and GitHub Action to cover a packaging gap:
AWS shipped AWS Emulator today - think LocalStack/Floci but native. Rust, built by agents (so hopefully it gets updated pretty fast). No public docker image though, and no GitHub action. So I filled that part.
AWS Emulator is generally available at no additional service fee. Source is on GitHub under the CC0 1.0 Universal public domain dedication, except third-party code in the vendor/ directory, which is under the Apache License 2.0. Setup details are in the user guide, and fidelity scores ship with each release.

articles.title: Jordan Belfort’s new AI voice startup, Tone, wants to sell like the 'Wolf of Wall Street' | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Years ago, as questions mounted about WeWork’s soaring valuation, I sat down with co-founder Adam Neumann. We were negotiating a stage interview, and he asked to meet me twice in the weeks leading up to it, once at a WeWork in San Francisco and again at his office in New York.
I knew full well that the numbers that SoftBank in particular had assigned to WeWork made little sense, but I came away understanding why investors wanted to throw in their lot with him.
It’s similarly easy to understand why people are enchanted by Jordan Belfort, the self-proclaimed “Wolf of Wall Street.” Belfort famously pleaded guilty in 1999 to securities fraud and money laundering tied to Stratton Oakmont, the Long Island brokerage where salespeople pushed penny stocks in pump-and-dump schemes while Belfort acquired a Southampton mansion, a 167-foot yacht, and at least one helicopter. (He destroyed the latter two while high on quaaludes and cocaine, as depicted in Martin Scorsese’s famous adaptation of Belfort’s autobiography, “The Wolf of Wall Street.”)
You might think someone who spent 22 months in prison and was ordered to pay $110.4 million in restitution to 1,513 victims wouldn’t get another shake. The victims ultimately received “far less” than they were owed, TMZ reported in July, noting that Belfort completed his court-ordered restitution obligations in late April of this year.
But Belfort, whose energy has a galvanizing quality, keeps resurfacing, including in recent years as a Miami-based sales consultant and one-time host of crypto workshops at his Miami Beach home. (A New York Times reporter attended a weekend workshop several years ago where the price of admission was one bitcoin or its equivalent value at the time of $40,000.)
Now he is moving into the intersection of what he knows best — sales — and the hottest trend on the planet, AI, building out a voice-based AI platform. The secret sauce is that it imbues its voices with the kind of tonality that wins deals, he says, for example, by phrasing declarative statements as questions (which “builds engagement”) and even whispering at times (which “implies scarcity of information”).
Belfort says the platform, called Tone, is already being used by companies that have more sales leads than their human teams can handle. Now, in a move that could also help expand its training data, Tone is launching a self-service platform for content creators and authors who want to turn their books into “expressive AI-generated narration.” Users can select from Tone’s AI voices or, as a voice-cloning feature rolls out, create a clone of their own voice.
It’s easy to argue the market is already saturated with AI voice startups and technologies, and Tone comes with added risk: Belfort’s co-founder in the business is longtime investor Shervin Pishevar, who has a controversial past of his own. We also can’t independently verify that the technology works as described (neither co-founder is an engineer).
But if my time with Neumann taught me anything, it’s that doubts about the numbers rarely get in the way of a good pitch. When Belfort looks for investors to back him in this new venture, finding believers won’t be too hard.
Here is part of our conversation, edited for length and clarity.
What have you built?
It’s a very unique way of going about building a voice, and it stems from a system of influence and persuasion I’ve been teaching since the late 1980s. It’s not just what you say, but how you say it. When you’re not in person, body language collapses into tonality. There are about 15 very powerful tonalities that people use all the time. The phrase I invented for this was “goal-oriented communication.” If I’m trying to be perceived as an expert, I apply tonality strategically.
Is this effectively trained on you?
It started that way. As a non-engineer, I went to first principles: How would I teach a human to do this? One tonality at a time. I have 30 years of super high-quality data , and I started teaching the model. It was a breakthrough moment, because it not only sounded exactly like me, it had nailed the tonality. Then I taught it a second one, and then how to link them. The key to all of this is data. Even the littlest bit of corrupt data dramatically negates the progress you’ve made.
How did you and Shervin Pishevar come together?
Shervin and I have been personal friends for a long time, and we were out for dinner one night. I had been pitched by an AI company that said it had an AI that could do selling. I listened to it. It was awful. But it put the idea in my head. I thought I was just going to teach models how to sell, but I couldn’t find a voice that was good enough. Necessity is the mother of invention, so we built our own.
Who are your customers, and how do they use it?
We have law firms and health insurance companies. We do a lot in polling and automobiles. It will take you through an entire health insurance sale. It asks qualifying questions, like what type of insurance you want, your budget, your ages. Then it chooses a plan and explains the features and benefits. Our latency is like 600 milliseconds. If the payment is too high, it’ll say it can bring the payment down and explain how to raise your deductible. If you don’t like the plan, it swaps you to a different one. It does literally the whole entire sale.
How does the AI handle a sales call that goes off script?
It never says, “That’s a great question,” unless it really is. I hate that. It’s so ingratiating. In any sale there’s a happy path, how we’d want the perfect conversation to go, and every last word can be mapped out. But people have questions and concerns, and they take you off the straight line. So the trick is a model that can carry that perfect conversation, handle anything thrown at it, answer elegantly and return to the straight line, without breaking rapport and without hallucinating — or, as a salesperson, lying. We’ve trained the model to do that.
Have you generated any revenue from Tone yet? Have you raised funding for it?
Revenue, probably about a million bucks — $700,000, maybe. We’ve raised friends and family and seed, about $10 million.
I want to address the elephant in the room. You have a fraud conviction. Pishevar has faced misconduct allegations that he denies. Why should a bank or a hospital or a consumer brand trust this product coming from the two of you?
All I can say for myself is that I did make mistakes. It was a very, very long time ago, and I’ve spent the last 20-plus years teaching people all over the world. I’ve been hired by companies all over the world to teach sales and persuasion. If some companies don’t want to work with us, that’s their decision. But I think there would be more than enough that would see the value of what we created.
What close rate does Tone have versus a typical sales force?
I still don’t think it’s quite as good as a top producer. A top producer in the field would outdo it call for call. I think that will change in the next six months to a year. To make a model respond this quickly, you’re not using frontier models. We’re using our own very small, very light models, so they don’t have quite as much intelligence. I think it will significantly outperform a mediocre closer.
Where is it used most effectively? Low-dollar sales opportunities? I’d think the more money someone is spending, the more human contact they’d demand.
I don’t think it’s about replacing humans. What I see most with customers is that they simply don’t have the human capital available. They could get a lot more leads than they have people to call, or they need coverage at different times of day or in different languages. I think there’s always going to be a need for great human salespeople. I really believe that.
You’re competing with ElevenLabs and Cartesia and a lot of other voice AI companies. Tone is your edge?
I don’t think sounding human is really what this is about. They’ll all sound human in six months or a year. It’s the application of tonality that makes us different: the intelligence behind when it chooses a certain tonality. We have a patent on it. ElevenLabs is a great company, and Cartesia as well, but those voices didn’t work for us.
The FCC ruled in 2024 that AI voices fall under robocall rules under the Telephone Consumer Protection Act. How does outbound sales calling work?
We only call opt-in. You’re not going to use AI to cold-call people. We would not allow that. You’d get sued by every TCPA lawyer in the world. It’s either opted-in leads or existing customers. The exception is polling, where there’s an exemption that lets you call private homes without opt-in.
How do you verify consent and prevent impersonation in voice cloning?
We could launch the cloning tomorrow. We didn’t. If you create a clone in our system, you speak into the computer, so we know who is creating it, and that person signs a consent. If someone wants to upload audio, which we don’t recommend, you’d have to match a live voiceprint in real time.
Who created the technology? You’re not an engineer, and Pishevar isn’t, either. I saw a name on the patent, Jordan Anthony Metzner.
No. Our VP of engineering is Ben Sussman. He’s a brilliant engineer. I’m the judge and the jury and the executioner of what sounds perfect. I’ll prototype something in the most obscene way, and my engineers rebuild it from scratch.
Do you charge per minute, or based on the outcomes customers see?
A combination. For streaming, it’s per minute. The content platform will be monthly subscriptions. And we have some clients where the bulk of our money is made through success.
Is this an independent company or something that belongs inside a larger AI company?
If the right offer came up, and it was substantial enough, and I thought it made sense, who wouldn’t entertain a conversation? But right now my plan is to raise a significant amount. I don’t think we need to own data centers, but we need enough reserve compute. I wouldn’t think I’d be selling it anytime soon, but who knows what the future brings.
Paramount+ released a documentary about you this summer. Did you watch it?
I didn’t. Believe it or not, I don’t watch or read anything about me, good or bad. I never read a comment. When you’re well-known, you have to live by who you are inside. I go by my own internal compass.

articles.title: Fable 5.2 creates an underwater world in a browser in only 96 KB — 40-line prompt creates impressive demo that runs at 180 FPS
articles.text:
Fable 5.2 creates an underwater world in a browser in only 96 KB — 40-line prompt creates impressive demo that runs at 180 FPS
Elegant effort is reminiscent of both old- and new-school demoscene.
Claude Fable 5.2 was released recently to mostly rave reviews, with both users and analysis outlets ranking it nipping at the heels of the much pricier Opus 5.5. Perhaps as practical proof of that claim, front-end developer Maksymilian Dendura took inspiration from the demoscene and had Fable roll his own virtual underwater world, Abyssal Garden, in only 96 KB of Javascript/HTML — you can check it out here.
The demo's 3D space and textures are all procedurally generated, meaning they're the result of mathematical equations rather than prebuilt 3D meshes, and all calculated on load. Using actual meshes and images for textures would otherwise take up a significant amount of space.
Building structures procedurally is difficult and has limitations, but it's exceedingly effective when used properly. Some games employ this technique for repeated elements like trees and grass.
Likewise, all the visual effects and even some texturing are done with shaders, which are small programs that change how a mesh or texture appears — for example, to make parts of an object shiny. Games use them extensively, as many players are aware, thanks to endless "loading shaders" screens or Unreal Engine's st-tu-tutering.
The result is definitely impressive, especially but not only as it's purely browser-based, relying on WebGPU and WebGL. Both are rarely-mentioned technologies that have actually existed for a long while now. As their names imply, they let developers render 2D and 3D graphics in a manner similar to that of OpenGL, but in a browser, using JavaScript as the base language.
The demo's most impressive fact is the simplicity of the prompt that got Fable 5.2 to build it. It's only about 40 lines long with word wrapping, and clearly illustrates the degree of autonomy that contemporary agentic AI has when given a specific, yet exceedingly open-ended task like this one. It's reasonable enough to assume the author did a few rounds of tweaking (and he has excellent artistic taste too), but the agent's acumen is nevertheless impressive.
Comparing this demo to an actual game is inevitable, but the reality is that demos have but an atom-sized fraction of the content of a full game, and are limited to little or no interaction, logic, or physics.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
Performance is decent for what is a great-looking but otherwise tiny and almost featureless space. The author says that he's getting 180 FPS at 1440p on an RTX 5070 Ti. Likewise, having this world in 97 KB sounds impressive, but it's actually gigantic for this type of demo, even if an X user further optimized it for 52 KB.
Regular computing users, including AI neophytes and acolytes, may not be aware that this kind of space-optimized programming for the purposes of visual/aural demonstrations is a discipline and art form that harkens back to the 1980s when 16-bit computers appeared — called the "demoscene."
By no means discounting the extraordinary fact that Fable did this nearly all by itself — which is the actual achievement here — code wizards have pulled off nearly impossible feats decades ago, including in browsers. The 2009 demo Elevatedn (17 years ago) has a comparable aesthetic, and includes music, in just under 4 KB (yes, four). There's even a browser version of it, taking up all of 4,777 bytes.
Hartverdrahtet (2012 — 14 years ago) has a highly complex 3D space, again in 4 KB. And old-timers in the audience will remember ".kkrieger", an FPS game prototype that fit in all of 96 KB, including meshes, textures, music, and sound effects... back in 2004.
Download the Tom's Hardware app for up-to-the-minute updates on iOS and Android. Also follow Tom's Hardware on Google News, or add us as a preferred source, to get our latest news, analysis, & reviews in your feeds.
Bruno Ferreira is a contributing writer for Tom's Hardware. He has decades of experience with PC hardware and assorted sundries, alongside a career as a developer. He's obsessed with detail and has a tendency to ramble on the topics he loves. When not doing that, he's usually playing games, or at live music shows and festivals.

It gave my iGPU a workout but maintained 60 FPS at a 720p-ish resolution on the lowest detail setting. I expected worse but it worked quite well. Reply

articles.title: Black Friday mit KI: Findet ChatGPT wirklich die besten Schnäppchen?
articles.text:
Black Friday mit KI: Findet ChatGPT wirklich die besten Schnäppchen?
Wer in den letzten Jahren rund um den Black Friday auf Schnäppchenfang war, hat vor allem die gängigen Preisvergleichsportale wie Idealo, Günstiger und Geizhals bemüht, vielleicht noch mit einigen Preisrecherche-Tools wie Camelcamelcamel oder Keepa Preisalarme gesetzt und bestenfalls noch die Tipps in Communitys wie Mydealz verfolgt. In diesem Jahr dürfte sich das ändern. Denn immer mehr Nutzer:innen haben erkannt, dass künstliche Intelligenz nicht nur gut darin ist, das geeignete Produkt in der Beratung zu ermitteln, sondern auch nach den passenden Preisen und Angeboten fahnden kann.
Laut einer repräsentativen Umfrage des Preisvergleichsportals Idealo von Oktober 2026 sucht schon heute jede:r fünfte Verbraucher:in mithilfe von KI-Tools oder -Assistenten nach Sonderangeboten. Auch Yougov hat im Oktober die Vorlieben der deutschen Käufer:innen untersucht: Demnach wird in diesem Jahr jede:r Zweite KI für die diesjährige Angebotssuche im Vorweihnachtsgeschäft einsetzen und immerhin 42 Prozent der Nutzer:innen wollen die KI gezielt für die Recherche nach dem besten Preis verwenden.
Doch sind ChatGPT, Gemini und Co. dafür wirklich schon reif und ist das Vertrauen in die Treffsicherheit der LLMs gerechtfertigt? Unserer Erfahrung nach ist insbesondere ChatGPT schon recht gut darin, Kaufinteressent:innen im Vorfeld zu beraten, etwa „einen Saugroboter, der gut im Beseitigen von Tierhaaren ist, unter 400 Euro kostet und nicht allzu laut ist“ zu finden. Dazu wählt die KI anhand hinterlegter Eigenschaften und Daten etwas Passendes aus, berücksichtigt (mehr oder minder zuverlässige) Testergebnisse und Kundenrezensionen und zeigt die passenden Angebote einiger Händler. Hier hatten wir Anfang des Jahres in einem Selbstversuch noch einige Schwächen aufgedeckt, die inzwischen weitgehend verschwunden sind.
Dass das so ist, dafür ist vor allem das Bewusstsein der Händler und Hersteller verantwortlich. Denn – nicht nur wir predigen es regelmäßig – die Auffindbarkeit und Validität der hinterlegten Daten sorgt dafür, dass zunächst die passenden Produkte gefunden und im nächsten Schritt auch die Angebote eines bestimmten Händlers aufgelistet werden.
Nicht nur ChatGPT kann Preisrecherche vernünftig abbilden
Besonderes Augenmerk liegt hier offenbar für viele Anbieter und Service-Betreiber auf ChatGPT. Wer etwa in der Vergangenheit auf Idealo für die Preisrecherche gesetzt hat, kann seit einigen Monaten das passende Plugin mit dem OpenAI-LLM verbinden. Der eigentliche Einkauf erfolgt dann allerdings weiterhin wie gewohnt über die Händler. Die Frage, ob man sich bei der Suche also weiterhin auf eine Preissuchmaschine verlässt, ist also eigentlich falsch gestellt – die Zukunft wird auf die Preissuchmaschine innerhalb der KI hinauslaufen.
Für die Preisrecherche kann es sich aber auch lohnen, auf Google Gemini zu setzen, weil hier inzwischen mehr als 60 Millionen Preislistings angebunden sind – Google Shopping sei Dank. Durch den strukturellen Vorteil ist die Google-KI grundsätzlich gut aufgestellt im Hinblick auf Produkteigenschaften und Preisrecherche. Allerdings ist selbst für Nutzer:innen, die hierfür ein geschultes Auge haben, insbesondere in der Mobilansicht nicht immer ganz klar, welche der Angebote gesponsert sind und wie die Empfehlungen zustande kommen.
Auffällig ist auch ein anderes Problem, das auch eine Untersuchung von Shopsavvy bestätigt: Nur bei einem Teil der Preisrecherchen entspricht das gefundene Ergebnis dem von Google Shopping. Die Untersuchung kam immerhin in einem Drittel der Fälle auf Abweichungen (übrigens in beide Richtungen). Auch bei unseren Tests gibt es bei nahezu allen Konstellationen im Rahmen der KI-Preisrecherche noch Fehler zu beklagen – und das unabhängig vom eingesetzten LLM:
Nicht immer sind die Preise wirklich aktuell, was darauf hindeutet, dass hier nicht mit Echtzeitdaten gearbeitet wird. Demnach nutzt die KI unterschiedliche Datenquellen, Aktualisierungsstände und Angebote der Händler.
Defizite bei den Suchergebnissen
Defizite haben die Suchergebnisse der KI allerdings auch noch in der Aufbereitung, die offenbar in den meisten Datenquellen weniger aussagekräftig im Hinblick auf die längerfristige Preisentwicklung ist. Hinzu kommt, dass die Varianten (etwa verschiedene Farben und Größen eines Kleidungsstücks) nicht immer treffsicher ausgewiesen werden. Das war tatsächlich in der Vergangenheit auch schon bei herkömmlichen Preissuchmaschinen ein Problem.
Eine weitere Einschränkung für den Nutzen der KI in diesem Kontext ist die Gefahr, an Fakeshops zu geraten. So hat etwa das auf Markenschutz spezialisierte Unternehmen Podqi bereits in einem Test ermittelt, dass sowohl ChatGPT als auch Gemini und Perplexity teilweise Angebote auf Fakeshop-Seiten empfehlen. Dazu wurden fast 6.800 Antworten der drei KI-Systeme analysiert. In 15 Prozent der Antworten von Perplexity tauchten problematische Websites auf, bei ChatGPT waren es acht Prozent, bei Gemini vier Prozent. Als problematisch wurden dabei sowohl gefälschte Markenshops als auch Anbieter von Produktfälschungen verstanden.
Immerhin in 57 Prozent der Fälle wurden diese ausdrücklich als Einkaufsmöglichkeit empfohlen, in weiteren 34 Prozent wurden sie ohne Warnhinweis erwähnt. Auch wenn die Untersuchung sich explizit auf US-Quellen bezog, sollten Kund:innen bei von der KI empfohlenen Onlineshops vorsichtig sein. Es dürfte nämlich nur eine Frage der Zeit sein, bis auch in Deutschland ähnliche Fälle bekannt werden. Auch wenn die KI-Anbieter hier schnell tätig werden dürften, bleibt also ein Restrisiko.
Als problematisch im Zusammenhang mit den (Pre-)Black-Friday-Rabatten hat sich aber noch etwas anderes erwiesen: In vielen Fällen ließ sich eine KI wie Claude von vermeintlichen Rabatten auf den Listenpreis blenden, während der Straßenpreis schon über längere Zeit deutlich darunter lag. Erst durch gezieltes Nachfragen sah die KI den Fehler ein, fand dann bei einer Preisrecherche zwar den günstigsten Preis, benannte aber einen absolut unbekannten Händler, obwohl mehrere große Shops denselben Preis anboten.
Wie KI Beratung und Preisrecherche kombiniert
Die eigentliche Stärke der KI beim Einkaufen liegt also nicht unbedingt in der reinen Preisrecherche, sondern (noch) eher in der vorgelagerten Beratungsleistung. Hilfreich war die KI – vor allem in Form von ChatGPT – übrigens bei einigen unserer Recherchen, bei denen Vorjahresmodelle angeboten wurden, wenn diese im Laufe des Dialogs als ausreichend angesehen wurden. Das funktionierte etwa bei einem Internetproblem mit einem bestimmten Kabelmodem recht souverän.
Allerdings war noch nicht in allen Fällen die Transparenz der Angebote gegeben. Zum einen wurde nicht in jedem Fall klar, ob ein Suchergebnis gesponsert war oder es andere Anreize gab, zum anderen wurden in einigen Fällen auch andere Produktvarianten, die sich im Detail unterschieden, mit aufgeführt. Das ist etwa bei einem Fernseher, der bestimmte Features nicht hat, ärgerlich, weil man es erst auf der jeweiligen Website des Händlers erkennt – wenn überhaupt.
Widersprüchliches gab’s auch im Hinblick auf kompliziertere Preise, wie sie im Mobilfunkmarkt üblich sind: So wurden uns bei der Recherche auch die Kaufpreise von Vertragshandys angezeigt, da diese mit subventioniertem Vertrag niedriger liegen als der Kaufpreis für das Gerät.
Sinnvoll ist es daher, die KI bestimmte Informationen, die einem wenig plausibel vorkommen, noch einmal verifizieren zu lassen und dabei sowohl auf eine Websuche zu setzen als auch die jeweilige Uhrzeit und Quelle einzufordern. In einzelnen Fällen hat die KI auch Preisverläufe einfach geschätzt, sodass einzelne Ausreißer nicht mit abgebildet wurden – das sollte man ihr deshalb generell untersagen.
Blind vertrauen sollte man der KI aber vor allem auch nicht bei den Preisangaben und bei den gefundenen Händlern. Denn in einigen Fällen wurden Versandkosten unterschlagen oder das Produkt war erst deutlich verzögert lieferbar. Und einige der recherchierten Shops verwiesen auf wenig vertrauenswürdige Händler.

articles.title: The open-source movement wants Jensen Huang back
articles.text:
The open-source movement wants Jensen Huang back
Supporters are signing a petition to reinstate Huang. But findings on Nvidia chips in China and a new Commerce rule are threatening open-source AI’s reputation and progress regardless.
This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here.
On Friday, a petition to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO of Nvidia began circulating on social media, and by Monday it listed some notable signatories, including Elon Musk and several influential Nvidia researchers. But comb through the more than 115,000 names and you’ll notice a significant faction of Huang’s supporters—higher-ups from Hugging Face, a hub for sharing AI models, and venture capital firms Andreessen Horowitz and Sequoia Capital—come from a particular slice of the tech world.
These names have a vested interest in the development of open-source AI, models that, unlike ChatGPT or Claude, can be downloaded and run independent of large tech companies. Supporters of such models say that concentrating AI in the hands of a few powerful companies will leave everyone else worse off (a concern that wouldn’t sound out of place among the AI industry's critics on the left, if so many open-source advocates weren’t also venture capitalists who stand to profit when startups can build on cheaper AI without paying Big Tech).
Huang had become a sort of ringleader for those who defend open source to policymakers against concerns that such models come with no guardrails and cede AI leadership to China, where the most powerful and popular open-source models are created. They now want their most influential voice returned to his post.
But it’s not just Huang’s extramarital affairs that threaten his (and Nvidia’s) credibility as an advocate for open-source AI. New research into China’s startups using Nvidia’s chips, and a new rule from the US Department of Commerce announced Monday, could deal a blow to both the movement’s reputation and its technical progress.
On Thursday, the day Huang resigned, ex-OpenAI researcher Will DePue published findings online suggesting that China’s AI companies had far more access to Nvidia’s advanced Blackwell chips than previously estimated. China is banned from accessing Nvidia’s most cutting-edge chips to help protect America’s AI lead.
It’s unclear how they would have gained access to the chips. DePue claims the results were verified by senior researchers at OpenAI and Anthropic, but an independent analysis has not confirmed the results. (DePue did not respond to a request for an interview. Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment.)
The findings do not establish that Nvidia helped Chinese companies obtain the chips, and the broader problem of chip smuggling was already known to extend well beyond Nvidia’s control.
But in suggesting that Nvidia may have profited from the rise of Chinese AI startups, whose models are increasingly being used by American companies instead of domestic alternatives, the findings do leave Huang in an awkward position. He has championed open-source AI as a way to strengthen American technological leadership. “Without open source, startups can’t thrive, university researchers can’t do research, you can’t teach AI, scientists can’t use AI,” he said last December during a talk about helping the US win the AI race against China.
It also makes the idea of reinstating Huang even more of a long shot. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent even said last week that Nvidia should not consider someone from inside the company to replace him. The new findings lower Huang’s chances further.
What happens next? Nvidia announced in September it would acquire Hugging Face for nearly $13 billion. Its support for open source also serves a straightforward financial interest: The more businesses that build their own models instead of forking over money to Anthropic and OpenAI, the more chips Nvidia can sell.
But a new rule from the US Department of Commerce could mean the models popular on Hugging Face will soon stop getting smarter. The rule aims to prevent Chinese companies from training models on Nvidia chips that they can’t own directly, but that they can access remotely in data centers in countries like Malaysia—a workaround that has helped China’s open-source models get so good.
The open-source world rallied around Huang because of his influence on policymakers. That was important, since the rise of China’s open-source models has splintered some in Trump’s orbit. If Huang is out, who is next?

articles.title: 4 éoliennes au lieu de 40 : la preuve spectaculaire des progrès de l'éolien en 28 ans — Frandroid
articles.text:
La multiplication des éoliennes à l’horizon n’est peut-être pas une fatalité. Si l’heure est toujours au déploiement de nouvelles capacités renouvelables, y compris pour l’éolien, les évolutions technologiques devraient permettre de rendre la transition énergétique plus discrète.
On en trouve un bon exemple au nord-ouest de la péninsule ibérique, dans la Bretagne espagnole, à savoir la Galice. L’une des régions les plus venteuses d’Espagne accueille le parc éolien de Coriscada, exploité par Endesa sur les communes de Mañón et Ortigueira, et dont l’énergéticien a lancé la modernisation fin septembre. Installé en 1998, ce parc est un témoignage de ce qui se faisait de mieux à l’époque. Il affichait une puissance cumulée de 24 MW grâce à la bagatelle de… 40 turbines ! Jusqu’ici, elles produisaient près de 47 GWh par an.
Du 10 au 30 novembre, le YUKA mini 2 500 passe à 599 € au lieu de 799 € ! Plug & Play, sans fil périmétrique à enterrer, zéro installation prise de tête. Bref, déballez, lancez, et dites adieu à la tonte !
Seulement voilà, en presque 30 ans, la technologie des éoliennes a fait un sacré bond en avant. De ce fait, les 40 éoliennes actuelles laissent la place à seulement 4 machines de 7 MW chacune, soit 28 MW installés contre 24 MW aujourd’hui ; la puissance injectée sur le réseau restera toutefois plafonnée à 24 MW, comme avant. Grâce à une plus grande capacité à fonctionner par vent faible, la production devrait en revanche croître de 78,5 % selon Endesa, pour atteindre presque 84 GWh par an.
Le chantier, mené par Endesa via sa filiale Enel Green Power España, doit s’étaler sur toute l’année 2027 : les essais des nouvelles machines sont prévus fin 2027, pour une mise en service complète en mars 2028. Endesa y consacre 36,3 millions d’euros, dont jusqu’à 6,79 millions d’euros d’aides publiques versées par l’IDAE, l’agence espagnole de l’énergie, dans le cadre du plan de relance.
    À lire aussi : 
8 500 éoliennes et panneaux solaires en accès libre : la boulette européenne
Le repowering est de plus en plus fréquent
Le renouvellement des premières générations d’éoliennes tend à s’accélérer à mesure que les années défilent. Désormais, il n’est pas rare de tomber sur des turbines qui dépassent la vingtaine d’années, en particulier en Espagne. Au tournant du millénaire, le pays était considéré comme pionnier des énergies renouvelables. Pour maintenir ces sites en production, plusieurs exploitants ont déjà sauté le pas : rien qu’en 2025, sept parcs ont été rééquipés, avec 20 éoliennes à la place de 147, selon l’Asociación Empresarial Eólica (AEE).
Selon l’Anuario Eólico 2026 de l’AEE, 9,77 GW des 32,9 GW éoliens installés en Espagne tournent depuis plus de 20 ans. Coriscada n’est d’ailleurs pas une première : à Aldeavieja, dans la province d’Ávila, 22 éoliennes totalisant 14,52 MW ont déjà laissé la place à quatre machines de 24 MW au total.
La technique du repowering consiste à maintenir en service un parc éolien en remplaçant entièrement les éoliennes par de nouveaux modèles. Dans ces conditions, il faut non seulement remplacer les turbines et les mâts mais également les fondations. Finalement, seul le raccordement est laissé tel quel, sauf besoin spécifique d’intervention. Le ministère espagnol de la Transition écologique estime qu’il faudra renouveler entre 10 et 12 GW d’éoliennes d’ici 2030.
À Coriscada, Endesa assure que les 40 éoliennes démontées ne finiront pas à la casse : une partie servira de pièces de rechange sur d’autres parcs du groupe, une autre sera revendue, et ce qui ne peut pas être réutilisé sera valorisé.
