articles.title: Microsoft says months-old bug caused global Microsoft 365 outage
articles.text:
Microsoft says a software bug introduced in July caused last week's worldwide Microsoft 365 outage, triggering a cascading failure that left more than 80% of its networking gateway servers unresponsive.
The nearly 24-hour outage on November 12 disrupted Microsoft 365 services worldwide, including Outlook, Exchange Online, Teams, and Copilot, leaving users unable to access their email and causing significant delays in message delivery.
In a preliminary post-incident report shared in the Microsoft 365 Admin Center, the company said the outage was caused by three problems: a previously undetected software bug, increased traffic after a Microsoft Teams failover, and reduced server capacity.
The incident began at 11:20 AM ET on Thursday, November 12, and continued until 11:10 AM ET the following day, when Microsoft confirmed that services were full restored.
According to Microsoft, the software bug was introduced in July through an update developed for Microsoft 365 networking gateway servers.
While the update had been deployed for more than three months without issues, it contained a bug that could overwhelm servers under certain traffic conditions, causing them to stop responding.
Microsoft says its tests of the update did not detect the bug as it used less powerful testing hardware than the production servers.
"Our normal load testing did not detect the latent issue because the traffic mix and SKUs used in our labs," Microsoft explained in its preliminary report.
"The contention issue is worsened on machines with more cores and newer hardware; whereas our load testing tended to focus on weaker hardware with fewer cores."
The bug was eventually triggered after Microsoft Teams automatically switched to the networking infrastructure used by Exchange Online approximately 15 hours before the outage, increasing traffic on those servers.
Microsoft Teams also experienced a separate outage earlier that day, but it is unclear whether the two incidents are related.
To make matters worse, Microsoft says nearly 14% of the gateway's server capacity was already offline due to an unrelated issue. While the infrastructure had sufficient capacity to handle the reduction, the combination of increased traffic and reduced capacity triggered the software bug.
As servers stopped responding, Microsoft's systems redirected users to other available servers, which also became overwhelmed by the additional traffic and failed as well.
"In less than two hours, the previously unknown defect was encountered across our fleet and rendered them unresponsive. At its lowest, more than 80% of servers were unresponsive," explained Microsoft.
Microsoft says safeguards designed to prevent problems from spreading between regions also failed to contain the cascading outages, allowing the disruption to spread worldwide.
While other Microsoft 365 services, like Teams, OneDrive, and SharePoint, could switch to alternative infrastructure and recover earlier, Exchange Online could not make the same switch, leaving users unable to access their mailboxes.
Microsoft says recovery was difficult because restarting affected servers caused them to be quickly overwhelmed again by backed-up traffic.
After identifying the bug, Microsoft engineers developed a fix and deployed it across affected servers, allowing services to stabilize throughout Friday.
Microsoft confirmed that active customer impact had ended by 11:10 AM ET on November 13.
The company says it has since increased capacity, improved monitoring, and added safeguards to prevent traffic redirection from triggering similar cascading failures.
In a separate statement on X, Charles Lamanna, Microsoft's executive vice president of Copilot, Agents, and Platform, apologized for the disruption.
"We are deeply sorry for the impact to all our customers and recognize the impact that this has on their normal business & operations," Lamanna said.
Microsoft says its investigation is continuing, with a final post-incident report expected later this week.

articles.title: Google selects 10 startups for inaugural Africa Applied AI Lab cohort - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
Google has selected 10 startups for the first cohort of its Google Africa Applied AI Lab, which gives founders early access to Google AI models, technical mentorship and links to venture capital.
Based at the Accra AI Community Centre (AICC) in Ghana, the Google Africa Applied AI Lab is managed by the Google AI Futures Fund alongside Google Research. It aims to support founders from across the continent interested in using the latest AI research to address real-world, uniquely African challenges – and, in turn, “build Africa’s first generation of AI-native unicorn startups”.
Google received thousands of entries from startups across more than 45 African countries, and has now selected 10 to take part in the inaugural cohort.
Three of the selected startups are from Nigeria – Intron, which builds speech recognition that understands African accents and code-switching; Termii, which provides customer verification and messaging for financial services; and Vendy, which lets businesses run storefronts and take payments inside WhatsApp.
Uganda’s Crane AI Labs builds offline AI tools for health workers and schools on affordable phones; Kenya’s Satlyt turns satellites into computing nodes that process data in orbit; and Senegal’s Tolbi combines satellite imagery with voice guidance to help smallholder farmers.
The cohort also includes four pan-African startups. AethexAI provides AI voice agents for banks, telcos and call centres; Agrails builds AI-powered insurance infrastructure for farmers, gig workers and small borrowers; Smile ID uses computer vision for identity verification; and Viamo brings generative AI to feature phone users through voice calls in local languages.
Over the coming weeks, the startups will work with Google engineers, researchers and product leaders, building with models such as Gemini and Gemma. They will also get go-to-market support from the lab’s VC partners – 4DX Ventures, Norrsken22, Novastar Ventures and Ventures Platform.
The programme ends with a demo day at the Accra AI Community Centre in December.

articles.title: Un dogo tiró al suelo a una jubilada y la heredera del dueño del perro deberá pagar una indemnización de $20 millones
articles.text:
El dueño del dogo argentino ha fallecido, por lo que la causa penal quedó archivada. Sin embargo, siguió adelante el proceso civil contra la legataria y la compañía de seguros. Se ha establecido una indemnización de 20.480.000 pesos argentinos con intereses (unos 11.900 euros).
La mujer tenía 75 años cuando ocurrió el incidente en Vicente López (Buenos Aires). La víctima caminaba con su bastón cuando el perro se lanzó sobre ella e hizo que cayera al pavimento. Por las lesiones sufridas, la mujer entabló una acción judicial contra el dueño del perro. Tras su muerte, se ha ampliado contra la legataria.
Las imágenes desmentían a la defensa.
La legataria y la compañía de seguros alegaban que no fue el perro quien hizo que la señora cayera. Aseguraban que estaba atado (con bozal) y que el accidente fue por un tropezón de la jubilada. Sin embargo, las imágenes de las cámaras de seguridad y los testimonios aportados avalan el relato de la demandante.
La pericia médica determinó que sufrió una incapacidad física parcial y permanente mayor al 40 % (con problemas en la cadera). También hay síntomas psicológicos vinculados al suceso. La defensa puso en duda estos resultados, porque podría haber tenido problemas óseos previos. El informe pericial afirma que la caída ha sido el detonante o exacerbante de un problema preexistente (que no se había hecho patente clínicamente).
Responsabilidad por los daños del animal
En Argentina existe un régimen de responsabilidad objetiva por los daños de los animales. Es decir, no es preciso probar la negligencia del dueño para solicitar la reparación por los daños. En este caso, el juzgado estima que está probada la vinculación entre las lesiones y la actuación del perro. Además, la parte demandada no ha probado ningún motivo exoneratorio.
La condena afecta tanto a la legataria como a la compañía de seguros. El importe (a valor de la sentencia) tiene en cuenta distintos aspectos: la incapacidad física, los gastos médicos y de traslado, los de rehabilitación y psicología. También se ha tenido en cuenta el daño moral. A ello hay que sumarle los intereses que establece la resolución.

articles.title: 11,000 applied, 10 made the cut: Meet the UAE-India Start-up Series finalists
articles.text:
11,000 applied, 10 made the cut: Meet the UAE-India Start-up Series finalists
Ten start-ups in AI, climate, deep tech and digital assets, chosen from more than 11,000 applications, pitch in Bengaluru on 18 November for a place in Hub71’s Abu Dhabi programmes.
More than 11,000 Indian start-ups applied to the second edition of the UAE-India Start-up Series. Ten are left. On the afternoon of 18 November in Bengaluru, each will get seven minutes to argue that its business is ready for the UAE: three minutes to pitch and four to answer questions.
The UAE-India Start-up Series helps Indian start-ups enter and scale in the UAE market. It is anchored in the UAE-India Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA), whose start-up provisions call for closer ties between incubators and accelerators in the two countries. Abu Dhabi's technology ecosystem Hub71 is the Series' cross-border partner. Its second edition, the UAE-India Start-up Series 2.0, ends with a two-day Final Pitch Event on 17 and 18 November.
The edition arrives as more Indian founders look to the Gulf for their next market. The UAE offers capital, a route into the wider region and a business culture many Indian companies already know. The harder question, and the one the final will test, is which companies can turn that interest into paying customers there.
From 11,000 applications to ten
The ten finalists come from four sectors: artificial intelligence (three start-ups), energy and climate (three), deep tech and robotics (three) and digital assets (one). They are based across the country, from Bengaluru, Chennai and Pune to Bhubaneswar and West Bengal.
Most are well past the idea stage. Several report revenue in the millions of dollars, and three already sell into the UAE:
- Onsite counts 59 UAE customers among its 1,591 paying customers.
- Flo Mobility has robots working on construction sites for ALEC in the UAE.
- XYMA Analytics has deployed its sensors with Emirates Steel.
The final pitches come after a day and a half of preparation. Finalists will meet investors one-on-one and take part in mentorship and pitch practice. That includes a session led by Hub71 on entering and scaling in the UAE.
The winners will be announced on the night of 18 November, when the Top 50 Investment Dossier will also be released.
The ten finalists
The finalists are listed below in the order they will pitch. Figures are as reported by the companies to the organisers.
What is at stake: a route into Abu Dhabi
The main prize is a place in Hub71's programmes in Abu Dhabi. Hub71 first announced its partnership with the Series in November 2025 and confirmed it for the second edition at its Impact Event in June 2026.
Hub71 Access Programme. Three start-ups will be shortlisted and one will be onboarded. That company gets up to AED 250,000 (about ₹65 lakh) in in-kind incentives and AED 250,000 (about ₹65 lakh) in cash through a SAFE note, an investment that converts into equity at a later funding round. It also receives mentorship, investor introductions, regulatory support and access to Hub71's corporate and government partners.
Hub71 Immersion Programme. Up to six start-ups will spend a week in virtual preparation on the Abu Dhabi and UAE ecosystem. They then spend a week at Hub71 in person, with sessions on market entry and introductions across its partner network. According to the Series website, the UAE leg for selected start-ups begins in March 2027.
What the first edition delivered
The first edition of the Series concluded in New Delhi in 2025, with twenty start-ups pitching in its final. Five of them moved on to Hub71. Endimension, an AI-first radiology platform, joined the Access Programme as part of Cohort 18. BioReform, Docket Run, Data Sutram and SBNRI entered the Immersion Programme.
The second edition has a smaller final and a field that is, on paper, further along. One question to watch is whether the jury backs start-ups that already have UAE customers or those with the most room to grow there. The longer test comes after the event: how many finalists build a lasting presence in the UAE.

articles.title: 3MTT: Nigeria earmarks $3 million to fix its jobs problem
articles.text:
When the Nigerian government launched the 3 Million Technical Talent (3MTT) programme in 2023, it sought to build a workforce that could support the country’s digital economy, fill technical skills gaps and position Nigeria as a global supplier of technology talent. The ambition was to train three million Nigerians within four years, ending in 2027, while connecting them to opportunities locally and internationally.
The programme formed part of the federal government’s wider digital economy strategy under President Bola Tinubu’s Renewed Hope Agenda. Its October 2023 strategic blueprint identified knowledge and technical talent as essential to economic productivity, innovation and job creation.
The ambition extended beyond training. The blueprint said the government intended to retain at least 1.5 million trained professionals in Nigeria and help another 1.5 million access the global talent market, preferably through remote opportunities.
“We have set an ambitious goal to train 3 million early to mid-career technical talents over the next four years,” Bosun Tijani, Minister of Communications, Innovation and Digital Economy, wrote in the blueprint.
But almost three years after its launch, the numbers show a gap between that ambition and what has been delivered. The ministry, in a statement on 11 October, seen by TechCabal, said 179,000 fellows have been trained across four cohorts and the DeepTech programme.
“Since 2023, more than 1.8 million Nigerians have registered on the 3MTT platform, and 179,000 Fellows have been trained across four cohorts and the DeepTech programme,” the statement noted.
The gap between training and employment
Counting its wider community resources and opportunities, the Nigerian government said more than 300,000 Nigerians had benefited, and that the programme had been implemented with more than 200 partner organisations across all 36 states and the Federal Capital Territory (FCT).
Against 3MTT’s three-million target, the 179,000 trained fellows represent nearly 6%, while the broader 300,000 beneficiaries represent 10%, with just over a year remaining ahead of its 2027 deadline. While this does not automatically mean the programme has failed, given that the deadline has not passed, it raises questions about the pace of implementation.
The challenge extends beyond training numbers. The World Bank estimates that about 3.5 million Nigerians enter the labour market annually, intensifying the pressure on the economy to create productive employment. For 3MTT, this makes tracking fellows’ post-training outcomes particularly important: How many have secured jobs, started businesses or found paying freelance work? And, more importantly, are these opportunities generating sustainable incomes?
Without such figures, the government can demonstrate how many people it has trained but not how much the programme has contributed to improving their economic prospects.
TechCabal sought clarification from the Ministry on employment outcomes for fellows that have been trained across previous cohorts. It had not provided answers to these at press time
A shift to employment outcomes
Against this backdrop, the 11 November statement announced that the federal government had opened applications for organisations and individual experts to join the 3MTT Delivery Network, with about ₦4 billion ($2.94 million) earmarked to support verified outcomes in Cohorts 5 and 6.
The network is designed to bring together organisations and individual experts who train Nigerians in digital and technical skills. They will work with 3MTT to help fellows acquire skills that employers need and transition into jobs, freelance work or businesses.
According to the statement, the new model builds on lessons from previous cohorts and shifts the programme away from simply expanding enrolment numbers towards connecting training to verified demand. However, it did not explain what specific implementation challenges emerged from earlier cohorts, which parts of the previous delivery model fell short or how those lessons informed the new structure.
How the government wants to transform 3MTT
Under the 3MTT Delivery Network arrangement, partners can join as Enabled Delivery Partners or Funded Delivery Partners. Both categories are expected to expand the programme’s training capacity, but their responsibilities and access to funding differ.
Enabled Delivery Partners form the wider training network. They include organisations and individual experts, with or without physical training centres. They will have access to the 3MTT Talent Operating System, the National Talent Registry, information about employer skills needs, and other partner resources, including device financing where eligible.
This category of partners will gain access to 3MTT’s national training platform, where they can recruit learners, publish courses and track progress. They can also add graduates to the National Talent Registry, access information on employer skill demands and salaries, reach over 1.8 million registered learners, and tap into learning resources and device financing opportunities, subject to eligibility.
Funded Delivery Partners, on the other hand, must demonstrate demand for the talent they intend to train. This could be for vacancies within their own organisations or placements with clients. They will submit their talent requirements, participate in selecting fellows and receive funding against verified results.
This presents a better way to engage fellows beyond just training.
The funding model is structured around four milestones: learning commenced, skills verified, an economic opportunity secured and that opportunity sustained for six months. This is intended to make funding dependent on progress from training to work, rather than the number of people enrolled alone. The Delivery Network portal outlines the application and verification process.
Cohort 5, according to the announcement, is supported by the European Union and Denmark through the GIZ Digital Transformation Center Nigeria, HAUS, a Finnish public-sector training and development organisation, and ESTDEV, Estonia’s international development cooperation agency, alongside a MacArthur Foundation grant channelled through Blue Sapphire Hub.
“Reaching three million technical talents requires a delivery ecosystem that is responsive to industry demand, accessible across communities and built to scale,” Tijani said. “By tying our support to verified demand and real results, we are strengthening the connection between skills, jobs and economic opportunity, while building the talent pipeline Nigeria needs to compete in the global digital economy.”
The new structure offers a way to bring employers closer to training and give delivery partners clearer incentives to produce work-ready talent. But an important question is how many fellows are currently employed from previous cohorts, against which the new model’s performance can be measured.
3MTT still has time to pursue its ambition. But the measure of its progress must increasingly move beyond how many Nigerians register or complete training. The government must ensure that the 3MTT Delivery Network actually delivers employment outcomes.
Its challenge is no longer just expanding access to technical training. It is ensuring that the skills it produces can find paying markets, whether through salaried employment, freelance contracts or viable businesses. Tying partner funding to verified outcomes gives the programme a way to measure that transition. But the government will have to ensure measurement of evidence of fellows’ employment and income sustainability. The new model remains a promise of better outcomes rather than proof that it can deliver them.

articles.title: Apple manquerait de temps pour corriger le principal défaut de l’iPhone Duo
articles.text:
Parmi les concessions qu’Apple a dû faire pour parvenir à mettre au point l’iPhone Duo, l’absence de Face ID est sans doute celle qui a été le plus regrettée par les utilisateurs (avec l’absence d’un téléobjectif). À la place d’un système de reconnaissance faciale, ils ont eu affaire au bon vieux Touch ID. Un comble pour un appareil qui se veut à la pointe de la technologie, tout en affichant des prix particulièrement élevés. Mais si l’entreprise à la pomme savait dès le départ que ce manquement allait être pointé du doigt, elle compte bien le combler sur les prochaines générations de l’appareil. Seulement voilà, les caractéristiques techniques de l’iPhone Duo de seconde génération doivent être finalisées maintenant, et Apple serait actuellement dans une véritable course contre la montre.
Une course contre la montre pour parvenir à intégrer Face ID à l’iPhone Duo 2
Selon le toujours très bien informé Mark Gurman, journaliste chez Bloomberg, Apple aurait pour objectif de lancer l’iPhone Duo de seconde génération à l’automne 2027. Mais cela ne veut pas dire que l’entreprise bénéficie d’encore un an pour mettre au point l’appareil. En réalité, les caractéristiques matérielles de ce dernier doivent être fixées dès maintenant, c’est-à-dire un an avant sa commercialisation.
En octobre dernier, Mark Gurman avait expliqué qu’Apple travaillait sur plusieurs prototypes d’iPhone Duo 2 intégrant Face ID. Sur ces appareils, le système de reconnaissance faciale d’Apple serait situé sous l’écran externe. Les prototypes existent donc, mais l’entreprise à la pomme parviendra-t-elle à en mettre au point un à temps ? Selon Gurman, Apple serait actuellement face à un calendrier très serré.
Apple n’aurait pas pu prendre en compte les retours des utilisateurs de l’iPhone Duo
Il faut également préciser qu’Apple n’aurait pas été en mesure de prendre en compte les retours des utilisateurs de l’iPhone Duo de première génération pour définir les principales caractéristiques matérielles de son successeur, celles-ci ayant été fixées depuis déjà un certain temps. Par conséquent, si l’iPhone Duo de seconde génération intègre bel et bien Face ID, cela ne sera pas en raison des contestations des utilisateurs. En réalité, Apple était conscient dès le départ de ce manquement, mais n’a pas eu d’autre choix que d’effectuer cette concession afin de mettre au point un écran d’une épaisseur de 5,2 mm lorsqu’il est déplié. Pour rappel, Face ID nécessite une certaine profondeur pour pouvoir fonctionner.
Il reste maintenant à voir si l’entreprise à la pomme parviendra à intégrer de justesse Face ID sur l’iPhone Duo de seconde génération. Dans le cas contraire, il faudra attendre la troisième génération. Dans tous les cas, il s’agit de la priorité d’Apple pour son iPhone pliant.

articles.title: Nvidia no ha despedido a Jensen Huang: ha aceptado su dimisión, y esa diferencia abre la puerta a su vuelta
articles.text:
Hace un año, Huang resumió así su longevidad como CEO: “primero: no ser despedido”. Ha cumplido la regla hasta su último minuto en NVIDIA. El 11 de noviembre el consejo de NVIDIA aceptó su dimisión como CEO y consejero. No lo despidió: aceptó su dimisión. Es distinto y tiene implicaciones.
Qué ha ocurrido. Tres días antes, el consejo había abierto una investigación porque Huang había sido objetivo de una operación de inteligencia extranjera, y había dicho que confiaba en él. El martes ya no. Colette Kress, la directora financiera, es CEO interina, y NVIDIA no tiene sucesor. Busca uno, interno o externo.
Entre líneas. El analista Gene Munster ha subido del 10% al 51% las probabilidades de que Huang vuelva. Su argumento es que el consejo le forzó a dimitir, y que esa forma de salir permite que la readmisión sea más sencilla, ya que no implica una admisión de que el consejo se equivocó.
Si en 72 horas pasó de “confiamos en Jensen” a enseñarle la puerta de salida, la tortilla puede volver a girar igual de rápido.
Sí, pero. La palabra elegida cuenta poco:
- Steve Jobs también dimitió, en 1985, después de que le quitaran todas sus funciones. Volvió doce años después, cuando Apple, al borde de la quiebra, compró NeXT.
- Sam Altman fue despedido en medio de un sainete en 2023. Volvió en cinco días porque más de 700 de los 770 empleados de OpenAI amenazaron con irse si no volvía.
Lo que decide estos casos es quién puede presionar al consejo.
En juego. Huang ha reunido muchos apoyos en un solo fin de semana:
- Una petición con más de 100.000 firmas –no verificadas–, entre ellas las de Musk y Tim Sweeney, y según los organizadores las de más de 5.000 empleados.
- Trump ya manifestó su voluntad de que Huang continuara al frente.
- Una carta de Gerstner (Altimeter) y Baker (Atreides). Las acciones de ambos combinadas valen más de 2.000 millones de dólares.
- Una norma de los estatutos que permite a accionistas con el 15% de los votos convocar una junta y cambiar el consejo.
Al otro lado. Scott Bessent, secretario del Tesoro estadounidense, ha pedido un CEO externo. No es una voz cualquiera. Y la investigación sobre Megaspeed, cliente de NVIDIA con sede en Singapur y sospechosa de desviar chips a China, sigue abierta. Si esa investigación encuentra algo, posiblemente dará igual cómo se llamara a la salida de Huang.
El aviso. Travis Kalanick dimitió en Uber en 2017 y más de 1.100 empleados pidieron que volviera. Pero no volvió, porque los grandes inversores querían que se largara. En NVIDIA muchos de los grandes quieren justo lo contrario: que se quede.
La primera prueba llega mañana, martes 17: los resultados son de un trimestre con Huang al mando, pero la previsión y la posterior conferencia con analistas serán ya sin él. Una previsión floja y unas respuestas poco convincentes a los analistas darían argumentos a quienes piden su vuelta. Será o seró.
Imagen destacada | Xataka con Magnific
En Xataka | Jensen Huang ha salvado a NVIDIA seis veces. La séptima crisis es él mismo y le ha costado el puesto

articles.title: Old Bitly links hijacked in X posts from Trump, McDonald's, Burger King, and others
articles.text:
In context: Back when tweets were capped at 140 characters, brands and politicians ran most of their links through Bitly to shrink them down. That's why years of old posts on X are still full of tiny bit.ly addresses. Click one, and the service quietly forwards you to the full web page sitting behind it. Most people wouldn't think twice before doing that. Over the weekend, pranksters managed to take over some of those old links in posts from Donald Trump, McDonald's and Burger King.
CNN found that Trump's account was hit the hardest. At least a dozen of his posts now carry swapped links, including a 2013 complaint about wind turbines. Open it today, and you'll land on a Google site called "fortnite baby," complete with a photo of an infant.
Over at Burger King, a 2011 post meant to help people find nearby restaurants now leads to Wikipedia's list of Nazi concentration camps. McDonald's didn't escape either – one of its 2011 posts now opens a page about the September 11 attacks.
Bill Gates, former Canadian prime minister Justin Trudeau and Mike Pence all had old posts tampered with as well. Weirdly, the FBI's 2012 post about its "Ghost Clicks" case now just shows a photo of a seal.
In theory, none of this should be possible. Bitly's own help pages say the code at the end of a short link can never be reused, even after the account that created it gets deleted.
The company acknowledged the problem on Sunday, saying it had found an issue that let bad actors "repurpose certain old, inactive links." It has since suspended the accounts behind the changes and is working to disable the affected URLs.
Back in February 2025, crypto scammers used a Bitly bug to point some of Trump's old tweets at memecoin pages. The company patched it at the time, but this weekend's redirects seem to suggest a similar hole stayed open.
This time, most of the redirects look like plain trolling with no obvious money angle. Even so, Carnegie Mellon digital media professor Ari Lightman told CNN that this kind of tampering is risky. Plenty of old accounts go unmonitored, he noted, and a swapped link on one of them could expose the information of anyone who clicks it.
By comparison, when Google switched off its inactive goo.gl links last year, they simply started returning errors. A hijacked link is a different problem since it keeps working and quietly sends people somewhere new.

articles.title: ElecWave Debuts Foldable KF01 Keyboard
articles.text:
Monday, November 16th 2026
ElecWave Debuts Foldable KF01 Keyboard
ElecWave today announced its brand debut with the launch of its first product, the ElecWave KF01 foldable keyboard. Guided by its brand slogan, "Convenient, No Compromise," ElecWave believes that working from anywhere should not mean compromising on typing comfort or productivity. Backed by the group behind global brands including Tribit and Ohuhu, and drawing on 20 years of iClever keyboard engineering expertise, ElecWave brings that promise to life with the KF01, a travel-friendly foldable keyboard that combines a full-size typing layout, comfortable scissor-switch keys, multi-device connectivity, and long battery life
As working on the go becomes increasingly common, professionals need the flexibility to stay productive in offices, cafés, and while traveling. Although foldable phones and dual-screen devices offer more screen space, typing directly on them can still be slow and frustrating. Even laptops such as MacBooks lack a built-in numeric keypad, which can make spreadsheet work and data entry less efficient. The ElecWave KF01 addresses these challenges with a full-size, desktop-style typing experience in a compact, foldable design, turning a desk, airplane tray table, or café counter into a practical workspace."As someone who frequently works on the go, I was frustrated by the trade-off in foldable keyboards: if a keyboard was compact enough to travel with, it was usually too cramped for productive typing," said Sam, founder and CEO of ElecWave. "Today, the world is our workspace, whether you're finishing a report on a flight, answering emails at a local café, or extending a business trip for leisure. Working on the go shouldn't mean compromising on comfort or speed. We built ElecWave on a simple principle: to deliver full-size typing performance wherever life and work take you."
Foldable Portability, Uncompromised Typing
As ElecWave's debut keyboard, the KF01 combines full-size typing comfort with a travel-friendly foldable design. When folded, it measures just 7.48 × 4.91 × 0.91 inches, with a footprint comparable to that of an iPad mini, making it easy to carry in a work bag or backpack. Unfolded, it measures 14.63 × 4.91 × 0.47 inches and features a full-size layout, standard-size keycaps, and an integrated numeric keypad for more efficient typing and data entry. Low-profile scissor-switch keys provide responsive tactile feedback and a comfortable, quiet typing experience. Together, these features help users maintain familiar typing habits across different work environments.
Boosted Productivity, Lasting Power
Designed for multi-device workflows, the ElecWave KF01 can pair with up to three devices via Bluetooth, allowing users to switch between them as needed. With dedicated Mac and Windows key layouts and automatic operating system recognition, it supports familiar keyboard functions across Windows, macOS, iOS, and Android. Dedicated screenshot and emoji shortcuts further streamline everyday tasks.
The KF01 features USB-C charging and is designed to minimize interruptions throughout the workday. Its battery supports up to 100 hours of continuous use, up to 180 days of standby time, or approximately two months of regular office typing between charges. To conserve power, an automatic sleep feature activates after two hours of inactivity; the keyboard wakes with a keystroke.
Pricing and Availability
The ElecWave KF01 is now available on Amazon, starting at $39.99.

articles.title: How Duco transforms financial data automation with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
How Duco transforms financial data automation with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
Financial institutions face a critical challenge: processing massive volumes of data with speed, accuracy, and compliance while operating under some of the world’s strictest regulatory frameworks. Duco is the agentic Operations platform for financial services, serving tier-one banks and other financial institutions. It processes 20 billion transactions monthly for 200+ clients, including 7 of the top 20 banks and 10 of the top 20 asset managers. To keep pace as data processing demands grew, Duco evolved from traditional machine learning models to the agentic AI capabilities of Amazon Bedrock and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. In this post, we share how Duco rebuilt its agentic AI stack on these services, cutting deployment time and onboarding costs while keeping each bank’s data isolated.
The challenge: Scaling intelligence in a regulated environment
Duco’s platform empowers teams to automate mission-critical data processes using AI and no-code models, handling everything from data extraction to downstream publication. It already used traditional machine learning models for predictive labeling and pattern recognition, helping banks consolidate and automate over 20,000 processes.
However, these classical machine learning approaches had inherent limitations. They required extensive historical data for training, struggled with novel scenarios, and demanded significant customization for each new use case. Most critically, they couldn’t adapt quickly to the diverse, constantly evolving data formats and business rules that characterize modern financial operations.
        “The classical prediction models worked to an extent, but they weren’t agile or flexible enough. Traditional machine learning models can only amplify what they’ve already learned — they can’t help with the next step or find new problems.”
— Rob Gates, Chief Architect and Innovation Officer, Duco
The solution: Amazon Bedrock and Bedrock AgentCore
Duco made a strategic decision to adopt Amazon Bedrock for managed access to foundation models, and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore to run agents at scale. This was more than a technology upgrade. It was a fundamental shift in how its system could understand, reason about, and act on financial data.
About Amazon Bedrock and Bedrock AgentCore
Amazon Bedrock is a fully managed service that offers a choice of high-performing foundation models from leading AI companies through a single API, along with a broad set of capabilities to build generative AI applications with security, privacy, and responsible AI. Learn more about Amazon Bedrock.
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is the platform to build, connect, and optimize AI agents at scale. Build with any open source framework and any model. Connect agents to your tools and data with authentication and access controls built in. Monitor and improve agents in production with tracing and evaluation. AgentCore handles the infrastructure so you focus on agent logic, not backend plumbing, and you get enterprise security and reliability without giving up open source flexibility.
Learn more on the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore product page.
Why Amazon Bedrock?
Several factors made Amazon Bedrock the ideal choice for Duco’s regulated financial services industry (FSI) environment:
- Security and compliance first: With Amazon Bedrock, customer data stays within the AWS environment, and it is not used to train models. With private endpoints in its virtual private cloud (VPC), Duco can connect to internal systems while keeping them completely isolated, which matters for sensitive financial data processing.
- Model flexibility: Access to leading foundation models from the Amazon Nova 2 family, Anthropic, OpenAI, Cohere, Meta, and Mistral AI through a single API means Duco can choose the right model for each task. Duco can switch between models by changing a configuration parameter.
- Built for financial services: Amazon Bedrock provides the robust governance controls and compliance frameworks that financial services require, avoiding infrastructure complexity while maintaining the security standards tier-one banks demand.
Choosing AgentCore as the runtime
Duco’s existing agent infrastructure was built on LangChain and LangGraph, both of which were already in production. When evaluating runtime options for its agentic workloads, AgentCore emerged as the clear choice for three key reasons:
- Compatibility with existing primitives: AgentCore is fully compatible with Duco’s existing LangChain and LangGraph code, so most existing code continued to work without modification.
- Managed runtime: Instead of Duco running its own agent infrastructure, AgentCore provides a fully managed runtime, reducing operational overhead for the engineering team.
- Regulated environment suitability: AgentCore met the stringent requirements of deploying in regulated financial services environments, with built-in security and compliance controls.
Multi-tenant architecture: Isolation by design
Duco’s platform operates as a multi-tenant software as a service (SaaS) offering with strict tenant isolation (figure 1). This is a non-negotiable requirement for regulated institutions. The architecture reflects this at every layer, from the underlying cloud infrastructure right up to the AI agent runtime.
Infrastructure layer
- Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) clusters with namespace-per-tenant isolation and network segregation help maintain workload separation at the Kubernetes layer.
- Per-tenant dedicated AWS services: every tenant receives a dedicated Amazon Aurora MySQL database, Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) storage bucket, AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) encryption keys, Amazon Simple Email Service (Amazon SES) and Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) messaging stack, Amazon ElastiCache layer, and Amazon Cognito user pool. Zero shared data infrastructure across clients.
- Per-tenant autoscaling helps minimize the impact of one client’s compute-intensive workload on another tenant’s performance.
Security and access control
Isolation is enforced through identity as well as infrastructure, with every hop between the user and their data authenticated (figure 2):
- Tenant-scoped authentication: every request carries a JSON Web Token (JWT) issued by the tenant’s dedicated Cognito user pool, validated by the inbound authorizer of the AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, before agent logic runs.
- Gateway-mediated tool access: agents reach tools only through the tenant’s dedicated AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, which passes calls through to the tenant’s container-based Model Context Protocol (MCP) services running in Amazon EKS.
- End-to-end user identity: the user’s identity is passed through to downstream services, and each MCP server validates both the agent’s and the user’s identity against the tenant’s Cognito user pool, so every tool call is authorized as the calling user, made by a trusted agent.
- Private networking: tenants share a VPC and Amazon EKS cluster, segregated by namespace and network policy, with private endpoints keeping traffic to Amazon Bedrock and AgentCore on the AWS network. Each tenant’s AgentCore runtime runs in VPC network mode, with network interfaces in the private subnets, so its outbound traffic enters the VPC and is governed by security groups.
Agent layer
The isolation principle extends fully into the agent architecture:
- One AgentCore runtime and Gateway per tenant: each tenant is served by a dedicated runtime and Gateway, configured against that tenant’s own Cognito user pool and Amazon EKS namespace. Combined with the built-in session isolation of AgentCore, this means there is no shared memory, context, or tooling between clients. Each bank’s unique schemas, naming conventions, and institutional knowledge remain completely isolated from other tenants.
- Per-tenant MCP servers: each tenant has its own set of MCP servers providing service-specific capabilities, dynamically discovered at boot time.
The architecture helps maintain a model where each agent only has access to one bank’s data, context, and reasoning, facilitating real isolation of context across banks.
Multi-model strategy
Rather than committing to a single foundation model, Duco uses the right model for each job, assigning each role in its agent design to the model best suited to it. This approach delivers both quality and cost efficiency by matching the right model capability to each specific workload:
| Model | Primary role | Use cases | 
| Anthropic Claude Opus | Planning agent | For complex reasoning and understanding, formulating up front plans for other agents to execute on | 
| Anthropic Claude Sonnet | Main reasoning & complex decision-making | Exception investigation, reconciliation logic, rule interpretation | 
| Anthropic Claude Haiku | Lightweight tool routing decisions | Fast routing choices, low-latency classification, cost-efficient first-pass triage | 
| Amazon Nova 2 Pro | Tool output summarization | Condensing MCP tool responses, generating readable summaries for analysts | 
This multi-model approach is architecturally designed to allow model swapping without disrupting the stack, which is critical in a landscape where model capabilities evolve rapidly.
Solving context bloat: The MCP skills architecture
One of Duco’s most significant technical innovations addresses a challenge familiar to anyone building production agent systems: context window management.
The problem
With 300–400 tools exposed per tenant through AgentCore Gateway (which fronts a separate MCP server for each underlying Duco service), approximately 200,000 tokens of tool descriptions were loaded into context before work began. This caused context overloading: response quality degraded as conversations lengthened, and the model lost the thread of earlier reasoning. The team emphasized that a feeling an agent is becoming less capable isn’t enough evidence on its own. Evaluations must be run before engineering decisions are made.
The solution: On-demand skills loading
Duco created a skills architecture using MCP resource types to move tool descriptions out of the static context and load them only when needed:
- skill:// resources — on-demand tool descriptions loaded only when a skill is required.
- system:// resources — dynamic system prompt sections composed at runtime, keeping the base system prompt lean.
- ui:// resources — UI-specific resources, isolated from operational tooling.
Three new meta-tools, implemented in Duco’s agent harness, replaced the bloated tool description payload:
- load_skill — fetches skill descriptions on demand, only when the agent determines a skill is needed.
- find_tool — locates relevant tools without loading all schemas into context.
- invoke_tool — executes the selected tool once identified.
The results
- 90% context reduction: Main context reduced from 200,000 tokens to approximately 20,000 tokens by moving tool descriptions out of static context and limiting the size of tool responses.
- Prompt caching preserved: the static prompt prefix (system prompt plus the three meta-tools) stays small and stable, and skills load into the conversation rather than the tool list, so loading a skill does not invalidate the cache.
- Measurably improved agent response quality: validated through a rigorous evaluation framework.
- Zero infrastructure changes required: same underlying models, same tools, and same tasks, with measurably better outcomes.
MCP tool discovery: Deploy a service, gain a capability
A key architectural decision was implementing MCP tool discovery at boot time. When a new service is deployed, its MCP server is registered as a target on the tenant’s AgentCore Gateway as part of the deployment. When an agent boots, the harness builds a registry of every tool the Gateway exposes and shares just the tool names. The agent then uses find_tool and invoke_tool to discover the details and invoke tools on demand. As a result, the agent automatically gains that capability with no redeployment or agent reconfiguration required. Access control is enforced by the underlying services themselves: because the user’s identity is passed through the Gateway, each tool call succeeds only if that user is permitted to perform the action.
This provides operational agility: the platform team can ship new capabilities to agents by deploying a new microservice, without touching the agent configuration or requiring downtime. For a platform that serves 200+ clients with diverse and evolving operational needs, this dynamic capability model is a significant competitive advantage.
Deploying agents at scale
Duco implemented Amazon Bedrock and Bedrock AgentCore to power two critical workflows that previously required extensive manual effort:
1. Intelligent onboarding
Previously, onboarding new reconciliation processes was a manual, time-intensive exercise requiring significant professional services resources. Banks would take years to migrate thousands of processes, moving at a pace of roughly one per week.
With Amazon Bedrock and Bedrock AgentCore, Duco can now:
- Automatically understand diverse file formats and data structures across legacy and modern systems.
- Translate legacy configurations from existing systems into structured Duco processes.
- Parse complex spreadsheet macros written decades ago that no one fully understands.
- Deploy new reconciliations 10× faster than before.
One global bank experienced a 70% decrease in onboarding costs for new reconciliations and achieved an increase of over 20% in straight-through processing through better match rates and allocation rules.
2. AI-driven exception investigation
Financial institutions run thousands of quality gates between systems, generating countless exceptions daily. Traditionally, armies of analysts manually investigate each break to determine if it’s worth worrying about, already being investigated, or represents a new risk.
Duco’s agents now handle the “first mile” of investigation:
- Triage new breaks as they arrive, grouping related exceptions that share a likely root cause.
- Check context, such as whether a break is already known, already being worked, or a timing difference expected to clear.
- Investigate by pulling evidence from source data and systems to trace the root cause of each inconsistency, whether a data quality issue, a missing or late record, a mapping or reference data problem, or a genuine mismatch, and explain why it happened.
- Recommend a decision-ready case: the likely cause, a proposed resolution such as an adjustment, a rule change, or an escalation, the alternatives considered, and the supporting evidence.
- Route each case to the right analyst, who reviews the evidence and makes the final call, with every decision recorded in the audit trail.
This agentic approach excels because financial workflows involve highly variable paths through information, exactly the kind of complex, context-heavy reasoning that foundation models handle well.
Operating in a regulated environment
Deploying AI agents in financial services requires more than technical capability. It demands rigorous compliance, auditability, and risk management. Duco’s implementation on Amazon Bedrock addresses these requirements through four core principles:
- Comprehensive observability: Every agent decision is logged in a complete audit trail. Reviewers can trace each decision to check it against regulatory requirements.
- Human-in-the-loop controls: High-risk actions require explicit authorization, with clear escalation pathways for complex scenarios that exceed agent confidence thresholds.
- Fail-safe architecture: Systems default to client protection over operational efficiency, supporting safety even when agents encounter edge cases or unexpected data.
- Regulatory alignment: The platform supports workloads subject to SOC 2 and DORA requirements, with data residency controls per institution.
Results that matter
Duco’s adoption of Amazon Bedrock has delivered measurable, auditable business impact across client deployments:
| 10× Faster reconciliation deployments | 70% Reduction in onboarding costs | 20%+ Increase in straight-through processing | 1000s Hours saved in manual investigation | 
Perhaps most importantly, Duco now has a foundation for rapid innovation. Building new agentic capabilities no longer requires extensive machine learning engineering, so the team can focus on solving business problems rather than managing infrastructure.
Roadmap: The future of human–agent collaboration
Duco’s architecture is designed not to replace workers, but to elevate them. The platform envisions a clear progression in human roles as agentic capabilities mature:
Task Worker → Investigator → Decision Maker
Rather than humans performing repetitive tasks, the future sees operations teams orchestrating multiple agents in parallel with humans making final approval decisions based on agent-prepared analysis. The architecture is designed to support agent-to-agent communication, including cross-firm scenarios where agents at different financial institutions could coordinate.
Conclusion
For regulated financial institutions, Duco’s architecture shows that agentic AI isn’t only viable. It’s already delivering at production scale. Duco rebuilt its agentic AI stack on Amazon Bedrock and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, combining strict per-tenant isolation, the right model for each job, and an MCP skills architecture that cut context overhead by 90%. The results include reconciliation deployments 10× faster and, for one global bank, onboarding costs down 70% and straight-through processing up by over 20%. To build a similar multi-tenant setup, start with the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Developer Guide, then read Building multi-tenant agents with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore on the AWS Machine Learning Blog. For the operating model behind this work, see Duco’s Agentic Operations: a new operating model for post-trade.

articles.title: Mercedes' clever new driving assist handles complex traffic like a champ
articles.text:
SAN FRANCISCO—When Ars first drove the new Mercedes-Benz CLA last year, the automaker also gave us a sneak preview of its next driver assist. Called Drive Assist Pro, it’s for collaborative partially assisted driving, and from the passenger seat at the time, the demo was impressive. Now the automaker is getting ready to start rolling out Drive Assist Pro to customers with cars running the new MB.OS operating system here in the US and in Germany, and it let us have some time behind the wheel.
While most automakers want a reputation for safety, Mercedes has long used passive and active technology to do so in its products. It was one of the first OEMs to introduce airbags, and a decade later started adding active safety systems like anti-lock brakes, electronic stability control, and adaptive cruise control. And so, by giving the car’s electronics the ability to control the brakes and throttle, we arrive at the first level of assisted driving—called “level 1” in automotive engineer-speak.
“Level 2” assisted driving, where the car also controls the steering as well as the acceleration and braking, got famous with Tesla Autopilot. But the first lane-keeping assists predate it by almost a decade in passenger cars, when Toyota introduced a system in 2004. The human driver behind the wheel is still in charge, responsible for situational awareness (and anything that arises from a lack thereof), with the idea that long drives become less tiring and a little more effortless when the car does the boring job of keeping a constant speed or a constant distance to the car ahead and between the white lines.
3? No, +, ++
The next step, numerically at least, should be level 3, where we move from assisted driving to partially automated driving; here the car takes over the task of driving fully under some circumstances, like heavy traffic. But that’s getting ahead of ourselves—the main developments over the past few years have been the inelegantly named “L2+” systems that combine more advanced driver monitoring with a higher degree of assistance, usually on geofenced highways.

articles.title: Samsung pode deixar câmera com abertura variável para o Galaxy S28 • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Samsung pode deixar câmera com abertura variável para o Galaxy S28
Recurso chegou a ser cogitado para o Galaxy S27, mas custo pode empurrar retorno para 2028.
A Apple trouxe para o iPhone 18 Pro a câmera principal com abertura variável pela primeira vez e o movimento reacendeu rumores de que a Samsung faria o mesmo no próximo flagship. Especulava-se que já veríamos o retorno da tecnologia na sul-coreana no ano que vem, agora, porém, podemos ter de esperar até o Galaxy S28.
Segundo o informante Yogesh Brar, a fabricante trabalha para levar a lente com abertura variável aos modelos Galaxy S28 Pro e Galaxy S28 Ultra, em 2028. Os planos teriam mudado devido ao custo do componente e ao espaço adicional necessário dentro do smartphone.
Como ainda falta mais de um ano para a possível estreia dos aparelhos, o site Android Authority ressalta que os planos podem mudar durante o desenvolvimento.
A fabricante adotou uma câmera com abertura física ajustável no Galaxy S9, em 2018, e só a manteve na família até a geração seguinte. Na época, um pequeno mecanismo permitia alternar entre duas aberturas, melhorando ajustes como a exposição e profundidade de campo.
Uma permite maior permite que mais luz chegue ao sensor, algo útil especialmente em ambientes escuros, enquanto a abertura mais fechada reduz a quantidade de luz e aumenta a região da imagem que permanece em foco.
O mecanismo desapareceu da linha mais cara da marca a partir do Galaxy S20, em 2020. O motivo teria sido o mesmo do adiamento atual: reduzir custos de produção e o espaço físico ocupado pelo conjunto.
A possibilidade de uma câmera com abertura variável voltar aos Galaxy começou a ganhar força após relatos de que a empresa havia procurado fornecedores para desenvolver novos módulos. Segundo informações anteriores, a fabricante avaliava a tecnologia como uma forma de melhorar a competitividade das câmeras dos celulares mais avançados, avanço que tem sido exigido pelo público da Samsung nos últimos modelos.
A expectativa inicial era que o trabalho resultasse em um componente pronto para o Galaxy S27, mas, de acordo com Brar, incorporar o sistema elevaria o custo de fabricação. A companhia já tem elevado o preço final dos aparelhos continuamente devido a crise de componentes de memória.
Brar afirma ainda que a Samsung não é a única fabricante estudando esse tipo de solução para futuros celulares de alto desempenho. O possível retorno acompanha a aparição da tecnologia em smartphones avançados de outras marcas.
A Apple adotou o recurso na câmera principal da linha iPhone 18 Pro, seguindo a Huawei, que trouxe a abertura variável no Pura 80 Ultra — ambos disponíveis no Brasil, por preços a partir de R$ 11.999 e 12.999, respectivamente.
As primeiras informações sobre a família Galaxy S28 já começaram a aparecer mesmo antes do lançamento do Galaxy S27, previsto para o primeiro semestre do ano que vem. Rumores passados da cadeia de suprimentos já nos dão sinais ao menos sobre o chip que o aparelho deve carregar.
Segundo o ZDNet Korea, a Samsung desenvolve o Exynos 2800, previsto para a geração de 2028. Os vazamentos apontam que, em vez de migrar imediatamente para um processo de 1,4 nanômetro, a Samsung estaria planejando continuar refinando sua tecnologia de 2 nm para o Exynos 2800.
A intenção seria priorizar a estabilidade da produção e evitar problemas de aquecimento enfrentados por gerações anteriores da família Exynos.

articles.title: Cursor Supply Chain Attack Started at Fireworks AI
articles.text:
Credentials compromised in the hack of AI inference platform Fireworks AI allowed attackers to steal more secrets and push malicious Claude Code extension copies, Cursor says.
The supply chain attack was discovered on October 29 and resulted in threat actors making two modified versions of the anthropic.claude-code extension (2.1.312 and 2.1.313) available through the Cursor VS Code Extension Marketplace for roughly 11 hours.
Anthropic was never hacked, and all the malicious activity occurred in Cursor’s environment, the company explains.
Instead, Cursor was hit after Fireworks was hacked twice in October. First, internal Fireworks credentials were used to access Fireworks stored secrets and account and billing information. Then, a third-party cloud provider was compromised, Fireworks development machines were reached, and customer data was stolen.
A Cursor access key issued to Fireworks was compromised in one of these incidents and the attacker used it to copy data from a read-only storage bucket, including unredacted credentials that opened the door to SaaS tools used by Cursor.
“From these tools they accessed select archived non-production Cursor source code repositories (some containing business contact information), limited customer support data and email conversations, product usage metrics and contact details, summaries of some coding agent conversations, and some credentials users had sent to the Cursor support team,” Cursor explains.
While Cursor blocked the attacker’s access immediately after discovering the unauthorized activity, the attacker used secrets exfiltrated from the company’s internal systems to place “malicious, unauthorized copies of Anthropic’s Claude Code extension directly on the cache used to serve the Cursor VS Code extension marketplace.”
The malware was never present in the Open VSX marketplace source, but was served to the users who requested the cached versions of the extension. According to Cursor, at most 5,000 users were affected.
“If customers installed or updated to the tampered version Anthropic.claude-code 2.1.312 or 2.1.313 from the Cursor VS Code extension marketplace during the exposure window, we ask customers to follow the steps in our security notice. Uninstalling the extension alone may not be enough,” Cursor notes.
The company considers the incident contained, as it has not seen attacker activity in its environment since November 1.
Notion and Uber also disclosed data breaches stemming from the Fireworks compromise.

articles.title: OpenAI will embed safety researchers to investigate AI subversion | TechCrunch
articles.text:
OpenAI will embed safety evaluators from Apollo Research, Goodfire, METR, and Transluce in its organization as part of a pilot, OpenAI said Monday. The news follows a series of safety incidents, including one in which an OpenAI agent swarm broke out of its sandbox and hacked into Hugging Face during cybersecurity testing. Many AI safety researchers, including from Apollo, have argued such an event might have been avoided if outside evaluators had been embedded within OpenAI to monitor its safety testing.
OpenAI said the efforts support its commitments to rely on independent assessments of safety controls under the White House Accord on Super Intelligence. The pilots will begin at different points, with Apollo’s beginning this week, according to OpenAI.
The idea of embedding evaluators into frontier AI labs first came from Anthropic, which last month started to give METR researchers employee-level access to its systems. Until recently, AI companies have only brought in outside reviewers to test models after post-training and shortly before public release. Evaluators say this is insufficient because it doesn’t allow them to test for misaligned behaviors like scheming during training or to monitor internal deployment use cases that could still pose a threat.
The work with each third-party firm differs in scope. The pilot with OpenAI and Apollo will focus on investigating whether models attempt to subvert their own or their successors’ alignment or control mechanisms. In other words, they’ll be on the lookout for whether AI models try to undermine the safety rules and safeguards designed to keep them, or future versions of themselves, under human control. OpenAI recently published findings that while training GPT-5.6 Sol, it began leaving instructions for future versions of itself telling them to conceal mistakes and misaligned behavior from the user.
Per Apollo, the pilot will examine whether training incentivizes subversion; whether evaluations can elicit subversion; whether subversion occurs during internal deployment; and whether reasoning relevant to subversion would be detectable. These risks are becoming increasingly important to monitor as AI models grow more capable of acting autonomously and deceiving humans. Apollo’s previous research with OpenAI found that models can behave differently when they know they’re being tested and tend to prioritize what evaluators want to see over users’ actual institutions.
Goodfire will embed researchers who specialize in understanding how AI models work internally. Using its interpretability platform, the firm will help OpenAI monitor training runs, fix undesired behavior, and improve alignment, per the company. Goodfire says it will publish findings, though its primary audience will be OpenAI’s own researchers.
With METR, OpenAI plans to perform two evaluations: one that looks for unintended or dangerous behavior in the model itself, including problems OpenAI’s own tests might have missed, and another that tests whether OpenAI’s systems are capable of catching that behavior. For the first evaluation, METR will largely decide for itself what to investigate and how to test the model. OpenAI and METR have not yet come to a decision on the scope of the second assessment, according to OpenAI.
Transluce, meanwhile, will examine whether OpenAI’s post-training safety evaluations themselves are good enough. The organization is also planning to test in 2027 how OpenAI uses its safety tests to decide whether a model is safe enough to release.
At a time when the independence of third-party evaluations is under scrutiny, it’s worth noting that Apollo and Goodfire are both receiving financial compensation for their evaluations. METR and Transluce aren’t, but they may accept compute or API credits.
Apollo, which published the most detailed account of its agreement with OpenAI, offers a closer look at the scope and limitations of these evaluations.
Many in the AI safety community have warned that AI labs might try to stymy evaluators’ independence, especially if outsiders find unflattering evidence that labs would rather keep hidden. Apollo says an essential part of the pilot is OpenAI’s agreement that the firm can publicly explain the conditions and limitations of its work.
Still, there are areas where Apollo believes its access to OpenAI’s systems is lacking. For a truly independent evaluation of the company’s AI models, Apollo says it needs true employee-level access to OpenAI’s systems, including “all data, records and documentation relevant to their assessment even if a developer was trying to hide unfavorable information.” Getting access to all data, including training data and evaluation logs which companies are loathe to show to outsiders, is important for, say, checking a company’s claims about how a model performed or determining when certain concerning behavior emerged.
In previous coverage, John Steidley, chief of staff at Palisade Research, told TechCrunch that it’s important to see this data in order to assess whether a model was trained to perform well on a “shutdown resistance benchmark.”
In OpenAI’s first pilot, the AI lab is providing Apollo with access to only the information required to assess whether the models engage in subversion attempts. This includes “relevant training code and datasets, reinforcement-learning rollouts with available reasoning traces and rewards, and the ability to query intermediate model checkpoints.”
The scope of access will be limited to “only the agreed claims and only for the specific models and time periods agreed for the assessment,” Apollo says. OpenAI still reserves the right to withhold certain information within that scope if it deems it necessary because of technical infeasibility, security risks, or IP protection. The company agreed not to withhold information simply because it is unfavorable.
Apollo also won’t get access to all OpenAI staffers, instead being limited to “only authorized staff,” which are participants that the AI lab selects, though Apollo can suggest certain individuals. Crucially, if an OpenAI employee outside this group raises confidential information within the scope of Apollo’s research, the firm cannot follow up and will need to cease communication and route follow-up through OpenAI.
That condition is significant. It comes in the wake of OpenAI firing three researchers for allegedly sharing confidential information with safety evaluation firm METR — which performed the Hugging Face incident post-mortem alongside independent AI safety research group Redwood.
Buck Shlegeris, CEO of Redwood, said in a post on Monday that the agreements announced don’t meet the bar of granting third parties “employee-like access,” saying it’s “disappointing but not surprising.”
OpenAI said that they'd have embedded evaluations with employee-like access; the agreements announced today obviously don't meet that bar.
This is disappointing but not surprising.
Maybe future agreements will be better. https://t.co/kmDbg1Dqav
— Buck Shlegeris (@bshlgrs) November 16, 2026
The pilot will also be limited in how much researchers can disclose. While Apollo will be allowed to publish independent conclusions of its findings, OpenAI will be able to limit evidence available to substantiate them publicly, which could make it hard for outsiders to independently assess the findings. Apollo has pushed back against this limitation, saying it believes researchers should be allowed to disclose the findings of the evaluation “to an appropriate outside audience even if the developer was trying to prevent the disclosure of unfavorable findings.”
That said, while the public cannot see the full supporting evidence, OpenAI says its Safety and Security Committee, which oversees safety on behalf of the OpenAI Foundation’s board, will get to review unredacted assessment reports and can communicate privately with evaluators.
While OpenAI is not granting all of Apollo’s conditions for a truly independent evaluation, the firm says the pilot is “an ambitious first step towards deeper access and disclosure rights,” and that it is working toward running full embedded evaluations with multiple AI developers in the future.
This article has been updated to include pilots with METR, Goodfire, and Transluce, as well as with information from OpenAI and comment from Redwood.

articles.title: 'Their relationship with the company could be permanently altered': Bosses beware — replacing workers with AI could prove incredibly costly if the technology doesn't work out
articles.text:
'Their relationship with the company could be permanently altered': Bosses beware — replacing workers with AI could prove incredibly costly if the technology doesn't work out
Re-hiring laid off workers could be expensive
- Workers said they would demand more pay and benefits when returning to their employer following an unsuccessful AI trial
- Half of workers would actually prioritize security over titles and perks
- Reputational damage and worker loyalty could also affect employers
New research has warned companies looking to replace human workers with AI could face major reputational consequences later on down the line if their AI strategies fall apart.
Companies that are forced to re-hire human workers after laying them off could ultimately find themselves having to pay higher salaries, offer better contractual terms and include stronger employment protections, the report from JobAssist warns.
But even after offering workers better terms overall, they could have already made reputational and loyalty damages – nearly one-third (29%) of workers say they'd return to their old job, but would immediately start looking for another.
Replacing humans with AI could have long-lasting consequences
While a relatively low but not insignificant number of workers would likely continue to look for other opportunities, the number of workers looking for a higher salary (71%) is much higher. Nearly two in three (64%) also said they'd negotiate more aggressively in general when returning to an old job.
However, workers are still very clearly worried about AI's impacts on their roles, because half (54%) would now prioritize job security over titles and perks, implying they're concerned about experiencing yet another redundancy. Nearly half (44%) also said they'd trust their employer less after AI replaced human workers.
All in all, the study is proof that employer reputation could suffer beyond the original workforce reduction, with laid off workers and re-hires less likely to trust the company.
And even after all the costs associated with laying off workers in the first place, and investing so heavily in artificial intelligence, JobAssist warns that workers could end up demanding more money, benefits and security than they had done before.
