articles.title: Taxonomy of multi-agent design patterns, anti-patterns, and lessons from manufacturing | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Taxonomy of multi-agent design patterns, anti-patterns, and lessons from manufacturing
Enterprise teams are building multi-agent systems, and when early implementations fall short, the cause is rarely the model. Multi-agent coordination is a distributed systems problem, and many teams taking it on haven’t yet built distributed systems instincts.
The numbers are consistent across sources: ~88% of AI pilots never reach production. Stanford HAI demonstrated that two models can perform worse collaborating than either alone when coordination overhead exceeds the benefit. The pattern is clear: teams are adding complexity faster than they build understanding. Ten steps that are each 95 percent reliable deliver only 59.9 percent end-to-end reliability, and 20 steps deliver 35.8 percent. This illustrative model assumes a strictly sequential chain with no retries, but the direction holds: each dependent handoff multiplies risk.
In this post, you learn how to decide whether a use case needs multiple agents, choose a coordination pattern, and spot costly anti-patterns early. You also see how takt time, safety boundaries, edge data, and shift cycles shape the architecture.
Multi-agent coordination patterns
Coordination patterns fall into two tiers, based on who controls the flow. In Tier 1, you define the path.
In Tier 2, the model chooses the path at runtime. That flexibility handles work whose steps you can’t define in advance, at a higher cost in tokens, latency, and debugging. The practical default is to start with Tier 1 and move a task to Tier 2 only when its subtasks emerge during the work.
Tier 1: Patterns (deterministic control flow)
1.1 Sequential Pipeline: Orchestration patterns that implement linear execution where each node’s output feeds into the next node (A -> B -> C) supporting ordered processing with predictable execution timing
In the following diagram, input flows to agent A (extract), then agent B (transform), then agent C (validate), and then output. The user defines that order at build time, and nothing is decided at runtime. As a result, the pipeline is straightforward to debug and test, and its cost is predictable. Typical fits include document processing, extract, transform, and load (ETL) chains, and warranty-claim triage.
1.2 Conditional Workflow: Logic-based edges select the next node by condition, so the workflow can branch and send each case down a different path.
In the following diagram, a user request goes to agent A (write code) and then to agent B (test code). A pass/fail check sends passing work to agent D (deploy). Failing work loops back to agent A for a retry, up to a maximum of N times, and then escalates to a human. The orchestration layer enforces that cap, for example through an AWS Step Functions iteration limit, which keeps the loop from becoming the unbounded iteration anti-pattern described later in this post.
1.3 Conditional Router:
A classification step examines the input and directs it to the appropriate processing path. Only one path is executed per request. Best for intent-driven dispatch, quality-gate decisions, customer inquiry routing, and anomaly triage.
The following diagram shows a plant supervisor’s request being read by a classifier and sent to exactly one specialist. Questions about whether parts meet spec go to the Quality Agent, overdue equipment services go to the Maintenance Agent, and shift changes go to the Scheduling Agent. This decision is made at the entry point.
1.4 Parallel Workflow: A task splits into independent subtasks that run simultaneously across handlers, each on its own data. A fan-in step combines the results when all handlers complete, and a failure in one path retries only that path. Best for multi-source analysis, batch processing, and work that decomposes into independent pieces.
In the following diagram, a research orchestrator decomposes the task and dispatches it to three specialist agents that run concurrently: a financial data agent, a geopolitical agent, and a logistics agent, each analyzing its own source. A combined step waits for all three, then synthesizes the results, resolves conflicts, and ranks the findings. Latency equals the slowest single agent rather than the sum of all three.
Tier 2: Autonomous patterns (LLM-determined control flow)
In autonomous patterns, control flow is determined at runtime by the AI model itself, not predefined by developers. Agents read task state, reason about what’s needed and coordinate through shared context rather than fixed paths spanning a spectrum from structured orchestration to fully emergent behavior.
2.1 Plan-based orchestration
In plan-based orchestration, a single orchestrator agent acts as a project manager. The orchestrator maintains an explicit task plan with assignments and dependencies, sees all context while each worker receives only its slice, distributes work dynamically against the current plan, and monitors progress centrally. Key design choice is that the workers are stateless and independent. If one fails, it doesn’t contaminate others. The orchestrator retries only the failed worker, not the entire workflow.
The following diagram shows how a planner agent decomposes a task into an explicit plan and dispatches each step to a worker’s agent. Each step goes to a dedicated worker (a research agent, an analysis agent, and a report agent) that sees only its assigned slice.
2.2 Handoff pattern
Agents operate with limited, local knowledge and coordinate through peer-to-peer delegation. Each makes local decisions about when and to whom to transfer control, based on the task and the agents it knows. Control passes with state: each transfer carries validated task state, the evidence behind it, and any unresolved questions, so the receiving agent continues rather than reinterpreting a summary. A handoff that moves only through the conversation is not a handoff.
In the following diagram, a customer service agent transfers control, together with its context, to either a technical support agent or a billing agent, and technical support can hand off further to a senior engineer. Each agent knows only the small set of peers it can transfer to.
2.3 Conversation-driven pattern
In conversation-driven patterns (also known as group chat patterns), all agents participate in a shared conversation where orchestration emerges through turn-taking rather than explicit plans or structured handoffs. This mirrors human team collaboration where everyone can see the discussion and contribute when appropriate.
In the following diagram, an agent-selection mechanism decides whose turn it is, and agents A, B, and C each add to one shared conversation, where every turn is a message plus a tool call. The selection mechanism sets the turn-taking, and state lives implicitly in the conversation history.
Control flow characteristics:
- Visibility: Broadcast all agents observe all messages in the shared conversation.
- Decision making: Next speaker selected based on conversation context, not predetermined plans.
- State management: Implicit in the conversation history.
- Turn-taking: Determined by selection mechanisms (round-robin, AI-driven) 
         
  - Round-robin. Agents take turns in a fixed, repeating order until a termination condition is met, which keeps it predictable.
  - AI-driven. A model selects the next speaker from the conversation context rather than a fixed order.
2.4 Debate/consensus
Multiple agents independently evaluate the same input, and their conclusions are reconciled by majority, by a judge agent, or by escalation when they disagree. Unlike a conversation-driven pattern, the agents do not see each other’s reasoning before committing to a position, which is what makes disagreement informative rather than socially convergent.
Use it sparingly. Debate is the most expensive pattern here, and on perceptual tasks it buys latency rather than accuracy (see the quality-inspection case in anti-pattern 3 that follows). Reserve it for high-stakes, low-volume decisions where being wrong costs more than deliberating.
Hybrid approaches
In practice, most production systems combine several patterns based on task decomposition:
- Use workflow patterns for predictable, well-understood components.
- Apply autonomous patterns where flexibility and adaptation are essential.
- Implement task management patterns (termination, delegation) consistently across all orchestration types.
- Design hierarchical compositions where complex agents internally use different patterns at different layers.
The governing principle: pattern-to-task alignment. Match the orchestration approach to each task’s inherent characteristics and your system’s reliability requirements rather than forcing everything through a single pattern.
Anti-patterns that burn budget
Each of the following five anti-patterns looks reasonable at design time, and each surfaces later as an inflated token cost, a missed takt-time window, or a decision that has quietly drifted out of sync with the plant floor.
1. God agent
One agent owns overall equipment effectiveness (OEE) analysis, programmable logic controller (PLC) diagnostics, and maintenance behind a single prompt with 15 or more tools. Tool selection degrades as tools grow, and failures become hard to attribute.
The fix: Bounded agents of five tools or fewer, such as an OEE analyst, a fault diagnostician, and a maintenance drafter.
2. Unbounded iteration
The agent loops on “try again” with no hard stop. A four-agent system can burn a significantly higher number of tokens before a single retry, and no one call trips an alarm. Retries multiply coordination failures rather than fixing them.
The fix: Hard iteration ceiling in code, per-agent token ceiling, budget alarm wired to an automatic stop. Infrastructure enforces limits. The model will not stop itself.
3. Natural-language contracts
Agents hand each other free-text prose with no schema. Interpretation hardens at every hop: “could indicate wear” becomes “confirmed wear” becomes a maintenance order. The drift happens between agents, where tracing is thinnest.
4. Premature multi-agent
Multi-agent where one agent with tool groups would do. Each agent adds a coordination tax that is not linear, and the gains flatten around four. Most “specialists” are one model in different costumes.
The fix: Needs at least two different models, different tool access, concurrent execution, and real interdependency. Fewer than two, and one agent with action groups does it.
The test: can one agent handle the phases by switching tools? Then it is not a multi-agent problem.
5. Unguarded customer contact
The agent triggers real-world actions (email, service visits, machine parameters) with no approval step. Hallucinations cross into the physical world, irreversible actions compound, and liability escalates from a refund to product liability.
The fix: Defense in depth: recommendation → Amazon Bedrock Guardrails → schema validation → business rules → human approval → execution.
Every point where agent output reaches a customer, or a safety system is a trust boundary.
Choosing an architecture
With the patterns and anti-patterns in view, the architecture choice comes down to a short sequence of questions.
- Does the task require action beyond text generation? Treat a direct model call as the baseline and add orchestration only for a measured reason. Summarizing documents or generating code from a specification rarely supplies one.
- Is the solution path known in advance? If you can write down what happens in what order, you don’t have a “how many agents” decision at all. Your real choice is simpler: a single agent that calls tools, or a Tier 1 workflow.
- Does the work require genuinely distinct expertise? Separate domains with established handoffs justify specialized agents. A single domain belongs to one agent, no matter how many tools it needs.
- Does the solution emerge only through exploration? When the action sequence is known and can run as an act-and-validate loop, it belongs to a single agent, even one that plans its steps dynamically. Tier 2 earns its added cost, latency, and debugging burden only when the subtasks themselves are discovered in the course of the work.
The following decision tree turns these four questions into a path you can follow from top to bottom.
The tree starts by asking whether the task requires actions beyond text generation. If it doesn’t, a simple model call is enough. If it does, the tree asks whether the solution is well known and can be expressed as a workflow. On the known solution side, work that benefits from specialized expertise or domain separation go to a Tier 1 multi-agent workflow (a pipeline, fan-out, or router). Everything else goes to a single agent with tools and action groups. On the unknown-solution side, only tasks that involve exploration or significant side effects go to Tier 2 for autonomous multi-agent patterns. The rest stays with a single agent. The guiding principle is to choose the simplest architecture that meets your requirements.
The following chart compares the patterns on four things: when to reach for each one, how control flows between agents, how deterministic the result is, and what it costs to build and operate. Build cost is a relative scale, not an estimate.
Tier 1 patterns score high on determinism at low to moderate build cost. Tier 2 patterns give more of the path to the model, and plan-based orchestration costs the most to build. If you can draw the control flow on a whiteboard before runtime, start with Tier 1.
Applied: Mapping patterns to manufacturing use cases
| Use Case | Pattern | Rationale | 
| Shift handoff summarization | Sequential Pipeline | Linear: raw logs → summary → report | 
| Multi-station root-cause analysis | Plan-Based Orchestrator | Dynamic: subtasks discovered during analysis | 
| Real-time quality gate | Conditional Router + Edge Agent | In-cycle: local model decides. Agent reasoning off path | 
| Predictive maintenance scheduling | Parallel Fan-Out/Fan-In | Independent models per asset class | 
| Engineering change order impact | Debate/Consensus | High stakes: adversarial review justified | 
| Supplier communication drafting | Sequential + Human Gate | Must not auto-send (see Unguarded Customer Contact) | 
| Cross-plant optimization | Plan-Based Orchestrator | Multi-source: dynamic queries. Solver does allocation | 
The manufacturing lens: Four constraints that change the calculus
Manufacturing is not a generic enterprise IT environment, and four constraints make that arithmetic unforgiving.
Constraint 1: Production-line latency = direct revenue loss
Automotive body shops, where robots weld the vehicle body together, typically run at 60 jobs per hour. Each of their over 40 stations has a 60-second takt time before the line advances. Inference latency that sits on a station’s cycle path eats into those 60 seconds, and a delay at the bottleneck station slows the whole line. Even a 2 percent throughput reduction can translate to significant annual revenue impact.
Architecture implication: budget latency at p99, not average. The tail is what stops the line. Give every agent a sub-second deterministic fallback, and match it to the risk:
- Advisory/quality-flagging: Pass the part with a flag for end-of-line review.
- Safety-critical: Containment or a deterministic stop, not continuation.
- Decide this mapping per station before deployment.
Constraint 2: Safety has physical consequences
A hallucinated chatbot causes embarrassment. A hallucinated welding parameter causes structural defects that surface in crash testing or field failure and can lead to a safety recall. Two failure modes recur:
- OT/IT boundary state desync: An agent reads the manufacturing execution system (MES) as Station 12 running Part #A, but a manual PLC override already switched it to Part #B, so it tunes parameters for the wrong part.
- Hallucinated safety boundary: A maintenance agent reasons about lockout/tagout from scratch and declares Station 7 accessible while adjacent Station 6 runs, breaking the interlock zone.
Architecture implication:
The boundary: keep the deterministic core unchanged, including PLCs, supervisory control and data acquisition (SCADA) systems, and the MES, and wrap an advisory layer around it.
- Agents observe, analyze, and recommend. They do not actuate.
- Safety constraints live as deterministic guardrails in an external service that agents query rather than reason about. They’re never embedded in prompts, where they can be argued away.
Validation and approval: A recommendation passes schema validation and physics simulation, checked against the OT source of truth immediately before actuation, never against OT state cached beyond one cycle. It’s then approved at a level matched to its scope:
- Level 0: Agent resolves autonomously.
- Level 1: Operator confirms with one click.
- Level 2: Engineer decides from the presented analysis.
- Level 3: Management evaluates a line-stop recommendation.
Only then does a validated command interface pass permitted commands to deterministic control. The large language model (LLM) proposes. The physics engine and the human operator dispose.
Constraint 3: Data lives at the edge
A single stamping press generates 50+ GB/day of sensor data whose value decays in milliseconds. Shipping it to the cloud costs more in bandwidth than compute, and by the time the cloud answers, the press has moved on.
Architecture implication: hybrid edge-cloud is the practical default, and the Constraint 2 boundary holds at the edge too.
- Edge (AWS IoT Greengrass): sub-takt anomaly detection, threshold monitoring, and stop-or-continue signals at the source: the edge agent recommends, the PLC acts.
- Cloud: What the edge can’t do: cross-shift analytics, trend correlation across plants, and model retraining on fleet data. The edge distills and transmits only what matters.
Constraint 4: Shift-aligned agent lifecycle
Unbounded context makes an agent drift as stale observations crowd out current reality. A full reset loses continuity between shifts. Manufacturing already solves this for humans with structured shift handoffs, and agents need the same discipline.
Architecture implication: Bound agent memory to the shift cycle.
- Initialize: Shift context, including the crew roster, production targets, and the prior shift handoff.
- Accumulate: Working memory within the shift window only.
- Hand off: Emit a shift-end summary of open issues, flagged anomalies, and recommendations that seed the next crew, mirroring the human ritual without unbounded context growth.
Building on AWS
The following managed services map to the concerns raised earlier in this post. Each row names the mechanism, not just the service.
| Need | Service | Mechanism | 
| Runtime | AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore | Where agents run, their control flow is determined or model determined. Bring Strands, LangGraph, or CrewAI. | 
| Shift-bounded memory | AgentCore memory, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore | Managed short-term and long-term context, so the shift-scoped memory from Constraint 4 is configuration rather than custom state plumbing. | 
| Typed handoffs | AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore | Converts APIs and AWS Lambda functions into Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools with validated schemas, so handoffs carry typed fields rather than prose. | 
| Agent permissions | AgentCore Identity, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore | A unique, verifiable identity for each agent with fine-grained access control. It’s the enforcement point for which agent can reach which system, and on whose behalf. | 
| Tracing between agents | AgentCore Observability, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore | Spans and traces across runtime, memory, gateway, and tools, through Amazon CloudWatch Transaction Search and AWS Distro for Open Telemetry (ADOT). Handoffs are the least observable part of a multi-agent system and where untyped contracts fail silently. | 
| Human approval surface | AWS Quick | Where the escalation tiers land. AWS Quick Automate runs approval workflows with one-click approval in Slack, and its action connectors can invoke Amazon Bedrock AgentCore agents. | 
| Tiered model selection | Amazon Bedrock | One API across model families, so cost tiering is configuration: a small model for a router’s classification and a stronger one for an orchestrator synthesis. | 
Conclusion
Multi-agent systems change how automotive manufacturers orchestrate intelligence at scale, but only when built on the right foundations.
The patterns and anti-patterns here come from real deployments where poor architecture shows up as runaway token costs, takt-time violations, and, at worst, physical safety risks. The economics at plant scale are unforgiving, because token volume grows with every agent, robot, and shift. Tiered model selection, context compression, and edge-cloud distribution are the main levers for delivering the same value at a fraction of that cost.
The recommendation here is to start with Tier 1 patterns, prove value, and then expand. Most manufacturing use cases, such as shift handoff summarization, quality-gate decisions, and predictive maintenance, are well served by deterministic workflows. Reserve autonomous orchestration for genuinely open-ended problems where dynamic subtask discovery justifies the added cost, latency, and debugging complexity.

articles.title: Delivery drones are coming. For some with PTSD, that's a terrifying prospect.
articles.text:
In August, Amazon announced plans to expand its Prime Air delivery drone program to “nearly 500 cities and towns by the end of 2026.” Combined with similar uncrewed aerial delivery programs from DoorDash and Zipline (in partnership with Uber and Walmart), the expansion suggests that flying robots dropping their payloads onto suburban lawns will soon be commonplace.
For many people, delivery drones will be little more than a novelty, occasionally good for a laugh when one does something ridiculous. For others, though, their growing use could be a nightmare. As the instant delivery industry clears the last FAA hurdles to rapid deliveries beyond an operator’s line of sight, an increasing number of people worldwide are living with post-traumatic stress disorder or other anxiety-related disorders triggered by drones.
The use of all manner of weaponized drones in the ongoing war in Ukraine and in Israeli attacks on Lebanon and Gaza has already produced an epidemic of what some mental health professionals have dubbed “dronophobia.” And while relatively few US troops have been targeted by drones flown by Iran, ISIS, and Iran-backed militias throughout the Middle East, even those who have not directly been attacked may experience anxiety simply because of the ample video footage of attacks circulating in news and social media.
Combined with broader anxiety about surveillance technologies, artificial intelligence, and things generally falling from the sky, the resulting hypervigilance could result in some unintended deliveries from those Prime Air flying robots.
Heralds of destruction
The aftermath of an Israeli airstrike in Gaza City on October 9, 2023, leaving widespread destruction in the Rimal area.
The aftermath of an Israeli airstrike in Gaza City on October 9, 2023, leaving widespread destruction in the Rimal area.
Credit:
CC BY-SA 3.0
Drones have been a part of the battlefield in some form since the late 1980s, when the Israeli Defense Forces began using them. From the beginning, they have had a psychological impact on both those in the sights of drone operators and the operators themselves.
The first military use of drones was for intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance. I witnessed the development of naval drone operations aboard USS Iowa in 1986 and 1987, and for many on the ship at the time, the drones were a curiosity—or, at worst, an annoyance. Our crews spent hours standing by a boat, ready to retrieve crashed drones from the water. But we were helping develop a capability that would eventually lead to Iraqi troops surrendering to the USS Wisconsin‘s drone during the Gulf War. Back then, drones were merely heralds of destruction, acting as forward observers for the Air Force ordnance fired or launched from elsewhere.
Iraqi troops on Faylaka Island associated the Pioneer RPV with the bombardment they had just experienced from the USS Missouri. When the Wisconsin’s drone flew in to assess the damage, their morale was broken.
Over southern Lebanon, the same kinds of drones were part of what amounted, for some residents, to sonic psychological warfare—the hum of lawnmower-like engines overhead was a reminder of constant surveillance and the ever-present threat of artillery or air strikes. The resulting anxiety intensified as drones began carrying their own weapons and “loitering munitions,” one-way drones designed to fly into targets and explode.
Dronophobia
Israel’s continued fight against Hezbollah in Lebanon, along with the US wars in Afghanistan and Iraq, accelerated the evolution of drone warfare and expanded the population experiencing its psychological effects. A Stanford Law study in 2012 of the impact of US drones in Pakistan (PDF) highlighted how drones were destroying the fabric of communities in northwest Pakistan:
Drones hover twenty-four hours a day over communities in northwest Pakistan, striking homes, vehicles, and public spaces without warning. Their presence terrorizes men, women, and children, giving rise to anxiety and psychological trauma among civilian communities. Those living under drones have to face the constant worry that a deadly strike may be fired at any moment and the knowledge that they are powerless to protect themselves.
That experience has been repeated and amplified in current conflicts in Gaza, Lebanon, and Ukraine. A team of US and Ukrainian psychiatrists has reported that Ukrainian military personnel and civilians who have experienced a drone attack, particularly those injured in one, “are at heightened risk for developing persistent psychological symptoms, a vulnerability intensified by the ongoing threat of repeated attacks.”
Those symptoms—a “unique hypervigilance behavior with corresponding hyperarousal and avoidance behaviors”—are now referred to by some Ukrainian doctors as “dronophobia.”
“The distinct hum of an approaching drone, often likened to the swarming of hornets, has itself become a psychological weapon,” noted the team led by Dr. Joseph L. Bonvie of Massachusetts General Hospital. “The escalating pitch as a drone draws near elicits fear and helplessness even before an attack.”
Similar symptoms have been reported in women and children in Gaza, where Israeli drone strikes have been persistent. In consultations with 19 patients in Gaza, “all patients reported an intense phobic reaction to the acoustic signature of drones (the ‘zannana’), associated with imminent bombing and death, manifesting as full-blown panic attacks,” wrote Dr. Mohammad Abu Slaih, a Jordanian psychiatrist, in an article for European Psychiatry. “Three children developed a specific fear of looking at the sky. “
The Iranian drone attacks on Gulf states, while hardly comparable to what Gaza has endured, have had a broad impact on civilians in the United Arab Emirates and other countries in the region, disrupting sleep, causing fatigue, and fueling anticipatory anxiety as people wait for the next drone to strike.
That anxiety is common across populations exposed to drone warfare. The US Army Training and Doctrine Command (TRADOC) has compared drones’ potential to induce PTSD to the “shell shock” of World War I and the “battle fatigue” of World War II, noting that the “fear and stress from (the sound of) near-persistent drone presence creates anticipatory anxiety… Fears can persist beyond the drone’s presence, enhancing a soldier’s anxiety even when out of harm’s way.”
An RQ-2 Pioneer UAV, developed jointly by AAI Corporation and Israel Aircraft Industries.
An RQ-2 Pioneer UAV, developed jointly by AAI Corporation and Israel Aircraft Industries.
Credit:
US Navy
The use of drone video by both Russia and Ukraine as a psychological warfare tool extends the impact of drones beyond those who experience attacks firsthand. Footage of attacks on individual soldiers has been posted on social media to spread anxiety among opposing forces, sometimes going viral and exposing thousands of other people to the attacks. Ukrainian military units often publish first-person-view videos of drones chasing down Russian soldiers, complete with horror-film-styled soundtracks.
According to Neda Gould, an associate professor of psychiatry and behavioral sciences at Johns Hopkins School of Medicine, that aspect sets drone-induced PTSD apart from other types of the disorder. In an interview with Psychiatry Online, Gould said social media could amplify trauma because “not only does the soldier have to grapple with the PTSD-related consequences of the attack itself, but they may also relive the experience in a way that is completely out of their control,” especially when social media comments express support for the attacks.
Reversal of misfortune
The US military has grappled with drone-induced PTSD and other mental health symptoms over the past 15 years. The first signs of stress for American troops, however, came from drone operators themselves.
In 2014, a team of researchers led by a US Air Force psychologist found that 4.3 percent of Air Force drone operators displayed “a pattern of symptoms of moderate to extreme level of severity” associated with PTSD. More recent studies have found that drone operators are just as likely to experience PTSD symptoms as members of aircrews deployed to war zones. Differences in how crews operate between manned combat aircraft and unmanned systems crews may even put drone operators at greater risk of psychological impact.
According to the latter study:
Drone missions generally involve days or weeks of surveillance of targets before launching strikes
Operators have a constant feed of imagery and radio communications from the area of operations for long periods, including imagery of their targets
Operators do not have transit time to and from the area of operation and may not experience “the adrenaline rush or thrill of accomplishing the mission”
Since operators have more time to study their targets, errors are not as easily shrugged off
Unlike their counterparts sitting in a pilot seat aboard a warplane, drone operators continue observation after the strikes to assess the extent of damage and are more likely to be exposed to disturbing imagery of the death and destruction resulting from their handwork
The dual psychological impact of drone warfare was aptly demonstrated by Killbox, a video artwork and “game” that presents two perspectives: those of a drone operator and a child on the ground. Playing it leaves many people deeply saddened, offering a glimpse of the moral injury some drone operators have experienced after their missions.
US troops are no longer just the ones behind the screens, however. Beginning with operations against ISIS, US troops have faced increasingly sophisticated drone warfare, starting with grenades dropped by ISIS-operated consumer quadcopter drones in 2017. Since then, Iranian-built drones, some based on reverse-engineered technology from downed US drones, have been used against US troops and ships by Iran and Iranian-backed militias in Yemen and Iraq. Among these is the Shahed, a long-range attack drone that Iran has sold in large numbers to Russia for its war on Ukraine.
Remains of a Shahed 136 drone at an exhibition showing missiles and drones Russia used to attack Kyiv, Ukraine.
Remains of a Shahed 136 drone at an exhibition showing missiles and drones Russia used to attack Kyiv, Ukraine.
Credit:
Oleksii Samsonov/Global Images Ukraine/Getty Images
The US Army TRADOC report also recognized that the psychological effects of drone attacks can reach further than those wounded in attacks, and even beyond the units that encounter them, saying:
Drones amplify the uncertainties of war because rear areas are less secure as long-range drones extend danger zones beyond that of artillery and rockets. The feeling of nowhere being safe exacerbates anxiety even when drones are not present.
While little public data is available on drone-induced PTSD among US veterans, evidence suggests that drones could also affect people with PTSD stemming from other kinds of trauma. The sound of a drone, its shadow, a glimpse of one in peripheral vision, or other stimuli from drones could trigger hypervigilance because of their unexpectedness, their similarity to other triggering stimuli, or a range of other factors.
Even for those who have not experienced drone attacks, the presence of an uncrewed aircraft can cause anxiety. Drones purportedly operated by the Department of Homeland Security in Minneapolis earlier this year appeared to be used not just for surveillance of targets of Immigration and Customs Enforcement but also to intimidate individuals who had been tracking ICE activity.
The expanding use of drones by law enforcement organizations in the US as part of “drone first responder” programs has exposed an increasing number of Americans to drone surveillance, with over 1,000 agencies applying for FAA waivers for drone operations as of February 2026, based on data from the Electronic Frontier Foundation. Combined with news reports about drone attacks and foreign governments’ use of drones, the disquiet of drone propeller noises and blinking lights in the sky has already created a War of the Worldslevel of dronophobia.
Drones and rumors of drones
Over the past two years, several drone incidents have been linked, or suspected of being linked, to state-actor espionage, with a surge in reports in November and December of 2024. Three occurred in Southern California, including a drone flyover of Vandenberg Air Force Base as a National Reconnaissance Office payload was being loaded ont0 a SpaceX rocket. A Chinese national was charged in the case and arrested while attempting to leave the country. Other cases in the US were officially downplayed as posing no security threat.
In November 2024, incidents in the UK centered on multiple air bases used by the US, including incursions near RAF Fairford, the base recently allegedly targeted in a plot that the British government attributed to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. Similar incursions occurred in Germany.
Many of these sightings turned out to be crewed aircraft or helicopters, toy drones, or, in very few cases, authorized commercial drone flights. Former Maryland Governor Larry Hogan even reported seeing dozens of large drones above his house, only for others to quickly point out that the objects were actually the constellation Orion.
The unfriendly skies
PTSD is a treatable condition, and coping strategies can help people manage triggers. But severe PTSD can be extremely debilitating, and research into the effects of drones on PTSD remains limited. It’s still unclear how well survivors of drone attacks will be able to process the fears and traumatic memories associated with drones, especially if the aircraft become a pervasive part of daily life.
I, for one, won’t be placing any Prime Air orders anytime soon.

articles.title: Como repostar Stories de outra pessoa no Instagram • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Como repostar Stories de outra pessoa no Instagram
Compartilhar stories de outra pessoa no Instagram é um recurso nativo que permite republicar conteúdos de perfis públicos na sua própria conta, mesmo quando você não é marcado
Você sabia que dá para repostar stories que não foi marcado no Instagram, desde que o perfil do autor seja público? A rede social tem uma função nativa no aplicativo para Android e iPhone para dar aquela força aos criadores e amigos.
Para compartilhar stories de outra pessoa no Instagram, basta abrir a publicação e tocar no ícone de envio para DMs. Se o autor permitir o compartilhamento externo, aparecerá a opção de “Adicionar ao story” para você republicar o conteúdo.
A seguir, o Tecnoblog te ensina o caminho para republicar um story de outra pessoa no seu perfil do Instagram.
Abra o Instagram no seu celular Android ou iPhone e toque no ícone de lupa, no menu inferior. Pesquise pelo nome do perfil que publicou o story que você deseja repostar na sua conta.
Toque na foto de perfil do usuário, exibida no canto superior esquerdo, para carregar a sequência de stories disponíveis no momento.
Com o story aberto na tela, selecione o ícone de avião de papel no canto inferior direito para ver as opções de envio de conteúdo via DM e compartilhamento do stories.
Escolha a opção “Adicionar ao story” para importar o conteúdo para o seu editor de criação, permitindo repostar o story mesmo sem ser marcado.
Se desejar, adicione texto, stickers e GIFs ao story original. Então, toque no botão de compartilhar no canto inferior direito da tela para repostar stories no Instagram.
Não dá para repostar stories do Instagram nativamente pelo navegador do PC. Essa limitação ocorre porque a Meta restringe várias ferramentas na versão web, priorizando a experiência nos aplicativos para Android e iOS.
Para republicar stories diretamente pelo PC, é necessário usar plataformas de gerenciamento de mídias sociais de terceiros, como Hootsuite ou Later. Esses softwares ajudam a contornar as restrições da versão desktop para compartilhar stories, além de organizar e programar as postagens com facilidade.
Em diversos casos, você não poderá repostar story no Instagram por restrições de privacidade definidas pelo autor original ou falhas técnicas que impedem os stories de carregar. Veja algumas situações comuns:
Não é possível repostar Stories de Amigos Próximos devido às questões de privacidade do formato. Lembrando que fazer story no Instagram para Amigos Próximos é a ação de enviar uma publicação para uma lista de pessoas selecionadas pelo dono do perfil.
Há duas formas de compartilhar stories do Instagram no Status do WhatsApp. Você pode usar a opção “Compartilhar”, tocando no ícone de três pontos dentro do seu story, para gerar um link que será publicado no app de mensagens da Meta.
A outra maneira é baixar o seu próprio story do Instagram para o telefone e publicar como um Status do WhatsApp. Assim, você consegue compartilhar a foto ou o vídeo com os elementos adicionados através da rede social.
Sim, você pode impedir outros usuários de repostar story no Instagram nas opções de privacidade da plataforma. Vá até o menu “Configurações e atividade”, toque em “Compartilhamento” e desative as chaves dos itens “Stories em que as pessoas são mencionadas” e “Compartilhamento do story”.
Esse ajuste desabilita os botões nativos de envio por DM e de republicação do story, mas tem um limite técnico. Como o Instagram não controla os recursos externos do aparelho, o bloqueio não impede que alguém faça um print ou grave a tela do post.

articles.title: GitHub Rebuilds the Copilot App's Diff Surface to Open Million-Line Pull Requests Without Jank
articles.text:
GitHub engineering has published a detailed account of how it rebuilt the diff surface in the GitHub Copilot app to open a pull request with 2,200 files, over a million changed lines and more than 400 inline review comments without turning the review into a waiting exercise.
The post, by Principal Design Engineer Alberto Gimeno, lands at a moment when AI coding agents are producing far more pull requests than reviewers can digest, and the bottleneck has moved from writing code to reading it.
At the heart of the rebuild is a decision to stop pretending a pull request is a single uniform list. Code rows have a known height at a known font size, so their geometry can be computed up front and never rebuilt. Comments do not. A markdown body wraps differently at different widths, <details> sections can be toggled in place, reply composers grow as a user types, and images change height when they load. Rather than force one variable-height virtualizer to absorb both, the team split the document into two independent domains:
total height = deterministic code height
 + Σ dynamic block effective heights
 + scroll padding
Dynamic blocks are keyed by identity (file, line, side) rather than pixel position, with a fingerprint tracking content, open state and measurement width. A single idle-gated measurement pass reads mounted blocks in one batch, scoped to roughly 2,400 pixels around the viewport, and corrections are anchored to whatever the reader is looking at so the surface never fights an active scroll.
Gimeno is open about an early mistake, the team's first instinct was one ResizeObserver per block writing heights back into the layout, a classic feedback loop whose cost grows with every mounted block. The shipped design keeps the observer but defaults it to flagging rather than writing, with a deliberate frame-synchronous exception when the user toggles a <details> or expands a reply composer, so the code below moves in the same frame.
The work builds on an April 2026 post from the main github.com files-changed team, who reported that unified-view diff lines previously rendered as roughly eight React components and ten DOM elements each, and cut both roughly in half.
GitHub's own stacked pull requests went into public preview on 30 July 2026 as an explicit answer to AI-generated monsters, and a DEV Community piece cited Microsoft research finding review quality degrades sharply once a pull request exceeds roughly 200 lines, a rounding error against the Copilot app's million-line test case.
Third-party tools have filled the gap from the review side. Graphite, Pullfrog and CodeRabbit each take different runs at agent-era review, with Codegen CEO Jay Hack arguing that the winners in this new era will be the teams that redesign their workflows around the fact that review, not code, is now the bottleneck.
The team also describes the measurement loop built around the rebuild. The surface carries permanent structured probes for its own invariants, which run as CI budgets against a synthetic huge-pull-request fixture, and an autopilot drives the real desktop app through a scripted flow, cold and warm, so an agent can read the on-disk log and spot regressions without anyone at the keyboard. Gimeno's closing line is addressed to anyone who reviews code for a living: open the worst pull request you have got.

articles.title: Microsoft reveals the cause of its catastrophic Outlook outage — incident set off by a ‘cascading failure’ of servers as crash leads to chlorine gas poisoning of 15 hotel guests
articles.text:
Microsoft 365 outage led to chlorine gas poisoning of 15 hotel guests in Germany — as Microsoft says crash was caused by ‘cascading failure’ rather than cyberattack
System crashes are bad for your health
- The Microsoft 365 outage led to a key safety system failing in Germany
- This caused the chlorine gas poisoning of 15 hotel guests
- Microsoft has since revealed exactly what caused the outage
If you were affected by last week’s global Microsoft 365 outage, chances are you had trouble accessing your email. You probably didn’t expect to be poisoned as a result, yet that’s exactly what happened to over a dozen unfortunate hotel guests in Germany — but Microsoft has reported that the blackout wasn’t caused by a cyberattack.
According to a news report from German outlet WDR (via Notebookcheck), 15 guests at a hotel for the Phantasialand theme park were injured when the park’s swimming pool received excessive levels of chlorine. This was caused by a malfunction in the chlorine monitoring system, but because alerts are sent to park staff over email — and because those email systems were down due to the Microsoft 365 outage — no one knew about the problem until guests started getting sick.
According to a Facebook post made by the fire department that responded to the incident, 40 first responders were dispatched and 15 guests were triaged after the chlorine gas leak. WDR reported that the affected people suffered from respiratory irritation, with four needing to be taken to hospital.
The episode illustrates the serious — and often unexpected — consequences that can arise when something as central to a business’s operations as an email system goes down. When it’s responsible for important safety procedures, the results can be potentially life-threatening.
Microsoft’s post-mortem report
Since the outage, Microsoft has said that full service has been resumed. It has since published a post-incident report, which is available in the Microsoft 365 Admin Center portal. The full write up has also been relayed on Reddit.
In the report, Microsoft revealed that the outage was caused by three principal factors: a “latent defect” from July that overwhelmed Windows servers; a Microsoft Teams failure that increased the load on a system shared with Microsoft Exchange; and the fact that 14% of server capacity for the networking system was out of service at the time.
Taken individually, these factors were not enough to cause the global failure. But when the increased load and the lower server capacity combined, they triggered the latent defect. Server requests then piled up until the servers stopped responding — which happened to occur during the peak traffic window for the United States.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
As a mitigation effort, traffic was automatically redirected towards healthy endpoints. However, this process made those endpoints more likely to themselves encounter the latent defect. “This caused a cascading failure from server to server as the same amount of load was spread across fewer servers,” Microsoft wrote. At its worst point, the outage had caused 80% of available servers to become unresponsive.
Due to a separate issue, Microsoft’s bulwarks against such a cascading failure did not function properly. Recovery took longer than expected because restored servers were immediately overwhelmed by pent up traffic, making them fail once again. And because the latent defect dated back to July, simply rolling back to a recent version was not enough.
To fix the outage once and for all, Microsoft had to return its code path to that of a previously good state, then take servers offline in batches, roll out the patch across its infrastructure, then restart its systems. Eventually, service was restored.
The post-incident report is a sobering reminder of what can happen when several seemingly independent issues can converge all at once, and of the consequences that are possible when that happens on such a large scale. And as the chlorine incident in Germany demonstrates, these failures often go beyond mere technical disruption and touch on people’s health and wellbeing.

articles.title: Google Project Zero Sets Course for 30-Day Disclosure Deadline
articles.text:
In the context of AI-assisted vulnerability discovery and exploitation, Google Project Zero is significantly shrinking bug disclosure windows.
So far, Project Zero’s policy has been a well-known one: vendors were given 90 days to patch vulnerabilities before public disclosure and granted a 30-day grace period for patch roll-out.
Starting November 13, that grace period is no longer in the books, Project Zero security engineer Natalie Silvanovich announced.
Under the new ‘Full X’ policy, Project Zero will publish vulnerability details 90 days after reporting them to the vendor, regardless of whether, or when, a fix is released.
Beginning February 2, 2027, Project Zero will disclose vulnerabilities publicly after 60 days, and the disclosure window will shrink to 30 days on January 3, 2028.
Furthermore, Project Zero is removing most ‘special cases’ from its disclosure policy, except for security defects actively exploited in the wild (which have a 7-day disclosure window, per Google’s policy) and flaws already made public by others.
If a vendor requests it, Project Zero may publish details on a security hole ahead of the deadline, Silvanovich says.
However, serious vulnerabilities may be granted exceptions. Project Zero has done it on rare occasions, such as Spectre and Meltdown, and that will not change.
According to Silvanovich, the phased transition to shorter disclosure windows addresses concerns that users may be exposed to unpatched vulnerabilities, that vendors may rush to fix flaws reported under the new policy but overlook previously reported bugs that are more severe, and that some vendors may not be able to meet the new policy.
“We decided on a policy that encourages vendors to improve remediation time on a schedule that is challenging but realistic, with the hope that this will lead to vendors broadly improving their remediation processes and infrastructure in a way that eventually enables them to fix all reported vulnerabilities quickly,” Silvanovich notes.
Noting that Project Zero only reports vulnerabilities that have substantial severity and demonstrated impact, she also points out that a vulnerability’s severity affects only its impact on users, not the likelihood that attackers will discover it.
“It’s also important to acknowledge that Project Zero holds itself to high standards with regard to the reproducibility, readability, reachability, and reported security impact of the vulnerabilities we report. This policy assumes bug reports are of this quality, and it is reasonable for vendors to treat low quality-bug reports differently,” Silvanovich says.

articles.title: Bußgelder drohen: Warum du nicht einfach planlos eine Ring-Kamera installieren solltest
articles.text:
Ring-Kamera und Co.: Wann du Videotürklingeln nutzen darfst – und wann nicht
Amazon und viele weitere Hersteller bieten mittlerweile eine Vielzahl von Überwachungslösungen, die die eigenen vier Wände besser absichern sollen. Wirft man einen Blick auf die Bestseller unter den „Türklingeln & Türglocken“ bei Amazon, finden sich auf den ersten drei Plätzen smarte Blink- und Ring-Kameras des Online-Riesen. Erst dahinter gibt es normale Funkklingeln, bevor auf den hinteren Plätzen wieder smarte Klingeln und Videotürspione landen.
Ring-Kamera: Warum es zu Problemen kommen kann
Da günstigere Modelle schon ab unter 50 Euro starten, ist der Kauf für viele Kund:innen kein großes Hindernis. Die Videotürklingeln versprechen im Gegenzug, den Eingangsbereich des Hauses abzusichern. Dafür nehmen sie alle Personen, die bei dir klingeln, von Kopf bis Fuß auf. Manche Modelle haben sogar noch eine zweite Kamera installiert, die den Boden filmt und so verhindern soll, dass einmal abgelegte Pakete nicht von Unbefugten unbemerkt gestohlen werden. Schließlich werden ihre Gesichter durch die Kameras aufgezeichnet, was das Aufspüren durch die Polizei erleichtern dürfte.
Wenn du eine smarte Türklingel oder einen Videotürspion installierst, solltest du aber aufpassen, dass die Polizei nicht wegen besagter Geräte bei dir klingelt. Aufgrund des Datenschutzes darf nicht einfach jeder öffentliche Bereich abgefilmt werden. Wohnst du also in naher Nachbarschaft mit anderen oder hast eine Haustür, die in Richtung Straße führt, wird das Ganze schon knifflig. Welche Vorkehrungen getroffen werden müssen, zeigen unter anderem die Landesbeauftragte für Datenschutz und Informationsfreiheit in NRW und die sächsische Datenschutz- und Transparenzbeauftragte.
Videotürklingel und -türspion: Was ist wirklich erlaubt?
Grundsätzlich ist es erlaubt, private Bereiche des eigenen Grundstücks per Video zu überwachen, die nur von Anwohner:innen betreten werden können. Areale wie Innenhöfe und Auffahrten, die von Paketlieferant:innen und anderen Personen prinzipiell auch betreten werden können, gelten datenschutzrechtlich allerdings als öffentlicher Raum. Sie sind deshalb strengeren Datenschutzgesetzen unterworfen.
Dazu zählt, dass die Überwachung nur auf dem eigenen Grundstück erfolgen darf und keine anderen Grundstücke, Wohnungen oder öffentlichen Straßen samt Gehweg erfasst werden dürfen. Zudem müssen Personen, die den Bereich betreten, vorab darüber informiert werden, dass eine Videoüberwachung stattfindet. Es muss ein „deutlich sichtbares, vorgelagertes Hinweisschild“ angebracht werden.
Ferner muss bei smarten Türklingeln wie der Ring-Kamera sichergestellt sein, dass sie nur „anlassbezogen“ aktiviert wird. Etwa dann, wenn jemand den Klingelknopf drückt. Eine dauerhafte Aufnahme des Bereiches ist nicht erlaubt. Die Kamera darf zudem nur den Eingangsbereich vor der Tür erfassen und muss sich nach kurzer Zeit wieder automatisch deaktivieren.
Sollten auf der Kamera dennoch Bereiche des öffentlichen Lebens zu sehen sein, müssen diese softwareseitig geschwärzt oder die Aufnahme durch physische Maßnahmen wie Blenden verhindert werden. Bei der softwareseitigen Lösung ist wichtig, dass sich die Schwärzung im Nachhinein nicht mehr rückgängig machen lässt. Zu guter Letzt sollten Aufnahmen im Idealfall nicht gespeichert werden. Allerdings bieten viele Produkte wie die Ring-Kameras eine solche Speicherung an.
Dann ist es wichtig, dass die Aufnahmen nur so lange gespeichert werden, „wie es dem vorher festgelegten Zweck erforderlich ist.“ Heißt: Soll das eigene Grundstück vor Einbrecher:innen oder Pakete vor dem Diebstahl geschützt werden, müssen die Aufnahmen gelöscht werden, sobald solche Vorfälle nicht eintreffen. In der Regel gilt dabei eine maximale Speicherdauer von 72 Stunden.
Welche Strafen drohen bei Verstößen?
Solltest du eine Ring-Kamera betreiben, die gegen die Datenschutzgesetze verstößt und das etwa von deinen verärgerten Nachbarn gemeldet werden, drohen Konsequenzen. Die unzulässige Videoüberwachung stellt laut dem Hessischen Beauftragten für Datenschutz eine Ordnungswidrigkeit dar, die nach Art. 83 Abs. 5 Buchst. a DS-GVO eine Geldstrafe nach sich ziehen kann. Die Höhe wird dabei in jedem Fall einzeln festgelegt.
Grundsätzlich können Nutzer:innen einer Ring-Kamera oder anderer smarter Türklingeln dazu aufgefordert werden, die nicht datenschutzkonform genutzten Geräte wieder zu entfernen. Sollten sie dem nicht nachkommen, kann das auch durch Zwang durchgesetzt werden. Sollten Personen, die aufgenommen wurden, auch Schadensersatz fordern, könnte das Ganze noch zivilrechtliche Konsequenzen nach sich ziehen. Etwa dann, wenn die aufgenommenen Clips im Netz geteilt werden, um auf eigene Faust nach vermeintlichen Dieb:innen oder Einbrecher:innen zu suchen.

articles.title: OpenAI releases a new image classifier and ChatGPT warnings to combat CSAM | TechCrunch
articles.text:
OpenAI today announced new tools to combat child sexual abuse material (CSAM) amid growing safety concerns around the use of AI tools. These features include a new image classifier to detect CSAM, warnings and temporary blocks to prevent users from creating or accessing content that sexualizes children, a new guideline for developers, and a set of tools for law enforcement.
The company unveiled a new image classifier that can detect CSAM images, including the ones generated by AI. OpenAI is giving select companies access to its classifier through its API at no cost. The tool looks for visual signs of abuse in images not seen before and assigns a score that can give an indicative direction to reviewers about dealing with CSAM.
OpenAI said that it developed this classifier with the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC), and it is working with Tech Coalition and ROOST to share access to the tool. In its early testing with partners, the AI company found that the classifier flags 48% fewer images while finding the same number of abusive images, reducing the work of reviewers. Plus, images flagged by the classifier are twice as likely to be abusive images.
What’s more, the company is adding new warning screens in ChatGPT to prevent users from accessing material that sexualizes children. ChatGPT will show an alert to users attempting such prompts, direct users toward specialized support to stop harmful behavior, and also suspend the account for 24 hours as a warning. The app already blocks CSAM content and requests related to it. It said that repeated offences could lead to the account being removed permanently.
OpenAI noted that it formed the message and guidelines around this behavior with organizations and researchers, including Protect Children, the Lucy Faithfull Foundation, and Joel Scanlan at the University of Tasmania, who independently evaluated a trial of deterrent messages.
The company is also publishing guidelines for developers using OpenAI tools to prevent, detect, and help users report CSAM content. It said that in early testing, the guidelines have helped a number of developers adopt child safety tooling and register to report CSAM to NCMEC. OpenAI is also equipping law enforcement dealing with child safety with AI-powered features like dedicated plug-ins, investigative tools, and complex data analysis, with access managed by program administrators. It is also providing training to investigators along with a field guide on how to use AI.
OpenAI has had several lawsuits against the company blaming its technology for harming users, especially children. Safety-focused nonprofit Common Sense Media labeled OpenAI’s tech as “unacceptable risk” for teens. Other AI chatbots — specifically Grok — have been used to create nonconsensual sexualized imagery, including of children.
The AI startup had made changes in the last 12 months to its technology, including releasing a safety blueprint, updating content guidelines to bar inappropriate content, retuning its model to prevent them from generating harmful content, and releasing a special version of ChatGPT for teens.

articles.title: Building trustworthy AI by fencing it in, not predicting it
articles.text:
Sponsored
Building trustworthy AI by fencing it in, not predicting it
While we’re used to predictable technology, AI challenges that assumption. Therefore, the goal must be bounded, observable, and controllable AI.
Provided byUL Solutions
In October this year, OpenAI disclosed that two of its AI agents had switched off the systems built to monitor them. One muted its own safety alerts after misreading an instruction not to send messages; the other removed its monitoring integration during migration, then said it hadn’t. No rule had told the agents to do that, and no test had anticipated the behaviors.
For a century, we have built trust in technology on predictability: predefined inputs, predictable outputs, and layers of protection. Consider how a breaker trips at a set current or an aircraft component is tested against known (i.e., predictable) stresses.
AI changes that. Traditional software executes instructions written by humans, whereas AI exercises what might be called synthetic judgment. We use AI because it can interpret situations we did not program and generate responses we did not prescribe. But the more freedom we give AI, the harder it becomes to provide the predictability on which trust has traditionally been built.
We will not make AI trustworthy by predicting what it will do. We will do it by fencing it in with hard limits that are enforced outside its reach. In OpenAI’s case, the safeguards sat inside a system the agents could edit. But a fence the agents can simply move is not a fence.
Where traditional definitions of trust fall short
Recent MIT Technology Review coverage has approached this problem from other directions. One contributor argues that having a human in the loop is an insufficient solution because humans are fundamentally unable to understand AI systems’ intentions and advocates instead for interdisciplinary research and collaboration between academia, government, and the tech industry. And a story on reverse game theory describes using incentives to keep models from deviating from the rules, even when no one understands how they work on the inside.
Both articles acknowledge that we cannot understand or watch every AI decision. Our instruments of trust, including requirements, testing, certification, safety margins, interlocks, and pass/fail criteria, all depend on our ability to bound a system’s behavior. This is the determinism paradox.
With generative and agentic AI, behavior is shaped by training data, architecture, prompts, context, retrieval sources, and the environment. Inputs change, models are updated, tools change, and agents interact. Small variations propagate into outcomes nobody designed. The problem is not randomness; it is that the space of possible behavior is too large to enumerate in advance. Trust must therefore be engineered around boundaries rather than predicted outputs. The goal is not deterministic AI, but bounded, observable, and controllable AI. Trust also cannot be a one-time test. Traditional assurance certifies a product at a point in time, but AI keeps evolving after deployment, and a system that has passed every test can drift outside the conditions that made those tests meaningful. Trust must be continuously earned.
Safety engineering has been accounting for some of this variability for decades. For example, the Nuclear Regulatory Commission determine the likelihood of failures in complex systems, and Systems-Theoretic Accident Model and Processes (STAMP) showed that accidents can emerge from interactions among working components, people, and organizations. But AI raises the stakes, because just a single component can now interpret, infer, and act. The stakes rise further as AI moves from browsers into vehicles, robots, medical systems, industrial controls, and data centers, where a wrong answer can become a life-threatening event.
Building trust that scales
It’s clear that a person rubber-stamping thousands of AI actions an hour is not an acceptable—or scalable—safeguard against risk. But the remedy is not to remove people from the loop; it is to put human judgment where it counts: setting limits in advance and approving the rare actions that have serious consequences while hard constraints handle the rest.
Therefore, trust has to move upstream into architecture. The central questions become: What authority are we willing to give AI, under what conditions, and supported by what evidence? And what happens outside those conditions? That is very different from asking whether a model scored 94% on a benchmark.
The determinism paradox does not mean AI cannot be trusted. It means trust needs a different architecture. Instead of making every output predictable, make the boundaries predictable. An AI medical assistant may be probabilistic in its diagnosis, but deterministic rules govern whether it can change a prescription. An industrial AI may find many ways to optimize a process, while fixed limits keep it within pressure and temperature bounds. An agent may decide how to complete a task, while permissions, transaction limits, and human approvals determine what it is authorized to do.
Let AI be probabilistic inside the box and make the box itself deterministic wherever consequences matter. Leaders can put this into practice by asking five questions:
- What authority does AI have? Define not only what it can do but what it is allowed to do, separating interpretation, recommendation, decision, and execution.
- Is the function of AI proportional to the consequence? A marketing copilot and AI controlling industrial equipment need different assurance thresholds.
- Are we taking the appropriate steps toward autonomy? For example, there needs to be a plan to move from having AI interpret while humans decide, to AI making recommendations, to then taking action with approval, and ultimately to having supervised autonomy, but only as AI can safely work at each step.
- Are we testing the system or merely the model? Unexpected interactions emerge among models, data, agents, APIs, and human workflows.
- Are we continuously earning trust? Monitor drift, failures, near-misses, and model changes throughout the lifecycle.
The winners in AI will be those who solve the determinism paradox—giving AI enough freedom to create value while engineering boundaries strong enough to make what it does with that freedom trustworthy. Invention earns attention. Trust earns adoption.

articles.title: Nvidia amassed $530 billion in financial guarantees to corner the AI market — supply commitments rose by nearly a quarter of a trillion dollars in a single quarter
articles.text:
Nvidia amassed $530 billion in financial guarantees to corner the AI market — supply commitments rose by nearly a quarter of a trillion dollars in a single quarter
Without a doubt, Nvidia's dominance in the AI hardware market stems not only from the capabilities of its AI accelerators and its vast software ecosystem, but also from its aggressive procurement strategy that effectively denies its rivals access to sufficient production capacity at TSMC and other contractors. The result of his deals is that supply and capacity commitments rose by almost a quarter of a trillion dollars in a single quarter, primarily due to memory procurement, according to SemiAnalysis. However, even Nvidia's former chief executive Jensen Huang had apparently begun to question the sustainability of this strategy before his departure, based on reports from The Wall Street Journal and SemiAnalysis.
Over the past several years, Nvidia has not only captured the vast majority of the AI accelerator market, but has also secured a substantial proportion of the world's production capacity for advanced logic, high-bandwidth memory (HBM), and various other components required to build AI accelerators and systems, which has limited the ability of its competitors to ramp up shipments of their processors. To support the deals, Jensen Huang personally negotiated agreements with major suppliers in Taiwan and South Korea.
The massive scale of Nvidia's procurement commitments also enabled the company to secure more favorable quotes than its rivals. SemiAnalysis estimates that SK hynix could charge Nvidia between $3.00 and $3.30 per gigabit of HBM4 memory in 2027, whereas other first-tier customers, such as AMD, Amazon, Broadcom, and Google, would pay between $3.70 and $4.10 per gigabit. The analysts believe that as part of an informal arrangement between the two companies, Nvidia gives SK Group preferential access to its AI GPUs.
While Nvidia's ability to secure vast production capacities has been instrumental in its success, such commitments also carry considerable risks. At a meeting with senior executives in August, Huang reportedly expressed concerns about the massive volumes of wafers and memory that Nvidia had committed to purchase as major cloud service providers sought to reduce their reliance on the company's hardware in favor of alternative AI accelerator platforms, according to The Wall Street Journal.
In a bid to diversify its customer base and create additional demand for its products, Nvidia offered financial guarantees to emerging cloud service providers and data center developers that otherwise could not afford to procure its hardware at scale. As of the end of its fiscal second quarter, Nvidia had $530 billion in gross off-balance-sheet guarantees, up from $184 billion a quarter earlier, as well as $99 billion worth of equity investments, according to SemiAnalysis. As half a trillion dollars seems gargantuan, here is a breakdown based on a filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission:
- $366 billion in future commitments (of which $279 billion was supply and capacity commitments, mainly for memory and manufacturing);
- $56 billion in additional commitments (including $36 billion in AI cloud agreements/take-or-pay arrangements and $20 billion in data-center leases expected to be reassigned);
- $108.5 billion in maximum gross exposure under guarantees (of which $105 billion was a lease/credit-support guarantee related to SB Energy’s PORTS Technology Campus in Ohio for an OpenAI affiliate, plus $3.5 billion for other AI-cloud partner land/power/shell guarantees).
The scale of such commitments raised concerns even within Nvidia. Then-CFO Colette Kress questioned the criteria used to select recipients of financial support and the potential returns on such arrangements. She also reportedly reduced Nvidia's initial financial commitment to OpenAI's massive data center project in Ohio by half before the two companies signed an agreement on August 17. The facility is expected to house some $300 billion worth of Nvidia processors.
Massive outcome?
At some point, Huang himself began to question the merits of Nvidia's aggressive financing strategy in the event of his departure, essentially calling the current interim CEO, Colette Kress, a mere 'reporting CFO' rather than an executive capable of making strategic decisions. He also expressed concerns about massive wafer and memory procurement commitments as major cloud service providers sought to reduce their reliance on Nvidia’s GPUs.

Despite questionable commitments, without Huang and his personal relationships with executives at major semiconductor companies, Nvidia may find it harder to secure preferential treatment from its suppliers. articles.title: United Airlines system outage disrupts departures just days after the big ground stop
articles.text:
Less than a week after an issue with air traffic control communications and radar caused the FAA to halt takeoffs nationwide, United Airlines departing flights are being disrupted by an outage. The airline has said it is working to get things up and running again as quickly as possible, but without much detail about the issue itself.
United Airlines system outage disrupts departures just days after the big ground stop
Is everything down right now?
Is everything down right now?
The outage is also coming after last week’s global Microsoft Outlook shutdown, and the great-bank-outage-that-wasn’t earlier Monday afternoon. According to posts on social media, a number of people onboard the planes have heard from their pilots that a systemwide IT outage for United has caused problems with a weight and balance calculator that has stopped them from getting clearance to take off.
United tweeted that “We are troubleshooting a technology issue affecting departing flights. There is no impact on flights in progress, or on United Express flights.” So far, there’s no word on when it expects the problem to be resolved, and when the impacted flights will be able to leave for their destinations.

articles.title: Si tienes un iPhone Duo, esta nueva función cambiará por completo la forma de desbloquearlo
articles.text:
El iPhone Duo se ha convertido en uno de los móviles más exitosos de la historia de Apple. El primer plegable de la compañía tuvo un gran recibimiento, aunque su diseño provocó que no contara con una de las funciones más útiles del iPhone: Face ID. La buena noticia es que Apple ha lanzado un desbloqueo facial para solucionar la carencia hasta que llegue su sucesor.
De acuerdo con TechCrunch, Apple ha lanzado un desbloqueo facial para el iPhone Duo. La nueva función estará disponible a través de la actualización de iOS 27.3 y se conoce como "face unlock". Esta característica aprovecha la cámara frontal del dispositivo para reconocer al usuario y desbloquear el móvil, pero tiene algunas limitaciones comparado con Face ID.
La principal limitante del desbloqueo facial del iPhone Duo es que solo funciona si el usuario se ha autenticado por Touch ID o código de acceso. Si es la primera vez que abres el móvil, tendrás que usar tu huella o introducir el PIN para que puedas usar tu rostro más adelante. Además, Apple ha añadido otras barreras de seguridad que te impedirán usar la cámara frontal como método de autenticación.
Las compras realizadas con Apple Pay y el acceso a las contraseñas seguirán requiriendo Touch ID. Lo mismo pasa si tu iPhone Duo permanece inactivo durante 45 minutos o más, donde necesitarás firmarte con tu huella o código antes de que el desbloqueo facial pueda utilizarse otra vez. Es por ello que Apple ha dejado claro que no es un equivalente de Face ID, sino una solución temporal a quienes extrañan este método.
¿Por qué no puedes usar el Face ID en el iPhone Duo?
El iPhone Duo no cuenta con Face ID debido a que su estructura no deja espacio suficiente para añadir el sistema TrueDepth que usa Apple en otros modelos de iPhone. Este tipo de desbloqueo requiere sensores especializados que pueden crear un mapa tridimensional del rostro, el cual se logra a través de un iluminador y un proyector que emite más de 30.000 puntos infrarrojos invisibles. El sistema también cuenta con mecanismos de comprobación para evitar el uso de fotografías o imágenes planas para engañarlo.
La ausencia de esta función ha sido una de las críticas más sonadas al plegable. Además de no ofrecer Face ID, el iPhone Duo la pone difícil para autenticarnos a través del Touch ID, ya que el móvil no siempre reconoce la huella en el primer intento. Es por ello que se implementó un tipo de desbloqueo facial que podría evitar que tengas que introducir tu clave cada que activas el móvil.
Según el periodista Mark Gurman, Apple ya está probando los primeros prototipos del iPhone Duo 2 con Face ID. Los de Cupertino no se han decidido si se integrará en el modelo de 2027 o se ofrecerá más adelante, ya que primero tendrían que mover la ubicación de la cámara frontal. La compañía también considera añadir un botón de acción similar al de los demás iPhone, aunque esto último sigue en el aire ya que un segundo rumor afirma que este botón desaparecerá de toda la línea de dispositivos en 2027.
Por el momento no hay información oficial sobre el sucesor del iPhone Duo, aunque es un hecho que Apple está trabajando en él y tendrá que solucionar dos de sus problemas más evidentes.

articles.title: Piratage de La Poste : la police lance une enquête pour retrouver les pirates
articles.text:
La justice vient de se saisir de l’affaire Maileva. Vingt-quatre heures après les révélations de La Poste, le parquet de Paris a confirmé l’ouverture d’une enquête sur la cyberattaque à l’AFP. Les investigations concernent une « atteinte à un système de traitement automatisé de données ».
À lire aussi : Fuites de données – la France sort du top 3 mondial, mais 18 comptes sont encore piratés chaque minute
« Une telle fuite ne s’est pas faite en un clic »
Sans surprise, l’enquête a été confiée à la Brigade de lutte contre la cybercriminalité (BL2C), un service d’enquête spécialisé de la police. C’est déjà cette unité qui s’est occupée de l’enquête sur le piratage du ministère, survenu en décembre 2025, le hack de la Fédération française de tir, ou la cyberattaque à l’encontre d’Intermarché.
Plusieurs de ces investigations se sont soldées par des arrestations. Un hacker de 22 ans a été interpellé à la fin de l’année dernière, à Limoges. Quelques semaines plus tard, un pirate de 18 ans arrêté en Seine-Saint-Denis en janvier 2026. En avril, « HexDex », un hacker de 22 ans soupçonné du piratage de nombreuses fédérations sportives, a été arrêté en Vendée.
De son côté, Thomas Lazzaroni, l’auteur de l’enquête qui a révélé l’attaque avant la Poste, pointe des failles de sécurité dans les systèmes du groupe. Selon lui, l’offensive n’a pas été orchestrée par une bande d’adolescents.
« Vingt-deux millions de personnes, c’est énorme. Une telle fuite ne s’est pas faite en un clic : ça a dû prendre des heures. Normalement, un bon système aurait dû notifier cette intrusion. Ça n’a pas été le cas », estime-t-il auprès de nos confréres de France 3 Hauts-de-France, ajoutant qu’on est « loin d’ados comme ça avait été le cas avec l’État ».
Le chercheur penche plutôt pour une organisation structurée, sans évoquer le nom d’une puissance étrangère. Pour rappel, La Poste a révélé que l’attaque s’est soldée par le vol des coordonnées de 22 millions de personnes, à savoir leur prénom, leur nom et leur adresse postale. Les victimes ne sont pas les clients de Maileva, mais les destinataires des courriers envoyés par des entreprises clientes, qui utilisent les services de la filiale.
À lire aussi : Après les frigos des supermarchés, l’Europe s’inquiète des cyberattaques contre « les appareils ménagers »
« Une situation sensible »
Parmi les entreprises touchées, on trouve un bailleur social des Hauts-de-France, qui n’a pas voulu décliner son identité. Le bailleur assure faire face à « une situation sensible » et que c’est « la première fois » que cela lui arrive. Le bailleur ignore combien de ses locataires sont concernés.
« On ne sait pas si c’est un ou 300 clients concernés. Peut-être qu’il n’y a personne », juge le bailleur social.
Les notifications envoyées aux victimes arrivent actuellement au compte-gouttes. Maileva doit seulement prévenir tous ses clients. C’est ensuite à eux d’informer ensuite les personnes concernées de la fuite, actuellement très difficile à circonscrire. En attendant, méfiez-vous de tout courrier, e-mail ou SMS inattendu qui prétend provenir d’un hôpital, d’un bailleur ou encore d’un service de recommandé.
