articles.title: The cost of making stablecoins work in Nigeria
articles.text:
This is Follow the Money, our weekly series that unpacks the earnings, business, and scaling strategies of African fintechs, financial institutions, companies, and governments. A new edition drops every Monday.
Nigeria now has rules that officially recognise stablecoins as payment and settlement instruments, giving issuers a framework to distribute tokens backed by fiat currencies. The Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) divides these tokens into two: naira-referenced and foreign currency-referenced stablecoins.
Stablecoins are digital currencies designed to maintain the value of currencies such as the naira or US dollar. Companies issuing them must hold enough money and other assets to back the tokens in circulation—which they create.
Under the new rules, foreign currency-backed issuers must hold up to ₦15 billion ($11.16 million) in minimum capital, while naira-backed issuers must hold ₦10 billion ($7.44 million). But the more consequential requirements concern what happens to customers’ money after they buy stablecoins.
Stablecoin holders cannot earn interest on their tokens, even though issuers can invest the money backing those tokens in interest-bearing assets. Cryptocurrency exchanges and other virtual asset service providers (VASPs) distributing regulated stablecoins cannot offer yield on behalf of issuers either.
The CBN has also restricted how issuers invest their reserves. Naira-backed issuers must keep part of their reserves in an interest-free account at the central bank and place other funds in approved financial institutions. This creates a difficult business model. Independent issuers must raise substantial capital to operate, but face limits on how much they can earn from the money backing their tokens.
These requirements could make stablecoins more useful for payments than savings, while giving commercial banks an advantage over independent issuers.
The money behind cNGN
Nigeria already has a privately issued naira-backed stablecoin, cNGN, which went live in February 2025. It is issued by a private company, Wrapped CBDC Limited, and is designed to maintain a one-to-one value with the naira.
Like other stablecoins, cNGN needs reserves to ensure that customers can exchange their tokens for money. Wrapped CBDC Limited holds those reserves in bank accounts and financial investments.
At the end of October 2026, cNGN had ₦4.41 billion ($3.3 million) in circulating tokens, backed by ₦4.67 billion ($3.48 million) in reserve assets, according to its attestation report. The issuer invested about ₦1.86 billion ($1.4 million) in money market funds, ₦786.1 million ($585,000) in fixed-term investments, and ₦621.6 million ($462,700) in Treasury and Open Market Operation (OMO) bills. The remaining ₦1.41 billion ($1.05 million) was held in bank deposits.
This means about 70% of the money backing cNGN was invested in assets that could generate returns. Some of its government securities carried annual interest rates between 17.5% and 19%.
The new CBN rules would require the issuer to operate a different reserve model. Naira stablecoin issuers must keep at least 20% of their reserves in an account at the CBN that pays no interest. Applying that requirement to cNGN’s October reserve portfolio would place about ₦935 million ($696,000) at the central bank.
At an annual interest rate of 18%, that money could generate about ₦168 million ($125,040) in a year if it remained invested at that rate. The mandatory CBN deposit would remove that earning opportunity.
However, the back-of-the-envelope math does not mean cNGN would lose ₦168 million ($125,040). Its reserves include assets earning different rates, and the company could fund the CBN deposit from investments or bank balances with lower returns.
The rules also limit money market fund investments to 10% of reserves.
In October, cNGN held ₦1.86 billion ($1.4 million), about 40% of its reserves, in those funds. Applying the new limit to the same portfolio would reduce that holding to about ₦467 million ($347,600), requiring about ₦1.39 billion ($1.03 million) to be moved elsewhere. The replacement assets could still earn interest. But issuers would have less freedom to decide where to invest their reserves.
Can you build a stablecoin company under Nigeria’s new rules?
You inherit cNGN’s October 2026 reserve portfolio. Rearrange ₦4.67 billion in assets to satisfy the new reserve rules without losing track of the money.
Move money between five reserve buckets. You have ₦4.67 billion to work with. Keep an eye on the rules as you allocate it.
Move the reserves
Drag the sliders or enter amounts directly. All figures are in ₦ millions. You can leave funds unallocated temporarily while rearranging your portfolio.
Compliance dashboard
1 / 3
Your reserve balance
Spread your deposits across banks
Split your commercial-bank deposits across three banks. Each must receive more than zero, and no bank can hold more than 30% of total reserves (₦1,401m).
The cost of locking away reserves
Moving 20% of reserves into a non-interest-bearing CBN account removes the opportunity to earn on that allocation. At an illustrative 18% annual rate, ₦934m could have earned about ₦168m in a year. This is not an estimate of actual lost profit.
This simulation tests selected reserve-allocation rules only. It does not model the separate ₦10bn issuer capital requirement, asset eligibility, liquidity tests or all concentration requirements. Passing the game is not regulatory approval.
The CBN is restricting investment income at both ends of the business. Customers cannot earn yield on their tokens, while issuers must keep some of the backing money in limited assets.
Stablecoins could become a tool for payments only
The restriction on customer interest could also affect how long people hold stablecoins.
In September 2026, Nigerian savings accounts paid an average annual interest rate of 5.36%, according to CBN data. One-month bank deposits paid 12.20%, three-month deposits paid 10.33%, while the Treasury bill benchmark stood at 16.24%.
At those rates, a customer holding ₦1 million ($744.29) in a savings account for a year would earn ₦53,600 ($40) if the rate remained unchanged. The same amount invested at the Treasury bill benchmark would generate an annualised return of ₦162,400 ($120.87). Holding ₦1 million ($744.29) in regulated stablecoins would generate no interest.
These products have different risks, access requirements, and liquidity conditions. Interest rates can also change. But the comparison helps explain why the new rules will disincentivise customers from holding stablecoins long-term.
Think about a trader who frequently sources large amounts of foreign exchange (FX) using stablecoins. The trader may need to keep funds in stablecoins to settle transactions quickly whenever opportunities arise. But if those funds sit idle for weeks, they earn nothing. Keeping the money in an interest-bearing account until it is needed could be more attractive, even if moving it into stablecoins later adds another step to the transaction.
This presents a problem for issuers. The longer customers keep their tokens, the longer the issuer can hold the reserves backing them and potentially earn interest. So, a customer who holds stablecoins for several months provides a more stable source of funds for investment than one who buys tokens and spends them within hours.
Yet, the new rules give customers little financial reason to leave large balances in stablecoins when they are not making payments. Issuers may still attract frequent users, but keeping their money between transactions could prove harder.
Without yield, it is one less financial incentive keeping customers from adopting stablecoins, especially the local-currency variations.
One coin.
Three layers of protection.
Under Nigeria’s new rules, the reserves backing a naira stablecoin must follow a defined structure. Here’s how the money is organised.
How 100% can be divided
Illustrative allocation, not fixed proportions. The CBN deposit must be at least 20%, cash and high-quality liquid assets at least 40%, and other eligible assets can make up the remaining balance. The CBN deposit does not count towards the 40% liquid-asset requirement.
The central bank vault
At least one-fifth of the reserve pool must be deposited directly with the Central Bank of Nigeria.
Ready-to-use liquidity
At least 40% must be held in cash or high-quality liquid assets, separate from the mandatory CBN deposit.
The remaining investments
Up to 40% can sit in other eligible reserve holdings, depending on how much is allocated to the first two tiers.
Extra protection, paid for by the issuer
Issuers must provide an additional overcollateralisation buffer of at least 2%, funded from their own capital to absorb reserve losses. It is not a fourth slice of the 100% allocation.
No single bank gets the whole pot.
Commercial-bank reserve deposits must be spread across at least three licensed Nigerian banks. No single bank can hold more than 30% of the total reserve pool.
And the rules don’t stop there.
Off limits: Corporate bonds, commercial paper, foreign-currency assets, equities, crypto assets, loans, commodities and real estate are excluded from the permitted reserve investments described in the rules.
This is part of the reason why digital asset companies in the United States have been pushing for yield inclusion in stablecoin issuance—or, at least, something similar under a new term, “rewards.”
In Africa, regulators are following a similar logic to protect their domestic financial sector from capital flight. Compared to private stablecoin issuers, banks and financial institutions run better-capitalised businesses that can protect customers.
This creates another challenge for stablecoin issuers. They need people to use their tokens for payments, but they also benefit when customers keep those tokens for longer.
cNGN’s trading volume underscores this difference between moving money and holding it. The naira-backed stablecoin has recorded about ₦451.7 billion ($336.2 million) in cumulative trading activity, yet only ₦4.41 billion ($3.28 million) worth of tokens was in circulation at the end of October.
That does not mean ₦451.7 billion ($336.2 million) passed into the issuer’s reserves. A token can change hands several times without bringing in additional money. The amount available for investment depends on how many tokens remain in circulation, not how often they are traded.
By prohibiting yield, the CBN may be encouraging stablecoins to compete as payment services rather than savings products.
Why banks may have an advantage
The cost of entering the market could make that competition harder. But critically, the rules also preserve the role of commercial banks in Nigeria’s financial system.
On the cost side, naira-backed stablecoin issuers must maintain ₦10 billion ($7.44 million) in minimum capital, separate from the reserves backing their tokens. That is more than twice cNGN’s ₦4.41 billion ($3.28 million) circulating supply in October.
The new rules also require naira stablecoin issuers to keep reserve deposits across at least three Nigerian commercial banks, with no single bank holding more than 30% of the reserve pool. Even when an independent company issues the tokens, commercial banks remain involved in holding the assets behind them.
Commercial banks have an advantage because they already hold customer deposits and operate the payment accounts through which much of Nigeria’s money moves. Independent stablecoin issuers must persuade customers to move money into their tokens. Banks already have that money and the relationships with customers who own it.
Banks have another advantage: they can issue deposit money tokens (DMTs) on their existing banking licences, allowing customers to use money already in their bank accounts to make payments through digital-token networks.
Take a Nigerian wholesaler paying a supplier ₦5 million ($3,721). If both businesses use a payment network that accepts tokens issued by the wholesaler’s bank, the wholesaler could convert ₦5 million ($3,721) from its account into five million tokens worth ₦1 ($0.00074) each and transfer them to the supplier. The supplier could then redeem the tokens for naira through the bank. The payment could be recorded and settled on the same network, potentially making it easier for both businesses to track.
The ₦5 million ($3,721) is not new money. It remains a claim against the issuing bank, even when represented by digital tokens. Unlike an independent stablecoin company, the bank does not need to attract a separate ₦5 million ($3,721) reserve to issue those tokens. It also doesn’t need a separate ₦10 billion ($7.44 million) stablecoin issuer capital base. However, lenders also face an interest-free reserve requirement, with the CBN requiring commercial banks to keep 45% of their eligible deposits as cash reserves, as of September 2026.
They must obtain CBN approval before issuing DMTs and remain subject to banking capital, liquidity, customer protection, and payment-system requirements. The advantage is that they can issue these tokens against existing deposits without creating a separate stablecoin reserve pool, helping to keep the underlying deposits within the banking system.
This could shape the future of Nigeria’s stablecoin market.
Customers gain another payment option but cannot earn interest from holding regulated stablecoins. Independent issuers can earn from permitted investments and services, but must operate within costly capital and reserve requirements. Banks remain involved in holding reserves and can develop competing digital payment products.
The likely outcome is that independent stablecoin issuers will have to compete on the speed, cost, and convenience of their payment services. Meanwhile, banks can offer similar digital payment services to customers whose deposits they already hold. Even if stablecoin payments grow, much of the money supporting those transactions could remain within the banking system.
Ultimately, Nigeria’s rules may favour stablecoin businesses that are good at payments, but the capital requirements could favour institutions that are already large.

articles.title: upGrad broadens its business with new workforce advisory venture
articles.text:
upGrad broadens its business with new workforce advisory venture
upGrad launches workforce advisory business as it expands beyond skilling, aiming to help organisations navigate AI-led transformation through integrated workforce strategy and implementation.
Edtech firm upGrad has launched upGrad Next, a workforce advisory business intended to help organisations redesign how they structure, hire, reward and develop employees as artificial intelligence (AI) reshapes work.
The move broadens upGrad’s corporate offering as it diversifies beyond skilling into higher education, professional courses, study-abroad services and enterprise learning. Its acquisition of Unacademy adds competitive exam preparation to its edtech portfolio, as the company, led by chairperson and co-founder Ronnie Screwvala, eyes a potential IPO.
Anandorup Ghose will lead Next as managing director, with Hrishikesh Godbole, Krishna Chaitanya and Dinkar Pawan among the initial team.
Screwvala described the launch as a response to the next phase of digital change. “The last decade, in many ways, was about the complete digital transformation of organisations. We see the next decade being about transforming the workforce to manage, and get strong returns from, the change that has already happened.”
Next will advise on organisational structure, recruitment, pay and workforce development, and help put those decisions into practice. upGrad said it will combine experienced advisers with AI and its skilling and hiring operations, with accountability for outcomes rather than consultant time billed.
Ghose, who has spent more than 24 years in HR and rewards consulting, worked as a partner at Aon and Deloitte and led the latter’s rewards consulting practice globally. He sees a gap between large technology transformation programmes and specialist products. “These demand experience and judgment. The next decade won't be won by those who adopt technology fastest, but by those who unlock human potential most effectively.”
His argument is that decisions about AI investment, job design and employee capability need to be made together. Technology adoption alone does not guarantee higher productivity.
Aon’s 2026 Human Capital Trends study found that 43% of organisations in India had deployed AI and a further 20% were piloting it, but translating investment into workforce outcomes remained difficult. The World Economic Forum’s Future of Jobs Report 2025 estimated that 39% of workers’ existing skill sets would be transformed or become outdated by 2030, while 63% of employers saw skills gaps as a major barrier to business transformation.
Consulting and technology firms are also combining these capabilities. In October 2026, KPMG in India and HR technology company PeopleStrong announced an alliance pairing workforce advice with AI-enabled human capital management software for employee data and HR processes. In September, Deloitte launched an Open Model Engineering practice to help organisations build and deploy AI tools for business use, and said it would hire and train specialists to work alongside clients. Both moves highlight the growing overlap between advice and implementation.
Meanwhile, the Government programmes are expanding the skills pipeline. The Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship said the Skill India Digital Hub’s SOAR programme now includes 50 AI and AI-application qualifications. By August 2026, more than 517,000 learners had enrolled and over 100,000 had been certified.

articles.title: HyperX Cloud III S Wireless, análisis: prometer más de 100 horas sin cargarlos parecía una exageración hasta que los probé
articles.text:
El mercado de los periféricos gaming está saturado de auriculares que intentan justificar su precio con lucecitas RGB, diseños variopintos o especificaciones a las que no todos sacan partido. Ahora bien, cuando me siento —de nuevo— frente al PC después de trabajar, lo único que realmente importa es que no me acaben doliendo las orejas, que no me deje tirado a mitad de la partida y que suene bien. HyperX lleva tiempo perfeccionando esta fórmula, y con estos cascos de diadema quieren evolucionar uno de los aspectos más relevantes: la batería.
He pasado las últimas semanas jugando a 'Project Zomboid', ‘WoW’ y 'Fortnite', entre otros, con los HyperX Cloud III S Wireless. No son unos auriculares premium prohibitivos para el bolsillo, ni pretenden competir con el sonido de unos monitores de estudio, sino que logran algo más sencillo: conformar un conjunto notable donde todo funciona como debe. Te cuento cómo ha sido mi experiencia usándolos.
✅ Cómpralos si...
- Juegas en casa y quieres un buen sonido y comodidad sin gastar una fortuna.
- Odias el “power off” en medio de una partida. Maravilla que sea sin cables con esta autonomía.
❌ No lo compres si...
- Quieres unos cascos de altísima gama y no tienes límite de presupuesto.
- Buscas unos auriculares polivalentes para salir con ellos a la calle.
- Necesitas imperativamente cancelación de ruido activa (ANC)
Lo esencial en 30 segundos
Los HyperX Cloud III S Wireless son unos auriculares circumaurales de gama media enfocados en el jugador de PC y consolas. Su reclamo es una batería que, en mis pruebas, supera las 100 horas cuando se usan con el pinchito USB de 2,4 GHz y muchas más si solo se usan vía Bluetooth. Por unos 150 euros, ofrecen transductores en ángulo de 53 mm, un chasis reconocible de aluminio y acero, y la clásica espuma viscoelástica de la marca. Prescinden de tecnologías costosas como el ANC en favor de ejecutar los fundamentos —comodidad, estabilidad y autonomía— de forma impecable.
8,3
A favor
- La batería: en 2,4 GHz, todavía dura más
- Muy cómodos. Se asientan de maravilla y no generan presión
- La conectividad dual (2,4 GHz y Bluetooth) es estable
En contra
- Carecen de rotación en las copas, algo que puede restar para ti
- No son unos auriculares discretos para sacar del setup de casa
- El micrófono cumple, pero no sustituirá a uno de mesa si buscas grabar o streaming
HyperX Cloud III S - Auriculares Gaming inalámbricos, Bluetooth, 2.4Ghz, PC, PS5, Xbox, Drivers 53 mm, DTS, micrófono 10mm, batería hasta 200h, Rojo-Negro
Nuestra experiencia con los HyperX Cloud III S Wireless
El triunfo de la comodidad. Hay auriculares que, pasadas las dos horas, me recuerdan que los llevo puestos. Me suele doler la coronilla con los auriculares cableados de Xbox Series, pero con estos Cloud III S Wireless no me ha sucedido en absoluto.
Se sienten bastante cómodos; no quedan holgados, sino muy bien asentados en la cabeza y las orejas. El peso ronda los 340 gramos, en la media de la competencia, pero el reparto de la presión está tan bien logrado que no he tenido quejas.
Es cierto que carecen de rotación lateral (swivel) en las copas; en mi caso no me penaliza, me basta con su inclinación, pero entiendo perfectamente que haya quienes puedan echar de menos ese punto extra de ajuste.
Una batería que dura. Prometer esas cifras en autonomía es un reclamo potente, pero vivirlo cambia la experiencia. He viciado a varios títulos en mi PC, entre ellos ‘Fortnite’, y me he olvidado de cargarlos.
Literalmente: es un lujazo la tranquilidad que transmiten, sea cual sea el momento que me los ponga. Funcionan bien tanto por Bluetooth como con el receptor USB, aunque para jugar (y para evitar cualquier tipo de latencia) es preferible tirar de este segundo.
Equilibrio. HyperX ha entendido muy bien a su público. Estos auriculares no buscan ser lo más de lo más en fidelidad, ni intentan que su micrófono compita con uno de condensador de mesa.
Su logro es reunir todas las piezas en un conjunto notable, y lo consiguen. El sonido tiene cuerpo, los pasos y disparos se posicionan bien en el estéreo, y el micrófono aísla lo suficiente como para que en Discord se escuche de forma clara.
Botones funcionales pero con margen de mejora. Me costó bastante acostumbrarme a la distribución de los botones. La rueda de volumen cumple, aunque se siente algo pequeña para mi gusto; sigo prefiriendo otras soluciones como la de Xbox, que permiten regular el nivel girando directamente el lateral.
Con los días, la mano acaba mecanizando el gesto. Por otro lado, la ubicación del botón de silencio para el micrófono no está mal, pero se echa en falta un relieve o una textura más diferenciada para no dudar al tocar a ciegas.
Un interruptor útil. Alternar entre los modos inalámbricos es sencillo gracias a un botón que conmuta entre ambos. Me ha venido bien puntualmente: estoy en el ordenador, me llega un audio de WhatsApp al teléfono, pauso el juego, le doy al botón de cambio e instantáneamente estoy escuchando el audio en los auriculares.
El móvil se conecta en apenas un par de segundos. Esa agilidad para cambiar de dispositivo sin tener que volver a emparejar le otorga una versatilidad mayúscula en el día a día.

HyperX Cloud III S Wireless, la opinión de Xataka
La marca ha sido pragmática con estos auriculares: pulir lo que importa cuando uno se sienta a jugar. Es cierto que por su precio, la inclusión de cancelación de ruido le habría sentado de maravilla para redondear el producto, pero están tan bien rematados que resulta difícil ponerle reproches más allá de eso.
Tampoco sería justo que penalizase en exceso al micrófono. Cumple en llamadas, sea a través de programas como Discord o ingame en títulos multijugador, cancelando el ruido ambiente de forma más que digna. No puedo negar que, como comenté en detalle, la disposición de los botones requiere un periodo de adaptación —especialmente por la rueda de volumen— y que la ausencia de rotación le resta ergonomía a fisonomías concretas. Sin embargo, en el cómputo global, sus virtudes pasan por encima de estas pequeñas sombras.
Los HyperX Cloud III S me han conquistado por una sencilla razón: prescinden de florituras para ejecutar de forma sobresaliente lo esencial. Sonido contundente y equilibrado, cómodos para jugar durante horas y la versatilidad de su conectividad completan unos auriculares notables. Quien busque rendimiento sin muchos extras, saldrá contento.
¿Te los recomiendo?
Sí, especialmente si te fatiga el uso de auriculares in-ear y buscas dar con unos que destaquen en ergonomía para tus sesiones de gaming. Aunque no desentonan escuchando música de forma casual, distan de ofrecer la fidelidad y el detalle de los dedicados. Su terreno es la partida y el sofá o escritorio.
Ahora bien, descártalos si quieres grabar podcasts o emitir en directo con la máxima calidad, si necesitas unos auriculares para viajar o si tu cabeza pide un aparato más personalizable. Tampoco son para quien busque unos auriculares de estudio de gama alta.

articles.title: Usable Security at Luxury Hotels - Schneier on Security
articles.text:
Usable Security at Luxury Hotels
Interesting case study from luxury hotels. Attackers used a fake booking request to gain access to a reservations inbox, where they copied genuine refund requests and got fraudulent ones approved.
This is a good illustration why “just don’t click on links” is bad advice. It can’t work when answering strangers’ emails is the job. Even worse, in this case the guest-first culture punishes hesitation. More interesting, the case study shows that splitting security between owner, operator, and brand leaves nobody accountable. And this is exactly the setting where blaming staff becomes the convenient answer.
TimH • November 16, 2026 7:22 AM
TFA: “We suspect a colleague opened the email and clicked the link, unknowingly giving the attackers access to the reservations shared inbox.”
So there was no front-end layer checking inbox content for such dubiosities? Or limiting access to specific computer MACs, or intranet IP ranges.
The ball is in the IT org’s court for not setting this up.
Same with IT who can’t set a limit of 5 CCs on emails to stop an email blast CCing every customer.

articles.title: How MoEngage built agentic customer engagement on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
How MoEngage built agentic customer engagement on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
This post was co-written with Ashwin Srinivasan, Nishan Das and Karthik Baile from MoEngage.
A marketing or product team member planning a weekend flash sale often opens three tools before writing a single line of copy. First they open the analytics dashboard to see what worked last time, then the content library to find the right tone, and then the campaign builder to build the campaign itself. Repeat that across email, push, SMS, and WhatsApp, and much of a marketing team’s week goes to navigating tools instead of making decisions.
The MoEngage Model Context Protocol (MCP) Connector gives an MCP-compatible assistant, such as Claude or ChatGPT, secure, tenant-scoped access to a brand’s segments, campaign history, and content library.
This capability points to a broader shift in software platforms. Beyond a user interface for business users and an API for engineering teams, a third layer is emerging, where a user describes an outcome in plain language and an agent carries out the steps across the platform. For a customer engagement platform, that means a capability already exposed as an API can become a tool an agent calls, and a campaign that once moved across several tools can move through one conversation instead.
MoEngage, the agentic customer engagement platform that more than 1,350 consumer brands use across channels including push, email, in-app, SMS, WhatsApp, and Rich Communication Services (RCS), set out to build this layer. MoEngage built Merlin AI, a set of artificial intelligence (AI) agents that work with live platform data. Marketing and product teams can now draft, analyze, and adjust campaigns from a single conversation, while agents decide what to send each customer. One customer, Glance, saw a 38% uplift in push notification click-through rates as a result.
MoEngage treated this as an architecture problem. The question was how to give agents secure, tenant-scoped access to live data without rebuilding hundreds of existing APIs. In this post, we walk through how MoEngage solved it with Amazon Bedrock and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, a platform to build, connect, and optimize AI agents at scale with any framework or model. The post covers the four agent modes in Merlin AI, how MoEngage exposed its existing APIs as MCP tools, and how the architecture keeps each tenant’s data isolated. It closes with the results MoEngage customers have seen and the pattern other software providers can reuse.
Solution overview: Four agent modes in Merlin AI
Merlin AI runs four kinds of agents. All four share the same foundation: foundation models in Amazon Bedrock for reasoning and generation, AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, for hosting, and MCP for standardized access to data. Across all four modes, Merlin AI uses Anthropic Claude Sonnet 4.6, Claude Sonnet 5, and Claude Sonnet 5.5 on Amazon Bedrock for reasoning, tool-call planning, and content generation. For the full list of models, see Supported foundation models in Amazon Bedrock.
Embedded agents in Merlin AI Studio
Merlin AI Studio places purpose-built agents at the exact point in the workflow where marketing and product teams do that piece of work:
- Copywriter generates personalized push and transactional copy that stays consistent with the brand voice.
- Designer produces a marketing banner or image from a text description.
- Segment Assist turns a plain-language audience description into the correct set of attributes and filters. For example, a marketing or product team member can ask for users who abandoned a cart in the last 2 hours.
- Jinja Assist converts natural-language requests into working Jinja and Liquid markup for dynamic content.
- In-app Template Builder creates responsive, accessible HTML templates for in-app messages, including gamified formats, lead-capture pop-ups, and surveys.
- Flow Assist turns a high-level idea into a ready-to-deploy customer journey. Behind the scenes, a sequence of specialized steps interprets the request, proposes paths, builds the flow structure, refines it with historical data, and packages it for deployment.
Conversational agents
Conversational agents work across campaigns, analytics, segments, and flows. A user can ask a question in plain language and the agent calls the right tools to answer it or act on it. The Campaign Insights Agent, embedded on the analytics page, delegates to specialized sub-agents. One sub-agent runs analysis across several metrics at once. A second diagnoses why a metric is underperforming, and a third compares performance across time periods or segments. A final step formats the findings into a clear answer.
Custom agents
Custom agents let lifecycle and customer relationship management (CRM) teams design agents that run continuously on MoEngage data and tools, inside rules the product and marketing team defines. Every agent shows its work through an activity log of the data it pulled, the decisions it made, the channels it touched, and the content it sent. Teams can run an agent with full autonomy or require human review before anything executes.
Decisioning agents
Decisioning agents act for each individual customer. Each agent decides what to say, when, how often, and on which channel, and it learns from every outcome. Product and marketing teams set the content, goals, and guardrails, and the agents handle the rest, with visibility into every decision. Offer Decisioning selects the best offer on web and app surfaces. Campaign Decisioning delivers 1:1 decisions across email, push, SMS, and WhatsApp. Together with workflow agents, this puts both halves of agentic marketing in one system.
Architecture overview
The architecture has four layers. Each layer has a single responsibility and can change without affecting the others.
- Clients. Merlin AI agents inside the MoEngage product, and external MCP clients such as Claude and ChatGPT, through the MoEngage MCP Connector, connect to the MoEngage MCP server. Clients that support MCP can connect.
- MCP server on AgentCore runtime. MoEngage hosts its MCP server on AgentCore runtime. The server exposes MoEngage platform capabilities as MCP tools. It does not run its own model. Reasoning happens in the agent that calls it.
- MoEngage platform APIs. The MCP server calls the same OpenAPI 3.0-compatible APIs that MoEngage customers already use. These APIs enforce existing permissions and data residency rules.
- Foundation models in Amazon Bedrock. Agents use foundation models in Amazon Bedrock to plan tool calls, generate content, and summarize results. For model availability by Region, see Supported models by AWS Region in Amazon Bedrock.
In a typical request, a user signs in to MoEngage and asks a question. The client sends the request with the user’s existing JSON Web Token (JWT). AgentCore runtime validates the token and starts an isolated session for that user. The agent asks a model in Amazon Bedrock which tools to call. The MCP server calls the MoEngage APIs with the user’s tenant context and returns the results. The agent then composes the answer.
The following diagram shows how these components connect.
Turning existing APIs into MCP tools
MoEngage opens its platform to agents through an MCP server and agent-callable APIs. Its platform APIs for campaigns, analytics, segments, content, and flows were already OpenAPI 3.0-compatible, so MoEngage used the FastMCP framework to generate MCP tools from those specifications. Each operation becomes a tool with a structured schema, a description, and parameter validation.
The following simplified example shows the pattern:
The tools fall into five groups:
- Campaign tools create, edit, schedule, and send campaigns across channels.
- Analytics tools query delivery funnels, click-through rates, conversions, and cohort performance.
- Segmentation tools list, inspect, and create segments from behavioral and attribute filters.
- Content tools manage content blocks, templates, and dynamic content rules.
- Flow tools inspect, pause, or modify automation journeys.
The tools come from the specifications, so they stay in sync with the APIs. When a team updates a specification, the tool definitions update with it.
Keeping tenants isolated and identity out of the model’s reach
A multi-tenant system cannot let a model decide whose data it is reading. MoEngage made three design choices to help prevent that. First, the MCP server reuses the existing authentication model, accepting the same JWT-based authentication that MoEngage APIs already use, and AgentCore runtime validates each token before a request reaches the server. Second, workspace and user context travel in request headers that AgentCore runtime forwards to the server rather than as tool arguments, so the model does not see these values and cannot change them. Third, AgentCore runtime runs each user session in its own isolated environment, so one user’s conversation cannot read another’s session state.
On top of this, Amazon Bedrock Guardrails apply content safety and personally identifiable information (PII) filters to agent responses. A backend-for-frontend layer then validates the structure of generated content before the MoEngage interface renders it.
Give users control over agents. Users set guardrails on what each agent can do, review every action in its activity log, and choose between autonomous and human-reviewed execution.
Why MoEngage chose AgentCore runtime
AgentCore runtime provides the production capabilities that a multi-tenant MCP server needs, and each one addresses a specific requirement of MoEngage’s workload. AgentCore runtime scales sessions as demand changes, so MoEngage does not plan capacity for traffic bursts across its customer workspaces. Each session runs in its own isolated environment by default, which keeps one brand’s conversation and data separate from another’s. The built-in JWT authorizer validates tokens against MoEngage’s existing identity provider, so the MCP server uses the same authentication model as the APIs.
Hosting on AgentCore runtime is also framework-agnostic. MoEngage can change models or agent frameworks without touching the MCP server, which matters as the agent layer evolves. Built-in metrics, logs, and traces through Amazon CloudWatch give MoEngage engineers visibility into every session. Together, these capabilities let the team focus on agent logic and marketing intelligence rather than hosting infrastructure.
Inference through Amazon Bedrock gave MoEngage two more benefits. Merlin AI agents run on Anthropic Claude Sonnet 4.6, Claude Sonnet 5, and Claude Sonnet 5.5 on Amazon Bedrock, and MoEngage moves between these versions through the same Amazon Bedrock API. MoEngage also pays per token instead of operating GPU infrastructure. Amazon Bedrock does not use customer prompts or responses to train foundation models, which matters for a system that processes customer engagement data at scale.
One campaign, one conversation
The following example shows how a user builds a campaign without leaving the conversation.
- Ask for the draft. The user types:
Draft a weekend flash sale push for our high-value segment, using the same tone as our best-performing December campaign. The agent calls the analytics tools to find the top December campaign, the segmentation tools to confirm the high-value segment, and the content tools to pull the brand voice. It returns a draft with several copy variants.
- Check what underperformed. The user asks:
Which push notifications last month had below 2% click-through rate (CTR), and what do they have in common? The Campaign Insights Agent compares those campaigns and reports the shared pattern, such as send time or audience overlap.
- Adjust the journey. The user asks:
Show me the drop-off at step 3 of our onboarding flow, and pause the SMS branch if it’s below 5% conversion. The agent reads the flow state through the flow tools and pauses the branch after the user confirms. This is the human-review mode in practice.
Each step uses the same tools that power the MoEngage interface. The user does not open a separate dashboard.
Results
Merlin AI agents on this architecture have been in production for more than 6 months. One customer, Glance, reached campaign go-live 50% faster and saw a 38% uplift in push notification click-through rates. With Merlin AI Copywriter, Glance teams also produce about three times more content variants per campaign.
Across the platform, MoEngage reports a 60–70% reduction in manual effort by marketing and product teams for channel, timing, and frequency decisions, and a 20–30% improvement in conversion rates from goal-based decisioning. Managed, pay-per-token inference in Amazon Bedrock reduced AI infrastructure costs by more than 50% compared with self-hosted models.
AgentCore feature availability varies by AWS Region. For supported Regions, see the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore documentation.
Conclusion
MoEngage made its platform agent-ready without rebuilding it. Existing OpenAPI specifications became MCP tools. AgentCore runtime provided hosting, authentication, and session isolation. Foundation models in Amazon Bedrock provided reasoning and generation. The result is a platform where marketing and product teams move from question to action in one conversation, where MoEngage engineers spend their time on marketing intelligence rather than infrastructure, and where agents handle workflows for the team and decisions for every customer while users stay in control.
The same pattern applies to other software providers with a mature API surface. Start from your existing specifications, keep identity outside the model, and let a managed runtime handle the production concerns.
To build your own MCP server on the same foundation, start with the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore documentation and follow the AgentCore runtime guide to host it. To choose a foundation model for your agents and review the security and data-handling controls, see the Amazon Bedrock User Guide. To generate MCP tools from your existing OpenAPI specifications, review the FastMCP documentation. To see Merlin AI in action, visit MoEngage Merlin AI. To plan a similar architecture, contact your AWS account team or Solutions Architect.

articles.title: AWS Nitro Sandboxes Put Each EKS Pod in Its Own MicroVM with One RuntimeClass Field
articles.text:
AWS has launched Nitro Sandboxes, which run an opted-in Kubernetes pod, ECS task, or EC2 workload inside its own lightweight virtual machine with a separate guest kernel, carved out of a running EC2 instance by the Nitro hypervisor. On Amazon EKS, the whole change is one pod field: runtimeClassName: isolated-sandbox or confidential-sandbox.
The feature is available in all commercial regions at no additional charge, and AWS positions it for workloads where the tenant or the code cannot be trusted, with coding agents named first. In an AWS blog post, Carlos Santana and Trishi Mehta write:
Each pod gets its own operating system, completely separate from the host and from every neighbor.
According to the EKS documentation, a containerd-shim-nitro-sandbox-v2 process on the parent instance launches a Firecracker microVM as a first-level guest with hardware-assisted virtualization, after which an agent inside the VM runs the pod’s containers through its own containerd and the two sides communicate over virtio and vsock. The result is a sandbox that shares neither kernel nor memory mappings with the parent instance or any other sandbox, while the containers themselves start unchanged. How the nodes get there depends on the cluster type: on EKS Auto Mode the two RuntimeClasses ship with every cluster and sandbox-capable nodes are provisioned on demand, whereas on standard EKS a team builds a sandbox-enabled AMI for its node groups or Karpenter.
(Source: Amazon EKS User Guide)
What separates the two modes is which side of the boundary is trusted. Isolated mode trusts the parent instance and not the guest, which is why kubectl exec, logs, and process listing keep working, whereas confidential mode treats the parent as untrusted and moves enforcement inside the VM: a Cedar policy generated from the pod spec pins image digests, arguments, environment, mounts and capabilities, exec and stdin are denied, the Nitro Secure Module measures the image and policy into PCRs, and a KMS key policy can release secrets only to a sandbox whose measurements match. Image layers can be encrypted as well, so the parent moves ciphertext it never reads.
That chain only holds if something checks the measurements, and the documentation says so: without a KMS policy or external verifier checking the PCR values, "the attestation measurement is recorded but never verified, and the confidentiality guarantees of confidential mode are incomplete." Separately from either mode, a network-isolated annotation boots the sandbox with no network device at all, which also removes DNS, NTP, IMDS and Pod Identity and breaks HTTP and TCP probes.
Sandip Das, an AWS Container Hero, read the documentation the same way and drew out what isolated mode leaves to the operator: the protection "only runs in one direction," so a compromised parent can still observe or tamper with unencrypted traffic and DNS, writes the pod's /etc/hosts, and can mint Pod Identity credentials for any pod on the node. He also lists prerequisites the blog post does not, among them Kubernetes 1.36 or later, a launch template with Nitro Enclaves enabled on managed node groups, without which "sandboxed pods sit in Pending," and Pod Identity rather than IRSA for credentials. On AWS's description of performance as near-native, he advises treating it "as a vendor claim" and benchmarking startup latency, I/O throughput and tail latency.
Beyond agents, AWS lists multi-tenant SaaS, regulated workloads, CI builds and remote IDEs, and points to the open-source agent-sandbox project for warm pools that hand out a pre-booted VM in about two seconds.
The constraints are on the considerations page, and the largest is GPU and device passthrough, which is not supported at launch because Firecracker cannot pass host devices into a guest, so GPU pods run without the sandbox class. Density is capped twice over: total sandbox vCPUs may not exceed five times the node's vCPU count, and neither may the number of sandboxes, halved on CPU-overcommit types, which gives a 4-vCPU node room for twenty 1-vCPU sandboxes or five 4-vCPU ones. Simultaneous multithreading costs more than the arithmetic suggests, because core scheduling stops two sandboxes sharing the sibling threads of one core and leaves roughly half the advertised vCPUs usable; Graviton, with one thread per core, is unaffected.
The nearest comparison is GKE Sandbox, which has offered a gvisor RuntimeClass since 2019 and more recently a microvm class built on Kata Containers and Cloud Hypervisor. gVisor intercepts syscalls in a user-space kernel, starts in under 200 milliseconds and supports CUDA on a subset of GPUs; Google's microVM option carries a fixed 250 mCPU and 130 MiB per pod, starts in one to two seconds and does not support GPUs. AWS has taken the VM side of that split and expressed its overhead as density and threads rather than per-pod resources.
On EC2, Amazon Linux and Firecracker are supported natively and patches are available for other virtual machine monitors. The EC2 User Guide carries the supported instance list and notes that snapshot, restore and live migration are not available.

articles.title: Shopify, Cohere leaders join call for Jensen Huang to be reinstated as Nvidia CEO | BetaKit
articles.text:
A pair of prominent Canadian technology leaders have joined a broader call demanding that US AI chip giant Nvidia bring co-founder and longtime head Jensen Huang back as CEO.
The news: After 33 years at the helm, Huang resigned as Nvidia CEO last week shortly after public allegations of affairs with two employees and an alleged Chinese spy tied to Singapore’s Megaspeed became public. Shopify co-founder and CEO Tobias Lütke and Cohere co-founder and CEO Aidan Gomez have signed an open letter asking Nvidia’s board of directors to reinstate Huang “pending an independent investigation and clear evidence that his removal serves the company.” That letter has now morphed into an online petition featuring more than 100,000 names. Several Silicon Valley leaders appear on the petition, but it’s not yet clear how many of the signatories are legitimate.
From the source: The letter demands that Nvidia “bring Jensen back while an independent investigation establishes the facts.”
As Lütke wrote on X after Nvidia announced Huang’s departure, “Generational blunder. At least based on the information that’s available.” In a reply, the Shopify CEO added, “Nvidia ends today, and is replaced with a thing cosplaying Nvidia. It will be run by custodians trying and failing to preserve the flame he ignited.”
The context: Nvidia sits at the centre of the ongoing AI boom, providing not only the hardware, models, and software, but serving as a key financier for other companies building in the space. Like many other tech firms, Ottawa-based Shopify is currently leveraging Nvidia’s offerings. Nvidia is also an investor in Gomez’s AI model-making firm, Toronto-based Cohere, as well as local self-driving tech developer Waabi. Canadian pension funds currently hold tens of billions worth of the AI chipmaker’s stock.
Final thought: Huang, who played a pivotal role in Nvidia’s ascent and did not leave a succession plan, has reportedly considered a comeback. While US President Donald Trump has said he is okay with that idea, his treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, has poured water on the notion, and Nvidia has reportedly ruled out the possibility of a return.
Feature image courtesy Wikimedia Commons.

articles.title: CEOs de tecnologia pedem volta de Jensen Huang à Nvidia • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
CEOs de tecnologia pedem volta de Jensen Huang à Nvidia
Campanha a favor de Jensen Huang tem apoio de grandes nomes da tecnologia, como Elon Musk, Tim Sweeney, Garry Tan e Travis Kalanick
Stand With Jensen — algo como “Esteja com Jensen” ou “Apoie Jensen”. Esse é o nome de uma campanha que visa fazer Jensen Huang voltar a ser CEO da Nvidia. O executivo deixou o cargo após enfrentar denúncias de escândalos extraconjugais. A parte mais surpreendente dessa história é que a campanha é apoiada por outros grandes empresários, entre eles, Elon Musk.
Na condição de cofundador, Huang estava na liderança da Nvidia desde 1993, quando a empresa surgiu. Sob seu comando, a companhia se tornou uma das mais valiosas do mundo, em grande medida, porque ajudou a Nvidia a se tornar líder no fornecimento de chips e tecnologias para aplicações de IA, bem como para computação de alto desempenho.
A despeito de seu notável histórico profissional, Jensen Huang se viu obrigado a renunciar ao posto de CEO da Nvidia em razão de denúncias sobre relacionamentos extraconjugais com os quais teria se envolvido, em especial, com uma mulher que supostamente faz espionagem para o serviço de inteligência da China.
O principal apoiador da campanha Stand With Jensen é Elon Musk, como já informado. O empresário argumenta que grande parte das relações comerciais estabelecidas pela Nvidia ao longo do tempo se deve à confiança que outros executivos têm na pessoa de Huang, indo além da mera formalidade, portanto.
Para Musk, a saída de Huang da posição de CEO pode enfraquecer a capacidade da Nvidia de manter e estabelecer novos acordos, dando a entender, nas entrelinhas, que isso seria ruim não somente para a própria empresa como para a economia americana.
Outros apoiadores incluem Tim Sweeney (CEO da Epic Games), Garry Tan (presidente da Y Combinator), Travis Kalanick (cofundador da Uber) e Tobias Lutke (CEO da Shopify).
A campanha não pede que todos os pontos polêmicos sejam esquecidos e que Jensen Huang retorne ao cargo de CEO como se nada tivesse acontecido, mas que o empresário tenha espaço para manifestar a sua versão e continue no posto enquanto as investigações perdurarem.
Além disso, a campanha pede para que as investigações sejam realizadas de modo independente e imparcial, que os resultados se tornem públicos e que o conselho de administração da Nvidia divulgue os critérios adotados para as decisões que afetarem o futuro da empresa.
Note que a campanha tem o apoio de grandes executivos, mas é pública. Até a publicação desta notícia, mais de 180.000 pessoas já tinham assinado a carta aberta em apoio a Huang, entre eles, milhares de funcionários e ex-funcionários da Nvidia.

articles.title: Instagram now lets creators add Amazon affiliate links in reels and feed posts | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Instagram announced on Monday that it’s launching an integration that will give creators a new way to earn by adding Amazon affiliate links directly in reels and feed posts. Creators can add up to 30 products per reel or 20 per feed post, which makes it possible for them to earn from multiple products through one piece of content.
While creators have long shared Amazon affiliate links through stories, DMs, and their bios, the new integration brings them to new parts of the app. The Meta-owned company told TechCrunch in an email that it has seen product links directly on creators’ reels and posts draw about twice as many clicks as the links in their bio.
By allowing creators to embed multiple product links directly in Reels and feed posts, the platform is expanding their opportunities to monetize content, while also giving them more flexibility in how they share recommendations. The change also strengthens the platform’s appeal to creators, as it continues to compete with rivals like TikTok and YouTube for their attention and content.
Instagram says adding products and affiliate links is free, and that it doesn’t take a commission on purchases or charge transaction fees.
Eligible creators can now connect their Instagram and Amazon Influencer accounts through the Monetization section of their Professional Dashboard. Once connected, Instagram automatically adds affiliate links when creators tag Amazon products in their content, with links directing viewers to the Amazon Shopping app. Connected affiliates also unlock image previews for their links, making it easier for viewers to recognize the products.
When creators connect their Amazon Associates account to Instagram, affiliate attribution is automatically applied to any Amazon product they add, even when they paste a regular product link, which wasn’t the case before, as they were required to add an affiliate URL.
Instagram says creators can also see each product’s estimated commission rate before adding it to a post or reel, with commissions continuing to be paid out by Amazon.
The new integration marks another step in Instagram’s efforts to expand its monetization tools while also making affiliate marketing more accessible for creators on its platform.

articles.title: In Get Huge, the manosphere is here to make friends — with deadly consequences
articles.text:
Before Clavicular and other manosphere streamers were introducing young guys to the concept of breaking their facial bones to become more attractive, there was an older generation of creators building massive followings with content focused on chemical biohacking. Were it not for steroid-obsessed influencers like Anthony “Tony Huge” Hughes launching YouTube channels over a decade ago, looksmaxxing might not have become such a prominent part of the digital media landscape in 2026. These creators became internet famous by presenting themselves as peak male specimens. But their larger-than-life online personas often concealed the truth about how sinister and toxic this kind of influencing can really be.
In Get Huge, the manosphere is here to make friends — with deadly consequences
Get Huge: Looksmaxxing to Death gets at the heart of how influencers are radicalizing impressionable men.
In Get Huge, the manosphere is here to make friends — with deadly consequences
Get Huge: Looksmaxxing to Death gets at the heart of how influencers are radicalizing impressionable men.
Hughes is the gravitational center of Get Huge: Looksmaxxing to Death — Hulu’s new three-part docuseries from director Stacey Lee. The series is both a deep dive into Hughes’ strange life and a fascinating exploration of how perilous the creator economy can be in the age of manosphere and looksmaxxing influencers. Through Hughes’ ever-expanding orbit of creators, Lee is able to highlight how lonely, impressionable men are all too easily radicalized by what they see and post online. And it makes clear that all these men are trapped in a deadly psychological prison of their own making.
Get Huge takes some time to touch on Hughes’ former life as a bankruptcy lawyer and supplement salesman who was investigated by the FDA for hawking unapproved performance-enhancing drugs. But most of the series takes place in Pattaya, Thailand, where Hughes spends his days producing content showcasing his extravagant life of nonstop partying and injecting substances that swell his muscles to huge proportions. Hughes takes pride in his image as a man with access to a harem of women, and the fact that his money gives him power over many of the people around him. He presents himself as the ruler of a small kingdom — and his entire brand is built on the idea that he can show people how to become more like him.
The men caught in Hughes’ aspirational fantasy aren’t just stateside fans who’ll never reach his muscle-y heights. He is also marketing himself to other established bodybuilding influencers who might be interested in joining his inner circle by following him to Thailand. These include a menagerie of biohacking / manosphere influencers who became vital parts of Hughes’ operation over the years. Leo Longevity (legal name Laith Abdallah Algaz), Elon Muscular (his legal name isn’t revealed), and Connor Murphy all built sizable social media presences of their own. But they were each compelled to move to Pattaya and join Hughes’ entourage by a powerful desire to feel connected to something larger and more fulfilling than their individual followings.
As Get Huge features clips of Hughes’ videos — the bulk of which are now only featured on Rumble and X following multiple account bans on YouTube and TikTok — you can see that he’s trying to sell his audience on his highly specific way of life. Hughes’ own videos make it seem like he’s living his dream surrounded by people who revere him. But with each interview, Get Huge makes it clear that for all of his posturing, Hughes has been living in something of a nightmare — one where many of his disciples have died under mysterious circumstances.
As these men explain why they were drawn to Hughes, you get the sense that looksmaxxing culture is a direct response to the widespread disaffection that followed the last decade of interconnected societal shifts, from the #MeToo movement to Donald Trump’s presidencies. Hughes seems very much like an entrepreneur profiting from men’s loneliness by convincing them that their lives would be better if they were part of his community. As Get Huge first maps out Hughes’ friendships, they all appear to be anchored by an odd, sometimes envious, but genuine kind of intimacy. But as the documentary digs deeper into its subjects’ lives, it becomes hard to see them as anything but emotionally stunted men who perform cartoonish masculinity for one another in ways that are psychologically unhealthy and, at times, physically dangerous.
Part of what makes Get Huge such an unsettling watch is how relatively calm and collected Hughes and the other interviewees are as they begin to discuss how many people in their circle have died in recent years. Hughes and Murphy grow closer as friends following Algaz’s death in 2023, but they seem to bond by making Algaz the butt of the joke in content produced after his death. Simply by letting these men speak frankly about their social dynamics, Get Huge reveals the manosphere as a space in which connections built on mogging and the objectification of women can quickly deteriorate into infighting and petty jealousy. Elon Muscular readily speculates that Murphy might have had something to do with Algaz’s death because Murphy openly jokes about it. And the entire situation becomes that much stranger and more grim when Get Huge reveals that Murphy drowned shortly after the series initially wrapped filming.
Though the deaths in Hughes’ circle bring a dark whodunit energy to Get Huge, the documentary emphasizes how much peril comes as a part of existing in the looksmaxxing space. Rather than trying to solve the mystery of how Algaz died, the docuseries presents his story as a cautionary tale. He’s an object lesson in how this lifestyle can warp a person’s perception of reality in a way that ultimately cuts them off from the kind of help they really need.
What might be most disturbing about Get Huge is the way it ends. The series follows Hughes to a youth bodybuilding event where he talks up his less-than-legal products to a new group of boys — some as young as 13. To keep his momentum going, Hughes has to appeal to a new, younger audience that doesn’t understand how everything about looksmaxxing is a performance. Though the docuseries gives you the distinct impression that people like Murphy and Algaz felt a true belonging with Hughes, its closing shots call into question how genuine any of his connections with other bodybuilders really are. By juxtaposing the deaths of Hughes’ adult acolytes with his focus on turning children into fans, Get Huge paints a clear picture of how the manosphere’s promise of emotional connection often ends in a twisted kind of exploitation. And that extractive energy feels foundational to a culture that runs on people turning every aspect of their lives into content.
All three episodes of Get Huge: Looksmaxxing to Death are now streaming on Hulu and Disney Plus.

articles.title: Hacker gets Doom running on a USB flash drive's built-in LCD, played by copying files — hacker dumps firmware from chip with scrubbed markings through an open debug port, then gets the game running with AI help
articles.text:
Hacker gets Doom running on a USB flash drive's built-in LCD, played by copying files — hacker dumps firmware from chip with scrubbed markings through an open debug port, then gets the game running with AI help
Key presses turn into bursts of reads and writes to play the game.
Doom now runs on a USB flash drive’s built-in LCD and is played by copying files to and from it, as hardware hacker Aaron Christophel showed in a teardown video. The marking on the drive’s display chip had been removed, but an open debug port let him extract its firmware, which enabled identification. He was then able to use AI to reverse-engineer the hardware and get the game running on the drive’s screen.
The off-the-shelf drive, the MOVESPEED MSSU10, has USB-A on one end and USB-C on the other, and the 128GB model, the smallest capacity in the range, cost him about 50 euros. Its screen normally shows status data such as transfer speed, how full the drive is, and its temperature.
The main flash controller is the Silicon Motion SM2320G, one we have reviewed in portable SSDs like the Kingston XS2000 and Lexar SL660 Blaze, with a separate C*Core CCM4101 microcontroller — which has 2MB of flash and a small amount of RAM to itself — for the 428 x 142 color LCD. The NAND carries SanDisk markings. All of this is fairly standard portable SSD hardware, aside from the display.
The drive’s metal body uses heavily glued plastic end pieces but, past that, the display lifts off first and unplugs. The board slides out after the USB-C end cap is removed, in this case with minor cosmetic damage inflicted. The display chip’s marking is scrubbed, most likely with a laser, by the hacker’s reckoning, which can hinder identification and tinkering. Luckily, a probe on the debug pads, ground, and a 3.3V pin connected on the first try, and memory was immediately readable.
The bootloader returned a version string dated 2023, followed by the full firmware, which helped greatly with identification. He says the chip is marketed as one for security — for fingerprint readers and access control, for example — but no related features were found to be enabled for this drive. He also discovered that, although the data sheet and stock firmware declare a 200 MHz operating clock frequency, it measured 40.2 MHz. This is unexplained.
One critical issue is immediately apparent: how do you play on a drive with no buttons? The display chip has no USB connection of its own and, from the connected PC or host, it only sees the storage controller’s activity, which it uses to gauge transfer speed. The primary storage controller has read and write counters, and the chip pulls these every 50 ms over I2C. Christophel says this is far easier than relying on a single physical button, as he did on a previous power bank mod.
The solution, then, is a PC script, doomctl.py, which turns key presses into small, timed transfers in each direction. The commands are simply encoded as transfer rates, at five levels per direction, and each read/write pair can map to a certain button combination. Arrow keys are for movement and turning, Space or Ctrl for firing and opening doors, and M for the menu, keeping it simple. Ordinary copying, without the script, can still steer, but the control scheme is much nicer.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
Performance is…well, not really playable at about 13 frames per second, although the game logic runs at Doom’s normal 35 ticks per second. This is why he names the chip’s clock as the biggest potential performance gain. The game itself is built on DMC100-DOOM, Artur Bieniek’s port for very small microcontrollers. Only the first map, E1M1, fits in the chip’s flash, and no sound is produced as the drive lacks a buzzer. Christophel did play the level end to end, noting the low resolution.
AI did the heavy lifting: the reverse engineering as well as the port, and Christophel said, “I would not be able to do such a thing in a few hours.”
The open-source project, with its code and prebuilt firmware published, is likely to draw attention and may spawn similar hacks. The tools required are relatively minimal, mainly a debug probe, and he does suggest backing up the stock firmware before trying. For his own unit, he put it back together to use as a normal drive, but one that can still play Doom, if so desired.

articles.title: Octopus Energy is bringing its sold-out plug-in solar panels to UK small businesses, says move was a 'no-brainer' following huge demand
articles.text:
Octopus Energy is bringing its sold-out plug-in solar panels to UK small businesses, says move was a 'no-brainer' following huge demand
SMBs can now buy Octopus Energy's plug-in solar panels
- UK SMBs can now buy the same solar panel kits as domestic users
- Business owners can choose between one or two 460W panels
- Annual energy bill savings of up to 23% are being targeted
Octopus Energy has announced plans to expand its plug-in solar scheme to small businesses across the UK after seeing immense success across its domestic applications.
The company's offering now also targets smaller organizations like cafes, shops and pubs - and being a plug-and-play system, it's especially friendly to renters who may not be able to install a more permanent solar array.
With its plug-in solar panels, Octopus says small businesses could save as much as 23% off their annual electricity bills by supplementing their consumption with energy generated on-site, though there will of course be an initial capital outlay.
Octopus Energy launches plug-in solar panels for SMBs, too
Much the same as its domestic offering, small businesses will be faced with a one-off cost of £450 for a single solar panel and micro-inverter, or £650 for a pair. Depending on energy consumption, the utilities giant envisions SMBs being able to pay off their initial investment in as little as three years.
"Energy bills are having a big impact on a small business’ bottom line," Octopus Energy for Business CEO Zoisa North-Bond explained. "Plug-in solar gives SMEs a simple way to generate their own cheap, green power – and because so many rent their premises, they don’t need to own a building or have a suitable roof to benefit."
One single panel generates up to 460W in peak conditions – that's 920W for the pair – and installing them is as easy as plugging them into an outdoor-rated three-pin domestic socket. Their dual setup daisy chains so that it only needs one socket, too.
Although a pair of panels could in theory generate up to 920W, they're limited to 800W per the UK's output limit. It's unclear whether that figure is under revision, but any future lifts could see Octopus' panels generate the full 920W.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
In an announcement, the utilities giant said a pair of plug-in panels could generate 828kWh in a year – the equivalent of around 2.2kWh per day (or nearly five full hours of operation for one panel). As is the case with any solar panel, 460W is only its peak capacity and plenty of factors, including sun strength, time of year and panel aspect, will impact how much it's actually generating at any given moment.
Because the panels are technically portable (if not a bit large), SMB owners can technically lift them and install them at new premises if they move. No electricians or complex scaffolding is required.
As for its domestic offering, which sold out its first 500 kits in just two weeks, nine in 10 (89%) customers opted for the 920W pairing.

articles.title: Cette marque de moto vaut 1,2 milliard d'euros dans un secteur où les faillites se succèdent
articles.text:
La moto électrique a tout d’un cimetière de start-up. L’italien Energica a été placé en liquidation en octobre 2024, le suédois Cake avait déposé le bilan en février de la même année, et LiveWire, la marque électrique de Harley-Davidson, doute de pouvoir tenir un an de plus.
Pendant ce temps-là, Stark Future, installée à Barcelone, roule sur un véritable tapis rouge. Ce lundi 16 novembre, son fondateur et CEO, Anton Wass, a annoncé à Reuters une levée d’au moins 150 millions d’euros sur la base d’une valorisation de 1,2 milliard d’euros. L’entreprise devient ainsi la première marque européenne de moto électrique à obtenir le statut de licorne, réservé aux start-up non cotées valorisées à plus d’un milliard de dollars (un peu moins d’un milliard d’euros).
Le fonds Highland Europe mène le tour de table, avec 1GT (le fonds de Morgan Stanley Investment Management) et Axon Partners Group. Les 1,2 milliard d’euros correspondent à la valeur de Stark avant l’arrivée de cet argent frais, soit 60 % de plus qu’en septembre 2025, quand l’entreprise était valorisée à 750 millions d’euros.
Anton Wass table aussi sur environ 150 millions d’euros de chiffre d’affaires en 2026 (contre 115 millions en 2025, soit 30 % de hausse) et sur un résultat d’exploitation positif cette année, dont il refuse de donner le montant. Dans son communiqué, Stark affirme enfin que la Varg est devenue la moto d’enduro la plus vendue au monde, devant ses rivales thermiques.
Pourquoi Stark tient là où Cake et Energica ont calé ?
Stark a misé sur une niche : le tout-terrain. La Varg est née en motocross (MX), puis elle a été déclinée en enduro (EX) et en supermotard (SM) homologués pour la route. De série, le moteur développe 60 chevaux, mais il est possible de le pousser à 80 chevaux dans la version Alpha, facturée 1 000 € de plus.
Et ce n’est pas le prix qui explique cet engouement, car avec un prix de départ de 11 999 € pour la Varg MX et 12 990 € pour les Varg EX et SM, Stark est plutôt dans le haut du panier. La raison se trouve dans les catégories couvertes par la marque. En tout-terrain, les motards roulent la plupart du temps par sessions de quelques heures. L’autonomie limitée des motos électriques si décriée compte donc moins que sur une moto routière.
Dans le cas de la Stark Varg SM, pour le coup destinée à la route, là aussi les longues balades sont moins fréquentes en raison du confort de ce genre de monture. C’est aussi le côté puissance instantanée de l’électrique qui va contribuer énormément au fun du supermotard.
Stark vise maintenant des motos plus grosses
Anton Wass explique la rentabilité par les marges. Stark détient toute la propriété intellectuelle de ses motos, et sa chaîne de valeur est selon lui « vraiment très courte », avec peu d’intermédiaires à payer. Surtout, la marque vend la Varg sur ses performances face aux thermiques, tant sur le plan économique que l’efficacité pure. « Nous n’essayons pas de forcer les gens à adopter un mode de vie durable, nous voulons simplement faire en sorte que l’option durable soit la meilleure option, même si vous ne vous en souciez pas », résume-t-il.
Interrogé en marge de la COP31, en Turquie, il juge ne pas avoir besoin des aides publiques pour avancer, mais souhaite en revanche qu’on taxe davantage les produits polluants et moins les produits dits « durables ».
Anton Wass revendique 5 % du marché du motocross, de l’enduro et du supermotard, qu’il estime à 3 milliards d’euros. Avec cette nouvelle levée, le patron vise désormais des catégories de motos plus grosses, sur des marchés qui pèsent 90 milliards d’euros, et compte y prendre 10 à 30 % de parts. Il dit avoir refusé des offres de rachat et espère que ce tour sera le dernier avant une entrée en Bourse, d’ici deux ans environ au plus tôt.

articles.title: 7 Tips For Complying with CJIS Password and MFA Requirements
articles.text:
Compromised passwords and gaps in multi-factor authentication (MFA) remain common ways attackers gain access to sensitive systems. For law enforcement agencies handling criminal justice information (CJI), protecting against these threats is also a matter of CJIS compliance.
The FBI's latest CJIS Security Policy sets clear requirements for password management and MFA. these are Priority 1 (P1) controls, so must be implemented immediately to comply. But this can be challenging, particularly across the complex IT environments that are common in law enforcement.
This guide contains practical tips to help agencies meet the latest requirements, strengthen their defenses against credential-based attacks, and make ongoing compliance easier to manage.
1. Enforce Stronger Minimum Password Lengths
CJIS requires user-selected passwords to be at least eight characters long, or six characters if generated by a credential service provider or verifier using an approved random number generator. However, we recommend going beyond these minimums and encouraging passphrases of at least 15 characters.
Longer passwords are generally harder to crack, and passphrases can be easier to remember than shorter passwords with complex combinations of symbols and numbers.
CJIS doesn't require traditional complexity rules, so focus on length and strength rather than arbitrary character requirements.
2. Block Weak and Compromised Passwords
Agencies must maintain a list of commonly used, predictable, and compromised passwords. This should include passwords exposed in previous breaches, dictionary words, sequential characters, and context-specific terms such as usernames or agency names.
CJIS requires agencies to update this list at least quarterly, and whenever organizational passwords are suspected of being compromised.
Solutions like Specops Password Policy with Breached Password Protection can simplify this process with CJIS-aligned password policy templates. You can create an unlimited custom dictionary of blocked words unique to your agency, with granular controls for blocking weak constructions.
Importantly, the Breached Password Protection feature delivers continuous screening against a growing database of more than six billion compromised passwords.
Secure your Active Directory passwords with Specops Password Policy
Verizon’s Data Breach Investigation Report found stolen credentials are involved in 44.7% of breaches. 
Effortlessly secure Active Directory with compliant password policies, blocking 4+ billion compromised passwords, boosting security, and slashing support hassles!
3. Reset Passwords Quickly and Give Users Clear Feedback
Agencies must force a password change whenever there's evidence that a credential has been compromised. Don't rely solely on scheduled password changes to address exposed credentials.
You must also check existing passwords against the breach list at least quarterly. More regular checks can help identify compromised credentials earlier, giving IT teams an opportunity to respond before attackers exploit them.
CJIS also requires users to select a new password immediately whenever compromise is suspected.
When a user does need to create or reset a password, rather than displaying a generic error message, provide clear, real-time feedback that helps users understand what makes a password weak and how to improve it.
Specops Password Policy delivers that support, making it easier to create strong, memorable passwords while reducing frustration and unnecessary help desk requests.
4. Protect Passwords in Transit and At Rest
Password security doesn't end with enforcing strong credentials. CJIS also requires passwords to be transmitted over encrypted, authenticated channels to prevent interception and man-in-the-middle attacks.
When stored, passwords must be salted and hashed using a suitable one-way key derivation function, making them more resistant to offline cracking if an authentication database is compromised.
Agencies should review how their applications and authentication systems handle credentials to ensure these protections are in place.
5. Require MFA For All Privileged and Non-Privileged Accounts
CJIS requires MFA for both privileged and non-privileged organizational accounts. Don't focus solely on administrator accounts. Standard user accounts can also give attackers access to sensitive data or provide a foothold for further attacks.
Review your accounts and access policies to identify where MFA is missing, including accounts belonging to employees and contractors.
6. Extend MFA Across All Relevant Access Methods
CJIS requires MFA for local, network, and remote access. Agencies should review authentication across their environment, ensuring that all systems that touch CJI are adequately protected.
Solutions such as Specops Secure Access helps agencies extend MFA to Windows logons, RDP, and VPN connections, with single sign-on (SSO) support for compatible SaaS applications through OIDC and SAML.
7. Make Sure Your MFA Methods Meet CJIS Requirements
CJIS specifies Authenticator Assurance Level 2 (AAL2), which requires two different authentication factors. This is a combination of something you know (like a password), something you have (like a smart card), or something you are (like a fingerprint).
Review your authentication methods to ensure they meet these requirements. Where possible, consider phishing-resistant MFA methods to provide stronger protection against credential phishing and adversary-in-the-middle attacks.
Keep Your Authentication Controls Effective
CJIS compliance doesn't end once you've implemented strong password policies and MFA. Regularly reviewing your authentication controls, checking for compromised credentials, and auditing Active Directory can help you identify security gaps before attackers exploit them.
As a starting point, Specops Password Auditor performs a free, read-only AD audit that checks for weak or compromised passwords and inactive privileged administrator accounts. You’ll get the results in an easy-to understand interactive report that highlights your current exposure.
By combining strong authentication controls with regular security assessments, agencies can reduce credential-related risks and make ongoing CJIS compliance easier to manage.
