articles.title: Aspirer, laver les sols et nettoyer les vitres : Ecovacs réduit ses robots jusqu’à 800 €
articles.text:
Aspirer, laver les sols ou nettoyer les vitres : Ecovacs veut automatiser toujours plus de tâches ménagères, et profite du Black Friday pour faire baisser le prix de trois de ses robots. Du 9 au 30 novembre, jusqu’au Cyber Monday, les remises atteignent jusqu’à 800 € selon les modèles.
Nous serons sans doute d'accord, le ménage n'est clairement pas l'activité préférée de tout le monde. Pour celles et ceux qui souhaitent automatiser le nettoyage des sols comme celui des vitres, Ecovacs met en avant trois appareils dédiés, avec des remises pouvant atteindre 800 € à l’occasion de ses offres Black Friday.
DEEBOT T90 MAX PRO : un robot aspirateur-laveur qui ne fait pas les choses à moitié
Le DEEBOT T90 MAX PRO mise sur une fiche technique musclée pour assurer aussi bien l'aspiration que le lavage des sols. Il embarque notamment une puissance d'aspiration de 40 000 Pa, associée à la technologie OZMO ROLLER 3.0, qui nettoie le rouleau en continu avec de l'eau propre tout en collectant l'eau sale au cours du processus de nettoyage.
Son rouleau de 27 cm exerce une pression de 4 000 Pa et tourne à 260 tours par minute. Son rinçage en continu est assuré par 32 jets d'eau, afin de limiter la propagation des saletés pendant le nettoyage. Son capteur LiDAR dToF cartographie précisément les pièces et optimise les trajets, tandis que TrueDetect 3D lui permet d'éviter câbles, chaussons et autres obstacles du quotidien.
Le robot peut aussi s'approcher des plinthes et des meubles grâce à la technologie TruEdge 3.0 (qui permet au rouleau à coussin d'air de se rapprocher des bords et des murs de 1,5 cm supplémentaire), tandis que son système ZeroTangle 4.0 limite les enchevêtrements de cheveux et de poils dans la brosse principale. De quoi réduire les interventions manuelles, notamment dans les foyers où les animaux de compagnie laissent régulièrement quelques souvenirs de leur passage.
Une fois sa mission terminée, le DEEBOT retourne à sa station OMNI, qui prend en charge plusieurs opérations d'entretien, dont l’indispensable lavage du rouleau à l'eau chaude à 100 °C. Le robot peut ainsi repartir pour un nouveau cycle sans réclamer une attention permanente.
Du 9 au 30 novembre 2026, le DEEBOT T90 MAX PRO passe de 599 à 449 €, soit 150 € de remise.
DEEBOT X12S OMNICYCLONE Care Kit : une station sans sac et une aspiration de 53 AW
Avec le DEEBOT X12S OMNICYCLONE Care Kit, Ecovacs propose une solution encore plus complète. Ce modèle reprend le rouleau OZMO ROLLER 3.0, avec ses 32 jets de rinçage, sa pression de 4 000 Pa et sa vitesse de rotation de 260 tours par minute. Il y ajoute une aspiration BLAST annoncée à 53 AW, soit une puissance supérieure de 60 % à celle de la génération précédente.
Le X12S dispose également de la technologie FocusJet, qui vient pré-pulvériser les taches tenaces pour les décoller avant le passage du rouleau. Son système AIVI 3D 4.0 lui permet par ailleurs de repérer les obstacles, notamment les câbles et les animaux, tout en adaptant sa trajectoire pour nettoyer au plus près des meubles. Il peut franchir des seuils jusqu'à 2,5 cm et des obstacles successifs atteignant 5 cm au total.
Mais sa particularité se trouve aussi dans sa station OmniCyclone, puisque celle-ci intègre le système PureCyclone 2.0, qui permet de vider automatiquement le bac à poussière sans sac jetable. Un choix qui limite les consommables à remplacer et simplifie encore plus l'entretien au quotidien. 
Cette version “Care Kit” vient ajouter trois filtres antibactériens, deux brosses latérales anti-enchevêtrement et une brosse principale supplémentaire.
Du 9 au 30 novembre, le DEEBOT X12S OMNICYCLONE Care Kit est proposé à 799 € au lieu de 1 299 €, soit 400 € d'économie.
WINBOT W3 OMNI : et si le nettoyage des vitres devenait lui aussi automatique ?
Les sols ne sont pas les seules surfaces à réclamer un peu d'huile de coude. Ecovacs s'attaque aussi aux vitres avec le WINBOT W3 OMNI, un robot lave-vitres accompagné d'une station multifonction qui automatise une partie de son entretien.
Le WINBOT W3 OMNI dispose de plusieurs modes de nettoyage, dont des options rapide, en profondeur ou ciblée. Il peut fonctionner sur secteur ou sur batterie, avec jusqu'à 130 minutes d'autonomie annoncées. Un câble composite associe alimentation et sécurité, tandis que le système de protection en 12 étapes contribue à sécuriser son utilisation sur les surfaces vitrées.
De son côté, la station propose un système Vortex Wash qui nettoie automatiquement les patins, sans qu'il soit nécessaire de les manipuler ou de les laver à la main. Seize jets haute pression et quatre disques de brossage se chargent de retirer les saletés en une minute environ.
A l’instar de ses cousins dédiés au lavage des sols, le Winbot W3 Omni bénéficie lui aussi de la technologie TruEdge, qui lui permet de nettoyer au plus près des bords et des angles, ainsi que de la navigation WIN-SLAM 5.0 pour organiser ses déplacements et éviter les obstacles.
Du 9 au 30 novembre 2026, le WINBOT W3 OMNI passe de 699 à 499 €, soit 200 € de remise.

articles.title: Los siete fundadores de Anthropic tendrán la mitad de los votos tras su salida a bolsa
articles.text:
Anthropic, la empresa del chatbot Claude, saldrá a bolsa con una estructura que da a sus siete cofundadores el 50,1% de los votos y a un fideicomiso el poder de elegir a la mayoría del directorio. Según la agencia AP, los expertos creen que el diseño deja a la compañía amplio margen para decidir qué cuenta como beneficio social.
La empresa fijará el precio de sus acciones el 18 de noviembre y empezará a cotizar en el mercado Nasdaq el 19, con el símbolo ANT. Ofrecerá 825 millones de acciones a un precio de entre USD 70 y USD 78, según su prospecto actualizado y el aviso de Nasdaq.
Antes de la oferta, la compañía emitirá una acción especial, llamada Clase F, a una sociedad formada por Dario Amodei, Daniela Amodei, Tom Brown, Jack Clark, Jared Kaplan, Sam McCandlish y Christopher Olah. Esa acción no da derechos económicos, pero concentra la mitad de los votos en los asuntos generales de los accionistas, según el prospecto.
El poder de los fundadores no es permanente: el documento indica que los votos pasan a los accionistas comunes cuando en la sociedad queden menos de tres cofundadores.
Un fideicomiso sin acciones elige al directorio
El segundo centro de poder es el Long-Term Benefit Trust, un fideicomiso de cinco fiduciarios sin interés financiero en la empresa, con experiencia en seguridad de la IA, seguridad nacional, políticas públicas y empresas con fines sociales. Controla una sola acción, de Clase T, que no tiene derechos económicos y que no puede vender, según AP.
Con esa acción, el fideicomiso elige y destituye a los directores de Clase T, que forman la mayoría del directorio. De los siete miembros, elige a cuatro; uno de esos puestos tiene salvaguardas, entre ellas un voto de los empleados si la empresa y el fideicomiso no coinciden. Los fundadores eligen a los otros tres.
AP precisó que ese séptimo director, con posible voto de desempate, no puede ser nombrado ni destituido sin el consentimiento del comité de nominaciones, que se espera que controlen los fundadores. El prospecto agrega que ni el fideicomiso ni los fiduciarios deciden la gestión diaria ni la estrategia de la compañía.
Los especialistas dudan del alcance de ese control
Stavros Gadinis, profesor de la Facultad de Derecho de la Universidad de California en Berkeley, dijo a AP que el fideicomiso solo puede pedir cuentas a la empresa hasta cierto punto. Si discrepa con los directores, deberá destituirlos, y podría no lograrlo con la mayoría.
Sarah Kreps, directora del Instituto de Política Tecnológica de la Universidad de Cornell, sostuvo que la prueba real llegará cuando el beneficio público resulte costoso. Planteó si la compañía revisará sus límites de seguridad ante la competencia de modelos de código abierto chinos, que responden casi cualquier pedido.
Anthropic, igual que OpenAI, es una sociedad de beneficio público, figura legal que obliga a equilibrar el interés de los accionistas con el bien común. Según AP, hay pocas cotizadas con ese formato y todas son mucho más pequeñas, como la marca de anteojos Warby Parker, la aseguradora Lemonade y la desarrolladora de software Veeva Systems.
La empresa transfirió 5% de sus acciones a un fondo de beneficio público, 846.840.960 títulos de Clase N, calculados al 30 de junio. Su directorio puede sumar hasta 2% más cada vez que el precio suba 50% sobre el hito anterior. Los cofundadores prometieron donar el 80% de su participación personal.
AP recordó que Google puso en su prospecto de 2004 el lema “No seas malvado”, que no era vinculante y que los críticos dicen que la empresa dejó atrás. Gadinis consideró que ser pública obligará a Anthropic a revelar más información, porque inversores y reguladores harán preguntas. El 18 de noviembre, Anthropic fijará el precio definitivo de la oferta, y el 19 sus acciones comenzarán a negociarse en Nasdaq.

articles.title: How flexible workspaces are changing the way companies think about offices
articles.text:
How flexible workspaces are changing the way companies think about offices
At TechSparks 2026, Manish Khedia of The Executive Centre discussed how businesses are moving beyond traditional office layouts and long-term leases to focus on flexibility, collaboration, and employee needs.
The COVID-19 pandemic changed how companies think about offices. After employees spent months working from home, businesses had to reconsider what would bring people back to the workplace and how to make that time productive.
At TechSparks 2026, Manish Khedia, Regional Managing Director at The Executive Centre (TEC), joined Shivani Muthanna, Senior Director – Strategic Content & Video at YourStory, for a fireside chat titled ‘The enterprise office 2.0: Space, strategy, experience redefined’.
The discussion covered how flexible workspaces, hybrid working arrangements, and employee expectations are changing the way businesses plan their offices.
From square footage to collaboration
For years, companies made office decisions based largely on location, square footage, the number of workstations, and the type of building. The pandemic changed those priorities, first by forcing employees to work from home and then by making companies reconsider how to bring them back.
According to Khedia, the challenge now is to create offices that employees want to visit, where they can work productively, collaborate, and have access to the facilities they need.
“I think all the companies are looking at how they can engage their employees to be more productive, not by giving them more work, but by creating an environment where they can collaborate,” he said.
As a result, businesses are looking beyond a premium address when choosing office space. They are considering the surrounding infrastructure, including technology parks, food courts, daycare facilities, and other amenities that make daily work more convenient.
Inside the office, the focus is shifting towards collaboration and employee experience. Companies are moving away from traditional hierarchical layouts toward spaces where people can exchange ideas, work , and think differently.
Khedia said businesses are increasingly treating offices as communities that support employees, rather than simply as fixed assets or status symbols.
Bringing offices closer to employees
Location remains important, particularly in large cities such as Bengaluru and Mumbai, where employees may spend two to three hours commuting each day. The time, cost, and effort involved are among the reasons companies are exploring hybrid working arrangements and the hub-and-spoke model.
Instead of operating from one central office, businesses can set up workspaces in different locations, allowing employees to work closer to home.
Khedia said the aim is to make time spent in the office more productive while reducing the burden of commuting. Employees have more time for themselves, while companies can provide spaces where teams can collaborate.
The shift is not limited to metropolitan cities. Khedia pointed to Ahmedabad, Kochi, and Coimbatore as emerging business hubs, supported by growing talent pools and improving infrastructure.
India’s expanding Global Capability Centre (GCC) ecosystem is also influencing office requirements. Companies are considering not only where talent is available but also whether a location has the infrastructure employees need to work effectively.
Khedia highlighted the quality of India’s commercial real estate developments and the amenities available in premium office buildings across the country.
For companies expanding into new markets, the growing network of business locations provides more options to access talent without requiring employees to relocate to major cities.
Why companies are choosing flexible offices
Business uncertainty is also changing how companies plan their real estate requirements.
Traditional office leases often require companies to commit to space for five to 10 years, based on projections of future growth. But as businesses become more agile, such long-term commitments can be difficult to make.
“If any multinationals come to India, they would first have to invest in real estate, thinking of a five-year horizon. Now, flexible office spaces have cut down on those uncertainties. They have ensured the companies can think for the next one or two years,” Khedia said.
Flexible workspaces allow businesses to start with smaller offices, expand, or reduce their space as required, and pay for what they use. This can help them manage real estate costs and allocate more resources to hiring and other business priorities.
Office design is changing as well. Traditional cabins and cubicles are making way for more open layouts that encourage interaction between teams. Companies are also incorporating greenery and biophilic design to make workplaces more comfortable and inviting.
Flexible workspace providers and landlords
Khedia said flexible workspace providers are increasingly working with traditional landlords rather than competing with them. Such partnerships can help property owners attract more tenants by offering businesses different ways to occupy office space.
“The flex office space is a true partner to the landlord. They're not changing the landscape, they're complementing the landlord to create a space which will invite more and more tenants to that building,” he said.
He pointed to the growth of the sector in India. When he began his career, flexible offices accounted for about 1% of overall real estate leasing. By the last financial quarter, that share had reached 23%, he said.
He also noted that flexible workspace absorption in India had increased from around half a million square feet to more than 17–18 million square feet.
Providers such as TEC now offer more than desks and meeting rooms. Businesses can access offices tailored to their requirements, including secure private units within a shared infrastructure.
This allows companies to maintain privacy while benefiting from flexible arrangements and opportunities to network with other businesses in the same building.
For companies entering a new market or expanding their operations, the model also reduces the need to set up and manage every aspect of an office independently.
Enterprise 2.0: Beyond the desk
Khedia believes the next phase of office development will focus more closely on employees' everyday needs.
This could include access to healthcare, childcare, food and other facilities within or near office buildings. Such amenities can make workplaces more convenient while helping businesses attract and retain talent.
For Khedia, Enterprise 2.0 is about moving beyond conventional office layouts to create workplaces that support employees throughout the working day.
As companies reconsider their real estate needs, flexibility, collaboration, and employee experience are becoming important factors in deciding what an office should offer.

articles.title: Amazon pierde 40 satélites tras la explosión de un cohete Vulcan: es un gran revés a sus ambiciosos planes
articles.text:
Por si el pique entre Elon Musk y Jeff Bezos no fuese ya algo legendario, este fin de semana el azar-o la tecnología- ha llevado sus diferencias a otro nivel. El CEO de SpaceX ha hecho historia recuperando por primera vez en el aire la segunda etapa de uno de sus Starship. Este, además, venía de depositar 26 satélites de nueva generación en su constelación Starlink. 24 horas después de este hito, Amazon pretendía añadir también unos cuantos satélites más a su propia constelación, pero en su caso, en vez de un éxito, todo terminó en desastre, con un fallo del cohete que los transportaba que impidió seguir aumentando el tamaño de la constelación Amazon Leo.
El suceso. Los 40 satélites iban a bordo de un cohete Vulcan Centaur, de la compañía United Launch Alliance (ULA), que partió de Cabo Cañaveral (Florida) a las 17:40 GMT (18:40, hora peninsular española) del domingo, 15 de noviembre. Unos 10 minutos después del despegue, hubo una anomalía que impidió que el cohete llegase a órbita para depositar los satélites. Hasta el momento ULA no ha dado información sobre las causas de esta incidencia que impidió depositar los satélites en su destino. ULA ya había tenido problemas antes con los propulsores sólidos de los cohetes Vulcan. Sin embargo, en esta ocasión estos han funcionado correctamente, así que el problema debe ser otro.
Más lejos del objetivo. En 2020, la Comisión Federal de Comunicaciones de Estados Unidos autorizó a Amazon para desplegar 3.236 satélites de telecomunicaciones en órbita terrestre baja. Por otro lado, se exigió que la mitad de ellos, 1.618, estuviesen en órbita para julio de 2026. Hasta ahora, se han puesto en órbita 400 de estos satélites, por lo que ya se ha incumplido este requisito. Además, están muy lejos de alcanzar una buena cobertura, por lo que se debe aumentar la cadencia de lanzamientos. Un suceso como el ocurrido este fin de semana no ayuda, sobre todo porque Amazon tenía mucha confianza depositada en ULA y ahora no tendrá más remedio que pensar en otros socios.
¿Y ahora qué? Amazon ya tenía contratados 38 vuelos Vulcan para lanzar más de 1.500 satélites de primera generación. Por desgracia, ahora tendrán que esperar a que concluya la investigación de ULA para poder volver a contar con su lanzadera. Es por eso que ahora el resto de socios de Amazon se han convertido en piezas indispensables para que la compañía logre sus objetivos. Un buen ejemplo de ello es la compañía Arianespace, con la que ya está contratado el siguiente lanzamiento de satélites Amazon Leo. Si todo va bien, este tendrá lugar el próximo 23 de noviembre, a bordo de un cohete Ariane 6.
Cabe destacar que, desde sus inicios, Amazon ha contado también en tres ocasiones con cohetes Falcon 9 de SpaceX para impulsar sus satélites. Sin embargo, dado que esta compañía es su principal adversaria, es lógico que quiera buscar otros socios con mayor potencial de convertirse en aliados.
Doble mazazo. Algo curioso de todo esto es que ha supuesto un mazazo para Jeff Bezos por dos motivos, ya que no afecta solo a Amazon LEO, sino también a Blue Origin. La primera etapa del Vulcan Centaur está impulsada por motores BE-4, fabricados por la compañía espacial de Bezos. No hay constancia de que sea este el motivo por el que ha fallado el cohete de ULA, pero lógicamente es algo que también habrá que investigar. En definitiva, no ha sido ni de lejos un buen fin de semana para Jeff Bezos. Que sí lo haya sido para Elon Musk, quien ya tiene más de 10.000 satélites en el espacio, no hace más que echar leña al fuego de su rivalidad.

articles.title: Irene Gramage, especialista en herencias: "Si en una herencia un hermano se aprovecha, hay que hacer un requerimiento notarial"
articles.text:
Cuando varios hermanos tienen que repartirse las propiedades de sus padres y uno se instala sin el permiso de los demás en una de las viviendas, el reparto puede quedarse bloqueado y acabar en los tribunales. Irene Gramage, experta en herencias, ha explicado en un vídeo de TikTok qué se puede hacer en esa situación. “Si en una herencia un hermano se aprovecha, hay que hacer un requerimiento notarial”, asegura.
El requerimiento notarial. Gramage pone como ejemplo el caso real de unos hermanos que, después del fallecimiento de sus padres, tienen que repartir las propiedades familiares- El problema llega cuando uno de ellos se va a vivir a una de las casas y se niega a firmar los documentos necesarios para seguir adelante. Si no hay respuesta, explica la experta, el siguiente paso sería recurrir a un requerimiento notarial para intentar desbloquear el reparto.
Esta vía está recogida en el artículo 1005 del Código Civil, que permite pedir al notario que avise al heredero de que dispone de 30 días naturales para aceptar o renunciar a la herencia. Y es que quedarse callado también tiene consecuencias, porque si no contesta en ese plazo “se entenderá aceptada la herencia pura y simplemente”.
Las llaves y el alquiler. Pero el requerimiento no es la única herramienta. Según Gramage, también se puede reclamar la entrega de las llaves de la vivienda al hermano que la ocupa. “Si no entrega las llaves del inmueble tendrá que pagar un alquiler al resto de hermanos”, asegura. Eso sí, esa compensación dependerá de las circunstancias de cada caso y de lo que se determine legalmente.
Una vía judicial cara. Si aun así no se llega a un acuerdo, cualquiera de los coherederos puede solicitar la división judicial de la herencia. En ese procedimiento, regulado en la Ley de Enjuiciamiento Civil, pueden intervenir un contador-partidor y peritos que valoren los inmuebles, a lo que hay que sumar los gastos de abogados y procuradores. Vamos, que no sale barato: “Eso va a costar un pastón”, advierte Gramage.
Por eso, si eres tú quien está pensando en quedarse en una de las casas, la experta recomienda pensarse bien las consecuencias antes de ocuparla y bloquear el reparto de los bienes.

articles.title: Google warns that fully-automated AI attacks are coming soon
articles.text:
Threat actors are now relying on agentic workflows powered by AI-based offensive frameworks to automate vulnerability discovery and exploitation, accelerating attacks to machine speed.
Although AI was initially used experimentally in the attack flow, Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) has observed its large-scale adoption by both financially motivated and state-sponsored threat groups.
A notable example is the use of CAIRN, an open-source multi-agent penetration-testing framework, in an attack against the U.S. aerospace sector, and suspected North Korean hackers using Claude Code to deliver malware.
The researchers estimate that in the next three months threat actors will be able to launch unsophisticated attacks that require "little to no human interaction" and rely mostly on multiple AI agents.
Their projection is that "sophisticated, fully autonomous" agentic attacks are likely to emerge in the next six months.
In an advisory last week, the FBI warned that multiple threat actors started weaponizing the ARTEX AI pentesting framework since August and launched attacks against organizations in the financial, government, technology, defense, healthcare, and other sectors.
Using AI to find and exploit flaws
Google says attackers now systematically abuse open-source pentesting suites to run fully automated attacks, including ARTEX, CAIRN, CyberStrikeAI, and HexStrike AI.
Attackers used these frameworks to carry out adaptive attacks against internet-exposed endpoints vulnerable to low-complexity flaws for which large language models (LLMs) could easily build exploits.
In one example GTIG highlights in its AI Threat Tracker report, hackers used a multi-agent system called ‘exploit_agent’ to fully automate vulnerability finding and exploitation in attacks targeting French media, entertainment, and education websites.
“In the past quarter, GTIG identified threat actors using LLM frameworks to fully automate vulnerability discovery and exploitation without a human in the loop for the first time,” Google says.
“More specifically, GTIG identified an exposed staging server hosting a multi-agent vulnerability research and weaponization framework, dubbed exploit_agent, that integrates with multiple frontier and local LLMs.”
Google discovered this framework from the attacker’s exposed staging server, which also included stolen victim data, reconnaissance information, webshells, and brute-forcing scripts.
The system analyzes software updates on popular web apps to find signs of security flaws and automatically attempts to exploit them.
Google warns that the deployment of such frameworks in attacks has dramatically decreased the time defenders have to patch their systems, while it also produces false leads.
The researchers noted the recent example of PHP2Shell, where hundreds of purported proof-of-concept (PoC) exploits, mostly AI-generated, appeared shortly after PHP announced the two flaws. This added a significant burden on defenders, as they had to verify the code and develop protections.
Other AI usage trends
Beyond automated attacks, Google spotted multiple attacks from UNC6836, an activity cluster with suspected links to “Midnight Neptune,” targeting cryptocurrency firms in North America and Europe, using modified Claude Code.
After the initial compromise, the attackers modified the Claude Code app's settings so that at launch it triggered the download of the SOMBERMEME backdoor.
Google reports AI is now routinely used in influence operations by state-backed groups, commercial vendors, and political networks.
According to the researchers, LLMjacking has become a widespread problem, with attackers increasingly exploiting this new revenue stream at significant cost to affected organizations.
Uncover email threats your existing defenses may miss.

articles.title: NGX Group acquires 10% stake in Nairobi Securities Exchange
articles.text:
The Nigerian Exchange Group Plc (NGX Group) has acquired a 10% equity stake in the Nairobi Securities Exchange (NSE) as it pursues a broader pan-African growth strategy.
The investment gives NGX Group a foothold in Kenya, one of East Africa’s key financial markets, and strengthens its presence beyond Nigeria. On Friday, the Nigerian stock market closed at $120.97 billion, and Kenya’s stock market was worth $31.45 billion.
It also builds on the group’s 2024 investment in the Ethiopian Securities Exchange as it pushes to establish commercial and institutional relationships with securities exchanges across the continent.
The move comes as NGX Group expands its regional footprint and African capital markets explore deeper integration to attract cross-border investments, broaden access to capital, improve liquidity, and facilitate multi-country initial public offerings (IPOs) such as the Dangote Cement share sale, which allowed Kenyan investors to participate through arrangements involving Kenyan capital market operators.
By taking equity positions in exchanges outside Nigeria, NGX Group is seeking to spearhead the integration of Africa’s capital markets while diversifying its investment portfolio and potential sources of returns beyond its domestic market.
According to the NGX Group, the Nairobi investment is intended to strengthen financial connections between West and East Africa and create opportunities for closer collaboration between the two markets.
“Both markets have already shown what closer collaboration can achieve for issuers and investors and a shareholding relationship gives that collaboration permanence. We remain focused on disciplined capital allocation and investments that deliver sustainable value to our shareholders over the long term,” Temi Popoola, group managing director and chief executive officer of NGX Group, said in a statement shared with TechCabal.
Umaru Kwairanga, group chairman of NGX Group, added, “African capital markets are at an inflection point, where integration is moving from aspiration to architecture. Exchange groups that commit patient capital to market infrastructure will help shape how capital flows across the continent.”
The NGX Group’s push into other African markets comes as its domestic business records strong growth, driven by increased digital access, which is bringing more investors into the market and boosting trading activity on the Nigerian Exchange.
In the nine months ending September 2026, the group’s gross earnings rose 64.8% year-on-year to ₦29.6 billion ($21.86 million), while profit after tax increased 86.4% to ₦14.7 billion ($10.86 million), already 40% higher than its full-year 2025 profit. Transaction fees, its biggest revenue driver, more than doubled to ₦20.7 billion ($15.29 million) as higher trading volumes and growing retail investor participation, increasingly through digital platforms, boosted activity. Over the same period, the NGX All-Share Index gained 61.43%, while equity market capitalisation grew 64.12% to ₦163.1 trillion ($120.46 billion).
The stronger financial performance gives NGX Group greater capacity to pursue its regional expansion ambitions as it looks beyond Nigeria for new sources of growth and investment returns.
While the acquisition is part of NGX Group’s strategy to build a more diversified exchange business, the extent to which these investments translate into increased cross-border listings, trading activity, and investment flows will depend on how effectively the exchanges convert their ownership relationships into operational collaboration.

articles.title: Tiny flaws in diamonds could unlock a quantum computing revolution
articles.text:
Tiny flaws in diamonds could unlock a quantum computing revolution
By treating qubits like individual molecules, scientists can now predict their behavior faster and more accurately
- Date:
- November 13, 2026
- Source:
- Princeton University
- Summary:
- Scientists have discovered a faster way to identify diamond-based materials that could power quantum computers and sensors at room temperature. The breakthrough has already revealed promising new quantum building blocks that could help unlock computing capabilities far beyond those of today's supercomputers.
- Share:
A new computational technique could accelerate the search for diamond materials capable of powering future quantum computers and highly sensitive sensors. Developed by a researcher at the U.S. Department of Energy's (DOE) Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory (PPPL), the method makes it much easier to identify promising materials for quantum technology, potentially opening the door to advances across many areas of science.
The approach has already revealed new candidates for quantum computing and sensing applications. The findings were recently published in ACS Central Science and have attracted attention from other researchers in the field.
One of the biggest challenges in developing quantum technology is finding materials that can maintain delicate quantum states under practical conditions. Many candidates require extremely low temperatures to function reliably. Diamond materials stand out because certain quantum properties can remain useful even at room temperature.
This capability could help advance technologies that are important to national research priorities and the development of next-generation computing. Quantum sensors promise levels of sensitivity and precision beyond those of conventional instruments, while quantum computers could eventually solve certain extraordinarily complex problems much faster than today's most powerful supercomputers.
Why Imperfect Diamonds Could Be the Key to Quantum Computing
Although diamonds are made of carbon atoms, a flawless diamond crystal is not enough to create a useful quantum computing system. The key lies in tiny irregularities within the crystal structure.
These imperfections, known as defects, can occur when a carbon atom is absent from its normal position, when another element replaces a carbon atom, or when both changes occur together. The atoms surrounding these defects can form qubits, the basic units used to store and process quantum information in quantum computers and sensors.
Finding the most useful defects, however, has been difficult. Accurately modeling their quantum behavior traditionally requires enormous computational resources, making it challenging to evaluate large numbers of possible candidates.
A Simpler Way to Discover Better Diamond Qubits
Mark Martirez, a staff research scientist at PPPL, developed a way to dramatically reduce the complexity of these calculations. Instead of simulating a much larger diamond structure, he isolates a small region containing just 16 to 30 atoms around a defect.
By "carving out" this tiny atomic cluster and treating it like a separate molecule, Martirez can use powerful computational methods that chemists have spent decades refining. These established techniques make it possible to analyze the quantum properties of diamond defects much more efficiently without sacrificing the high level of accuracy needed for the calculations.
"Because we're treating the qubits as molecules, the cost of calculating these defects is equivalent to the cost of just modeling a simple molecule," Martirez said. "This method really opened the floodgates" in terms of how qubits can be assessed.
The new technique allows researchers to calculate how different qubits respond to laser light and microwave pulses far more quickly than before. Using this approach, the team identified promising defects involving boron and oxygen that could serve as new types of qubits.
New Diamond Defects Reveal a Spectrum of Quantum Colors
Light plays an important role in how scientists interact with diamond qubits. Researchers use lasers and microwave pulses to manipulate their quantum states and retrieve stored information.
Much of the previous work in this area has centered on a defect known as the nitrogen-vacancy center. This structure forms when a nitrogen atom takes the place of a carbon atom in a diamond crystal, while an adjacent position that would normally contain another carbon atom remains empty.
Under laser illumination, this type of defect can emit red light when it occupies a particular quantum state.
The newly investigated defects offer different optical properties. Oxygen defects can produce blue light, while those involving boron emit ultraviolet light.
These differences could make it possible to combine several types of qubits within a single quantum device. Because each type responds differently to light, researchers might be able to interact with one group of qubits without disturbing another.
"One could imagine, then, combining different qubits of different responses, so you can basically probe one qubit but not the other," Martirez said.
Beyond identifying new candidates, the findings suggest a broader change in how researchers approach quantum technology. Diamond qubits have traditionally been studied primarily through physics, but understanding their underlying chemistry could provide additional ways to design them.
Martirez believes that researchers could eventually engineer qubits for particular functions using principles similar to those applied when chemists create specialized molecules, including compounds designed for new medications.
How Quantum Chemistry Could Transform Future Research
The potential benefits extend well beyond the development of quantum computers themselves. Martirez sees an intriguing possibility in which advances made possible by quantum chemistry eventually lead to quantum technologies that help improve the field of chemistry.
In other words, quantum chemistry could develop the very tools needed to "enrich itself" in the coming decades.
A practical quantum system containing multiple qubits could make molecular calculations substantially more accurate. That would allow scientists to study increasingly complex chemical structures, including large biological molecules and proteins, with a level of detail that is difficult to achieve using conventional methods.
"We could describe larger molecules, biomolecules, proteins and everything like that in a more accurate way, and that could improve all the chemical-adjacent industries, such as pharmaceutical science and materials science. Even our fundamental understanding of molecular systems could be enriched."
Such improvements could have far-reaching implications for pharmaceutical development, materials research, and the fundamental study of how molecules behave.
Martirez also hopes the research will encourage more chemists to explore solid-state physics. Although building advanced quantum computers is often viewed as a challenge primarily for physicists, he argues that chemistry offers valuable expertise that could help accelerate progress.
"At this moment in time, there's a great emphasis on building the first state-of-the-art qubit computer," he said. "But it's not just physicists who should be participating in this research. Chemists have decades of developed intuition about chemical systems that could be easily translated into understanding defects in solids as well."
By bringing these disciplines together, scientists may be able to develop more effective ways to discover, understand, and eventually engineer the quantum materials needed for future technologies.
The research was funded through PPPL's Laboratory Directed Research and Development program under prime contract number DE-AC02-09CH11466, with additional support from the DOE Office of Science, Office of Fusion Energy Sciences.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Princeton University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- John Mark P. Martirez. A Chemist’sGuide to Solid-State Qubits: DiamondColor Centers as Embedded Vacancy-Centered Molecules. ACS Central Science, 2026; 12 (10): 1578 DOI: 10.1021/acscentsci.6c00548

articles.title: Microsoft says Project Helix is a console that plays PC games, not a PC that plays console games
articles.text:
The takeaway: Microsoft's next-generation Xbox, code-named Project Helix, is being built as a console that can run PC games, not as a Windows PC adapted to play console titles. Jason Ronald, Xbox's vice president of next generation, made that distinction in an interview published in the company's new digital Xbox 25th Anniversary Magazine.
Rumors and official hints have long pointed to a Helix that could play PC games and open the door to rival storefronts such as Steam and the Epic Games Store. That led many observers to expect something closer to a gaming PC, running a custom version of Windows that could also handle console games. Some rumors went further, saying Microsoft might license the hardware to manufacturers like Asus so they could release their own Helix-based boxes.
Ronald described the product the other way around. "We're very clear on the design goal: Helix is designed to be a console that is also capable of playing games from your PC," he said. "It is not a PC that can also play console games. The goal is making it easy, intuitive, and instant to access my games. But if you're a hardcore gamer or a power user who wants to have that deeper level of customizability across settings and performance options, you can absolutely go do it."
That framing matches reports that the Xbox team favors a customized, console-focused operating system rather than a conventional Windows desktop. Microsoft has confirmed that Helix's OS is being built on Windows, but the experience will be tailored to gaming.
Ronald confirmed that the Helix interface "will be its own." It won't be designed from scratch, though. He said the interface will draw on what Microsoft learned from the ROG Xbox Ally handheld and Xbox mode for Windows, both of which bring game libraries from different sources into one front end. Helix appears set to take the same approach and present games from several libraries in one place, so players don't have to jump between separate launchers.
The library itself is a big part of the plan. Ronald called Helix the "ultimate gaming machine," one that "removes all the barriers of play that have historically existed." On the console side, that means access to games spanning four generations: the original Xbox, the Xbox 360, the Xbox One, and the current Xbox Series X|S.
On the PC side, Ronald said the aim is to "remove the arbitrary constraints between console and PC games," a long-standing divide that has kept the two libraries apart even though both run on Microsoft platforms.
His remark about deeper customization points to a hybrid performance model. Consoles usually lock graphics settings in place, and PC players expect a slew of graphics and performance settings they can adjust. Ronald's comments suggest Helix owners could get more control over settings and performance than traditional console users, while the default experience remains simple for everyone else.

articles.title: Modernizing mainframe Assembler to Java using Amazon Bedrock and AWS Transform | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Modernizing mainframe Assembler to Java using Amazon Bedrock and AWS Transform
Imagine a batch job that has run every night for decades without failing, and the only person who understands its code is about to retire. We have seen this situation again and again while working with banking, insurance, and airline customers. Their Assembler programs still run critical business operations, but fewer people can read them each year. Rewriting them by hand takes years, risks breaking business rules nobody remembers writing, and still depends on the same experts who are leaving. Amazon Bedrock and AWS Transform change that equation.
This post shows you a multi-stage transformation methodology using Amazon Bedrock, Kiro IDE (an AI-powered integrated development environment), and AWS Transform that can help reduce modernization time compared to manual approaches while maintaining business logic integrity through validation checkpoints. You will learn how to systematically extract business rules from Assembler code, convert them through an intermediate COBOL stage, and deploy modernized applications as Java Spring Boot services on AWS.
Prerequisites
Before starting the modernization process, make sure you have:
- Active AWS account with least-privilege AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissions for Amazon Bedrock, AWS Transform, and Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3).
- Access to Amazon Q Developer or Kiro for AI-assisted code analysis.
- Access to AWS Transform for COBOL to Java conversion.
- Access to Amazon Bedrock with appropriate foundation models (FMs).
- An Amazon S3 bucket configured for source code and artifact storage, with encryption and Block Public Access enabled.
- Knowledge of the target business domain and application functionality.
- Availability of business and technical subject matter experts (SMEs) for validation sessions.
- Source Assembler code inventory with available documentation.
- Test data sets with expected outputs for functional equivalence testing.
Solution overview
You can transform legacy mainframe Assembler applications tightly bounded with COBOL into Java Spring Boot applications built for the AWS cloud through a systematic five-phase approach. This multi-stage methodology, converting Assembler to COBOL as an intermediate step before Java transformation, reduces risk and preserves business logic with greater reliability than direct Assembler-to-Java conversion. The intermediate COBOL stage provides a structured, human-readable format that subject matter experts (SMEs) can validate before final transformation. This makes sure that business rules remain intact throughout the modernization journey. The following sections describe both the current mainframe architecture and the target cloud-focused state.
Current state
Your current architecture represents a traditional mainframe environment where Assembler programs execute batch processes, connected with COBOL, interact with databases, and process files. At its core, JCL (Job Control Language) jobs trigger Assembler program execution at scheduled intervals. These programs read input from VSAM (Virtual Storage Access Method) and sequential files and perform operations against IBM Db2 for z/OS. Your business logic executes using low-level register operations (direct CPU register manipulation) and memory management. Output is written back to files or database tables, and job completion status is reported through JCL return codes. All of this runs on IBM z/OS mainframe infrastructure.
Target state
The modernization solution helps you transform legacy mainframe Assembler applications into Java applications built for the AWS cloud through a multi-phase, AI-powered workflow. The architecture uses Amazon Bedrock and Kiro IDE for AI-assisted code analysis and business rule extraction, and AWS Transform for automated COBOL-to-Java conversion.
If COBOL source code is already available, you follow the conventional approach and provide it directly to AWS Transform for conversion to Java Spring Boot applications.
With this solution, you can achieve:
- Reduced transformation time compared to manual approaches.
- Systematic business logic preservation through validation checkpoints.
- Human-in-the-loop validation at critical stages.
- Automated code conversion with functional equivalence testing.
You begin the transformation workflow by analyzing Assembler code to generate Business Rules Extraction (BRE) documentation. You then create detailed functional specifications with human-in-the-loop refinement. The validated specifications guide the Assembler-to-COBOL conversion, generating intermediate COBOL code that bridges the gap between low-level hardware instructions and business-oriented constructs. This COBOL code undergoes functional equivalence testing before AWS Transform converts it to Java, with validation checkpoints at each phase to reduce risk and verify business continuity.
Business rules extraction with AI
The quality of your Business Rules Extraction (BRE) directly impacts transformation accuracy, so focus carefully on this phase. Use Amazon Bedrock, through Kiro IDE or the Amazon Bedrock console, along with AWS Transform for mainframe to extract and document business rules from your Assembler source code.
You can use the prompts in this post directly in Amazon Bedrock through the Chat Playground, or within Kiro IDE using its built-in AI chat and Spec panel. Replace the placeholder values with your actual Assembler code and context before running.
Amazon Bedrock is the inference platform behind the first four phases: business rules extraction, specification creation, Assembler-to-COBOL conversion, and validation. Choose a foundation model with strong code reasoning and a large context window, because Assembler programs are long and dense. Set the temperature to 0 so you get consistent output across runs. To process many programs, call the same prompts through the Amazon Bedrock Converse API and store each output in your Amazon S3 bucket so it can feed the next phase. Amazon Bedrock doesn’t use your prompts or model outputs to train AWS models or share them with third parties. For details, see Data protection in Amazon Bedrock. Use sanitized test data instead of production data or personally identifiable information (PII).
The more context you provide to the AI, the better it understands the business intent behind the code. Include relevant documentation, data dictionaries, and available business context alongside the Assembler code when prompting.
Note: Save the output of each prompt as you go. You will need them as inputs in the next phase.
Example prompt for context-aware analysis:
You can customize this prompt by adding domain-specific terminology from your business context. When you run this prompt, you will see structured JSON output that you can use for automated validation and direct integration with downstream transformation tools. Data mapping accuracy directly affects conversion quality. Incomplete mappings can lead to lost or corrupted business logic.
Validate with SMEs
Treat AI-generated BRE documents as drafts, not final outputs. Have subject matter experts review and validate the extracted rules before moving forward. Document discrepancies in a validation log and update the BRE based on SME feedback before proceeding to specification creation.
To help SMEs validate the rules, supplement textual BRE documents with visual aids like flowcharts and data flow diagrams. Maintain a validation checklist covering business rule accuracy, data mapping correctness, edge case handling, and error condition completeness.
Extracting spec-driven data flow
After you validate business rules with SMEs, translate them into detailed functional specifications that will guide code conversion. This spec-driven approach confirms that business requirements are clearly documented and agreed upon before code transformation begins, reducing costly rework later.
Use the extracted BRE documents to create complete functional specifications that guide COBOL code generation. These specifications should include program overview, COBOL data structures, process flow design, and business rules coverage mapping.
Example prompt for functional specification generation:
You can adjust the data structure specifications based on your COBOL standards. When you run this prompt, you will receive a complete functional specification with full traceability from business rules to COBOL structures, ready for SME review and direct integration with Kiro for code generation.
Converting legacy Assembler to COBOL
With validated functional specifications in hand, the next phase uses these structured outputs to guide the Assembler-to-COBOL conversion. The intermediate COBOL step helps you bridge the gap between low-level hardware instructions and business-oriented constructs, which helps you verify that business logic is preserved before the final Java transformation.
Example prompt to guide the conversion:
You can modify the formatting requirements to match your organization’s COBOL standards. When you run this prompt, you will generate COBOL code designed to be syntactically correct, logically equivalent to the original Assembler, and fully traceable, with comments linking each code section back to specific business rules from the BRE document. Once generated, rigorously validate the COBOL code before proceeding to the final Java transformation.
Validating the transformation
You should treat testing as an ongoing activity throughout the transformation process, not only a final phase. Your functional equivalence validation between Assembler and COBOL code should employ a comprehensive testing framework that systematically evaluates syntax correctness, structural alignment, logic equivalence, data flow integrity, business rules coverage, and specification compliance.
Example prompt to guide the testing:
You can customize the validation thresholds based on your quality requirements. When you run this prompt, you will receive a comprehensive validation report with actionable recommendations for addressing gaps in program structure, conditional logic, data transformations, and traceability between the original Assembler instructions and the modernized COBOL implementation.
COBOL to Java transformation
In the final phase, you use AWS Transform to automatically convert validated COBOL code into Java Spring Boot applications. Generate production-ready Java code with the intelligent refactoring in AWS Transform. This refactoring preserves the business logic validated in previous phases while introducing modern design patterns, including dependency injection, repository patterns, and service layers.
You can deploy the resulting Java applications on AWS infrastructure to achieve cloud scalability and resilience while maintaining the same business functionality as your legacy mainframe systems. This cloud-focused approach replaces monolithic mainframe architecture with modular, maintainable code that can be independently deployed, monitored, and enhanced.
For detailed step-by-step instructions, refer to the AWS Transform Refactor Workshop.
Lessons learned
When you apply this methodology in practice, here are the key lessons that can shape your approach:
- Human-in-the-loop validation is essential for transformation quality. Amazon Bedrock and Kiro IDE can help improve business rule identification, but AI-generated documents should always be treated as drafts. SME review is essential at every critical stage, not only during extraction, to catch domain-specific logic, edge cases, and business context that AI tools may overlook. This human oversight can help reduce post-deployment defects compared to automated conversion without structured checkpoints.
- The intermediate COBOL step reduces risk. You will find the multi-stage approach (Assembler to COBOL to Java) with validation checkpoints at each phase more reliable than attempting direct conversion. The intermediate step helps you verify business logic preservation before committing to the final Java transformation.
- A spec-driven methodology helps you prevent rework. Creating detailed functional specifications before code conversion catches misunderstandings early. With structured JSON specifications, you can also automate validation and direct integration with transformation tools.
- Incremental validation helps you accelerate your overall timeline. Testing after each transformation stage, rather than waiting until the end, helps you detect issues early and reduces overall rework. Quality gates at each phase help confirm the output is ready for the next stage.
Conclusion and next steps
In this post, we walked through a systematic, AI-powered approach to transform legacy mainframe Assembler applications into Java applications built for the cloud on AWS. This approach combines Amazon Bedrock and Kiro IDE for intelligent business logic extraction with AWS Transform for automated COBOL-to-Java conversion. By following a multi-stage methodology with validation checkpoints at each phase, you can help accelerate modernization timelines while preserving critical business logic integrity.
To evaluate the full service landscape and understand how the components fit together, start with the AWS Mainframe Modernization documentation. When you’re ready to see the pipeline in action, the AWS Transform Refactor Workshop walks you through the end-to-end process with sample workloads you can run in your own environment. If you’d like to discuss how this approach applies to your specific environment, contact an AWS representative.
Tell us about your modernization journey and share your thoughts in the comments.

articles.title: Alpine Linux Users Urged to Patch OpenSSH Authentication Flaw
articles.text:
A recently disclosed vulnerability in OpenSSH lets an unauthenticated attacker log into accounts that should have no usable password. The issue, named *sshole and tracked as CVE-2026-123158, affects Linux systems running OpenSSH with the musl C library and which don't use PAM. Security researchers now report that attackers are exploiting it in the wild.
The flaw comes from the way OpenSSH checks passwords when musl handles the underlying crypt() call. On an affected system, a password longer than 256 bytes causes musl to return an error value. That value is an asterisk, the same character Linux uses in /etc/shadow to mark an account as having no password. OpenSSH then treats the returned asterisk as a match and permits the login.
The conditions to exploit the vulnerability are however quite narrow. The server must run OpenSSH before version 10.6p2, be built against the musl library rather than glibc, and operate without PAM. It must also have at least one account with a SHA-256 or SHA-512 password hash and another account marked with an asterisk in its shadow entry. When those conditions are met, any password between 257 and 1,024 characters can authenticate against the passwordless account.
Alpine Linux is the most prominent distribution affected, as it uses musl and its default OpenSSH configuration does not enable PAM. Other musl-based environments, including OpenWrt, Buildroot and Yocto, may also be affected where the same configuration applies. Systems using glibc, PAM, Dropbear or OpenBSD are not affected.
"Accounts that should never take a password at all (root, your key-only deploy user, ldap users, the default user on alpine's aws and azure images) take any password longer than 256 characters."
Ozgun Kultekin, *sshole
Ozgun Kultekin, a security researcher at Wakefield, published the technical explanation on the *sshole site. Kultekin traces the problem to two musl changes made in 2012: the first replaced the NULL error return from crypt() with an asterisk, and the second added a 256-byte limit to SHA-512 password hashing, so longer inputs caused an error. Together, the changes produced a value that could be mistaken for a password hash.
The OpenSSH side of the problem dates from a 2016 fix for CVE-2016-6210, which was a timing attack that could reveal whether a username existed. To make responses take a similar amount of time for valid and invalid users, OpenSSH borrowed the salt from another account and hashed the supplied password anyway. That workaround also applied to real accounts whose shadow entry contained an asterisk.
Kultekin writes that the issue remained unnoticed for roughly a decade because the vulnerable combination was uncommon in testing. OpenSSH is tested on OpenBSD and glibc-based systems, while many Linux distributions route authentication through PAM, which does not call crypt() for asterisk entries in the same way. Kultekin says the bug was found after building OpenSSH in several configurations and testing about 17,600 unusual login attempts.
"On alpine's official aws and azure images that's the default `alpine` user, and it has passwordless `doas`. so it's root"
Ozgun Kultekin, *sshole
On Alpine's official AWS and Azure images, the default alpine user is marked as passwordless and can use doas without a password. This means that an attacker who reaches that account can therefore obtain root privileges. Dan Goodin reports for Ars Technica that the issue can give unauthenticated access to high-privilege accounts within seconds on affected systems.
OpenSSH 10.6p2 contains a fix. Operators who cannot update immediately can disable password authentication by setting PasswordAuthentication no in the SSH server configuration and restarting sshd. Kultekin also advises checking authentication logs for evidence that an account with no password accepted a password. The project has published a detection and background repository.
The vulnerability is being actively exploited. Goodin notes that GreyNoise reported that honeypots in Southeast Asia had been attacked by a group it is tracking known as GT10, which reportedly deploys a backdoor which supports shell commands, reconnaissance and persistence. Goodin reports that watchTowr linked the activity to botnets and cryptocurrency operations, while Previdian recorded 20 exploitation attempts from 13 IP addresses in nine countries. The United States Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency added CVE-2026-123158 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 9 November, according to Hackread.
Red Hat has said that its products are not affected because they do not meet the required combination of musl and no PAM. Amazon has likewise marked Amazon Linux 2 and Amazon Linux 2023 as not affected. That does not remove the risk for teams running Alpine-based containers, embedded devices or custom musl builds. Administrators should look for SSH servers built against musl, check whether PAM is disabled, review shadow entries for asterisk-locked accounts, apply OpenSSH 10.6p2 and restart the service.
The vulnerability was publicly disclosed on 5 November and exploitation reports followed within days. For organisations with internet-facing SSH services, the immediate action to take is fairly straightforward: update OpenSSH, restart it, and remove password authentication where it is not needed.

articles.title: Sam Altman says he wants everyone ‘to have a lot of RAM’
articles.text:
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman is once again addressing his controversial comments on PC RAM purchases. “I want to be clear, I want people to have a lot of RAM, I think everybody should be able to buy a lot of RAM for their own computer,” Altman said today. “I think the home tinkering is great.”
Sam Altman says he wants everyone ‘to have a lot of RAM’
Altman suggested we all ‘share this memory’ and said, ‘I think the home tinkering is great.’
The comments were made onstage at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World summit on Monday.
Altman’s remarks on RAM stirred up controversy last month. In an appearance on the Cheeky Pint podcast, Altman said that it’s “quite terrible” for everyone to have RAM in personal computers rather than in data centers. He later followed up on those comments in posts on X earlier this month, saying, “i want you to have so much ram” and saying the original remarks had been “taken out of context.”
AI companies have been buying up the world’s memory supply for data centers, leading to ongoing price hikes on everything from phones to game consoles. Altman commented on supply chain issues, saying OpenAI has “been constrained by different things at different times,” like memory, rack assembly, data center capacity, or “some random component.”
Onstage today, Altman went on to say that “a few years ago we started saying the world needs to build a lot more memory supply chain in particular.” He acknowledged how RAM prices have soared over recent months, saying:
“The world did not build out that much, and now we have seen DRAM prices — I don’t know exactly, but maybe they went up 5x, 7x, something like that. I think it would be much better if the world just had a lot of memory. That comment, which I think got misinterpreted, but there is a true part of it, which I will stand by is that, if we’re going to be in this memory supply shortage, then in some sense — whether or not we’ll decide to do it, because I think there are other tradeoffs like people having their own at-home inference — the optimal thing would be, can we share this memory and have it working 100 percent of the time rather than sometimes off in someone’s edge device? Again, optimal use of this limited supply. Maybe it’s not the reason to make the decision but that’s what I was trying to say.”
Altman also commented on Jensen Huang’s resignation as Nvidia’s CEO, saying he “doesn’t know enough” to say if Huang should be reinstated.

articles.title: Telegram Widgets Hit by RCE Demos, Malware Warning Days After Launch
articles.text:
Kaspersky has warned that a vulnerability in Telegram’s newly launched widgets may have been exploited in the wild to deliver the WebRAT malware. The warning came shortly after researchers showed what they described as remote code execution through the new feature.
In a November 13 post on its Russian-language Telegram channel, the security firm said it had observed malicious activity that it suspects is tied to the flaw. According to the company, exploitation took place when users visited certain Telegram channels.
Kaspersky said the activity results in a PowerShell script running without the user’s knowledge. The script fetches and launches WebRAT, a piece of malware also known as Salat Stealer.
WebRAT is a Rust-based trojan that gives attackers control of the infected system. It can also steal cryptocurrency wallet and Telegram account data.
Kaspersky did not share technical details on the exploitation, or say how many users were targeted. Its main recommendation was “do not launch widgets in Telegram until a fix is released.”
Telegram CEO Pavel Durov promoted the widgets feature on X on November 10, saying that any message on the platform can now become an app.
A day later, researchers at V12 posted a video on X with the caption “Any telegram message can now become RCE.” The video showed an interaction with a bot causing the Calculator app to open on an Android phone.
Telegram replied the same day, saying the Android issue “was fixed yesterday, and the fix was deployed to all users earlier today.”
V12 later published a second video, saying it had another RCE exploit that worked against the supposedly patched Telegram client for Windows. In the researchers’ view, letting QuickJS, a JavaScript engine, run inside messages without a sandbox creates a large attack surface.
Durov has dismissed the reports. “No one could be hacked just by receiving a message,” he wrote on X on November 13.
According to Durov, an attack required the user to first start a third-party service, and that scenario has since been fully patched on the server side. He challenged skeptics to hack his own account.
SecurityWeek has reached out to Telegram for comment and will update this article if the company responds.

articles.title: How the World’s Most Advanced AI Infrastructure Supply Chain Invents the Future
articles.text:
Deb Shoquist leads operations at NVIDIA, overseeing the supply chain and manufacturing behind its AI platforms. That description sums up the job, but it doesn’t begin to encompass what Shoquist has made possible over decades.
Shoquist, her team and their global network of manufacturing partners enable NVIDIA to introduce world-leading technologies year-round.
Much of the team’s success comes down to her deep relationships with some of the world’s most accomplished manufacturers, including TSMC, Foxconn, Wistron, SPIL, King Yuan Electronics (KYEC), Unimicron, Lumentum, Coherent and Amkor. TSMC has partnered with NVIDIA since 1998. SPIL and KYEC were assembling and testing its chips more than two decades ago.
For Shoquist, those relationships grow stronger through each challenge solved together on the factory floor, as every generation of technology demands more from the people and tools behind it.
Ask her about the global network she relies on, and she starts with the people. There’s the supplier in Taiwan so eager to get production moving that he calls her at 3 a.m. with a fix to the latest problem. There are the factory workers in Vietnam whose only ask of her are more tools to get more work done. She remembers the partners that supported NVIDIA when it was small, and the work they’ve done to help each other grow.
Shoquist meets with key suppliers quarterly and spends six weeks each year on the road visiting partners in Taiwan, China, Korea, Vietnam and the U.S., where conversations move from meeting rooms to factory floors.
Recently, she paused her travels to accept the 2026 Dr. Lisa Su Woman of Innovation Award — and to share how she finds the right people and companies to imagine and produce at massive scale technology that has never been built before.
Q: How would you describe your job to someone outside NVIDIA?
A: At the most basic level, our job is to convert designs into the physical world. Our design team creates a blueprint, and our job is to transition it into a reliable, high-performance supply chain.
A matchmaker is probably the best analogy. You have to find the partner that matches your ramp style and has the technology that can meet the needs of very precise designs. The supplier has to be financially strong enough to invest in our ramps. They have to be highly technical. And they have to be willing to do something that has never been done before.
If you don’t have all three, you can’t create products at the volume and speed that we need. You need those three legs, and in some cases, if you only have two, you have to invest in the company to make them a partner.
Q: What’s an example of that in practice ?
A: Amphenol’s cable cartridge is the most complex interconnect assembly they have ever built. When I recently visited the Vietnam factory, now in full production, I was struck by the level of precision required to build a product of this complexity.
In this large cable cartridge, there are 1,500 small cable legs. Each one requires a very precise assembly to yield a quality level of less than 1 DPPM, or defect part per million. Amphenol built over a hundred automated lines to produce this product at the speed and scale we require. That takes know-how and technology, but it also takes heart, willingness and dedication.
Creating anything of that complexity and precision with a supplier forges the partnership. The partners NVIDIA maintains are the ones who supported us when we were small, and yet are willing to scale with us today.
Q: What changed as NVIDIA went from selling chips to building systems and platforms?
A: When we were primarily a chip manufacturer, we were small, and the semiconductor industry was at scale. In that environment, it was about picking the best technology match for the products we envisioned.
As we became a data center systems company, we needed more partners. But we’ve also now entered into new technology areas where the scale of the supply base is still developing.
For example, our optical component partners have the technology and the willingness, but they don’t yet have the scale or capital to build fabs for the volume we need. To grow, we needed to support and invest, like we did with Coherent and Lumentum.
Beyond that, with products like CPO (co-packaged optics), we’re creating entirely new supply chains with scale partners that are new to the optics world. Leading the integration of talent across the supply chain is the key to driving this incredible technology to high volume quickly.
Q: You clearly enjoy spending time with supply partners, and in particular on the factory floor. What have you learned there over time that can’t be learned anywhere else?
A: Over 20 years, you meet many individuals key to the success of your supply. You meet not only the CEOs, but also the people that are running the production floor. These are the people that really know the problems of manufacturing.
If you don’t have a tight working relationship with the people deeper in the organization, then it’s hard to have an open dialogue about any challenges. But when you have tight relationships, they want to help you, and they feel comfortable enough telling you, “I need better technical support on the floor. I need more quality engineers. We need a better design. We need to automate this. We need more buffers of material.”
That’s what 20 years of working with our suppliers has taught us. It’s year after year of learning from people, getting to know people deeper in the organization and creating the trust where they can tell us what we need to do to be successful with them.
Q: Demand for NVIDIA technology is already massive and growing. Your job is to make sure NVIDIA’s volume can keep up. How do you make it happen?
A: It goes back to relationships. When you decide that you’re going to push a line hard to increase volume, you have to have the relationships. You have to know their processes in detail. You have to know their people in detail, and they have to trust you. Only then are you in a position to ask them for special favors, because you can do it surgically, and your ask is credible and reasonable.
And when you’re successful together, they’re happy, you’re happy, and the appreciation for the partnership deepens. We all appreciate those that make us successful.
Q: How do you prioritize resources across the supply chain?
A: You need to first understand what the most critical components are, and protect and prioritize production around them. We need wafers like we need air. And the critical component is the TSMC chip. As it comes out of assembly every week, we decide what factory gets what chip.
Every week, we look at factory performance. If a particular factory yield is low, if their time of ownership is not at the level we want, they don’t get more chips that week.
We keep track of every chip, from the identification number on the die all the way to the customer invoice. If you want to be our supplier, you have to support that traceability process. With that process, we took the time it takes from chip out at TSMC to system out at Foxconn and Wistron from five to two weeks when supply and demand requires it.
Think of the supply chain as a large circulatory system with pathways everywhere — and when you need to accelerate any branch of it, you have the power to do that. We have the capability to do that. It’s empowering and exciting.
Q: What’s an example of a time things didn’t go as planned? How did you, the team and your partners find a way forward?
A: We were getting ready to go to volume production with Foxconn and Wistron for the compute board of NVIDIA GB200. The last step in the process was a test managed by an automated handler — a completely new approach for us, developed to meet the demands of high-volume throughput for these complicated products. During the initial ramp, the throughput was significantly below plan.
The operations director of Taiwan manufacturing made the call that to protect the product and shipments, he needed to disable the entire process and return to manual test loading. Our manufacturers backed him without question and brought in the necessary manpower to meet the immediate needs, literally hundreds of operators. That kept production moving, but would not solve the throughput requirement of full production.
As with any operations problem, the root cause had many elements to it: test tray assembly, test tray design, automation hardware design, automation control software, product yield. From all viewpoints, it was a difficult problem to resolve quickly.
That’s when we executed the NVIDIA swarm. Teams from NVIDIA design engineering, operations industrial, and product and test engineering, as well as from Foxconn automation engineering, flooded the line with talent to redesign and reactivate the line before the scale ramp hit.
This is not an unusual occurrence when there is a problem in operations. All teams at NVIDIA are street fighters — action-oriented, and know no organizational boundaries. We say that “the mission is the boss,” but we also live “the mission is the boss.”
Q: What makes this work so exciting for you?
A: Operations is a very empowering place to be at NVIDIA. Our team is designing and implementing changes to the supply chain constantly to meet the strong demand of our new products. The challenges are understandably high, but we’re always given the resources we need to be successful. The only thing between our goals and our success is our own creativity. That is exhilarating.

articles.title: Telus pulls out of two government-backed AI data centres in Vancouver | BetaKit
articles.text:
Telus has pulled out of two AI data centre projects in Vancouver that former CEO Darren Entwistle announced alongside federal AI minister Evan Solomon just six months ago.
The news: Daily Hive reported on Saturday that the Canadian telecommunications giant is no longer partnered with local real estate developer Westbank on the AI data centre projects. When reached for comment, Westbank confirmed to BetaKit that Telus is no longer a partner on the two Vancouver projects. It did say, however, that it’s proceeding with the projects as planned and that a new partnership will be announced in the coming months.
When reached for comment, Solomon’s office deferred to Telus about its decision, but said Canada remains committed to building secure, sovereign computing capacity; Telus did not respond by press time.
From the source: According to an anonymous source quoted by The Globe and Mail, a lack of local support caused Telus to reconsider the project. Hundreds of people protested the data centre projects over the summer, and the sites are still awaiting municipal decisions, including rezoning and an upcoming city motion that could impose stricter requirements on data centre owners. The Globe’s source noted that the level of opposition in Vancouver would have made it challenging to proceed, but that Telus is still open to opportunities at these sites in the future.
The context: The Telus data centres were announced in May and were among the first to advance under the enabling large-scale sovereign AI data centres initiative, a federal program announced earlier this year designed to build domestic AI compute infrastructure and reduce reliance on foreign-owned systems. The proposed facilities included a 100,000-square-foot, repurposed facility in the Mount Pleasant neighbourhood, as well as a 400,000-square-foot development adjacent to Vancouver’s BC Place stadium.
Telus’ withdrawal from the project comes as the telecom giant is also facing mounting debt and is working to rejig its non-telecom sectors of the business. Its stock has fallen nearly 25 percent year-to-date.
Final thought: The recent federal budget pledged to enable Canadian AI companies to access 500 megawatts of sovereign AI compute as foreign hyperscalers like Meta, Anthropic, and Microsoft buy up space in Canadian data centres. As building up sovereign compute capacity continues to be a government priority, a Westbank spokesperson said the firm has already chosen its new partners, who are Canadian and “will meet sovereignty requirements.”
Feature image courtesy Telus.

articles.title: Serena Williams winds down her VC firm, launches new fund, seeks $200M | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Serena Williams and longtime business partner Beth Ferreira announced Monday the launch of an early-stage firm called Starfire Ventures.
The firm is seeking to raise $200 million in capital to back AI-native companies that are “solving critical, underserved problems for individuals across the experience economy,” including in areas such as fintech and health and wellness, the fund said in a press release announcing its launch.
This fund is separate from Serena Ventures, which Williams founded in 2022. A rep for Starfire confirmed that Serena Ventures has recently cut its last check, though a team remains to support the existing portfolio. Serena Ventures backed more than 100 companies and raised over $100 million in capital. Ferreira worked as an advisor and general partner at Serena Ventures and has co-invested with Williams since 2015 when they backed MasterClass’ seed round.
This new firm, Starfire, is a continuation of that business partnership, with Williams saying in the press release that it was “designed to live beyond” them and that the goal remains to broaden “access to capital” and create “opportunities for more people to participate in the ownership and growth of transformative businesses.”
This piece and headline were updated
