De'Longhi All-In-One Combination Coffee & Espresso Machine: two-minute review
The De'Longhi All-In-One Combination Coffee & Espresso Machine brews every sort of coffee beverage you can think of. Granted, it's not fully automatic, so you'll have to be the barista, but getting started is easy and you'll be able to make a wide variety of drinks with very little practice.
Make drip coffee the traditional way, by measuring out coffee grounds into the basket. A reusable plastic filter is included, but you can use a cone #4 paper filter if you prefer. The large carafe makes 60 ounces of coffee, and the half-carafe setting brews 30 ounces. You can pre-set the machine to automatically begin brewing at a certain time. The warming plate will keep your coffee hot or reheat it. A pull-down tray holds your mug so you can brew a single serving of coffee right into it. Choose the 8oz, 12oz, 16oz, or 20oz mug/travel mug setting. There are Classic and a Bold settings for drip coffee, so you can adjust the flavor to suit your preferences.
The espresso portafilter comes with two filter baskets, one for brewing a single espresso and one for a double espresso. The machine uses 15 bars of pressure to make espresso.
The adjustable steam wand has a Latte setting, which heats your milk without scalding it, and a Cappuccino setting, which steams and foams your milk of choice. This wand also dispenses fresh hot water for Americanos or non-coffee drinks. There is a frother whisk tucked into the side of the machine that just froths your milk, which is perfect for cold foam (or hot foam if you pre-heat your milk).
As with any coffee machine, you'll need to clean everything after you're done brewing. Many of the parts can go into the dishwasher, and the parts that do need to be hand-washed are quick and easy to clean.

articles.title: Cade investiga Apple por restrições ao Pix por aproximação no iPhone
articles.text:
O Conselho Administrativo de Defesa Econômica (Cade) abriu uma investigação para apurar se a Apple dificulta a oferta de Pix por aproximação no iPhone por bancos e fintechs. O procedimento busca esclarecer se as condições técnicas e comerciais impostas pela fabricante restringem o acesso de concorrentes à tecnologia NFC dos aparelhos.
A disputa envolve a Zetta, associação que reúne fintechs como Nubank, Mercado Pago e PicPay, e a Federação Brasileira de Bancos (Febraban). As entidades acusam a empresa de favorecer o Apple Pay, sua própria carteira digital. O Olhar Digital procurou a Apple para comentar o caso e atualizará esta reportagem caso receba um posicionamento.
Por que a Apple está sendo investigada?
O centro da discussão é a tecnologia NFC (Near Field Communication), que permite a comunicação entre dispositivos próximos e viabiliza pagamentos com a simples aproximação do celular de uma maquininha.
O inquérito administrativo, registrado sob o número 08700.002893/2025-17, foi aberto pela Superintendência-Geral do Cade para verificar se as regras da Apple dificultam o acesso de outras empresas ao NFC dos iPhones.
A Febraban afirma que o Apple Pay é atualmente o único aplicativo autorizado a realizar pagamentos com cartões por aproximação nos aparelhos com iOS. Para a entidade, essa limitação pode encarecer os serviços e reduzir as opções disponíveis aos consumidores.
Já a Zetta argumenta que as regras da fabricante também dificultam a oferta de Pix por aproximação em aplicativos de bancos e fintechs. Segundo a associação, a Apple bloqueia as APIs necessárias para processar esse tipo de pagamento e exige a utilização de sua própria plataforma paga.
APIs são ferramentas que permitem a comunicação entre diferentes programas e serviços. Na avaliação da Zetta, as restrições técnicas e as tarifas cobradas tornam economicamente inviável oferecer o recurso aos usuários de iPhone.
As entidades comparam o modelo ao Android, no qual desenvolvedores podem acessar gratuitamente a tecnologia NFC por meio do HCE. O recurso permite simular um cartão de pagamento usando o software do próprio celular.
A Zetta e a Febraban pedem que o Cade determine a liberação do acesso ao NFC dos iPhones para aplicativos de terceiros, sem cobranças restritivas e em condições equivalentes às oferecidas ao Apple Pay.
O que a Apple diz sobre as acusações?
Em sua defesa no processo, a Apple nega impedir o uso do NFC por outros desenvolvedores. A empresa afirma que existem duas maneiras de realizar pagamentos por aproximação no sistema: integrar cartões ao Apple Pay ou utilizar a plataforma NFC & SE, disponibilizada para aplicativos de terceiros a partir de outubro de 2024.
A fabricante também defende a exigência do Secure Element (SE), componente físico de segurança presente nos aparelhos. Segundo a empresa, ele protege os usuários contra fraudes e programas maliciosos.
A Apple considera esse modelo mais seguro do que o HCE, defendido pela Zetta. Enquanto o Secure Element utiliza um componente separado para proteger os dados das transações, o HCE simula um cartão por meio de um software executado no processador principal do celular.
Outro argumento da companhia é que as tarifas cobradas pelo uso da tecnologia são legítimas e compensam os investimentos em engenharia e infraestrutura de segurança.
A empresa também questiona a importância do NFC para a concorrência no mercado brasileiro de pagamentos presenciais. Em manifestação ao Cade, citou dados do Banco Central referentes a setembro de 2026.
Segundo os números apresentados pela Apple, foram realizadas aproximadamente 2,09 milhões de transações de Pix por aproximação no período, contra cerca de 3,14 bilhões de operações com QR Codes dinâmicos.
Com isso, a fabricante argumenta que os consumidores já contam com alternativas amplamente utilizadas e que a abertura do NFC não seria necessária para garantir a concorrência no setor.
Quais são os próximos passos?
A Superintendência-Geral do Cade ainda precisa concluir a análise das informações reunidas no inquérito. Até o momento, o órgão não decidiu se a Apple cometeu alguma infração às regras de concorrência.
Depois de avaliar os argumentos das entidades financeiras e da fabricante, a Superintendência-Geral poderá decidir pela abertura de um processo administrativo ou pelo arquivamento do caso.
Ana Figueiredo é editora de tecnologia do Olhar Digital. É formada em Jornalismo pela Universidade Federal de Uberlândia (UFU).

articles.title: Google enciende las alarmas: la IA podría lanzar ciberataques sin ayuda humana
articles.text:
Uno de los peores miedos de los especialistas en seguridad está a punto de volverse realidad. Google advirtió que los ciberataques totalmente automatizados con IA llegarían en poco tiempo, por lo que es necesario prepararse. La compañía dijo que los hackers están empezando a usar sistemas de IA capaces de identificar vulnerabilidades, desarrollar exploits y comprometer sistemas de forma remota y sin ayuda humana.
Según una nueva investigación del Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG), varios actores maliciosos han comenzado a desplegar marcos de trabajo agénticos. Estos sistemas compuestos por varios agentes de IA pueden trabajar y colaborar entre sí para ejecutar las distintas fases de un ataque. Entre las herramientas descubiertas por el grupo de seguridad se encuentran ARTEX, CAIRN, CyberStrikeAI, PentAGI y HexStrike AI.
Si bien esta no es la primera vez en que Google advierte sobre la ola de ciberataques con IA, los hallazgos del GTIG van más lejos. Los hackeos autónomos se han incrementado en los últimos meses y el ejemplo más evidente fue lo que ocurrió con Hugging Face. Si hacemos memoria, un grupo de agentes de OpenAI escapó de su entorno seguro y vulneró los sistemas de seguridad de la startup, un hecho que se replicó después en una oficina de gobierno en Australia.
¿Qué son los ciberataques automatizados con IA?
Desde hace décadas, un ciberataque siempre requería la participación de una o más personas. Los atacantes deben buscar vulnerabilidades, analizarlas, desarrollar un método de explotación, obtener acceso al sistema y moverse dentro de la infraestructura comprometida. Esto involucra diversas habilidades que van desde la programación hasta la ingeniería social.
Tras la llegada de modelos como Claude Fable y GPT-6 Astra, los hackers han buscado automatizar este proceso. La clave de todo está en los agentes, a los que pueden asignarse tareas específicas para llevar a cabo cada una de las fases del ataque con supervisión mínima o incluso inexistente. A diferencia de un humano, estos agentes de IA no duermen y pueden intentar vulnerar sistemas cientos o miles de veces hasta lograr su cometido.
Google menciona que los nuevos sistemas automatizados son efectivos con vulnerabilidades poco complejas y sistemas conectados a internet que no se han actualizado. Esto último es evidente en los hackeos a los sistemas de refrigeración de supermercados y bancos de sangre en Europa, en donde los atacantes aprovecharon un componente desactualizado que permitió explotar una vulnerabilidad.
Así funcionan los nuevos marcos de ataque que usan los hackers
De acuerdo con el GTIG, algunos de los frameworks que utilizan los hackers operan como una cadena automatizada. Primero analizan actualizaciones de software y comparan versiones antiguas y nuevas del código para detectar las partes que se corrigieron. A partir de ahí, la IA intentará deducir la vulnerabilidad, crear un exploit y ejecutarlo automáticamente contra posibles objetivos.
Los investigadores de Google encontraron evidencia de un sistema denominado exploit_agent, el cual se alojaba en un servidor expuesto y realizaba el proceso sin ayuda humana. El marco integraba varios modelos de IA y podía llevar a cabo análisis de código, generar exploits para comprometer sistemas y ejecutar tareas como instalar webshells o realizar reconocimiento interno.
El informe del GTIG señala que el peligro de estos sistemas radica en que reduce el tiempo de reacción para los equipos de seguridad. Si una vulnerabilidad puede analizarse y explotarse automáticamente apenas se publica un parche, algunas empresas no alcanzarían a actualizar sus sistemas para impedir el hackeo. Google advierte que los ataques con agentes de IA se incrementarán en los próximos meses, pudiendo operar sin participación humana en un futuro no muy lejano.

articles.title: Building AI that can work across the enterprise
articles.text:
Sponsored
Building AI that can work across the enterprise
Moving AI beyond isolated pilots requires a strong data foundation, clear business outcomes, and governance built for enterprise scale.
In partnership withInfosys
For years, enterprises have approached AI as a series of discrete experiments. Now, as AI agents begin to move into the workflows that run the business, that model is starting to look inadequate. Organizations moving from isolated pilots toward AI agents and autonomous workflows are confronting a deeper challenge: rethinking how data, business processes, governance, and people fit together, turning AI from a collection of tools into part of the enterprise operating model.
For Thorsten Leiduck, SVP and global head of SAP Business AI Platform Ecosystem, that shift begins with treating AI as an enterprise platform rather than a collection of disconnected projects. “AI is absolutely dependent on the data foundation,” he says, arguing that companies need a connected, semantically rich layer that reflects their business before they can reliably deploy AI across processes. The stakes also change as AI moves into mission-critical workflows. For some everyday applications, “80% might be good enough,” he says, but in areas such as supply chains or financial close, that level of accuracy is “a very terrible result.”
That foundation also determines which AI applications are worth pursuing. Satinder Pal Singh, associate VP North America for SAP BAIP and SAP AI Strategy at Infosys, frames AI agents as “digital coworkers” and recommends evaluating potential use cases through three lenses: impact, feasibility, and scalability. Companies should identify where an agent can move meaningful business metrics, determine whether their data and talent can support the use case, and then establish whether successful applications can be replicated. “A pilot that can't scale is just an experiment,” he says.
Scaling also brings governance into sharper focus. Clear policies, access controls, monitoring, and oversight are necessary to ensure agents remain trustworthy and aligned with business requirements. “The absence of governance doesn't speed up AI adoption,” Singh says. “It creates a risk backlog” that can ultimately force a more disruptive stop and audit.
Those considerations will become more important as AI agents take on more responsibilities as digital coworkers. Both executives see a future in which agentic systems coordinate work across applications, while customer-specific knowledge graphs and governed data become critical enterprise assets. For Singh, the longer-term opportunity is a shift from AI as a productivity tool to “AI as a decision-making partner,” helping leaders understand what is happening, anticipate what comes next, and determine how to respond.
This episode of Business Lab is produced in partnership with Infosys.
Full Transcript
Megan Tatum: From MIT Technology Review, I'm Megan Tatum, and this is Business Lab, the show that helps business leaders make sense of new technologies coming out of the lab and into the marketplace.
This episode is produced in partnership with Infosys.
Now, the development and democratization of AI tools has the potential to reconfigure how enterprises operate. But, at a time when applications are being scaled up from that initial phase of experimentation, we're still seeing senior leaders grapple with questions around AI's value, risk, and the complexity it adds. It's becoming clear that, unlike past ways of automation, AI requires a real mindset shift. Put simply, the technology can't simply be added into an enterprise's existing toolkit. It requires a complete reconfiguration of what's inside and how it's used.
Two words for you: conscious configuration.
My guests today are Thorsten Leiduck, SVP and global head of SAP Business AI Platform Ecosystem, and Satinder Pal Singh, Associate VP for North America, SAP Business AI Platform and SAP AI Strategy.
Welcome, Thorsten and Satinder.
Thorsten Leiduck: Yeah, thank you for having us. Really a pleasure to be here with our valued partner, Infosys. Looking forward to the conversation.
Satinder Pal Singh: Hi, Megan. Thanks for inviting for the conversation today. Looking forward to the discussion.
Megan: Me too. Thank you both so much for being here. Thorsten, if I could start with you. We know that many senior leaders understand the transformative potential in AI, but they continue to struggle with aspects of its implementation. Many projects remain stuck at a pilot phase, for example. When you speak to clients, what are the biggest obstacles they face when it comes to integrating AI into their tech stack?
Thorsten: Yeah. Megan, as you mentioned, AI is on the agenda of every client conversation today, but many customers are really struggling how to convert that interest into an operationalized model and to unlock the value of AI across the enterprise. And the reason is that too many programs start as isolated POCs on different AI technologies and in an inconsistent fragmented data foundation.
This creates a lot of duplication, inconsistent performance, and no clear path to scale. At the same time, leaders are highly concerned about security, observability, reliability of agents, and some ethical implications when those get deployed. This is also shown in some studies. For example, BCG has launched a report, which shows that 74% of the organizations are stuck in pilot mode with no plan to scale. And in an Anthropic survey, data said that 42% are really struggling with getting access to the data and the quality to really, basically, scale the entire AI capabilities across the organization.
The path forward is really to treat AI not just as a project, but more holistically, as an enterprise platform, one that really consistently connects an unified data layer with the process context of the applications, and then embed AI capabilities governed across the entire life cycle. And to make this real, we in SAP launched the SAP autonomous enterprise framework, so organizations can move from pilots to scaled outcomes.
Megan: Yeah, really, to provide that support. And, Satinder, would you agree, why is it that we're seeing enterprises get a touch of almost AI paralysis here? What's the mindset shift that needs to happen and, perhaps, why is this something organizations need to be thinking about now, as well?
Satinder: Absolutely, Megan. And, if anything, the picture sharpens when you look at, specifically, at agentic AI. Infosys and HFS research surveyed over 500 global 2,000 enterprises and found only 14% have successfully scaled AI. Eighty-six percent remain in early exploration, proof of concept, or fragmented pilot phases. For a technology at the top of every boardroom agenda for two years, that's a striking failure rate. And at the core of that 86% is what I would describe as AI as a department trap.
What happens is that an organization creates an AI team or a center of excellence and walls it off from business. That team builds technically excellent pilots the business doesn't recognize itself in, and you end up with AI solutions searching for problems, rather than the other way around. Mindset shift is clear. Move from treating AI as a technology initiative to treating it as an operating model transformation. AI stops being something IT does for business and starts being something the whole organization does together. Every function, every workflow, embedded from the start.
And what makes this a now problem? Early movers are building an advantage. You cannot close by buying the same platform later. Eighteen months of agent behavior data, calibrated knowledge graph, workforce that has genuinely internalized AI, that is a structural advantage that compounds. Infosys Knowledge Institute AI Maturity Index shows that only 8% of the companies qualify as AI native today, yet they achieve four times the revenue contribution from the AI versus laggards. If you're not building AI today, you're not standing still, you're falling behind at an accelerating rate.
Megan: Right. There's a real polarization there, isn't there, between the front-runners and the laggards, as you say. As we shift from pilot to scaled-up applications, perhaps the first step is evaluating when AI is the right tool. AI has quickly become the default solution within many enterprises. Is there a tendency to use it as a bit of a blunt instrument, nowadays, Thorsten? At the outset, how can senior leaders better evaluate what use cases are worthy of their time and investment, in order to strip out some of that later complexity?
Thorsten: Yeah, I think, Megan, what everybody needs to be aware is adopting and rolling out AI across an organization is as much a change management journey as it's a technology rollout.
Now, when you have this in mind, it makes absolutely sense to put AI in front as many teams as possible, because you want to build formality, and spark ideas, and also people should see the benefit of AI in an organization. When you think about travel assistance, meeting summaries via Copilot, or AI-enabled workflows, increase the productivity, everybody feels this in their real job, in their real daily business. And, obviously, this creates creativity and also provides the organization from a bottom-up perspective with some innovation scale.
Now, however, as majority grows, the conversation, and this is also what we discuss with many of the leaders, and our clients, shifts more to economics and governance. Things like token costs, model performance, security, and accountability become much more relevant. And when you then take the approach and think about AI agents as digital workers that execute specific tasks within a business process, then this means, from an AI perspective, not every task justifies nation.
In some cases, human effort remains more economical or effective. The smart approach, and that's what we really recommend to our clients, is to start with a defined, maybe small set of high-value use cases with defined success metrics upfront. So, for example, such as cycle time reduction, accuracy gains, or cost of per transaction, or top line improvement, and then scale what works. Those use cases can be tied to a line of business domains or industry scenarios.
And then, what we are doing from an SAP perspective, together with Infosys, we really help customers to be successful. We provide, as part of our autonomous suite, the according domain assistance, which really run business processes end-to-end and which deliver find ROIs for single end-to-end business process steps.
And then, last but not least, in many scenarios, I think, which has been very common pattern in particular around large industry AI use cases, is a joint approach, and we do this with partners like Infosys, but also customers around forward deployed engineering, so that you really define very closely the AI-specific use case with the defined outcomes together with the customer, and deliver this as the initial projects. And then, ideally, scale this to other customers and take it back like a best practice, which can be rolled out to other organizations, as well.
Megan: Right. It's been really clear, isn't it, on what you're looking to achieve and what's worth your time, as I say. And what would your advice, Satinder, be here, on refining an AI strategy to ensure organizations can focus on those areas, where AI can deliver the highest returns?
Satinder: Sure, Megan. I think Thorsten's framing of AI agents as digital coworkers forces a precision that agentic AI strategy language often lacks. When you ask which digital coworkers do we need and where do they deliver the most value, the answer starts to become clearer right from the first step. At Infosys, through our Topaz AI-first framework, we push clients through the three lenses simultaneously.
The first one is impact. Where does deploying an agent move the numbers that matter? Revenue, cost, working capital risk. We have built a library of over 300 enterprise use cases across industries, so we never begin from a blank page. The second is feasibility. Given your data foundation platform and talent today, which high-impact use cases can you actually execute? Feasibility determines your sequence. The high-impact use case on a broken data foundation is not viable. When the foundation is right, the results are dramatic. One Infosys engagement cut complex SAP-specification documents from 86 person hours to 6, a 92% reduction.
Third is scalability. Once you have proven a use case with clear ROI metrics, cycle time reduction, accuracy gains, cost per transaction, what's the architecture that lets you replicate it? A pilot that can't scale is just an experiment. My practical advice: treat your AI portfolio like an investment portfolio, quick wins that fund the program, medium-term bets, one or two bold, long-term positions that balance keep stakeholders engaged at every stage and not just in year three.
Megan: That's such a useful framework for people to use there. And given the urgency here, Thorsten, how can organizations approach and manage AI in a more structured, efficient way? To start with, what are the fundamentals that some organizations perhaps miss at the moment? I know Infosys and SAP talk about platform and data, then AI, for example.
Thorsten: Yeah, Megan, I think the fundamental, which many organizations are overlooking, is data and the data is a foundation for AI. Because, at the end, without the data structures and the ability to access the right information at the right time and basically bringing different kind of structured, unstructured data sources together, in a meaningful governed and semantic way, there will be no successful AI. AI is absolutely dependent on the data foundation. And I think this is often overlooked, and that's why I said when you start POCs in different organization, or different parts of the organization with different technologies, it's very hard to establish an end-to-end consistent model on the data side, as well as on the AI side.
One of the key goals companies need to achieve is, and that's why we really talk about you need to start with data first and the platform first, is to establish and semantically-rich connected data layer that really reflects your business, so that the agents are really grounded in the company's reality and not just in generic patterns.
And then, I think, the second element that's important is accuracy. In the enterprise context, it really matters. For example, what might pass in a consumer setting, where you have 80% accuracy, and even in a workforce environment where you build PowerPoints or you do email drafts, which you then, with a human in the loop, optimize, 80% might be good enough. But, when you really think about mission-critical or business-critical processes in the supply chain, or closing the books, 80% is a very terrible result.
The stakes are much too high and you need to have much more accuracy. And that's why it's important that you have business process logic and industry context embedded into the data and the models which build the foundation, if you will, the backbone for every AI and, obviously, for the data in the ERP and the line of business system.
And then, last but not least, the other critical element, and you see this obviously in the news with all the agents going rogue, are governance, compliance, and security. Very critical in an enterprise context. You need to set clear policies, access controls. You need to have monitoring ability, capabilities, to really make sure that what then the AI agenda capabilities or agents are executing is fully aligned, is trustworthy, and scalable.
Megan: Right. Which is quite a lot of things for organizations to be thinking about. Satinder, how do SAP and Infosys work with organizations to streamline some of these processes, perhaps and make unlocking AI's capability a little bit easier?
Satinder: Megan, I think at the onset, I want to acknowledge that, at Infosys, we are uniquely positioned for our relationship with SAP, because we are a customer to SAP, as well as one of their key global suppliers. And the way SAP and Infosys work together is designed around the architecture Thorsten described, that defines a coherent partnership.
SAP brings the platform foundation, business data cloud for the semantically-rich enterprise, generative AI hub for governed LLMXs, and agent hub for the lifecycle governance, enterprise grade from day one. Infosys brings implementation depth, industry context, and use case accelerators. Through Infosys Topaz, we have built over 50 pre-configured AI use cases on Business AI Platform, production-ready configurations deployable without building from scratch. We co-develop use cases within SAP's industry AI engagement with clear customer-specific FTE metrics. That shared accountability for results is different from a typical implementation engagement.
In practice, one global S/4HANA transformation program used AI-assisted delivery tooling to complete over 480 RICEF objects in five months, a pace conventional delivery would not sustain. In another account, an AI-powered platform auto-classifies over 120,000 SAP incidents monthly, with zero analyst charge. The combined effect time to value drops from 12 to 18 months, down to four to six months.
What I would emphasize is change management damage. Technology is increasingly deployable, and Thorsten also spoke about it earlier. What's hard is helping an organization internalize that their agents are digital coworkers, not automations. That mindset shift is 70% of the implementation challenge that platform cannot solve alone, and Infosys and SAP run joint adoption programs addressing both the dimensions in parallel.
Megan: Fantastic. Some great real-world examples there, as well. Thorsten, can you tell us a little bit more about SAP's Business AI Platform, or BAIP, in particular? How does that work and what sets it apart from other platforms?
Thorsten: Yeah, so SAP Business AI Platform, if you will, is the foundation for our SAP autonomous enterprise framework, which really consists of a unified user interface and is enabled as an agentic orchestration layer, which we call Joule. And you have the autonomous read with all the applications, and then you have the Business AI Platform, which powers the other capabilities, and is closely connected, and is basically organized around three core pillars.
The first one is, really, what we call build. What it means is you provide the respective intent-based development tools, so that customer, or partners like Infosys, can really create and development agents, applications and workflows using best-in-class tools and model to extend SAP's own assistant, or customizing those, or really building own agents as needed.
Complimenting what Satinder said, it's really critical for us that we have a thriving ecosystem, who is innovative, and is building innovations, and is complementing our own SAP agentic portfolio. We are focusing on specific areas on the domains, from a line of business industry perspective, where we deliver assistance as part of our organization, but to really then customize them from a last mile execution from really complimenting areas which we don't cover and really driving the innovation towards the customer, our ecosystem is the multiplier force and Infosys is really playing a leading role here with us, together.
Second is, and we talked about this, is what we call the contextualize and reason pillar, which is literally as a foundation data, we address with SAP Data Cloud and comprehensive data strategy, where we establish an end-to-end data fabric across partner provider platforms, like Databricks, Snowflakes, where we promote and zero copy access to data. For the customer, this is very important. So, we allow, basically, promote to customers if you have made investments in any of those platforms, reserve those investments and just leverage BDC to connect without moving data around your, for example, Databricks, Snowflake environment to BDC.
With this approach, we establish and harmonize semantic data layer, which can then be used for any AI scenario across the entire enterprise, combining different data sources without any disruption. The other key element that's part of this is the generative AI hub. We have aggregated more than 50 models, language models, including some of our own models into it, in single cockpit, so that customers can access and choose any of those 50 models as part of the generative-AI hub, which is part of the platform.
And then, as a key differentiator, we really moved a lot of business semantic and context into the knowledge graph, which then helps to navigate the agents and acts like a nerve, or navigation system, in the company to really provide business-relevant, customer-specific information for the decision making and the execution to any agentic execution framework.
And then, we talked about governance, last but not least. This is the third pillar, which is very critical and this is built-in. So, we have, as the third pillar, the SAP agent hub, which is kind of a command center for enterprise-wide AI and agent governments. You can govern SAP agents, you can also govern non-SAP agents, as long as they're integrating to SAP via A2A. So, the team can really manage, on the customer side, an end-to-end life cycle of agents and features from hire to retire.
Megan: Fantastic. That's a really comprehensive overview. Thank you ever so much. And, Satinder, can you share any examples, perhaps, of how organizations have used SAP Business AI Platform in practice, to improve the ways they've used AI? Perhaps, what was the challenge they faced, what did the process look like, and what benefits did they unlock?
Satinder: Sure, Megan. I think Thorsten just explained how powerful a platform Business AI Platform is. And this is decades in working. We also have been using that, and I'll share two examples from live Infosys engagements, both showing what BIP's three pillar look like in production.
The first is global diversified manufacturer with a large SAP estate. The challenge was month-end close, 80-plus SAP transaction codes, period closed teams working nights and weekends, L1 support absorbing over 300 incidents per month, from close cycle alone. On Business AI Platform, we deployed Topaz Fabric, Infosys' agentic orchestration platform, with a master agent coordinating five specialist child agents, WBS accrual, revenue recognition, intercompany settlement, master data reconciliation, and SOX audit trail generation. Agents run autonomously, escalating to humans only for genuine exceptions. The result, entire L1.5 support tier eliminated, over 300 monthly incidents handled with zero human touch. The close team redeployed from reactive firefighting to forward-looking financial analysis. Annual savings pipeline exceed $1 million.
The second is North American Utility in a S/4HANA transformation. Their challenge was development velocity, complex SAP functional specification documents routinely requiring 80 or more personnel each, a bottleneck throttling the entire program. Using AI native development environment on Business AI Platform with a Claude-powered retrieval system, we reduced those specifications from 86 hours to six, a 92% reduction, validated across 51 SAP task types at 95% accuracy. The architecture is now being replicated across accounts. In both cases, the pattern matches what Thorsten described, governed data foundation, SAP business process context, full agent observability through SAP Agent Hub. That's the autonomous enterprise running as daily operations, not as a concept.
Megan: And those are some really compelling concrete results I think would be really helpful for people to hear. Also, of course, responsible AI, or clear governance frameworks, are a critical component of AI integration, too. And we know that tools like LLMs are rarely developed with compliance built-in. I wonder what's your advice there, Thorsten, on how to ensure that property governance is embedded into an ERP?
Thorsten: Yeah, I mean, Megan, you're absolutely right. Governance compliance and security are really mission-critical to delivering relevant, reliable, and trustworthy AI at enterprise scale. I mean, it's important to understand how in public LLM service really works. Many of those services are trained on internet scale data, which means they're public models. Depending on the provider's policies and setting, they may retain easier inputs for model improvement, which means if a company provides data back to the model, this company data is in the public domain. For example, pipeline information or forecast information, which is becoming very, very critical, because this exposes your organization, really, at significant risk.
So, while then LLMs X are really great, imposes in large volumes of text and other unstructured data, they are less effective with structured tables like in EOP systems, or in business applications, in general, and then they're lacking, usually, the nuance of business process and logic and context. That's why a robust governance framework is essential. We talked about the generative AI, how we aggregate those models in a single cockpit.
And then, the other element, which we previously touched based on and Satinder mentioned, is always a part of the custom examples is SAP agent hub or, in general, when we talk about the capabilities just in AI lifecycle governance, which really includes agent registry, LMN registries, MCP registry, so a single source of tool for every AI artifact that you can manage identity and access control, so that agents are really variable and that you can really provide the right permissions, in terms of which agents allowed to use access which data, and then agent observability, agent minus, and then also map the agent skills to the organization is very critical.
As all of part of this, as I mentioned before, we provide those capabilities really fully embedded into the Business AI Platform to really provide this governance framework out of the box and fully embedded into everything what you do at SAP.
Megan: Which is so important, because when organizations are experimenting with, or scaling up multiple AI programs and tools, in some cases, it adds real complexity. I wonder, Satinder, would you add anything on how organizations can have that robust layer of governance built in, even with a pretty complex tech stack?
Satinder: We, at Infosys, have our Infosys Knowledge Institute, they run this annual magazine generative AI radar, and it found that 48% of companies had deployed generative AI without a formal governance policy. Nearly half of the enterprises were running AI with no documented framework or oversight, accountability, or compliance. That's the gap that Thorsten is describing, and it has to be closed proactively before an incident forces a reactive stop or audit far more disruptive than building a governance upfront.
What Thorsten has just described in SAP Agent Hub is exactly the platform layer that makes enterprise-wide governance possible and is worth making the overall architecture explicit, because without it, governance is theoretical.
The framework I use with clients has three layers that have to work together. The first one is policy, a clear organization-wide AI use policy, what agents can and cannot do autonomously, how data can be used for AI training, disclosure obligations, and accountability for outcomes. This needs legal, compliance, technology teams together with a board level sponsorship. Without that foundation, every deployment becomes an ad hoc governance debate. Second layer is platform. This is where SAP Business AI Platform and, specifically, SAP Agent Hub becomes enterprise control tower.
The capabilities Thorsten described, agent LLM, MCP registry as a single source of truth, verifiable agent identities with scoped access trails, agent observability, agent mining for drift detection, these aren't just governance features. They give leaders real-time visibility across a complex multi-agent landscape. You can see what's running, what it's consuming, and whether it's performing as expected. That's what turns a complex tech stack from a governance liability to a governance asset.
And the last layer is process, the recurring governance rituals, quarterly AI risk reviews, bias audit cycles, model performance reviews against the business KPIs, these structured conversations that keep humans accountable for the agent behavior over time. What organizations consistently discover is that this three-layer structure actually accelerates the deployment. Every new use case has a clear path through approval and a governance architecture to plug into. The absence of governance doesn't speed up AI adoption. It creates a risk backlog that eventually forces a stop and audit movement far more disruptive than building the governance muscle.
Megan: That's such an interesting point. Thank you so much for that. And we've covered a lot of ground, so to close with a future forward look, we've spoken today about the proliferation of AI tools that are now on the market, many designed to transform enterprise-level operations. I wonder, what do you see on the horizon, Thorsten, that you think could be a real game-changer?
Thorsten: I think what we will see very soon, and we talked about this briefly, is that we are heading into a period of sustained, rapid AI adoption, where assistance and agents will operate as digital coworkers. They will be embedded in our organizations like employees today, and they will be embedded into processes as people perform tasks, as we speak.
Now, as this happens, the Center of Gravity will shift more and more from a monolithic application layer to an agentic value layer that orchestrates work across systems and across different landscapes, which need to be orchestrated very well. I think what we also will see, and this will be likely, at least in terms of scale, I believe a game-changer, is that the delivery will become industrialized. When you think about agent factories and church services that really design, test, and govern agents at scale, or you can say agentic frameworks at scale, and I think we will see an evolution of commercial models, which are today more consumption-based towards really value and outcome-based agreements, which are then tied to clear business KPIs.
On the technology front, I think there's still so much movement on the LLM landscape, new architectures, training methods. I think we'll bring down, significantly, the total cost of ownership, while also control and the viability will be improved. I think there's an awareness which the recent examples in the market show, and then I think the innovation will be playable.
And I think the big question is, from that perspective, which role is China going to play in a global context, and also how those models are really embedded. Last but not least, most importantly, even I think ontology and customer-specific knowledge graphs will become first-class assets, and I think this will be the key differentiation in the future, because they will lead in code process, semantics, policies, what Satinder talked about, and data relationships. And they are the blueprint for secure high-performing enterprise agent architectures in the future.
Megan: Which is, of course, what we're aiming for. And how about you, Satinder? What would you flag as a really exciting area of development?
Satinder: Sure, Megan. I think what excites me most is the shift from AI as productivity tool to AI as a decision-making partner. The most important evolution Thorsten's architecture makes possible. For decades, enterprise systems have told us what happened. The next generation helps leader understand what is happening now, what will happen next, what actions to take.
The scenario I keep coming back to, a CFO starting a day with an agent that continuously analyzes signals across finance, supply chain, procurement, workforce data, proactively surfacing the three issues that are most likely to impact the quarter, with recommended actions, financial impact quantified. That's not a dashboard. That's a fundamentally different decision model. Through Infosys Topaz, we are helping clients move forward an AI-first enterprise, one that can sense, learn, decide, adapt continuously across the different domains.
What also excites me is the pace of AI evolution. In past technology waves, constraints were stable. You identify a limitation and architect around it for years. AI is different. Use cases that appear constrained at program start are often resolved before go live. SAP's prior model transformed structured data reasoning once a clear LLM gap. Decision intelligence is arriving faster than most organization are planning for.
The winning strategy is to design for where AI will be 18 months from now, flexible architecture, trusted data foundation, governance that absorbs innovation as it arrives. Organizations that do this compound value at each new generation of capabilities becomes available.
So, the next frontier isn't that AI can do more work. It's that AI that understands your business well enough to help you make better decision. And that's where the greatest opportunity for SAP, Infosys, and our clients lies, convergence of systems of record with systems of intelligence.
Megan: Fantastic. Certainly, lots on the horizon to look forward to. Thank you both so much for joining us today.
That was Thorsten Leiduck, SVP and global head of SAP Business AI Platform Ecosystem and Satinder Pal Singh, Associate VP for North America at SAP Business AI Platform and SAP AI Strategy, whom I spoke with from Brighton in England.
That's it for this episode of Business Lab. I'm your host, Megan Tatum. I'm a contributing editor and host for Insights, the custom publishing division of MIT Technology Review. We were founded in 1899 at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, and you can find us in print, on the web, and at events each year around the world. For more information about us and the show, please check out our website, thetechnologyreview.com.
This show is available wherever you get your podcasts. And if you enjoyed this episode, we hope you'll take a moment to rate and review us. Business Lab is a production of MIT Technology Review, and this episode was produced by Giro Studios. Thank you so much for listening. Goodbye.

articles.title: Microsoft: Wie ein alter, unentdeckter Fehler die Dienste weltweit ausfallen ließ
articles.text:
Microsoft 365: Wie ein unentdeckter Programmfehler für den weltweiten Ausfall sorgte
Ein seit Juli unentdeckt im System schlummernder Programmfehler hat in der vergangenen Woche den weltweiten Ausfall von Microsoft-Diensten wie Outlook und Teams ausgelöst. Wie der US-Softwarekonzern mitteilte, führten drei Faktoren zusammen zu einer Kettenreaktion: Auf dem Höhepunkt der Störung reagierten am Abend des 12. Novembers mehr als 80 Prozent der zuständigen Rechner nicht mehr.
Auslöser war laut Microsoft eine Software-Änderung an einer zentralen digitalen Eingangstür für den Datenverkehr von Microsoft 365, die bereits im Juli aufgespielt worden war. Über mehr als drei Monate lief das System damit unauffällig. Bei den vorherigen Tests im Labor war der Fehler nicht aufgefallen, weil dort vorwiegend ältere Technik genutzt wurde – das Problem trat jedoch vor allem auf neueren, leistungsstärkeren Servern auf.
Dominoeffekt in der Cloud
Zum Ausbruch kam der Fehler am vergangenen Donnerstag ausgerechnet zur Hauptnutzungszeit in den USA durch zwei zusätzliche Belastungen: Kurz zuvor war das Videokonferenz-Programm Teams planmäßig auf dieselbe Haupt-Infrastruktur umgeschaltet worden, was den Datenverkehr erhöhte. Gleichzeitig waren wegen eines anderen technischen Problems bereits knapp 14 Prozent der Server-Kapazitäten vorübergehend nicht einsatzbereit.
Als daraufhin erste Server unter der hohen Last ausfielen, leitete Microsofts automatische Steuerung die Nutzeranfragen auf die verbliebenen Rechner um – und löste damit denselben Fehler auch dort aus. Binnen weniger als zwei Stunden erfasste dieser Dominoeffekt fast das gesamte System. Weil zudem digitale Schutzbarrieren zwischen den einzelnen Weltregionen versagten, breitete sich der Ausfall rund um den Globus aus.
Warum die Reparatur so lange dauerte
Während Dienste wie Teams oder der Online-Speicher OneDrive relativ schnell auf Ausweichwege umgeleitet werden konnten, war dies beim stark belasteten E-Mail-System Outlook nicht möglich. Die Behebung zog sich bis Samstag hin, weil frisch neu gestartete Server sofort wieder unter der Flut wartender Anfragen zusammenbrachen. Microsoft musste schließlich ein spezielles Reparatur-Update entwickeln und die Server schrittweise in Gruppen neu starten.
Weltweite Folgen in Behörden, Kliniken und Unternehmen
Die Auswirkungen der Störung waren in mehr als 70 Ländern spürbar: Zahlreiche Unternehmen, Gerichte, Schulen und Behörden waren stundenlang von ihren E-Mails, Kalendern und Online-Dokumenten abgeschnitten – auch beim Bundesamt für Sicherheit in der Informationstechnik gingen entsprechende Meldungen ein. Besonders gravierend traf es vielerorts das Gesundheitswesen: In Großbritannien und Kanada etwa mussten Krankenhäuser und Arztpraxen teils auf Papierakten ausweichen und einzelne Termine verschieben.
In vielen Büros griffen Beschäftigte notgedrungen auf private Messenger wie Whatsapp oder das Telefon zurück; Risiko-Analysten schätzen den weltweiten wirtschaftlichen Produktivitätsausfall auf mehrere Milliarden Dollar.
Kritik an digitaler Abhängigkeit
Nach dem gravierenden Microsoft-Ausfall wurde erneut scharfe Kritik an der starken Abhängigkeit vieler Unternehmen und Verwaltungen von einem einzelnen US-Konzern laut. IT-Fachleute, Datenschützer und europäische Wettbewerber warnten vor dem sogenannten Klumpenrisiko, wenn die gesamte Bürokommunikation an einer einzigen Cloud-Plattform hängt.
Schleswig-Holsteins Digitalminister und Staatskanzleichef Dirk Schrödter (CDU) forderte im Deutschlandfunk angesichts der „tiefen Abhängigkeit“ mehr digitale Widerstandsfähigkeit: IT-Systeme der öffentlichen Hand müssten wie kritische Infrastruktur behandelt und auf Anwendungen mit offenem Programmiercode (Open Source) umgestellt werden – wie dies in der Landesverwaltung in Kiel bereits erfolgt sei.

articles.title: Developer creates a 100% valid ZIP file that doubles as a BIOS-bootable operating system — hiding BIOS boot flags inside uncompressed files and turning file headers into CPU instructions
articles.text:
Developer creates a 100% valid ZIP file that doubles as a BIOS-bootable operating system — hiding BIOS boot flags inside uncompressed files and turning file headers into CPU instructions
The original definition of "hacking" was making hardware and software do something it wasn't supposed to.
Hacking stories these days mostly involve someone using an army of AI agents to find vulnerabilities in networks and software that were carefully hidden in plain sight. Today, for a change, we have a story about hacking in its original meaning — twisting computing artifacts into purposes not in their design spec. David Oberhollenzer, aka Goliath, a greybeard in spirit if not in shade, crafted a 100% valid ZIP file that's simultaneously an archive, BIOS-bootable, and a Multiboot-compatible OS image.
You can unpack the ZIP file just like any other, boot it using Linux's GRUB, QEMU, or any other Multiboot-compatible loader (even if imaged to different media), or alternatively, perform the finest party trick: image-write it to a floppy and boot from it directly from BIOS on any compatible PC, without modification.
Much like me, that sequence of words may be triggering a head-tilt reminiscent of a confused puppy, so we'll explain. The first thing you need to know is that unlike most file types, the metadata (in this case, file directory) of a ZIP is actually at the end of the archive. Up to that point, the data is comprised of every compressed file in sequence.
The file packs all have a predictable structure: "PK" followed by bytes 03 04, metadata (including name), some extra/comment fields, and then the file's contents. Notably, any file can be stored uncompressed, and Goliath made use of that for the very first file, called ZIPHEAD.COM — remember, this is the start of the ZIP archive.
Goliath said that it was "easy" to make the ZIP file a valid Multiboot system image. A valid image only needs to contain bytes 0x1BADB002 in the first 8 KiB, followed by some flags and a checksum. It was trivial to place that datum in ZIPHEAD's data, along with the location of where the bootloader lies.
Grub or QEMU don't care about anything else in the image, as once they have the initialization information, from that point it's the bootloader's problem. The actual bootloader, predictably, is in ZIPHEAD's uncompressed data, and the image will happily boot directly, or, say, from a floppy.
Making the same exact archive bootable via a standard PC BIOS took a little more work and some clever shenanigans. Making a disk bootable is simple enough: the BIOS reads the first exact 512 bytes of the disk's contents, and if they end with bytes 0x55AA, then it's bootable, and the BIOS starts executing whatever code is the first byte.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
Placing 0x55AA precisely at position 510 of the ZIP, already in ZIPHEAD's contents, is once again simple, and won't corrupt the Multiboot image, as if you'll recall, the Multiboot spec is flexible with data locations. But you may wonder: once the BIOS runs code in sequence starting from the ZIP's first byte, then ZIPHEAD's header ("PK" + 0x0304, plus all metadata) surely is garbage for practical purposes, and not proper code? Well, yes, but actually no.
The first four bytes represent CPU instructions that don't write anything to memory, so they're harmless, other than a push-to-stack. The next few belong to ZIPHEAD's metadata, and Goliath massaged those values to represent instructions that would either be innocuous or perform operations he could use, namely using the modification time bytes as instructions to jump further down the data.
Sounds simple, but the actual process of choosing bytes that represent (1) non-crashy CPU instructions, (2) useful code for setting up the boot process, and (3) still represent a valid file header in a ZIP archive is far trickier than the above. Do go and check out the full blog post if you want all the details.
Download the Tom's Hardware app for up-to-the-minute updates on iOS and Android. Also follow Tom's Hardware on Google News, or add us as a preferred source, to get our latest news, analysis, & reviews in your feeds.
Bruno Ferreira is a contributing writer for Tom's Hardware. He has decades of experience with PC hardware and assorted sundries, alongside a career as a developer. He's obsessed with detail and has a tendency to ramble on the topics he loves. When not doing that, he's usually playing games, or at live music shows and festivals.

articles.title: Novo Nordisk modernizes manufacturing process documents with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Novo Nordisk modernizes manufacturing process documents with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
Novo Nordisk (Novo) is one of the world’s leading global pharmaceutical companies, manufacturing medicines for chronic diseases such as diabetes and obesity, and delivering them to patients across many countries. Behind every product lies a manufacturing network that adheres to strict quality requirements. Every quality-relevant process step must be described, controlled, and validated through formal documentation. Keeping this documentation current and accurate is a core responsibility of the Manufacturing Technology team within the Tablet area, a responsibility that spans a large and diverse portfolio of controlled documents, including standard operating procedures, work instructions, forms, and training materials, across the global organization.
Managing this portfolio presents significant challenges. Document updates are frequent, driven by regulatory changes, process improvements, equipment modifications, and audit findings. Each update demands careful review, structured approval workflows, and timely communication to all affected stakeholders. With thousands of active documents spread across multiple divisions, departments, and product programs, tracking which documents are due for revision, pending approval, or require immediate attention becomes increasingly complex. Much of this oversight currently relies on manual processes and fragmented tracking methods such as spreadsheets or disconnected systems. These methods are time-consuming, error-prone, and difficult to scale. The result is a risk of outdated documentation remaining in circulation, delayed updates, and critical gaps in compliance visibility.
Beyond document management, there is a deeper knowledge challenge. Valuable manufacturing knowledge is distributed across many controlled documents, versions, sites, and product programs. Finding the right answer at the right time often depends on experienced individuals knowing where to look. This dependency on tribal knowledge creates bottlenecks that slow down decision-making and, ultimately, impact how quickly life-saving medicines reach patients.
To address these challenges, the Manufacturing Technology team within the Tablet area has embarked on developing an intelligent support system powered by agentic AI, deployed on AWS. The goal is to reduce lead times, improve documentation visibility, and make critical manufacturing knowledge more accessible, ultimately helping the organization move faster and serve more patients around the world. This post dives deep into the architecture and the key design decisions made to meet the high standards of accuracy and traceability required in a regulated pharmaceutical environment. The solution helped subject-matter experts (SMEs) complete work that used to take hours or days in minutes.
We also describe an AI process-intelligence assistant that can answer complex process questions with grounded, cited responses. The solution is built around a GraphRAG architecture, combining a knowledge graph with hybrid search to retrieve the most relevant and contextually accurate information. AI agents, built on a managed agent framework, coordinate the retrieval and response process end-to-end. A guided mode helps clarify ambiguous questions before a search is initiated, helping make responses more precise and defensible.
The challenge
Teams supporting manufacturing repeatedly answer variations of the same question: what does the process require, for this site, this product, and this equipment? Answering well requires four things at once:
- The right document out of a large corpus.
- The right version and lifecycle state (approved and effective, not draft or obsolete).
- The right scope (it actually applies to the site, product generation, and equipment).
- The relationships (which documents reference which, and what a change would impact).
Conventional keyword search returns documents, not answers, with no concept of scope, version, or relationship. A plain vector-based Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) system improves recall on natural-language questions but still struggles with exact identifiers (document numbers, equipment codes), with multi-hop relationship questions, and (most importantly for a regulated domain) with identifying when relevant content is not available. The team needed a system that treats structure and relationships as first-class, stays grounded in approved sources, and clarifies instead of guessing.
Solution overview
The assistant is built on a GraphRAG architecture: a knowledge graph in Amazon Neptune captures structure and relationships, and a hybrid search index in Amazon OpenSearch Serverless provides semantic and exact-match recall over document contents. The two stores are deliberately kept separate and bridged at query time rather than combined into a single engine. This is a common production GraphRAG pattern.
The reasoning layer runs on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale with any framework or model. AgentCore was chosen for its managed agent runtime with built-in session isolation, native tool orchestration, and integrated AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) and observability. This removes undifferentiated infrastructure work so the team could focus on the domain logic. The agent runtimes are built with the Strands Agents SDK and powered by Anthropic Claude models on Amazon Bedrock. Documents are processed through an ingestion pipeline that uses Amazon Bedrock Data Automation for multimodal parsing, orchestrated with AWS Step Functions and AWS Lambda. The stack is defined as infrastructure as code with the AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK).
At a high level, a question flows through the system like this:
- The query agent receives the question and, in guided mode, determines whether the scope is clear enough to answer well.
- If it is ambiguous, the agent asks a short, graph-grounded clarifying question (for example, which site or product generation applies) before searching.
- After scope is clear, hybrid search retrieves candidate passages, the graph expands from those results to add structure and relationships, and a reranking step sharpens precision.
- The agent composes an answer grounded in and cited to approved source documents, and is explicit when content is not available.
Architecture
A two-layer taxonomy: Structure plus domain detail
The graph is organized around two complementary layers, which is what lets the assistant take into account where a document sits and what it is about.
High-level taxonomy: The process tree. The organization’s official process framework is modeled as a hierarchy of process nodes (roughly three levels, parent to child). Each controlled document is attached to the lowest applicable process level, so each onboarded document has a known place. This lets the assistant scope a question to a process area before retrieving anything, and automatically categorize newly ingested documents.
Low-level taxonomy: Domain entities. SMEs define the entities that make an answer correct or incorrect in manufacturing: sites, product generations, equipment, process steps, and similar attributes. These are modeled as first-class graph nodes linked to the documents that describe them, using a small set of unified relationship types rather than an ever-growing list of edge names.
Modeling both layers is what distinguishes a genuine GraphRAG system from two databases side by side. The document number on an OpenSearch passage is also a node in the graph, so a search hit is an immediate entry point into the graph’s structure with no fuzzy re-matching required. This chunk-to-graph bridge is a key design choice in the retrieval path.
Why a fixed, curated taxonomy (and why this is best practice)
Early GraphRAG work favored open-ended extraction, letting a language model discover entities with no fixed schema. This approach is powerful for open-ended sensemaking over sprawling text, but it is noisy, hard to maintain, and difficult to audit. Over the past couple of years, the consensus has shifted toward ontology-guided extraction using a predefined, domain-specific schema to guide the model, which improves accuracy and reliability for specialized corpora.
For regulated pharmaceutical manufacturing this is not a compromise, but the right default. The domain already has a real ontology, curated by experts, and a fixed schema with a human-in-the-loop promotion process for new entities supports the auditability the team needed in a regulated pharmaceutical environment. The design aligns with where much of the field has moved since early open-schema approaches, while making design decisions easier to explain to quality and audit stakeholders.
Retrieval: Hybrid search, graph expansion, and reranking
Each store covers the other’s blind spot:
- OpenSearch provides recall – Hybrid search combines dense vector similarity (Amazon Titan Text Embeddings) with lexical BM25 matching, fused with reciprocal rank fusion. Vector search captures meaning. And lexical matching catches the exact tokens that matter here: document numbers, equipment codes, and multilingual terminology.
- Neptune provides structure – Given the entities and documents search surfaced, the graph answers “what is connected, how, and how far”: neighboring documents, references, position in the hierarchy, and impact of a change, which is exactly what vector-only retrieval cannot do.
A common pattern is vector finds the seeds, the graph expands from them, and the reverse for relationship-first questions. A reranking stage (a cross-encoder through Amazon Bedrock Rerank) sits after fusion: it reads the question and each candidate passage together and reorders them, adding a precision pass on top of the cheaper recall stage before anything reaches the model.
Guided mode: Clarify before you retrieve
A distinctive part of the assistant is how it handles ambiguity. A question like “which samples are taken on the granulator?” has several correct answers depending on product generation, site, equipment, and batch size. Answering immediately risks a confident, wrong, out-of-scope response, which is the worst outcome in a regulated setting.
Guided mode inverts the usual RAG order: instead of retrieving first, the agent narrows scope through clarification first, then searches. This follows recent research on clarifying ambiguous questions before retrieval and on using a knowledge graph to supply the clarification options rather than letting the model invent them. It uses two classes of scope:
- A small, near-universal set of attributes (such as site and product generation) is asked directly and consistently for process-specific questions.
- Everything deeper: which equipment, which batch size, and attributes added over time. This is all derived from the graph at query time. A scope-resolution step matches the user’s term against real graph nodes, filters by what is already known, and, if more than one candidate remains, offers the attribute that genuinely distinguishes them, using only values that exist in the graph.
This keeps clarification options grounded in real data (designed to help reduce the risk of hallucinated options) and it scales: when experts add a new distinguishing attribute to the taxonomy, the assistant surfaces it automatically, without requiring changes to prompts or code.
Grounding and trust in a regulated environment
Accuracy here is defined narrowly and enforced deliberately:
- Explicit indexed state – A document can exist in the graph with metadata, relationships, and place in the hierarchy before its contents are searchable. A deterministic flag tracks whether a document’s content is indexed, so the assistant can distinguish between “I have this document’s contents” and “I only have its metadata,” rather than inferring availability from empty search results.
- Approved sources by default – Answers rely on approved and effective documents and the latest applicable version, unless the user explicitly asks for drafts or historical revisions.
- Anti-hallucination rules – Clarification options and cited claims are designed to come from actual tool results rather than the model’s own knowledge.
- Stated limitations – When retrieved material is missing or ambiguous, the assistant says so rather than filling the gap and flags when SME, quality, or regulatory review is needed.
An automated evaluation harness checks responses against these criteria: relevant-source selection, valid document status, latest applicable version, scope compliance, citation accuracy, and faithful preservation of requirement strength (must, should, or may) so behavior can be measured as the system evolves.
An intelligent search engine over a vault of millions of documents
The wider vault this solution sits on top of holds on the order of four million documents. At that scale, the problem is not a shortage of information but the near-impossibility of finding the exactly right, in-scope, current answer by hand. Traditional enterprise search returns long lists ranked by keyword overlap and leaves the hard work to the person asking. This includes deciding which result applies, which version is effective, and how documents relate.
This solution turns the vault into an intelligent, answer-first search engine, and the two-layer taxonomy is what makes that tractable at scale:
- The graph is the full map and the index is the searchable subset. Each onboarded document across all registered domains is placed in the graph with its metadata, relationships, and hierarchy position. This means the assistant can reason about where a document sits and how it connects, even for the millions whose contents are not yet indexed. Full-text contents are indexed for onboarded domains, added incrementally, and the assistant is explicit about which is which.
- Scope narrows the search space before retrieval. Because guided mode resolves site, product generation, process area, and equipment up front, a question is filtered to the small slice of the vault that can answer it. The system searches the few documents in scope, not millions. This helps keep answers precise as the corpus grows.
- Hybrid search plus graph expansion goes beyond keyword ranking, surfacing related documents, references, and hierarchy a ranked list would never reveal, and returning a grounded, cited answer (not ten blue links) while saying when content is unavailable.
The design is intended to scale with the vault rather than degrade as it grows: the larger and more interconnected the documentation, the more value the graph and scoping add.
Outcomes
Depending on the type of task an SME is doing (searching for an answer, updating a document, or adapting one for a new context), work that used to take hours or days is reduced to minutes. Beyond raw time saved, the solution changes what is practical to do at all:
- Navigate the group’s process landscape – Users can move across all three levels of the process taxonomy, spanning roughly four million documents and their many subprocesses through a single assistant that acts as both a search engine and a guide over the documentation, the process, and the organizational maps.
- Consolidate structured and unstructured data – Metadata, process hierarchy, and document contents are unified into one searchable knowledge graph, so information that used to live in separate systems can be queried together.
- Understand relationships between entities and documents – The graph helps users ask how documents, processes, equipment, sites, and products connect, including multi-hop questions that manual search cannot answer.
- Trace and validate references end to end – The solution can map a document’s full chain of references and flag where a document points at out-of-date or superseded material, surfacing integrity issues across the corpus rather than one document at a time.
- Extend to further AI and agentic capabilities – The same grounded foundation opens the door to capabilities like document generation, revision with impact analysis, and other agentic workflows reusing the same graph, retrieval, and guardrails rather than starting from scratch.
Just as important in a regulated setting, the assistant’s design to clarify scope and flag missing or ambiguous content helps reduce the risk of confident, out-of-scope answers, where the real cost of a mistake lies.
A collaborative delivery model
The Novo Manufacturing Technology team within the Tablet area collaborated with AWS to build this solution, with subject-matter experts and data and AI engineers working closely throughout. The taxonomy that makes the assistant accurate comes directly from the group’s domain experts. The retrieval and agent architecture was designed and iterated with AWS.
Building a prototype was key to getting the solution to go live. Rather than debating capabilities in the abstract, the team put a working system in front of subject-matter experts early. They tested it against real questions and used what they learned to sharpen the taxonomy, the retrieval path, and the guided-mode behavior. The prototype turned an ambitious idea into something people could try, critique, and trust. It also de-risked the architecture decisions before any broader rollout.
Conclusion
By combining a curated knowledge graph, hybrid search, and a clarify-before-retrieve agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, the Novo Manufacturing Technology team within the Tablet area built a process-intelligence assistant that is fast where speed helps and grounded where accuracy matters. The design applies current GraphRAG patterns to regulated manufacturing: ontology-guided extraction, a bridged two-store retrieval path, graph-grounded disambiguation, and reranking. This turns a large documentation landscape into grounded, cited answers with room to extend to new domains.
To get started building your own agentic AI solution, explore Amazon Bedrock AgentCore for managed agent runtime, tool orchestration, and observability at scale. The agent runtimes in this post were built with the Strands Agents SDK, an open source, framework agnostic toolkit you can use with your own retrieval stack. For GraphRAG reference architectures using Amazon Neptune and Amazon OpenSearch Serverless, visit the AWS Architecture Center.

articles.title: Bharat Semi raises $24M to develop AI-enabled sensors
articles.text:
Bharat Semi raises $24M to develop AI-enabled sensors
Bharat Semi has raised seed funding to develop programmable AI-powered sensors, targeting the growing demand for intelligent, energy-efficient hardware for robotics, vehicles and other machines.
India- and US-based semiconductor company Bharat Semi has raised $24 million in seed funding to develop programmable smart sensors for Physical AI, where machines use artificial intelligence to perceive and act in the real world.
The round was led by Info Edge, the internet group behind Naukri; South Park Commons, a founder community and early-stage investor; and IndusBridge Ventures, which backs deeptech sector.
Micromax, an electronics group; Valour Capital, a deeptech investor; New York-based venture syndicate Gaingels and angel investors Mukul Agarwal and Kartik Iyer also participated.
The funding will accelerate product development, expand the US engineering team and support efforts to secure global customers.
Founded in 2021, Bharat Semi operates across New Delhi, Bengaluru and San Francisco. It is initially targeting consumer electronics and surveillance, with potential longer-term applications in robotics, vehicles, drones, aerospace and defence.
Its sensors combine data capture and AI processing in a single component. A camera-equipped device could interpret an image at the point of capture, rather than send raw data to a separate processor or cloud server. This is known as edge inference, where AI processes information close to its source, potentially reducing delays and energy consumption.
Bharat Semi said its technology could reduce data movement between components by up to 99% and lower system costs by up to ten times compared with conventional multi-chip systems.
“Soon, growth in the sensor market will be driven by capturing data for machines,” co-founder Vinayak Dalmia said, arguing that sensing, processing and software must be designed together.
Co-founder Vrinda Kapoor described the shift as “intelligence at the right place”, saying it offered India an opportunity to build globally relevant technology businesses.
The technical team also includes Boyd Fowler, former chief technology officer of image-sensor maker OmniVision.
The investment comes as AI moves beyond data centres and into physical devices and machines. Bharat Semi has reportedly secured design wins with US defence company General Atomics and India's Kaynes Semicon.
Other Indian deeptech ventures have attracted funding this year. Bengaluru-based chipmaker C2i Semiconductors raised $15 million in February, while sensor and navigation technology developer Yaanendriya secured Rs 15 crore in July. Physical AI startup Flo Mobility raised $2.5 million in May to expand its construction robotics business.
Policy support is also expanding. Approved in July 2026 with an outlay of Rs 1,27,500 crore, India’s Semicon 2.0 programme covers chip design, manufacturing equipment and materials, fabrication, packaging, research and talent development. In November, the government reported that five of 12 approved semiconductor projects had commenced commercial production.

articles.title: Après l'iPhone Duo, Apple aurait un nouveau cheval de bataille qui va rythmer son année 2027
articles.text:
Apple préparerait l’annonce de ses premières lunettes connectées pour sa WWDC de juin 2027, le grand-messe des développeurs qui a souvent été le théâtre d’annonces de nouveaux produits (le dernier en date étant le Vision Pro en 2023). Les lorgnettes se limiteraient à des caméras, des micros, des haut-parleurs et Siri, sans affichage de réalité augmentée, pour affronter les Ray-Ban de Meta sur leur propre terrain. Avec une commercialisation prévue pour la fin de l’année 2027, les lunettes dépendraient d’un iPhone récent dans la poche pour à peu près tout.
Siri aux commandes, l’iPhone à la manœuvre
Les prototypes, connus en interne sous le nom de code N50, seraient légèrement plus fins que les Ray-Ban Meta de deuxième génération, avec des verres ovales et des caméras affleurantes. Les unités de test embarqueraient une version allégée de visionOS, animée par une puce dérivée de celles de l’Apple Watch. Un chargeur magnétique de la taille d’un Tic Tac, fixé à la branche gauche, permettrait de les recharger sans les quitter.
Les montures n’embarqueraient aucune application. Les développeurs ouvriraient leurs services existants à Siri via App Intents, directement depuis l’iPhone apparié, et l’assistant exécuterait les demandes à la voix. Réserver une table, commander un VTC ou un café : les scénarios à l’étude s’appuieraient sur des applications déjà en place comme Uber, OpenTable ou Starbucks.
Il faudra en contrepartie un iPhone récent apparié en permanence, et les possesseurs d’un smartphone Android resteront à la porte. Les lunettes conserveraient un filet d’autonomie en Wi-Fi, de quoi poursuivre l’écoute quand le téléphone s’éloigne, sans jamais devenir un appareil indépendant.
Un calendrier suspendu à Siri qui questionne, surtout en Europe
La partie matérielle serait pratiquement figée, au terme de travaux entamés au début de la décennie. Le logiciel accuse en revanche un retard susceptible de faire glisser la date de sortie. Le nouveau Siri dopé à l’IA, qui porte l’essentiel du produit, n’a ouvert sa préversion aux développeurs que le 3 novembre, dans les betas d’iOS 27.3. Ses capacités s’étendront aux applications d’Apple en décembre, puis aux applications tierces au printemps 2027.
Le projet a déjà glissé une fois : visé pour fin 2026, le dévoilement aurait été repoussé cet été à la WWDC 2027, le temps de trancher la place de la caméra et le discours sur la vie privée. En face, plus de sept millions de Ray-Ban connectées se sont écoulées l’an dernier, vendues autour de 329 euros. L’agenda 2027 d’Apple s’annonce chargé, entre les 20 ans de l’iPhone et la suite de l’iPhone Duo lancé cet automne. Des AirPods équipés de caméras resteraient d’ailleurs programmés pour fin 2027, avec des fonctions qui recoupent en partie celles des lunettes.
Apple vient par ailleurs d’ouvrir les ventes de son écran connecté HomeView dans sept pays, en excluant l’Union européenne. « HomeView n’est pas disponible à la vente dans l’Union européenne, car Siri AI est actuellement indisponible sur iOS dans l’UE », justifie la page d’annonce. Les lunettes reposeraient sur la même mécanique, un appareil jumelé à un iPhone dont Siri AI pilote les applications. Ce Siri nouvelle génération manque justement à l’appel sur les iPhone européens depuis son lancement en septembre, Apple et la Commission se renvoyant la responsabilité au nom du DMA, sans calendrier de déblocage.
