articles.title: La caída global de Microsoft se debió a un fallo introducido por la compañía hace meses y que tumbó el 80% de sus servidores
articles.text:
La caída global de Microsoft se debió a un fallo introducido por la compañía hace meses y que tumbó el 80% de sus servidores
El incidente, que se prolongó durante más de 18 horas, afectó a millones de usuarios de algunas de las aplicaciones más populares de la tecnológica, como Outlook, Teams, Copilot, Word, Excel o Power Point
Los fallos que experimentaron el pasado jueves y viernes varios servicios de Microsoft se originaron en una sobrecarga de los servidores de la compañía. Esta sobrecarga, a su vez, vino provocada por la implementación defectuosa de una serie de actualizaciones que venía desarrollando la compañía desde hace meses. Así lo asegura la tecnológica en un comunicado difundido esta mañana, en el que también vuelve a pedir disculpas a sus clientes por las molestias causadas.
La citada actualización se empezó a ejecutar en julio y no se observaron problemas. “Durante más de tres meses, el cambio se implementó en todo el mundo sin impacto”, ha dicho esta mañana en la red X Charles Lamanna, vicepresidente ejecutivo de Copilot, Agentes y Plataforma en Microsoft. Pero unas quince horas antes de la interrupción, Teams registró un error en el uso de los servidores, lo que “aumentó la carga” y cambió los patrones de tráfico.
More details on the root cause can be found in the Microsoft 365 Admin center, and an abridged version can be found below. 
We are deeply sorry for the impact to all our customers and recognize the impact that this has on their normal business & operations. 
The incident on… https://t.co/p8mUHxDe67
— Charles Lamanna (@clamanna) November 16, 2026
Lamanna explica también que, cuando esto sucedió, casi el 14% de la capacidad de los servidores “estaba fuera de servicio debido a un problema no relacionado del día anterior”. Eso hizo que la sobrecarga tuviera un impacto más fuerte de lo normal en el sistema, que colapsó al no poder absorber un aumento súbito del tráfico de datos. “El tráfico redirigido aumentó la probabilidad de que el mismo problema ocurriera en los puntos finales restantes. Esto causó una falla en cascada de servidor a servidor”, explica Lamanna. Fue como un efecto dominó: en menos de dos horas, el problema se había extendido por todo el mundo, afectando en su punto álgido a más del 80% de los servidores que gestiona la compañía en todon el planeta.
Una vez caídos los sistemas, restaurarlos no fue sencillo. “La recuperación tomó más tiempo de lo habitual porque, a medida que los servidores regresaban al servicio, eran inmediatamente abrumados por el tráfico en espera y se volvían no responsivos nuevamente”, indica Lamanna. “Dado que el defecto principal de código era un error latente de varios meses anteriores, nuestros mecanismos normales de reversión y pruebas no pudieron revertir rápidamente el cambio”, añade.
Cuando identificaron el fallo, los ingenieros de Microsoft desarrollaron una actualización “que devolvió la ruta de código al estado previamente conocido como bueno”. Para poder aplicarla y que no volviera a colapsar todo, lo que hicieron fue ir aplicando los cambios en grupos de servidores fuera de servicio, que después se reiniciaron y pusieron en marcha. “Este proceso se aplicó cuidadosamente a grandes cantidades de infraestructura a la vez (por ejemplo, más del 50% de una región)”, indica Lamanna.
Microsoft no dio oficialmente por zanjado el problema hasta el sábado por la mañana, casi un día y medio después de iniciarse la crisis. El propio Lamanna ha dicho en X que se conocerán más detalles sobre el incidente “durante esta semana”, cuando se complete la revisión post-incidente.
Hacia las 18.30 hora peninsular española del pasado jueves día 12 de noviembre, miles de usuarios empezaron a notar que algunos servicios de Microsoft funcionaban mal. El fallo se prolongó durante más de 18 horas, afectando a millones de usuarios de al menos 70 países. En España no provocó problemas significativos en la Administración, que pudo seguir prestando sus servicios sin problemas. Otros países, como Japón, Australia o Malasia, sí tuvieron que interrumpir servicios críticos.
El servicio afectado de Microsoft 365, que incluye programas como Word, Excel o PowerPoint, cuenta con más de 450 millones de usuarios corporativos y 95 millones de clientes particulares. El programa Teams, de videoconferencias y otras funcionalidades para entornos laborales, cuenta con más de 320 millones de usuarios. La aplicación de correo electrónico Outlook también fue uno de los afectados.
Todos estos programas son desde hace años herramientas de trabajo fundamentales en muchas oficinas de todo el mundo. De ahí que la incidencia de la caída de los sistemas fuera especialemente severo en el sector privado.

articles.title: Mercedes voudrait rendre sa Classe C électrique beaucoup plus abordable
articles.text:
Mercedes est une marque particulièrement active sur le marché des véhicules électriques. Après une première génération de modèles sous la gamme EQ, la marque à l’étoile a revu sa stratégie en déclinant les noms de modèles thermiques pour des voitures électriques. La nouvelle Classe C électrique adopte cette stratégie et devrait bientôt voir sa gamme se compléter de trois nouvelles versions, dont deux plus abordables.
Deux motorisations plus abordables prochainement
La gamme de la Mercedes Classe C électrique est actuellement composée de la Classe C 400 4Matic, version de lancement avec 489 chevaux venant de deux moteurs offrant une transmission intégrale. La batterie est une NMC de 94 kWh permettant une autonomie de 762 km en cycle WLTP.
Quelques semaines plus tard, la Mercedes Classe C 300 4Matic a rejoint le catalogue, toujours bimoteur avec quatre roues motrices, mais cette fois avec une puissance totale de 421 chevaux. Cette motorisation est associée à la batterie de 85 kWh pour 682 km d’autonomie.
Mercedes devrait ajouter à la gamme prochainement les Classe C 200 et 250, se passant de la transmission intégrale pour devenir des motorisations à propulsion et à moteur unique. Ainsi, la Mercedes Classe C électrique deviendrait plus accessible.
La Classe C électrique bientôt plus accessible ?
La Mercedes Classe C 200 devrait utiliser une batterie LFP de 64 kWh. L’autonomie devrait approcher les 600 km selon nos estimations, en s’appuyant sur l’efficience de la Classe C, le seul moteur arrière et la boîte à deux rapports pour moteur électrique de Mercedes. L’utilisation d’une batterie LFP et du moteur unique permettra de réduire drastiquement le prix de la Mercedes Classe C électrique. Une batterie LFP est 40 % moins coûteuse à produire par kWh qu’une NMC. Actuellement, la Mercedes Classe C débute au tarif de 62 999 euros. La Classe C 200 pourrait être plus proche de 50 000 euros.
De son côté, la Mercedes Classe C 250 devrait aussi utiliser un seul moteur. La puissance n’est pas encore connue à ce stade, avec une batterie de 85 kWh. L’autonomie totale devrait approcher les 700 km WLTP, une version idéale pour les grands rouleurs souhaitant maîtriser leur budget.
La recharge des Mercedes Classe C 200 et 250 devrait toujours être rapide en raison de la plateforme 800 volts, mais l’énergie récupérée en 10 minutes sera moins importante que sur les 300 et 400. En effet, plus la batterie est petite, moins le pic de charge peut être important.
Enfin, Mercedes devrait aussi lancer une Mercedes Classe C électrique plus dynamique, plus sportive. Une déclinaison AMG est au programme en 2027. Évidemment, cette version sera plus coûteuse que celles actuellement au catalogue, mais aussi plus exclusive. La Mercedes Classe C électrique devrait bientôt avoir cinq versions à son catalogue, une gamme fournie pour répondre à plusieurs usages.

articles.title: New NoisyTCP vulnerability lets attackers crash Linux servers
articles.text:
An 11-year-old Linux kernel vulnerability, dubbed NoisyTCP, affects almost all Linux distributions and lets attackers crash systems running Nginx, Apache, and SSH servers with default configurations.
According to Hyunwoo Kim, the security researcher who discovered it, this pre-authenticated remote corruption flaw (tracked as CVE-2026-99288) stems from a NULL pointer dereference weakness in the Linux kernel's TCP networking subsystem.
Unauthenticated attackers can trigger it remotely via maliciously crafted TCP packets that exploit the timing between SYN cookie handling and socket hashing to crash the kernel and operating system on targeted servers.
However, while CVE-2026-99288 exploits cause a kernel panic and take down the host, they don't allow threat actors to alter data or gain arbitrary code execution.
Kim added that although attackers can exploit this vulnerability against any Linux system that receives TCP packets directly and runs Nginx, Apache, or an SSH server, "the race window is narrow, so triggering it against a quiet bare-metal server can take a long time."
"Due to a race condition during lockless socket lookups, recycled socket memory can be accessed before it is properly initialized and hashed. A remote attacker could exploit this issue by generating network traffic that drives socket reuse, triggering a NULL pointer dereference and kernel crash that results in a Denial of Service (DoS)," the Red Hat security team explained.
"To trigger this vulnerability, a stale ehash lookup and the freeing and reallocation of an existing request socket must proceed concurrently in different RX contexts. Packet processing has to be spread out by using the difference in receive hash between IPv4 fragments and regular TCP packets, so it can be triggered against servers that have two or more RX queues, or where RPS distributes packets across multiple CPUs," the researcher said.
While a CVE-2026-99288 patch is already available and a fix was already merged into the mainline Linux kernel two weeks ago, the researcher advised those who can't apply it or upgrade immediately to disable SYN cookies (which will unfortunately lower protection against SYN flood attacks) and serialize to a single RX queue to block the race required for successful exploitation.
In May, Kim also disclosed Dirty Frag, a Linux local privilege escalation flaw that chains RxRPC (CVE-2026-43500) and xfrm-ESP (CVE-2026-43284) page-cache write flaws to gain root access on major distributions, including Ubuntu, Red Hat Enterprise Linux, CentOS Stream, and Fedora.
More recently, in July, he also disclosed Januscape, a 16-year-old Linux kernel vulnerability that enables attackers to escape a virtual machine and run arbitrary code on the host.

articles.title: A hidden limit of space and time could unlock electronics 100,000 times faster
articles.text:
A hidden limit of space and time could unlock electronics 100,000 times faster
- Date:
- November 7, 2026
- Source:
- University of Regensburg
- Summary:
- Scientists have discovered a surprising quantum limit that prevents electrons from being tracked with unlimited precision in both space and time. The breakthrough could pave the way for manipulating chemical reactions and developing electronics hundreds of thousands of times faster than today's technology.
- Share:
Quantum physics places fundamental limits on what scientists can know about the behavior of particles. Werner Heisenberg's famous uncertainty principle states that certain properties, such as a particle's position and momentum, cannot both be measured with unlimited precision. This restriction is not caused by flaws in scientific instruments. It is built into the laws of nature.
But position and time are different. Heisenberg's uncertainty principle does not impose the same restriction on these quantities. Now, researchers have experimentally demonstrated another fundamental limitation: an electron's location and its behavior over time cannot both be determined with arbitrary precision. Known as the "space-time limit," this newly observed relationship could have major implications for the future of quantum technology and ultrafast electronics.
The discovery comes from an international collaboration involving research groups at the Regensburg Center for Ultrafast Nanoscopy (RUN), led by Profs. Jascha Repp, Rupert Huber, Franz Giessibl, and Klaus Richter, along with a team at the Max Planck Institute in Hamburg led by Angel Rubio.
Watching Electrons Move at Incredible Speeds
Understanding how matter behaves at the smallest scales is essential for developing the next generation of technology. Advances in clean energy, quantum computing, and powerful electronics for artificial intelligence all depend on knowing how chemical reactions unfold, how light interacts with materials, and how electrons travel through electronic devices.
However, even the sharpest microscopic photographs cannot reveal the full picture. Scientists also need to observe how these processes change over time, effectively creating slow-motion movies of events occurring at the atomic scale.
At RUN, researchers are developing ultrafast microscopes capable of recording the movements of electrons, atoms, and molecules with extraordinary precision in both space and time. About ten years ago, scientists in Regensburg used ultrafast scanning tunneling microscopy to resolve the movement of a single molecule across space and time for the first time.
Tracking individual electrons presents an even greater challenge. At these microscopic distances, electrons can move roughly a thousand times faster than atoms and molecules, with important changes taking place over just attoseconds.
To appreciate how extreme these scales are, consider that an atom is approximately ten million times smaller than a millimeter. An attosecond is one-billionth of a billionth of a second. The difference between an attosecond and a second is comparable to the difference between one second and the entire age of the universe.
Making these measurements is especially difficult because electrons do not behave like ordinary objects. Their motion follows the unusual laws of quantum mechanics rather than the familiar rules of classical physics.
Ultrafast Lasers Reveal Quantum Tunneling
To observe electron behavior at these extraordinary speeds, the researchers built a new laser system that provides much finer time resolution than earlier experiments. The system allows them to control and study the quantum motion of individual electrons directly.
In the experiments, carefully timed laser pulses drive electrons from an extremely sharp metal tip toward a silver surface. The distance they travel is only a few atomic diameters.
The researchers detect this movement by measuring the resulting electrical current. To determine exactly when the electrons move, they use two pulses of light separated by a precisely controlled interval.
Simon Maier, the lead author of the paper, explains: "By varying the time interval between the two laser pulses, we can directly observe how the electrons respond."
This approach revealed clear evidence of electron motion occurring on attosecond timescales. It showed that the laser pulses could transfer electrons within these incredibly brief intervals while allowing scientists to observe the process as it happened.
What makes the result particularly remarkable is how the electrons travel. Instead of moving like conventional particles, they behave as quantum waves. This allows them to pass through an energy barrier separating the metal tip from the silver surface, even though classical physics predicts they should not have enough energy to cross it.
This phenomenon, known as quantum tunneling, is somewhat like an object passing through a solid wall without breaking or damaging it.
"Our measurement can be understood as a high-speed camera for the electron wave packets, since you can see at what point in time the tunneling process takes place," explains Katharina Glöckl, a doctoral student and co-author of the publication.
A Surprising 500-Attosecond Delay
To understand the measurements more deeply, researchers working with Prof. Angel Rubio performed sophisticated quantum simulations of the electrons' behavior near the "space-time limit."
Their calculations closely reproduced the experimental findings and uncovered another remarkable detail. The electrons did not respond to the light field instantaneously. Instead, their motion lagged behind it by approximately 500 attoseconds.
At such extreme scales, several fundamental features of quantum physics become important simultaneously.
For example, the researchers found that the laser pulses could not be described entirely by treating light as a wave or entirely by treating it as individual particles called photons. Their effects displayed characteristics of both descriptions. This combination was essential for exploring electron behavior so close to the "space-time limit."
The team also discovered that controlling electron motion over extremely short intervals changes how the electrons are distributed in space. Quantum mechanics describes these electrons using wave packets, which represent how their wave properties extend across different locations.
The relationship between the timing of electron motion and the spatial extent of these wave packets revealed the central limitation behind the discovery.
A Hidden Tradeoff Between Space and Time
Raffael Spachtholz, another co-author of the study, explains: "The more precisely we want to pin down the electron's position in time, the more energy we need to provide. And as a result, the electron wave packet spreads out more spatially."
In other words, improving the precision of an electron's timing comes with a cost. The more tightly researchers define when its motion occurs, the more broadly its quantum wave packet spreads through space.
To examine this relationship experimentally, the team placed a single atom on the surface to confine the electron wave packets to an extremely small region immediately before the laser pulses arrived.
This setup allowed the scientists to directly measure the connection between the electrons' spatial distribution and the timing of their motion.
Importantly, even when the electrons received substantial energy from the laser pulses, their wave packets remained sufficiently localized for microscopy with atomic spatial resolution and attosecond time resolution.
The findings provide experimental insight into a fundamental space-time constraint that scientists had previously only suspected. They also make it possible to systematically investigate how changes in electron motion over time affect the spatial structure of quantum wave functions.
Could Quantum Electronics Become Hundreds of Thousands of Times Faster?
Beyond revealing a new aspect of quantum behavior, the discovery could open the door to technologies that operate on timescales far beyond the capabilities of today's electronics.
One especially promising possibility involves using precisely controlled electron wave packets to influence chemical reactions.
Transferring a single electron to a molecule represents the smallest possible transfer of electric charge. But when that electron is concentrated within an exceptionally small region of space and time, the resulting local peak current density can reach as much as 1 trillion amperes per square centimeter.
Such extreme conditions could give scientists new ways to control chemical bonds and observe how molecules change during reactions.
"In the future, we want to use such wave packets to specifically trigger chemical reactions and observe, on the relevant length and time scales, how chemical bonds can be broken or altered," explains Prof. Jascha Repp enthusiastically.
The implications could extend well beyond chemistry. Greater control over electron motion may eventually help engineers develop electronic devices and quantum information systems that operate at speeds approaching the fundamental limits of electron dynamics.
"In the long term, the insights gained could also contribute to operating electronics and quantum information processing at the intrinsic speed limit of electron motion itself -- hundreds of thousands of times faster than the currently dominant CMOS technology," adds Prof. Rupert Huber.
That possibility remains a long term technological goal rather than an achievement demonstrated in the current experiments. Nevertheless, the findings provide a new foundation for exploring how electrons can be manipulated at the smallest distances and shortest timescales.
For Repp and Huber, the results suggest that the range of potential applications is extraordinarily broad. They believe that future advances in controlling electrons at the space-time limit may ultimately depend more on human creativity than on the constraints imposed by nature.
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of Regensburg. Original written by Karoline Stürmer. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:

articles.title: Avec le Magic 9 Pro Max, Honor veut se mettre les vidéastes dans la poche
articles.text:
Avec le Magic 9 Pro Max, Honor veut se mettre les vidéastes dans la poche
Alors que la concurrence facture ses flagships au prix fort, Honor prépare un smartphone censé défier les références du marché, avec la promesse d'une expérience vidéo hors norme et un prix encore inconnu que l'on espère plus doux.
Déjà lancé en Chine, le Honor Magic 9 Pro Max s'apprête à débarquer en France début 2027. Son objectif ? Se faire une place face aux iPhone 18 Pro Max et Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra, sans se contenter d’empiler les superlatifs.
Honor Magic 8 Pro
Un air d’iPhone, une finition qui fait mouche
Avec son cadre et son dos en aluminium d’un seul tenant, ses discrètes antennes et son écran presque sans bordures, le rapprochement avec Apple saute aux yeux. Mais le résultat est soigné. En main, ses 233 g se ressentent, malgré une épaisseur de 8,59 mm, mais le poids est bien réparti.
L’afficheur Oled de 6,8 pouces adapte sa fluidité jusqu’à 120 Hz et promet 10 000 cd/m² de luminosité — uniquement sur de petites zones HDR évidemment. Le verre NanoCrystal Shield et les indices IP68/69/69K rassurent côté résistance. Sous le capot se cache le nouveau processeur Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 de Qualcomm, 12 Go de RAM, 256 ou 512 Go de stockage et une batterie de 7030 mAh, compatible avec la charge filaire à 100 W et jusqu’à 80 W sans-fil.
Son ambition ? Remplacer aussi votre caméra
Au dos, deux capteurs de 200 mégapixels s’occupent des clichés classiques et du zoom optique x3,5. Ils profitent d’une stabilisation CIPA 8.0 pour limiter les tremblements. Un ultra grand-angle de 50 Mpx et une caméra selfie de 55 Mpx complètent l’ensemble, avec reconnaissance faciale 3D à l’avant.
Mais c’est surtout sur le terrain de la vidéo que le constructeur entend se démarquer. Outre sa puce maison H1, Honor collabore avec ARRI, spécialiste des caméras utilisées au cinéma, pour proposer la 4K à 60 images par seconde (i/s) et le format LogC3, idéal pour retravailler les couleurs après tournage. Ajoutez le codec professionnel APV, un micro directionnel et des accessoires en option, dont une cage SmallRig et des convertisseurs 200 et 500 mm : les vidéastes sont clairement visés.
L'appareil tourne sous Android 17 via MagicOS 11 et dispose d'un bouton dédié à l’IA Gemini, un déclencheur photo et une interopérabilité avec l’univers Apple (AirPods, iCloud, transferts façon AirDrop). Le mode portrait Studio Harcourt reste au programme, tout comme les sept ans de support logiciel promis. Une belle promesse sur le papier, qu'il faudra évidemment confirmer lors d'un test complet. Quant au prix français, il reste encore mystérieux, mais on peut toujours espérer que l'ancienne filiale de Huawei joue la carte de l'agressivité tarifaire pour bousculer ses rivaux.

articles.title: With Qwen4-Max, Alibaba puts the open source jacket back on the hanger
articles.text:
With Qwen4-Max, Alibaba puts the open source jacket back on the hanger
Alibaba has officially unveiled Qwen4-Max, the first model in its next-generation Qwen4 family, with a focus on complex professional tasks and autonomous AI agents.
The Chinese tech titan teased the new Qwen4 family last week, taking to X to promise improvements in coding, reasoning and real-world knowledge, while initially making Qwen4-Max available in preview through several of its products.
Now, the company has formally detailed the model’s capabilities, pitching it as an always-available “AI teammate” capable of tackling everything from software development to scientific research.
However, Alibaba appears to be keeping its most powerful model proprietary, despite the open-weight releases that have helped establish Qwen as a major force in the AI realm.
Under the hood of Qwen4-Max
In a blog post published on Monday, Alibaba revealed that Qwen4-Max is built on a new mixture-of-experts (MoE) architecture comprising 2.4 trillion backbone parameters, with 71 billion activated for each token. It also includes another 328 billion parameters dedicated to a technique called “N-gram Embedding,” which helps the model process patterns in text more efficiently.
The model supports images as well as text, and comes with a one-million-token context window, allowing it to process large amounts of information in a single interaction.
Qwen4-Max is available through Alibaba’s QwenCloud platform, with API pricing starting at $1.50 per million input tokens and $4.50 per million output tokens. It can also be accessed through QwenWork, Qoder and QwenStudio, while Vercel has added Qwen4-Max to its AI Gateway, allowing developers to use the model through coding tools such as Claude Code, Codex and Cursor.
Alibaba claims the new architecture delivers substantial improvements over its predecessor, Qwen3.8-Max, particularly when performing complex tasks involving multiple tools and extended periods of autonomous execution.
On Work360, an internal benchmark developed to assess professional tasks across hundreds of specialised fields, Qwen4-Max scored 52.69 compared with 47.74 for Qwen3.8-Max. Alibaba also claims the newer model uses between 24% and 35% fewer tokens on that benchmark, depending on the reasoning effort selected.
The company reports even greater token savings on Terminal-Bench 4.0, a test of AI agents’ ability to carry out tasks in a terminal environment, where token usage fell by nearly half compared with Qwen3.8-Max.
Alibaba says those improvements, combined with lower API prices, reduced the average cost of completing a task in its Work360 evaluation by 62%, from $4.43 to $1.67.
Of course, those are Alibaba’s own results. Independent testing by Artificial Analysis offers another perspective, awarding Qwen4-Max a score of 43 on its Intelligence Index, placing it 38th among 81 models in the comparison. That puts it slightly above the median score of 41 for models in its price category, but lagging leading competitors such as Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5.2 (65), Google’s Gemini 4 Carbon (60) and OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra (57).
Artificial Analysis also calculated an average cost of $3.27 per task across its evaluations, while noting that Qwen4-Max generated 127 million output tokens, considerably more than the median of 78.6 million among comparable models.
Alibaba pulls its weight(s)
The proprietary nature of Qwen4-Max is particularly notable given Alibaba’s recent history. When the company introduced Qwen3.8-Max in August, it made an unusual commitment: for the first time, it would release the weights underlying one of its flagship Max models, allowing developers to download and run a version on their own infrastructure.
That marked a departure from Alibaba’s previous approach, with Qwen3.6-Max-Preview and Qwen3.7-Max both remaining proprietary. In hindsight, Qwen3.8-Max looks more like an exception than the beginning of a broader shift towards open weights.
The announcement followed Alibaba’s efforts to demonstrate that its models could compete with leading proprietary systems from the likes of Anthropic. As The New Stack reported at the time, the company had already been making increasingly ambitious performance claims for its Qwen family.
Qwen3.8-Max also arrived with a demonstration of autonomous software development, in which an AI coding agent worked on a project over 16 days, producing hundreds of commits and more than 100 pull requests.
However, the open-weight promise initially attracted scepticism when Alibaba announced the model release before making the files available.
“That is not a technical footnote; that is the API business model wearing an open source jacket for the launch photo.”
In reactions gathered by The New Stack, independent AI consultant Jeff Brokaw questioned the significance of advertising downloadable weights that developers could not yet obtain. He also drew parallels with Chinese AI startup Moonshot AI’s Kimi K3, which had similarly been promoted as an open-weight model ahead of the files becoming available.
“That is not a technical footnote; that is the API business model wearing an open source jacket for the launch photo,” Brokaw said at the time.
Alibaba, for its part, did eventually follow through on August 12, publishing the underlying Qwen3.8-2.4T-A95B weights — but there were notable strings attached. The downloadable model came under a custom licence, versus the more permissive Apache 2.0 terms Alibaba had used for various earlier Qwen releases. Businesses operating “model-as-a-service” or AI work assistant products, with combined revenue exceeding $50 million over any consecutive 12-month period, were required to obtain a separate commercial licence, although internal use was exempt under specified conditions.
The licence also required certain commercial products with more than 100 million monthly active users, or $20 million in monthly revenue, to prominently display the model’s name.
For comparison, Xiaomi released its MiMo-V2.6 models under the permissive MIT licence in September, alongside technical documentation and a public record of its reinforcement-learning training costs. The company also committed to publishing thousands of training environments and associated tools, giving outside developers a potentially deeper view of how the models were developed.
Alibaba was willing to wear the “open source jacket,” while keeping some of its most valuable capabilities behind a commercial API. And with Qwen4-Max, the company appears to be putting that jacket back on the hanger.
The released Qwen3.8-Max weights also represented a more limited version of the hosted product, lacking some of the capabilities available through Alibaba’s API, including native image input.
In other words, Alibaba was willing to wear the “open source jacket,” while keeping some of its most valuable capabilities behind a commercial API. And with Qwen4-Max, the company appears to be putting that jacket back on the hanger completely — no downloadable weights have been announced for the new model, and Alibaba has made no commitment to publish them.
On X and the accompanying blog post, Alibaba did say that the “open weights of smaller Qwen4 models will be released,” although it has yet to specify which models or when they will become available. But for Qwen4-Max itself, developers remain reliant on Alibaba’s hosted services or third-party API providers.

articles.text:
This article is brought to you by VicOne.
VicOne identified an initial set of 28 zero-day findings in less than two days using AI-assisted research across software and tools supporting the Physical AI ecosystem. These include projects developed or maintained by Google, NVIDIA, and Meta, among others.
Based on initial validation, all 28 findings are classified as zero-day vulnerabilities. The count may change following vendor and vulnerability-authority review, and some findings do not yet have CVE tracking numbers.
Many of these tools help teams train, simulate, test, and operate robots. Weaknesses in them could influence the models teams build, the test results they trust, and the instructions sent to robots.
These findings create two demands for robotics teams: responding as AI helps uncover weaknesses faster, and assessing how each one could affect robot safety and operations.
What AI changes about vulnerability discovery
Vulnerability discovery involves examining code, tracing how systems communicate, and testing whether a suspected weakness can actually be exploited. AI can accelerate parts of this work, helping researchers analyze more software in less time. Attackers could use similar capabilities.
When the weakness is a zero-day — previously unknown and without an available fix — faster discovery can leave teams with little time to respond. While that exposure does not necessarily mean an attack has occurred, teams still need to determine whether they use the affected software and what an attacker could access or change.
Where the findings sit across the robot lifecycle
VicOne’s findings span three stages of the robotics lifecycle: development and training, simulation and validation, and deployment and runtime. Weaknesses at each stage could affect what a robot learns, how it is tested, and how it is controlled.
Figure 1. In this research set, 75% of findings involved development, training, simulation, or validation tools, highlighting risks that can arise before a robot is deployed.VicOne
The following scenarios show how a compromised component could influence the robot at each stage.
- Development and training: Hidden changes can reach the finished robot
A team downloads a pretrained model to adapt for its robot. Loading a malicious file could give an attacker access to the training system, allowing changes to training data or the model itself. A manipulated model could behave normally during routine testing but respond incorrectly to a particular object, scene, or command after deployment. The risk can enter through a tool the team trusts, before anyone attacks the robot directly.
- Simulation and validation: A passing test could give false confidence
Importing a compromised scene or robot model could give an attacker access to the simulation environment. With sufficient control, the attacker could alter simulated sensor readings, physical conditions, or test results. A robot could then appear to pass tests that should have exposed unsafe behavior, leading the team to approve it for real-world use on the basis of misleading evidence.
- Deployment and runtime: Operators could lose visibility or control
An attacker could exploit weaknesses to change files that influence motion planning or send malicious map data that crashes the operator’s monitoring display. Compromising a remote-operation computer could also put the instructions sent to the robot at risk. Depending on the system and its safeguards, these weaknesses could alter robot movement or leave operators unable to see what is happening and respond promptly.
These are potential consequences and not demonstrated outcomes for every finding. Actual effects depend on the attacker’s access, the system’s design, and whether other safeguards prevent the changes from reaching physical behavior.
In a separate demonstration, VicOne researchers provide a concrete example of a weakness affecting a protective function. The researchers exploited a vulnerability to prevent a robot’s remote-stop command from working. The case shows why teams need to test whether safeguards remain effective when the software supporting them is compromised.
Video 1. VicOne researchers demonstrate a vulnerability that prevents a robot’s remote-stop command from working. VicOne
A published patch still needs to be proven safe
AI can shorten the search for weaknesses, but a robotics team still needs to determine whether a fix is safe to deploy. Even after a software maintainer releases a patch, teams must identify affected systems, check compatibility, and verify that the update preserves intended behavior.
An earlier successful test remains useful evidence. However, a newly discovered weakness may reveal conditions that test never examined.
Three questions can help teams respond:
- Where do we use the affected software? Include training computers, simulation environments, and deployed robots.
- What could the weakness change? Assess whether it could affect models, test results, operator visibility, or robot behavior.
- How do we verify protection? Confirm that the fix addresses the weakness and that the updated system still operates as intended.
When immediate updating is impractical, teams may need temporary safeguards, such as restricting access to an affected service, while a validated fix is prepared.
From discovery to safer deployment
As details from the 28 findings become available through coordinated disclosure, the next step is for robotics manufacturers is to connect each finding to its potential effect on development, deployment, and robot behavior.
That work also requires understanding how threats could affect robot behavior and how to protect systems already in operation. VicOne Radeis helps teams identify potential zero-day vulnerabilities, assess AI model and system security, and use simulation to evaluate how these risks could affect robot behavior before deployment. VicOne Rthena supports threat detection and responses within approved policies during operation.
Figure 2. Cybersecurity strengthens robot safety evidence throughout the lifecycle. VicOne helps teams test safety limits against manipulation before deployment and monitor the conditions behind safe behavior in operation.VicOne
Faster vulnerability discovery matters when teams can turn findings into action: identify what needs attention, verify that safeguards still hold, and confirm that a fix does not introduce new risks. That is how cybersecurity strengthens robot safety as systems continue to change.
For a deeper look how cybersecurity can affect robot safety, download our white paper, “Why Robot Safety Depends on Cybersecurity: Protecting the Information That Safety Decisions Rely On.”
VicOne is a Physical AI cybersecurity company protecting vehicles and robots from cyber threats that can alter behavior and compromise safety. Headquartered in Tokyo, Japan, the company provides automotive and robotics organizations with software and services to identify cyber risks early, assess their potential safety impact, and protect systems in operation, helping maintain safe, reliable behavior across real-world deployments.

articles.title: NVIDIA CUDA-X Libraries Give Agents the Tools to Accelerate Scientific Discovery
articles.text:
With expanded NVIDIA CUDA-X libraries, including cuPhoton, cuPotential and cuSpa, researchers can sift through vast amounts of data to accelerate research, from astrophysics and materials science to single-cell biology.
The speedups are helping scientists analyze larger datasets and model more complex systems.
The new libraries give AI agents the tools to help researchers make discoveries faster than ever.
Bringing Black Holes Into Focus
Seeing a black hole takes a telescope the size of Earth. The Event Horizon Telescope links radio dishes worldwide, generating petabytes of data that can take months to process.
With NVIDIA cuPhoton.xBeam, a module within the cuPhoton Toolkit, black hole observations from the Event Horizon Telescope can now be correlated orders of magnitude faster than ever. Analysis that once took over a month now takes eight minutes.
By combining global radio dishes into Earth-sized aperture, cuPhoton delivers unprecedented astronomical imaging resolution. cuPhoton successfully correlated observations of powerful black hole jets J1924 and 3C279 in the night sky — making it a reality to reconstruct a Messier 87* black hole galaxy in real time.
The entire pipeline, from data loading and processing to visualization, runs on distributed multi-GPU systems or a compact NVIDIA DGX Spark system, helping scientists study how gas spirals inward under a black hole’s powerful gravitational pull.
Steering Fusion Simulations
Sustaining plasma at millions of degrees is essential to achieving stable, continuous fusion energy. But simulating its behavior is costly: on petascale systems, a single time step can take days, with simulations running for weeks. Experiments also generate data faster than traditional pipelines can process it, often leaving scientists waiting until experiments end to analyze results.
Pacific Fusion researchers used NVIDIA cuPhoton.xLens module to extract insights while plasma simulations run, helping them visualize what’s happening as results emerge.
The NVIDIA cuPhoton.xLens module extracts insights while plasma simulations run, helping researchers understand what’s happening as results emerge. Researchers can couple the entire pipeline with an NVIDIA Nemotron-powered agent running locally on the same system, enabling interactive analysis that can help steer simulations in real time to inform fusion reactor target and chamber design.
Exploring Potential Medicines
Molecular simulations help scientists evaluate drug designs before costly laboratory experiments. NVIDIA cuPotential, built on work by researchers at Simons Foundation’s Flatiron Institute and D. E. Shaw Research, accelerates existing simulation software by up to 3x while improving calculation stability and accuracy. It expedites synthetic data creation for generative AI models, finding previously unknown molecular binding sites and calculating the strength of molecular interactions.
NVIDIA is working with Schrödinger and the AMBER, NAMD, GROMACS, LAMMPS and Open Molecular Software Foundation communities to bring cuPotential acceleration to molecular dynamics engines and workflows.
Cadence, Fathom Therapeutics, Topos Bio, Genesis Molecular AI and Terray Therapeutics are adopting it for drug discovery.
Accelerating Materials Research
Daviator, a collection of batched GPU kernels for the widely used Vienna Ab initio Simulation Package, is coming to NVIDIA ALCHEMI — delivering quantum-mechanical calculations up to 22x faster and at up to 75% lower cost. With Daviator, researchers building simulation models can now use GPU acceleration across atomistic systems of all sizes to generate the millions of calculations of atomic interactions needed for model training and inference, including for small systems that previously ran faster on CPUs.
At Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, the NVIDIA DAQIRI networking library connects a high-speed electron microscopy detector to GPU processing, moving analysis into the experiment itself. Researchers can identify useful signals, discover previously unknown regions of interest and decide what to measure next while measurements are being taken.
The workflow supports atomic-resolution materials studies that can distinguish elements, laying the groundwork for future automated experiments.
Revealing Biology at Scale
The newly open source cuSpa accelerates cell polygon calculations, enabling developers to generate massive spatial graphs for next-generation patient and cancer models at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, with a 900x speedup compared with using CPUs.
Codeveloped with scverse, the rapids-singlecell framework accelerates single-cell analysis — and is now available in a single, agent-ready container. Using the tool, Therna Biosciences processed data 200x faster for therapeutic design. 10x Genomics integrated rapids-singlecell in its new Sentira platform, helping academic researchers, biopharma teams and foundation model builders accelerate the path from large-scale spatial data to biological insights.
And the NVIDIA GPU-accelerated HMMER library, also open source, accelerates the annotation of predicted protein sequences, supporting data preparation for biological foundation models. At Basecamp Research, benchmark searches ran up to 84x faster than with standard HMMER, reducing the time required to annotate the large biological datasets used to train the company’s therapeutic design models.
Explore NVIDIA CUDA-X libraries. Learn more in this technical blog on GPU-powered black hole reconstruction.

articles.title: Customize answers per tenant in Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Customize answers per tenant in Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base
With retrieval instructions in Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base, you can customize answers per tenant. The same product and policy documents often serve several audiences, such as customers in different regions or internal teams, and each audience needs its own answer. You set the voice, format, retrieval guidance, and answer policy that agentic retrieval applies to each request. Before this feature, you couldn’t set the answer style, so agentic retrieval could use a different style from one request to the next. For a fixed voice or structured output, you had to turn off response generation, call a model yourself, and maintain the prompt in every application.
Now you write that guidance once, as a managed, versioned Amazon Bedrock resource, and each request references it. When you change an instruction, you can pin a version so that each application switches to the new version when you’re ready.
Take AnyCompany Smart Home, a fictitious company that sells a home controller and room sensors in three sales regions. Its customer assistant serves all three regions, and its support, field sales, and legal teams use internal assistants that they built on the same documents. AnyCompany defines each region and internal team as a tenant here, and each needs a different answer. A customer in Sales Region Central needs Spanish with day/month/year dates, and a support agent needs a short ticket note. To keep the example compact, every tenant queries one knowledge base. However, agentic retrieval can search up to five knowledge bases in a single request, and the tenant’s instruction applies to all of them.
Retrieval instructions change how the assistant answers, but they aren’t an authorization or data-isolation boundary. Use metadata filters or separate knowledge bases to control what each tenant can retrieve. In this post, we show how to give each tenant its own answers from shared knowledge bases while keeping each tenant’s data separate. By the end, you can roll out a change to one tenant’s instruction and confirm which version answered each request.
Why tenants need their own instructions
Tenants that share documents still differ in language, date and money conventions, voice, and which policy values they can quote. A retrieval instruction has four fields for these differences:
- persona: who the assistant is, including identity, tone, and language.
- answerFormat: how the answer is structured, including how it cites sources.
- retrievalGuidance: how the agent interprets the question and what it prioritizes when it searches.
- answerPolicy: whether and how to answer, including questions outside scope.
The persona, answerFormat, and answerPolicy fields apply only when generateResponse is true, which is the default, and retrievalGuidance applies either way. For details, see Create and manage retrieval instructions. Table 1 shows how the answer to the same return question changes when the request includes the Sales Region Central instruction and names the customer’s region.
| Compared | No instruction | With the instruction and the customer’s region | 
| Answer | Every region’s return window, then a question about where the unit was bought | 45 days from delivery, in Spanish | 
| Last line | None | Source: central-returns-addendum.md | 
Table 1: The same return question with and without the Sales Region Central instruction
These patterns come up across industries. An enterprise software provider can run one assistant for many of its own customers. Each customer uploads its policies, standard operating procedures, and company values, and persona and answerPolicy give each one its own voice and rules. A regulated enterprise can put a fixed disclaimer in answerPolicy and a set citation form in answerFormat, so every answer includes both. A team that sends answers to downstream code can get strict JSON from an answerFormat, without a separate generation step. In each case, the documents are shared, and the voice, format, and policy change from caller to caller.
How retrieval instructions work
An instruction belongs to your AWS account and AWS Region, not to a knowledge base, and goes through these stages:
- Create – CreateRetrievalInstruction returns HTTP 202.
- Review – Amazon Bedrock reviews the instruction’s fields asynchronously, and you poll for the result. If the review fails, lastTransitionStatusReasons says why.
- Activate – A passing review makes the instruction ACTIVE, and DRAFT points to its current content.
- Version – CreateRetrievalInstructionVersion saves an immutable numbered version.
- Apply – A request names the instruction and, optionally, a version, which defaults to DRAFT.
- Report – The first Planning trace event includes appliedInstruction.
Scope and trade-offs
Instructions set voice, format, conventions, and policy wording. They don’t limit which documents the agent can retrieve, and they don’t choose the tenant’s own values, which come from naming the tenant in the request. Use metadata filters or separate knowledge bases to limit what each tenant can retrieve.
Solution overview
Each tenant gets its own instruction and metadata filter. The instruction sets the voice, format, and policy of the answer, and the filter limits which documents the agent retrieves. Your backend chooses both from the authenticated tenant, so one shared knowledge base can serve every tenant. In Figure 1, your backend maps the authenticated tenant to an instruction version and a metadata filter, and adds a short tenant line to the message. Then it calls AgenticRetrieveStream on one shared managed knowledge base.
The same pattern works with a separate knowledge base for each tenant. A request can query a shared global knowledge base and the tenant’s own knowledge base together, each with its own filter.
The example uses 32 short, fictitious AnyCompany Smart Home policy and product documents for the AnySmartProduct-5 home controller and AnySmartProduct-6 room sensors. They’re stored in an Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) bucket, and each has region, audience_team, and sensitivity metadata. Each of the six tenants, three regions and three teams, has its own instruction pinned to version 1. Two restricted engineering notes belong to no tenant, so no tenant’s filter should return them.
The code is in the GitHub repo, in Python and TypeScript, and runs in the US East (N. Virginia) Region (us-east-1) by default. To use another AWS Region, set AWS_REGION. For the latest Region support, see Supported AWS Regions.
Prerequisites
You need the following:
- An AWS account with permissions to create retrieval instructions, AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles, and an S3 bucket.
- One or more managed knowledge bases, with a metadata file for each document you want to filter on.
- Python 3.10 or later and a current version of the AWS SDK for Python (Boto3). Older Boto3 versions don’t include the retrieval instruction operations.
- A current version of the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) for control-plane commands. AgenticRetrieveStream has no CLI command, so call it through an SDK.
- Optional: an AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) customer managed key, if you want to encrypt instructions with your own key.
Examples use Python with these two clients. Later snippets leave out the client setup and import lines.
Create a retrieval instruction for each tenant
The Sales Region Central instruction sets the language, date and money formats, and policy wording:
To create and pin each tenant’s instruction:
- Select a tenant key, such as sales-region-central, for the name and the tenant tag.
- Enter the instruction fields for that tenant.
- Send CreateRetrievalInstruction with the content and tags.
- Poll GetRetrievalInstruction until lastTransitionStatus is neither CREATING nor UPDATING.
- If the status isn’t ACTIVE, read lastTransitionStatusReasons, revise, and update.
- Create a version and record it in your release configuration.
This code runs steps 3 and 6. The repo version adds the polling for steps 4 and 5.
An update replaces the whole instruction, including the description, so resend every field you want to keep. To encrypt an instruction with your own key, set customerEncryptionKeyArn when you create it. You can’t add or change the key later. Your key policy also needs the statement in Encryption of retrieval instructions.
Keep tenant data apart with metadata filters
An instruction doesn’t limit which documents the agent retrieves. On a shared knowledge base, a Sales Region North customer’s question can return the Sales Region Central and South addenda, and even notes that no tenant should see. To keep each tenant to its own documents, add a metadata filter built from the authenticated tenant, or give the tenant its own knowledge base. A request can still query the tenant’s knowledge base alongside shared ones. Figure 2 compares the three approaches.
A metadata filter keeps one knowledge base to sync and maintain, but every document needs accurate metadata, and your backend must build the filter correctly on every request. A separate knowledge base per tenant isolates tenant data by design, but each tenant adds a knowledge base and data source to create, sync, and pay for. You can combine them: one request can query a shared knowledge base and the tenant’s own knowledge base, each with its own filter.
With a tenant filter or a separate knowledge base, the agent retrieves only documents the tenant is entitled to, so answers don’t quote other regions’ values. An answer policy that limits the assistant to one region helps, but without a filter an answer can still quote another region’s value.
Build the filter on your server from the authenticated tenant, because Amazon Bedrock applies whatever filter the request sends:
This filter uses the equals, andAll, and orAll operators on document metadata. It isn’t per-user access filtering through userContext.
Answer policies are best effort. A line such as “Never share restricted engineering notes” can keep values out of the answer. If the notes are retrieved, though, an answer can still name the mechanism or record ID. To keep restricted content out of answers, exclude it with a metadata filter.
Answer as the tenant
For each request, your backend sends the tenant’s instruction ID and version, the tenant filter, and a tenant line. A tenant line is a short sentence, such as Customer sales region: Sales Region Central., placed before the question:
Here’s the same return question answered with three tenant instructions on one knowledge base, trimmed:
A tenant line tells the agent who is asking, which helps the answer quote that tenant’s values. It doesn’t set the tenant’s language, answer format, or date and money formats, so pair it with the tenant’s instruction. Without the instruction, a Sales Region Central answer can come back in English, without the Source: line, or in the wrong date format.
Without an instruction, a customer answer can also quote internal discount tiers from a document the tenant can retrieve. An answer policy that forbids them, like the Sales Region Central one, can keep them out, but to make sure, filter out the document that contains them. Team formats such as the ticket note aren’t guaranteed on every answer, so validate the format in any code that depends on it.
Instructions change how an answer is written. The facts still come from the documents the agent retrieves, so compute exact values such as a return deadline in your application.
Cover users who belong to a region and a team
A request can reference only one retrieval instruction. When a user belongs to both a region and a team, that instruction has to cover both. For example, a support agent in Sales Region South needs the support team’s voice and the region’s date and money formats. Table 2 compares two ways to set that up for N regions and M teams.
| Approach | Instructions to maintain | Applies the region’s formats | 
| One combined instruction for each region and team pair | N x M, plus the N region and M team instructions you already have | Yes | 
| The team’s instruction, with the region named in the tenant line | N + M | No, the team’s formats apply | 
Table 2: Two ways to cover a region and a team with one instruction
Start with the team’s instruction and a region tenant line, which keeps the count at N + M. Add a combined instruction only for pairs whose formats differ from the team’s default. Neither approach limits what the agent retrieves, so keep the tenant filter on every request. A filter also can’t remove a value from a shared document the tenant is entitled to, such as a global policy that lists every region’s dates. As of this writing, the default quota is 50 retrieval instructions per account per AWS Region, and you can request an increase. Combined instructions add up quickly, with 15 for 3 regions and 3 teams and 65 for 10 regions and 5 teams.
Scope tenant roles with instruction tags
If your application calls agentic retrieval with the same role for every tenant, IAM can’t tell tenants apart, and your code alone chooses each request’s instruction and filter. When each tenant’s requests run under that tenant’s own credentials, tag conditions add a second check on which instruction a request can apply and who can change it. Those credentials can come from a role per tenant or a role assumed with a tenant session tag.
AgenticRetrieveStream has no IAM resource. To apply an instruction, the caller needs bedrock:GetRetrievalInstruction on the instruction’s Amazon Resource Name (ARN), so that’s where the tag condition goes. These attribute-based access control (ABAC) statements from the example’s AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) app scope one tenant:
With these statements, a tenant’s applier role can apply only instructions tagged with its tenant, and its tenant admin role can manage only those instructions. The platform admin can manage any tenant’s instructions. Require both tag conditions on TagResource. With only the request-tag condition, a tenant admin can retag another tenant’s instruction into its own scope. To add a tenant, add its key to the tenantRoles context value and deploy the AWS CDK app again with the same trustedPrincipalArn. Apply permission doesn’t limit retrieval, so scope bedrock:Retrieve to each role’s knowledge bases. ListRetrievalInstructions can’t be scoped by tag, so keep instruction names free of sensitive information.
Trace each answer to a tenant and version
As Use retrieval instructions with agentic retrieval describes, the first Planning trace event includes appliedInstruction, with the ID and version of the instruction that was applied. Log it with the tenant ID:
For every event type, see the AgenticRetrieveStream API reference. To capture the applied instruction, check for the first Planning event in the loop that reads the answer:
For an audit record outside your application, use AWS CloudTrail. CloudTrail logs Agents for Amazon Bedrock Runtime operations, including AgenticRetrieveStream, as data events. A trail records data events only after you enable them. For details, see Monitor Amazon Bedrock API calls using CloudTrail.
Release instruction changes one tenant at a time
Amazon Bedrock doesn’t route traffic between versions. Keep a release configuration for each tenant, pin its version on every request, and canary, promote, or roll back by changing that pin. The trace confirms which version served each request, not whether the new version answers better, so gate each promotion on your own checks. This release configuration is from the repo’s router:
To change one tenant, update its instruction, wait for the review, create a version, and move only that tenant’s pin. For example, moving the support tenant to version 2 leaves the other five tenants on version 1:
A pin fixes the instruction, not the exact wording of each answer. During an update review, DRAFT keeps serving the previous content. A version create or a second update during the review fails with HTTP 409, so poll until the review finishes, as the retrieval instruction rollout steps describe.
More ways to use retrieval instructions
Retrieval instructions aren’t only for multi-tenant setups. The same fields work for a single application, such as an assistant that has to return JSON for downstream code or keep one voice across every answer. The repo has code for the first three.
Return structured JSON
An answerFormat can replace your own generation step:
With this answerFormat, agentic retrieval can return the JSON directly, so you don’t need a separate generation step. Validate the JSON in your code before you use it.
Serve several audiences
Give each audience its own persona and answerFormat, such as a customer answer and a ticket note, so the same knowledge bases can serve them all without mixing their formats.
Apply one instruction across knowledge bases
Several retrievers can share one instruction version:
Keep a consistent brand voice
Set identity, tone, and language once in persona, such as “Use a friendly, concise tone. Reply in the language of the question.”
Add disclaimers or citation formats
Put required lines in answerPolicy and citation forms in answerFormat, and give a realistic citation example, such as Source: central-returns-addendum.md, instead of a placeholder.
Hand off questions outside scope
Use answerPolicy to name the fallback, such as “If the documents do not answer the question, say so and give the support contact.”
Teach domain vocabulary
Use retrievalGuidance for acronyms and preferred sources, such as “Treat model numbers as exact-match terms.” Check the Planning trace events to see how the agent searched. Use filters, not guidance, to limit what it retrieves.
Best practices for writing retrieval instructions
Follow these practices when you write and roll out retrieval instructions:
- Add a tenant line to the message. It helps the answer quote the tenant’s own values.
- Bind filters to the authenticated tenant on the server. Amazon Bedrock applies whatever filter the request sends.
- Pin versions in production. Test on DRAFT, then promote by changing the pin.
- Wait for each review to finish. After a create or update, poll until the review succeeds before you create a version. A version create during a review fails with HTTP 409.
- Treat answer policies as best effort. To keep a documented fact out of answers, filter out the document that contains it.
- Validate formats your code depends on. Formats such as a ticket note aren’t guaranteed on every answer.
Clean up
To avoid ongoing charges, delete the retrieval instructions with the following commands. Then follow the cleanup steps in the repo README for the knowledge base, data source, S3 bucket, and roles.
Conclusion
Retrieval instructions give each tenant its own voice, answer format, date and money formats, and answer policy on shared managed knowledge bases. Pair them with metadata filters to keep tenant data apart and pinned versions to roll out changes one tenant at a time. The trace shows which version answered, and CloudTrail can record the AgenticRetrieveStream calls. Tag conditions add a check when tenants have their own credentials.
To get started, see the AgenticRetrieveStream API reference and the GitHub repo. To learn more, read Agentic retrieval for Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base.

articles.title: Black November: Galaxy A57 atinge a maior queda de preço desde agosto • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Black November: Galaxy A57 atinge a maior queda de preço desde agosto
Galaxy A57 (128 GB) traz tela de 120 Hz e câmera de 50 MP; celular custo-benefício da Samsung sai por menos da metade do preço no Pix com cupom no Mercado Livre
O Galaxy A57 de 128 GB está saindo por R$ 1.587 no Pix com cupom HOJEPRATEC no Mercado Livre. O smartphone acessível da Samsung, com câmera de 50 MP e tela de 120 Hz, atinge o menor preço desde agosto segundo o Achados, com desconto de 52% sobre o base de R$ 3.299 na Black November 2026.
Mas seja rápido: o cupom é válido apenas nesta segunda-feira (16).
O A57 é o melhor celular custo-benefício de 2026. Seu kit de câmeras inclui wide de 50 MP com OIS e ultrawide de 12 MP, que captam belas cenas ao ar livre, macro de 5 MP para aproximações de elementos pequenos e frontal de 12 MP, que tira ótimas selfies. Todas filmam em 4K.
Seu chip Exynos 168 e os 8 GB de RAM sustentam apps em multitarefa e algumas funções do Galaxy AI. Os 128 GB de espaço interno podem ser expandidos com planos de armazenamento na nuvem.
A tela de 6,7″ Super AMOLED+ é uma evolução sutil da Super AMOLED, que oferece melhor qualidade de imagem. A taxa de 120 Hz e o brilho de até 1.900 nits reproduzem imagens com cores vibrantes, alta fluidez e visibilidade garantida.
O corpo de alumínio do A57 é revestido de ambos os lados pelo vidro Gorilla Glass Victus+, resistente a arranhões e pancadas. A certificação IP68 confere proteção em cenários como poeira intensa e mergulhos acidentais.
Sua bateria de 5.000 mAh resiste por até dois dias de uso, segundo a Samsung. O suporte ao carregamento rápido de 45 W via cabo USB-C permite receber uma carga de 60% em 30 minutos.
O Galaxy A57 de 128 GB (R$ 1.587 no Pix com cupom HOJEPRATEC) será atualizado até o Android 22 e possui conectividade 5G, Wi-Fi 6E, Bluetooth 6.0 e NFC.
A Black November 2026 já começou, e o Mercado Livre e outras lojas oferecem desde 03/11 diversas promoções em eletrônicos com cupons e condições especiais, em preparação à Black Friday, que ocorre dia 27 de novembro.
Acompanhe os Achados do TB no Telegram ou WhatsApp e não perca nenhuma oferta.
Aviso de ética: ao clicar em um link de afiliado, o preço não muda para você e recebemos uma comissão.

articles.title: Uber Data Breach Impacts 150,000 People
articles.text:
Uber is notifying roughly 150,000 drivers that their personal information was stolen in a data breach involving a third-party services provider.
The company learned of the incident on October 9 and immediately severed its data connections with the provider and launched an investigation.
On October 13, the investigation determined that the hackers used compromised service provider credentials on October 7 to access data Uber had shared with the provider.
According to Uber, the hackers accessed images of driver’s licenses and personal information such as names, addresses, dates of birth, driver’s license numbers, and government-issued ID numbers.
The company says that the data was stored in an environment created and managed by Uber’s Cloud Security team. While alerts were enabled, none were triggered because the threat actor used valid credentials.
“The service provider’s compromised credentials did not provide access to other Uber systems. The investigation remains ongoing,” the company said.
Uber has filed data breach notifications with multiple US states, including California, Iowa, Massachusetts, South Carolina, Texas, and Vermont, and reportedly notified the Texas Attorney General’s Office that a total of 149,346 people were affected.
Uber is providing the potentially affected individuals with free credit monitoring and fraud assistance services.
Uber did not identify the service provider in its breach notifications, but a company spokesperson confirmed to TechCrunch that the incident involved Fireworks AI, a cloud platform for running and fine-tuning open source AI models.
Fireworks initially said it had found no evidence that customer personal information, models or datasets had been accessed. However, in a November 9 update, the company acknowledged that the breach also affected account and billing information, as well as some customer datasets and incomplete models.
SecurityWeek has emailed Uber for additional information on the data breach and will update this article if the company responds.

articles.title: Verafin alum-led Verlo nabs $4.5 million to build AI operating system for wealth managers
articles.text:
Verlo has closed $4.5 million CAD in seed funding to reduce the administrative burden facing wealth managers using AI.
The news: The St. John’s startup, which bills itself as “the compliant AI operating system” for independent financial advisors and wealth management firms, announced the round on Monday. Toronto’s Staircase Ventures led with support from returning local backer Pelorus VC and angel investors, including founders and key executives from Canadian tech success story Verafin. The all-equity, all-primary capital financing round closed in October and brings Verlo’s total funding to $6.5 million. Verlo, which went live in March, aims to help wealth managers save time on admin work and focus more on growing their businesses without adding operational overhead. The startup plans to put this capital towards product development, adding another 10 employees to its 15-person team, and expansion in the United States.
From the source: “Verlo has the product, team, and traction to win,” Staircase Ventures founder and managing partner Janet Bannister said in a statement. “When we met Brent, we were immediately impressed by his tenacity, vision, bias for action, and understanding of the nuances of building great products in heavily regulated industries.”
The context: Verafin, which built financial crime detection software for banks and credit unions, sold to US stock exchange Nasdaq in 2020 in a massive, $2.7-billion USD ($3.8-billion CAD) cash deal. That deal was by far Atlantic Canada’s largest-ever tech exit, and still represents one of the country’s overall biggest to date. Like other Newfoundland and Labrador-based tech startups, Verlo’s Verafin connections run deep. Pretty, who launched Verlo in 2024, previously spent nearly five years leading AI workflow automation at Verafin as a product manager both pre- and post-acquisition. As founder and CEO Brett Pretty told BetaKit over email, “Working at Verafin was the best education I’ve ever gotten.” The startup’s team also features a number of other former Verafin staff with experience building software for the tightly regulated financial services industry.
Final thought: While legacy wealth management software providers are beginning to introduce AI, Pretty said in many cases, they “feel more like add-ons to existing workflows” than truly integrated, transformative tech. Verlo is betting that it can move the needle even further by ensuring all of its clients’ data is searchable to AI agents capable of helping advisors automate tasks like financial planning, portfolio reviews, client onboarding, and more.
Feature image courtesy Verlo.

articles.title: Original Mass Effect composer shares how a blind audition got him the job after BioWare ‘gravitated’ toward his demo music — ‘No one knew whose music was attributed to which composer’
articles.text:
Original Mass Effect composer looks back on the audition process for the ‘mystery’ RPG codenamed ‘SFX’ and how he had to ‘earn’ the job through a blind audition — ‘They gravitated to mine and were very happy to find out it was me!’
Sam Hulick was also chosen, and his demo music would later become 'Uncharted Worlds'
- Original Mass Effect composer Jack Wall recalls how he landed the job at BioWare
- Wall says he created demo music for the "mystery" RPG dubbed "SFX," and BioWare chose him after a blind audition
- He says, "They gravitated to mine and were very happy to find out it was me! I love that story because I had to earn it"
Jack Wall, the composer for the original Mass Effect, has shared the story of how he landed the job on BioWare's now-iconic sci-fi role-playing game (RPG).
In an interview with TechRadar Gaming, Wall recalled that he was offered a chance to audition for Mass Effect after working on Jade Empire and "had a pretty good time doing that."
"Of course, then it had a code name: 'SFX'," Wall recalled. "It was a mystery."
The composer explained that he created some demo music, then got a call shortly after from BioWare producer Shauna Perry, who told Wall they did a blind audition of all the entries to single out their favorite.
"No one knew whose music was attributed to which composer," he said. "They gravitated to mine and were very happy to find out it was me! I love that story because I had to earn it."
Wall continued, saying, "I went to BioWare in Edmonton to do our kickoff meeting, and they said there was this one composer, Sam Hulick, who did this one piece that they really liked (the demo that became 'Uncharted Worlds'). I think I said, 'Why did you hire me?' (laughs)."
'Uncharted Worlds' is, of course, one of Mass Effect's most memorable tracks, and Hulick also came on board, too.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
"He was very young in his career at the time, so they were reluctant to hire him outright on his own, but having us both made sense," Wall said. "I honestly love that piece, and Sam killed it."
The Mass Effect and Mass Effect 2 scores were a collaborative effort, featuring Wall, Hulick, Richard Jacques, and David Kates, with Jimmy Hinson lending his talent on the sequel. They're two of the best RPG soundtracks of all time, and according to Wall, the other BioWare developers had their favorite tracks.
Namely, 'Vigil', 'Uncharted Worlds', 'The Normandy', and 'The Citadel', Wall said, adding that game director Casey Hudson called him after he'd completed 'Noveria' and told him, "This was his dream piece fulfilling the brief he had asked for initially."
"From ME2, of course, 'Suicide Mission', 'The Illusive Man' and 'Reflections'," Wall added. "I’m going from memory here, so opinions on the dev team may vary!"
Wall also told TechRadar Gaming that 'Suicide Mission' was one of the first things he and Casey Hudson worked on together and is "Probably to date one of the 10 best endings for a video game ever."
