articles.title: Exclusive: Mazama Energy has a solution for geothermal’s biggest drilling problem | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Success in geothermal energy is guided by two basic goals — drill fast and drill deep. Hit both targets, and geothermal startups have a good chance at being cheaper than nearly every other source on the electrical grid.
But while the goals might be straightforward, they’re anything but easy. Drilling fast generates heat, which damages equipment, and so does drilling deep.
Those two foes are what led Mazama Energy to develop a new technology, called Carbon Chill, that uses carbon dioxide to cool the drill bit and bring cuttings to the surface. The technology will not only let the company drill deeper, but also faster. The startup gave TechCrunch an exclusive look at Carbon Chill.
“Our rate of penetration increased 20% over the already very high rates we were achieving,” Sriram Vasantharajan, co-founder and CEO of Mazama Energy, told TechCrunch.
Speed has other advantages in geothermal. Drilling represents about 25% to 30% of the total cost of building a power plant, so reducing drill time can bring costs down significantly.
If geothermal startups succeed in drilling faster and cheaper, they stand to help reshape the grid in the 2030s. Hyperscalers are already planning the facilities that will enter operation at the end of the decade.
Mazama has been working on the problem for years now. In October 2025, the Khosla-backed startup said it had drilled a well in Oregon that reached 629˚ F (331˚ C), and a more recent well has surpassed 700˚ F, Vasantharajan said. In September, the startup raised $135 million in a round led by Centaurus Capital and Doerr Capital.
Mazama hopes that its new carbon dioxide-based cooling technology will help it prove that geothermal energy from super-hot rock is a viable contender in the electricity market.
Already companies like Google and Meta have started to explore the use of geothermal energy, in part because the potential is enormous: A report from the National Laboratory of the Rockies said that geothermal could generate between 26.5 to 57 terawatts of electricity in the U.S. alone. If just 10% of the conservative estimate were developed, it would more than double the U.S.’s peak generating capacity.
Geothermal experts have identified super-hot rock — in which temperatures exceed 752˚ F (400˚ C) — as a promising way to improve the performance of individual wells. At those temperatures, water turns “supercritical,” a gaseous-like liquid state which carries five to 10 times more energy than water from traditional geothermal wells. By harvesting more energy from each well, developers have to drill fewer of them, bringing costs down.
Accessing that heat can be challenging for traditional drilling methods. Most geothermal drillers use “mud” — a combination of water and other compounds to keep the bit cool and clear cuttings from the borehole. But mud can only bring temperatures down so much. Eventually, they become so hot that electronics in the drill bit, which help keep it on course, start to fail.
High temperature-rated electronics exist, but they’d be cost prohibitive, Vasantharajan said.
Instead of mud, Mazama injects liquid carbon dioxide down the center of its drill string. As it travels deeper, it gets heated by the rock around it, which turns it supercritical, too. Then, just before it reaches the drill head, Mazama has it flow through a valve that looks a lot like a rocket nozzle. As the gas expands, it escapes through the cone-shaped nozzle and rapidly cools, absorbing heat from the electronics and the drill bit.
“I look at [carbon dioxide cooling] as a binary,” he said. “Without such technologies, I am, today, not able to drill these horizontal wells at super-hot rock temperatures.”
That capital injection will help Mazama drill more wells deeper. By next year, Vasantharajan said his company hopes to complete a single well that’s capable of generating up to 15 megawatts of electricity.
“What was just a dream or a quest, I can tell you with confidence is now a promise,” he said. “We see a path towards this commercial super-hot rock geothermal.”

articles.title: Mission gescheitert: Vulcan-Centaur-Rakete erleidet „Anomalie” und verliert 40 Amazon-Satelliten
articles.text:
Mission gescheitert: Vulcan-Centaur-Rakete erleidet „Anomalie” und verliert 40 Amazon-Satelliten
Am 15. November 2026 gegen 18:40 Uhr deutscher Zeit startete die Vulcan-Centaur-Rakete der United Launch Alliance in Cape Canaveral, Florida. An Bord der Rakete befanden sich insgesamt 40 Leo-Satelliten von Amazon. Mit den Satelliten plant der Konzern, ein Satellitennetzwerk für Internet aufzubauen und damit ein Konkurrenzprodukt zu Elon Musks Starlink zu liefern. Doch diese Pläne haben jetzt einen kleinen Dämpfer erfahren, wie Space berichtet.
Warum ist die Vulcan-Centaur-Rakete abgestürzt?
Der Start der Rakete verlief noch reibungslos. Auf X postete die United Launch Alliance nur sechs Minuten nach dem Start erste Aufnahmen, um den Launch zu feiern. Vier weitere Minuten später kam es allerdings zu einem Zwischenfall. Wie die ULA schreibt, trat zehn Minuten nach dem Launch eine „Anomalie“ auf, wodurch die Rakete nicht mehr imstande war, die Leo-Satelliten von Amazon in den Erdorbit zu befördern.
Die Meldung über den gescheiterten Flug erfolgte nur eine Stunde nach dem Start der Vulcan-Centaur-Rakete. Dementsprechend betont die ULA, dass es noch keine genauen Informationen darüber gibt, welcher Zwischenfall für das Scheitern gesorgt hat. Die ULA will in den kommenden Tagen sämtliche Daten auswerten und anschließend einen ausführlichen Bericht samt möglicher Korrekturmaßnahmen für künftige Flüge veröffentlichen.
Bei vorherigen Starts gab es schon Probleme mit der Vulcan-Centaur-Rakete, die schon seit Januar 2024 im Einsatz ist. Der aktuelle Launch war insgesamt der fünfte. Bei zwei Starts fiel nur etwa 30 Sekunden nach dem Start eine SRB-Düse von der Rakete ab. In beiden Fällen konnten die Missionen aber erfolgreich durchgeführt werden. Die US‑Space-Force, die die Rakete ebenfalls für zwei andere Missionen genutzt hatte, hatte seither davon abgesehen, die Rakete zu nutzen.
Seit dem letzten Launch sind nunmehr neun Monate vergangen. Noch Ende Oktober schrieb die ULA: „Unser Team hat enorme Fortschritte gemacht, die SRB-Anomalien zu verstehen, die bei vorherigen Vulcan-Flügen aufgetreten sind und mehrere potenzielle Fehlerquellen offenbart haben. Diese wurden durch neue Designs und Prozessverbesserungen bei der Düse mitigiert.“
Wie lang die Untersuchungen der ULA andauern werden, ist nicht bekannt. Amazon hat sich noch nicht dazu geäußert, ob die gescheiterte Mission Auswirkungen auf die Pläne für das Leo-Satellitennetzwerk hat. Aktuell hat das Unternehmen noch einen weiteren Launch geplant. Am 23. November 2026 sollen insgesamt 36 Satelliten in den Erdorbit befördert werden, allerdings mit einer Arianespace-Rakete, die von Kourou in Französisch-Guayana abheben soll.

articles.title: The Apple Watch Series 12 is cheaper than ever ahead of Black Friday
articles.text:
If you’re still sporting an Apple Watch that launched five or so years ago, now is a good time to upgrade. Apple’s latest smartwatch, the 42mm Apple Watch Series 12 with Wi-Fi and GPS connectivity, has dropped to a new all-time low of $329 at Amazon, Best Buy, and Walmart, beating the October Prime Day price by $20. If you prefer a larger size, the 46mm model is on sale for $379 ($70 off) at Amazon, Best Buy, and Walmart, which is also $20 lower than the previous best price.
The Apple Watch Series 12 is cheaper than ever ahead of Black Friday
Apple’s latest smartwatch introduces AI-powered audio features, redesigned health sensors, and faster charging.
The Series 12 stands out compared to previous models with its new AI-powered Audio Intelligence features, which are made possible by Apple’s new S11 chip. For example, the watch can alert you when it detects sounds like a doorbell, alarm, or even a baby’s cry, while other upcoming features like Live Rewind and Siri Recap lets you look back at a transcript of the previous 15 seconds of conversation and get a high-level overview of the conversations you had that day. The new chip also makes Siri more responsive, so you can get answers to questions with less waiting around.
It’s not all about AI, though. The Series 12 also features redesigned health sensors that can now track your heart rate every five seconds even when you’re not exercising, which is particularly help if you have a chronic condition and need to keep a closer eye on your heart rate. It also introduces a new readiness score to help you decide how prepared your body is for the day. Other highlights include easier navigation with simple pinch gestures, and faster charging, which helps to make up for the fact that battery life is rated at up to 24 hours on a single charge, just like the previous-generation model. In our testing, the watch went from 20 to 64 percent charge in just 20 minutes, making it relatively easy to top up while showering or getting ready for the day.

articles.title: Can Indonesian researchers ever win a Nobel? Not without overhauling the research ecosystem
articles.text:
Will Indonesia ever win the Nobel Prize? That question probably pops into some Indonesians’ minds whenever Nobel season starts in October.
The reality is that there are no shortcuts to a Nobel. Breakthroughs recognised by the committee almost always stem from foundational work done decades earlier — often when it is impossible to foresee the practical payoffs.
Take the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine awarded to Peter Hegemann, Georg Nagel and Karl Deisseroth for pioneering optogenetics — a breakthrough technique that uses light to control nerve cell activity.
Read more: Bagaimana alga mengantarkan ilmuwan pada Nobel Kedokteran dan cara baru memahami otak
Interestingly, the road to optogenetics began with research that seemed to have nothing to do with medicine. Hegemann was initially investigating how the single-celled green alga Chlamydomonas swims towards light. His collaboration with Nagel eventually led to the discovery of channelrhodopsin — a light-sensitive protein that acts as an ion channel.
By 2005, Deisseroth’s team showed that channelrhodopsin could be harnessed to control neuronal firing with light. What began as a humble inquiry into pond algae laid the groundwork for optogenetics — now an indispensable tool for mapping and manipulating the brain.
This trajectory illustrates the road to the prestigious award: Nobel-worthy breakthroughs emerge from ecosystems patient enough to let basic research mature before demanding immediate benefits.
But can Indonesia’s research ecosystem nurture that kind of long game?
It all comes down to funding. Again.
The most glaring bottleneck in Indonesia’s research ecosystem is funding. The country’s R&D spending remains low, lagging far behind its ASEAN peers.
Data from the National Research and Innovation Agency (BRIN) paint a sobering picture: in 2024, Indonesia’s total R&D expenditure stood at around US$2.8 billion — a meagre 0.23% of gross domestic product (GDP). Higher education shouldered 71.02% of that spending, while the private sector contributed a negligible 14.96%.
Neighbours tell a different story: the private sector drove 51.37% of R&D in Malaysia (2022) and roughly 74% in Thailand (2021). The lesson is structural: a nation’s scientific muscle depends not just on how much it spends, but on who funds it.
How should public research funds be accounted for?
Researchers must naturally account for every public fund they spend: explaining what they investigate, how funds are allocated and what discoveries emerge. Yet not all grant systems in Indonesia define “results” the same way — and rigid metrics can easily distort scientific work.
Take Indonesia’s 2025 Research and Community Service Guidelines. Under the Regular Fundamental Research scheme (PFR), grantees are mandated to publish at least one paper in a reputable international journal every single year.
Research benchmarks are indeed necessary. But when success hinges on short-term milestones — like annual publication quotas — scientists are almost guaranteed to play it safe, pursuing predictable findings over ambitious, high-risk discoveries.
Take Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman, who jointly won the 2023 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for work that began more than two decades earlier.
In 2005, the pair made a critical breakthrough: modifying mRNA’s nucleosides could suppress harmful inflammatory responses to synthetic mRNA. After years of funding rejections, skepticism and painstaking refinement, that fundamental discovery unlocked the mRNA vaccines and therapies that ultimately saved millions of lives during the COVID-19 pandemic.
By comparison, Japan’s Grants-in-Aid for Scientific Research program, known as KAKENHI, still demands strict accountability: recipients must report on expenditure, track ongoing milestones, and submit comprehensive final evaluations.
KAKENHI explicitly urges researchers to disseminate their findings globally — via peer-reviewed journals, international partnerships, and academic conferences. Crucially, the guidelines avoid treating rigid publication targets as make-or-break funding criteria.
Lessons from Asia’s research ecosystems
In 2025, China boosted its R&D spending to roughly 2.8% of GDP. Its investment in basic research surged by 13.3% year-on-year – comfortably outstripping its 8.2% overall growth in R&D expenditure.
Meanwhile, Singapore committed S$S37 billion (around US$28.77 billion) to its Research, Innovation and Enterprise 2030 (RIE2030) plan. The blueprint balances market-driven applications with solid backing for open-ended fundamental science and homegrown scientific talent.
Both countries operate under distinct economic realities and strategic priorities. Yet they share a common thread: fundamental science remains an indispensable pillar of their national policy.
Boosting Indonesia’s research budget is crucial, but cash alone will not fix the system without deeper industry involvement and long-term backing for university laboratories. Accountability matters, too – but evaluation frameworks must be flexible enough to give unorthodox, exploratory ideas room to breathe.
Read more: Ribuan riset dan paten Indonesia terjebak di “jurang maut” karena tak dipakai industri
After all, scientific inquiry is inherently unpredictable. Hypotheses fall flat, experiments fail and dead ends are part of the process. A project that yields no marketable innovation within five years may still unearth foundational knowledge that sparks a breakthrough decades later.
Grant systems must therefore make room for rigorous science whose outcomes cannot be mapped in advance. Such work still demands robust evaluation – just not through the same narrow, transactional metrics applied to off-the-shelf product development.
The Nobel is a byproduct, not the destination
Indonesia does not need a glitzy roadmap to a Nobel Prize; it needs a dependable research ecosystem. That means reliable funding, smarter resource allocation, sensible evaluation metrics and real avenues for international collaboration.
Read more: Bukan (hanya) soal anggaran. Bagaimana dana riset dibelanjakan juga penting
Every nation dreams of its own Nobel laureate, and Indonesia is no exception. But the medal itself cannot be the end goal.
For Indonesia, the real debate is not a false choice between applied projects with immediate payoffs and curiosity-driven basic science. The challenge is designing an ecosystem flexible enough to nurture both, knowing full well that groundbreaking research runs on its own clock.
What matters far more is fostering a research ecosystem that empowers scientists to pursue bold, open-ended questions – even when the tangible payoffs are years or decades down the line.

articles.title: CUDA at 20: How the Platform Transformed Scientific Computing
articles.text:
This week at SC26, NVIDIA is marking two decades of CUDA by honoring the researchers, developers and engineers who helped make GPU computing a foundation for modern science and AI.
CUDA’s 20th anniversary presents an occasion to reflect across computing eras, from the people who wrote the very first CUDA programs to the AI developers building on their work today.
At the platform’s core is this developer community whose experiments, tools and persistence expanded what accelerated computing could do.
From SC06 to SC26
NVIDIA announced CUDA in November 2006 and brought it to the scientific community at SC06, giving scientists and developers a familiar, high-level programming model for using GPUs. It fundamentally extended accelerated computing beyond graphics use cases to accelerate demanding applications for science, simulation and more.
In the two decades since, developers have used CUDA to advance Nobel Prize-winning AI research, accelerate scientific applications on supercomputers and support visual effects in Oscar-winning films.
Today, more than 11 million developers build on CUDA across the computing stack.
Honoring the Architects of Progress
Now, at SC26, NVIDIA is looking back at some of the CUDA luminaries who’ve spearheaded breakthroughs in science and AI:
At the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, biophysicist Klaus Schulten’s team helped connect GPU computing with molecular biology through Nanoscale Molecular Dynamics and Visual Molecular Dynamics, tools for molecular simulation and visualization. In 2013, researchers at Illinois, the University of Pittsburgh and Vanderbilt University used CUDA-accelerated tools to help resolve the HIV capsid’s atomic structure. They combined experiments with simulations on Blue Waters, one of the world’s most powerful supercomputers at the time.
In a critical breakthrough in AI, University of Toronto researchers Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever and Geoffrey Hinton used CUDA to train AlexNet on just two NVIDIA GPUs. Their image-recognition system won the 2012 ImageNet competition, helping demonstrate the potential of GPU computing for deep learning.
That connection between computing and scientific discovery is seen with AlphaFold, which predicts protein structures. Demis Hassabis and John Jumper shared the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for protein structure prediction. Their team’s publicly released AlphaFold 2 software uses CUDA for GPU execution.
These are just a few of many examples that show how one generation’s work creates opportunities for the next. With 1,000+ NVIDIA CUDA-X libraries, developers are now reshaping industries and giving machines the power to see, learn and reason — from discovering new medicines and designing next-generation factories to advancing autonomous vehicles, modeling financial markets and unlocking quantum computing — and more.
Start building with the CUDA Toolkit and visit the 20-Year CUDA Celebration Event Wall at NVIDIA’s booth at SC26.

articles.title: Sam Altman diz que indústria de IA ficará bem sem Jensen Huang na Nvidia
articles.text:
O CEO da OpenAI, Sam Altman, acredita que a indústria de inteligência artificial (IA) continuará avançando mesmo sem Jensen Huang no comando da Nvidia. Apesar de reconhecer a importância do executivo para o desenvolvimento do setor, ele afirmou que a demanda por IA é forte o suficiente para manter o mercado em expansão.
As declarações foram feitas nesta segunda-feira (16), durante o evento Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World. Foi a primeira vez que Altman comentou publicamente a saída de Huang da fabricante de chips, após o executivo deixar o cargo de CEO na semana passada.
Questionado sobre a possibilidade de o fundador retornar à liderança da Nvidia, Altman evitou tomar partido. “Não acho que eu saiba o suficiente para responder a essa pergunta”, afirmou.
Sam Altman demonstra empatia por Jensen Huang
- Embora não tenha defendido diretamente a volta de Huang, Altman demonstrou solidariedade ao executivo e destacou sua contribuição para o setor de tecnologia;
- O CEO da OpenAI afirmou que Huang é um de seus heróis e que é difícil imaginar a revolução da IA sem ele e a empresa que construiu;
- “Heróis têm defeitos”, acrescentou Altman ao comentar a trajetória do fundador da Nvidia;
- O executivo também disse ter empatia pessoal pela situação de Huang. A declaração tem contexto particular: em 2023, Altman foi afastado temporariamente do comando da OpenAI pelo conselho de administração, mas acabou sendo reconduzido ao cargo poucos dias depois;
- A comparação entre os episódios ganhou força no setor de tecnologia, especialmente porque parte dos executivos e investidores que defendem a volta de Huang vê semelhanças entre os dois casos.
Leia mais:
- OpenAI diz que o mundo deve aceitar riscos para evoluir com IA
- Sam Altman visita Samsung para discutir futuro dos chips de IA
- Sam Altman diz que RAM deveria ficar em data centers, não nos PCs dos usuários
OpenAI depende de investimentos e chips da Nvidia
A declaração de Altman também chama atenção pela relação comercial entre as duas empresas. A Nvidia é uma das principais fornecedoras de chips utilizados no desenvolvimento e na operação de sistemas de IA da OpenAI.
Mais recentemente, a fabricante concordou em oferecer garantias de até US$ 105 bilhões (cerca de R$ 560 bilhões) para respaldar o projeto de data center da OpenAI em Ohio.
O acordo faz parte de relação financeira mais complexa entre as companhias. A Nvidia investe no crescimento do mercado de IA e, ao mesmo tempo, ajuda a financiar empresas que compram seus próprios chips.
Questionado sobre a possibilidade de a saída de Huang afetar esse tipo de financiamento, Altman disse não estar preocupado. Segundo ele, a Nvidia é uma empresa gigantesca e suas garantias continuam inspirando confiança no mercado.
Demanda por IA deve sustentar o setor
Altman reconheceu que a ambição de Huang e sua capacidade de impulsionar grandes projetos tiveram papel especialmente importante na expansão da IA.
Ainda assim, o executivo acredita que o mercado não sofrerá consequências significativas com a saída do fundador da Nvidia. “Há tanta demanda, está tão claro que a IA é real, que as pessoas querem usá-la, e as receitas e a demanda estão crescendo tão fortemente que acredito que a indústria ficará bem”, afirmou.
A avaliação contrasta com as preocupações de parte do mercado de tecnologia, que teme que a saída de Huang leve a Nvidia a rever os riscos financeiros assumidos para sustentar a expansão da infraestrutura de IA.
Por enquanto, Altman prefere não opinar sobre o futuro do executivo na fabricante de chips. Sua avaliação é que, apesar da importância de Huang, o crescimento da IA não depende exclusivamente de sua permanência no comando da companhia.
Rodrigo Mozelli é jornalista formado pela Universidade Metodista de São Paulo (UMESP) e, atualmente, é redator do Olhar Digital.

articles.title: Are AI Agents The New Semiconductor IP?
articles.text:
Agents are emerging as reusable design tools, but trust and use models remain challenging.
Key Takeaways:
AI agents are emerging as a new category of reusable design capability, but with a twist. Rather than providing tightly defined design blocks, agents can be used to explore different options, integrate them, and use those changes to improve designs.
At the leading edge, soft IP developers have been customizing their code for large customers for more than a decade to boost performance and/or reduce power. But that customization is typically narrow and costly, and optimizations for one design may not directly transfer to derivative chips — especially multi-die assemblies at the leading edge.
Agents, in contrast, can be used to customize different functions with little or no human intervention, and they can self-optimize for different workloads and use cases, and some agents can even adjust for aging hardware. And they can do all of this much faster than a human, even though an experienced engineering team is needed to verify those results and recommendations.
“We have in-house specialized AI agents to do different things, to do spec analysis, RTL generation for design, for formal and functional verification, and then CDC linking, and place-and-route,” said William Wang, CEO of ChipAgents. “We provide our optimized agents to a customer, and sometimes a customer builds their own AI agent. But there are some similarities with the IP business. Sometimes we’re specifically building an agent for one customer for a particular flow, which is similar to what happens in the IP business. What’s different is that we can do it in a very short amount of time. With IP, you need 10 months. Our cycle is much shorter because AI agents are very easy to customize. In some cases we can give solutions to the customer the same day.”
Those solutions still need to be verified and debugged. But the ability to sort through many different options quickly is an attractive formula, especially with rapid evolution of AI.
“I draw parallels to the early 2000s gigahertz wars, where all of a sudden everything was multicore,” said Mo Faisal, CEO of Movellus. “Now we’ve gone from,’ Everything is going to be a GPU,’ to ‘Oh, no, it’s CPUs and GPUs, and this is a one-to-one ratio.’ So effectively we’re going through the same architectural churn that we go through every 10 to 15 years.”
The business of agents
Business models still need to solidify around agents. but they also need to be flexible enough to evolve at the same pace as the technology.
“If you look at how the EDA industry has evolved, we’re not selling perpetual licenses anymore,” said Rob Knoth, senior group director of Strategy & New Ventures at Cadence. “We moved to time-based licenses many years ago. Now we see similar things as agents roll around. They’re hitting up the tool usage even more because they want to find answers quickly, and they’re trying lots of experiments. So putting together more of a consumption-based model is really good because customers know how to use that.”
This isn’t a simple transition, though. While the promise of agents is significant, their adoption in chip design will take time. In addition, security and permissions aren’t always well-defined.
“There are some things where you’d really rather sell an agent than sell the software,” said Wally Rhines, CEO of Silvaco. “People are trying to figure out if anybody in EDA is actually pricing based upon tokens rather than traditional pricing models. It doesn’t seem like anyone is, but their customers are all talking about it. I’m very much open to selling an agent that will automate [manufacturing equipment] calibration, then jump back to my store of synthetic simulated data against the physical data. We don’t get to see the physical data, but we do know how many tokens our agents consumed. It’s a way that EDA can sell a product, get the benefit, and no one ever sees the underlying data that companies want to keep proprietary.”
Divide and conquer, but with caveats
One of the big changes with the shift from generative AI to agentic AI is the need for orchestration, and this has broad business implications. Orchestration is basically a blueprint that defines how tasks are assigned, how agents access tools and data, and how that work is coordinated. But it’s especially challenging if multiple agents execute at the same time and their actions overlap.
“What’s different about traditional AI and agentic AI is the coordination of multiple agents that are working in parallel, but doing different types of work,” said Robbie Williamson, vice president of customer engineering for cloud AI at Arm. “It’s not like there’s a unique workload that we haven’t seen before. It’s more about how do you coordinate all of these at the CPU level, and have enough bandwidth, memory, etc., to do all of this at scale. Instead of an individual making a request and driving AI, we have computers that can do it much faster. The transition that we see when we talk to hyperscalers is now about what they need from the CPU. With training, that wasn’t as important because you’re just batching the job and waiting for it to come back.”
That creates a new hierarchy in the design flow. “What has happened with this multi-agent workflow is that, in an organization, you’re trying to design a chip,” said Prith Banerjee, senior vice president of innovation at Synopsys. “When they’re having a problem with the PPA, some engineers say they know exactly what changes to make to lower the power. They’ll do clock gating. But when you clock gate power, then it changes something else. It increases the area. So some area will come in — and this is exactly what happens in the real world with coordination when multiple people come together to design a system. The human manager is coordinating the activities of the human agents in the world of a multi-agent framework. We have agents for EDA tools and agents for the CAE (computer-aided engineering) tools. We have simulation with three core solvers — CFD (computational fluid dynamics), HFSS (high-frequency structure simulation) for the electromagnetics, and mechanical for the structural part. In the EDA world, we have things for the implementation, and things for sign-off. Each of these tools has sub-areas, and we have agents to do these things. But what was happening by a team of engineers coordinated by a human manager is now being done by a hierarchy of agents with that framework.”
That changes some of the dynamics in chip design in not-so-subtle ways. Soft IP is often portable across process technologies, but it typically requires optimization and validation. AI agents can automate those tasks by coordinating EDA tools and weighing alternatives, and they can work with traditional IP to optimize specific functions in the context of a larger design.
“One of the key implications of agentic workflows is disaggregation,” said Niels Faché, senior vice president for Keysight‘s Design Engineering Software business. “We believe in platforms. Now we have to see how everybody’s going to deal with that because a platform is a very sticky concept. Many of our customers invest in customizing our platform for their needs. It’s very hard to move away from it. It’s the same for Cadence and Synopsys, but we believe that ultimately customers want that flexibility. We take an open approach to this, where we accept that disaggregation is going to happen. We need to play to the strength of our simulation capability and our understanding of the application. Customers still wanting to work with us on creating their workflows will need help with orchestration, so we need to be experts in that domain, while the most sophisticated customers will do it themselves.”
That requires some fundamental changes for EDA companies. “With AI, that’s a different model where human engineers work with digital engineers or agents,” Faché said. “So now we have to redesign our products. You’ve heard about MCP (Model Context Protocol) servers where we look at a product and ask, ‘Okay, how can we modularize it to provide access to different capabilities with the proper APIs?’ All of that coding is typically done in Python. That would then allow an agent to stitch together a code-based workflow. Our job is to make sure that our customers get this MCP functionality. We also provide examples so that an agent can learn from them and say, ‘Okay, based on these examples, I understand how this works. And now I’ve got a request for a new design, and I can organize that work based on what I’ve learned.’ That’s the world we’re moving toward, and we already see that with our front-runner customers. They are already building these agentic workflows. That means we need MCP servers, and we need all the proper documentation so we can train these agents.”
What else can agents do?
How much freedom to give agents isn’t entirely clear. AI is opaque, and unlike traditional IP, it needs to be observed from the outside. This becomes more complicated as more agents are assigned to different but connected jobs.
“Orchestration is going to be a big challenge, and it will become an even bigger challenge,” said Stelios Diamantidis, chief product officer at Cognichip. “As agents become smarter, they can deliver some outcomes, and it’s been proven to work in many other spaces, as well. But putting all these agents together to drive them as a cohort toward an answer to a problem can also have some interesting challenges. We’re still working with models that generally do not understand the deep physics of the chip design problem, and that means a lot of the logic being baked into agents. But what happens when those agents begin to disagree? Are we going to have ping-pong effects and convergence issues in EDA? We’re no strangers to those effects.”
This is particularly true with multi-die assemblies. “The stack is very heterogeneous,” Diamantidis said. “You’re looking at a model that was trained with sources that generally we don’t know very much about. You have agents that have been given enough logic about a problem by enough different people that the combination of agents and models is now a fairly chaotic model. You put them all together and you get chaos times chaos.”
These challenges help explain why IP and EDA companies are working to tightly integrate agents into existing tools.
“When you look at how we’re applying agents into our data center design and operation tooling, agentic AI coupled with physics-based simulation is great at being able to integrate large amounts of disparate data, ask questions, run experiments, evaluate the output of those experiments, and then do the loop again,” said Cadence’s Knoth. “And what’s very unique about the space we operate in is that, as opposed to other industries, we don’t need a person to look at the results and say that’s right or that’s wrong. EDA has the tools that we’ve used for decades to grade the decisions. ‘That floor plan worked better. It lowered the power.’ Or, ‘That floor plan was worse. The power went up, the heating was worse.'”
Establishing a hierarchy for agents is important, but it’s not always straightforward. “So you have one agent with different sub-agents to do different things, and then we have a multi-agent solution,” said Wang. “We released a multi-agent solution last year. So for debugging, your SoC is so big that it makes it hard to optimize performance. You need multiple agents to have parallel access to different contexts to do the job. Similarly, with formal, you have multiple agents looking at doing the debugging and being able to optimize the design. Those are extremely critical. So you need multi-agent coordination. In the future, we’re going to have virtual chip companies with virtual AI engineers working together, collaborating from this agent organization, and then maybe a part of the chip companies will be virtual in the future.”
That, in turn, could accelerate the adoption of agents.
“There could be a time where we start looking at agentic workloads and try to figure out how we can model those in pre-silicon to improve IP around that, and what that means in terms of the design of the CPU itself and our CSS offerings for those building their own,” said Arm’s Williamson.
Trust and verification
The bigger question is how much autonomy chip designers will be willing to give agents.
“The cost of a mistake is $500 million at 3 or 2 nanometers,” said Ankur Gupta, executive vice president of Siemens EDA IC products. “That’s why these engines have to remain deterministic. They have to remain high-fidelity. We, of course, use reinforcement learning, unsupervised learning, and we’ve been doing that for more than a decade. But the way we measure the result of that learning capability is whether we are still delivering a trusted outcome. So that doesn’t change.”
There’s more to the trust equation than just the outcome, though. It harkens back at least a few decades to the challenge of sharing process data that chipmakers and chip companies consider to be their IP.
“All of these agent technologies and models are pretty good at understanding the language components,” said Gupta. “But the physics component is still the big challenge. And if you think about SLMs, LLMs, where are they going to get the vast amounts of data from, because the whole universe of semiconductor and electronics designs is very siloed and customers are concerned about their IP. Everybody wants on-prem, but that argument persists because you’ve got the foundry, which is not giving up anything.”
Foundries do share PDKs with end customers and EDA companies, but they tightly restrict access to them, which makes it more difficult to train AI and to share models. And because AI is opaque, it becomes even more difficult to convince people to share data.
Nevertheless, the adoption of agents continues to grow. “The analogy is to what the human engineer is doing in a company,” said Synopsys’ Banerjee. “You do not have a single engineer doing the entire design of a chip or a system. You have teams of engineers, and teams of engineers are managed by managers, by directors, by vice presidents. And you have that hierarchy because individuals are doing different things, which they are skilled at. Then the manager coordinates their work. So the early work in AI applied to EDA was to make the tools go faster, better PPA. This is what we did with our DSO.ai (design space optimization). The early work on AI was GenAI. It was generating a script. So you ask a question. ‘I am struggling with this Fusion Compiler. What setting should I use?’ And based on hundreds of questions and answers, this thing essentially is a ChatGPT targeted to this particular line of questions. So it’s an agent for RTL assistance, or whatever.”
AI agents can even be used to fine-tune existing steps in the design flow. “In general, we want to have some very commonly used workflow agents,” said ChipAgents’ Wang. “For example, when you’re building an accelerator chip, it’s very different from a CPU. So how do you do verification? Do you do more formal, less formal? It’s a very different methodology. Having that flexibility is really critical. You don’t want to build a workflow that is very rigid so people cannot customize it. The platform needs to allow you to customize for your specific chip while also being general enough.”
Conclusion
“The model brings a lot of intelligence, so the agent doesn’t have to be terribly smart,” said Cognichip’s Diamantidis. “It can be there to introduce some guardrails and add some additional skills. But right now we’re flipping it. We’re saying, ‘You know, we don’t have billions of examples of hardware, and they’re spread out in all these different silos. So we can’t get them in one place. We can train a model that’s very focused on what it does and put everything on the agent, but that makes it top-heavy, and top-heavy things tend to lose their balance. That’s one of the big challenges.”
So even though AI agents are being integrated into traditional workflows, chip design is still cautious about when and where to deploy it.
“Should agents be managing the hardware that is running all kinds of agents? The answer is yes,” said Movellus’ Faisal. “Is that going to be easy? I don’t think so, because the silicon industry that is enabling the intelligence and adopting all of that for internal tooling and even management is probably the slowest and most conservative. A $500 million silicon program failure is a big deal. There are going to be all kinds of management agents that will be needed — managing the rack, managing thermals, managing workload orchestration.”
While agentic AI won’t replace traditional IP, it could impact the design process in which that IP is used. Change is coming, but there are still a lot of challenges and unknowns ahead.

articles.title: NVIDIA and Lambda Disclose First Production Co-Packaged Optics Cluster... It is FINALLY real
articles.text:
For SC26, NVIDIA and Lambda discussed their first production co-packaged optics (CPO) cluster. The industry has worked to move CPO from the lab to production for decades. Many in the industry will tell you it is a few years out, but Lambda has already deployed it in production in a cluster with over 10,000 GPUs.
NVIDIA and Lambda Disclose First Production Co-Packaged Optics Cluster
We covered NVIDIA’s co-packaged optics extensively during the company’s Hot Chips 2025 presentation. NVIDIA’s first version of the packaging is in its Quantum-X switching product, while Spectrum-X will be an updated second-generation part.
NVIDIA is using an array of 18 pluggable light sources on the front of the chassis, as shown in the photos above, to generate light en route to the switch package’s optical modules. Those light sources are pluggable, meaning they can be serviced, which was one of the key inhibitors to CPO in switches when the light source was integrated. Light sources tend to be the parts that fail in pluggable optics, so making them serviceable was an important innovation. Likewise, on the switch package side, making the connections at least somewhat serviceable helps with deployment.
Downstream, NVIDIA’s Quantum-X CPO switch pictured above has 144 MPO/MTP ports, each at 800Gbps. Something interesting is that with only 18 light sources, instead of 144x 800Gbps optical modules (or 72x dual 800G modules), there are actually fewer light sources that can fail than in a traditional switch, and it becomes easier to cool them compared to having a larger array of individual pluggable modules.
Final Words
One of the biggest benefits of the deployment is that by moving the optics to the switch package rather than the front-panel pluggables, numerous high-speed copper links do not need to drive signaling over relatively long distances from the switch chip to the front cages. As a result, CPO can significantly lower power consumption so that more GPUs can fit in the same footprint. After all, in a power-limited environment, ultimately the more power that can be used for GPUs directly impacts the revenue that can be generated per Watt of power available to the cluster.
Lambda and NVIDIA may have a short on the cluster up, but let me be clear: it exists and is running today, putting NVIDIA at the forefront of deploying CPO. I think it is actually just being announced this week as part of SC26. As a fun aside, I was at OCP Summit 2026 a few weeks ago when I heard during another vendor’s keynote that CPO was still years away from deployment. It turns out it is already deployed. We no longer have to ask if or when CPO will finally be deployed. The big question now is what the adoption curve will be.

articles.title: FritzOS 8.50 und 8.51 kommen auf weitere Fritzboxen: Wer die Updates jetzt laden darf
articles.text:
FritzOS 8.50 und 8.51 kommen auf weitere Fritzboxen: Wer die Updates jetzt laden darf
Schon seit geraumer Zeit warten Fritzbox-User:innen auf das große Update FritzOS 8.50. Hersteller Fritz hatte erste Neuerungen zunächst mit der Labor-Version 8.40 testen lassen. Jetzt ist die Beta-Phase für erste Fritz-Router vorbei und die finale Version von FritzOS 8.50 wird in immer größeren Schritten für einzelne Geräte freigegeben.
Welche Fritzboxen bekommen FritzOS 8.50 und 8.51 jetzt?
Die Liste der Fritzboxen, die jetzt mit der Release-Version FritzOS 8.50 ausgestattet werden, ist mittlerweile schon stark angewachsen. Unter den Kandidaten befinden sich auch Router und Repeater, die direkt ein Update auf die Version FritzOS 8.51 erhalten. Am Funktionsumfang ändert sich dadurch nichts. Der Hersteller verweist bei den Ankündigungen auf X stets auf die Übersichtsseite von FritzOS 8.50.
In den kommenden Wochen und Monaten dürfte Fritz noch mehr Modelle für die Aktualisierung freigeben. Wer nicht so lange warten möchte, kann wie erwähnt bei manchen Modellen das Labor-Update zu FritzOS 8.40 installieren, das erste Funktionen von FritzOS 8.50 mit sich bringt. Beachte allerdings, dass es sich um Testversionen des Updates handelt, die noch Probleme bereiten können. Diese Modelle dürfen schon die finale Version von FritzOS 8.50 laden:
- Fritzbox DSL/Fiber 7-90 (direkt auf FritzOS 8.51)
- Fritzbox 7530 AX
- Fritzbox 7690
- Fritzbox 7682 (direkt auf FritzOS 8.51)
- Fritzbox 7630 (direkt auf FritzOS 8.51)
- Fritzbox 7632 (direkt auf FritzOS 8.51)
- Fritzbx 6690 (direkt auf FritzOS 8.51)
- Fritzbox 6690 Pro (direkt auf FritzOS 8.51)
- Fritzbox 6670 Cable (direkt auf FritzOS 8.51)
- Fritzbox 6660 Cable (direkt auf FritzOS 8.51)
- Fritzbox 5630
- Fritzbox 5690
- Fritzbox 5690 XGS (direkt auf FritzOS 8.51)
- Fritzbox 4690 (direkt auf FritzOS 8.51)
- Fritzbox 4630 (direkt auf FritzOS 8.51)
- Fritzbox 4050 (direkt auf FritzOS 8.51)
- Fritz Repeater 3000 AX (direkt auf FritzOS 8.51)
- Fritz Repeater 6000 (direkt auf FritzOS 8.51)
- Fritz Mesh Set 4200 (direkt auf FritzOS 8.51)
Was steckt in FritzOS 8.50?
Die größte Neuerung von FritzOS 8.50 ist ein DNS-Filter. Dadurch kannst du Werbeeinblendungen auf einer Vielzahl von Geräten im Netzwerk einfach ausblenden. Das gilt etwa für Smartphones, Tablets und verbundene Smart-TVs. Daneben bietet die Myfritz-App in Verbindung mit FritzOS 8.50 einen Smart Check. Darüber wird dir in der App der Status deiner Fritzbox und deines gesamten Netzwerks angezeigt. Die App gibt dir zusätzlich Empfehlungen, mit denen du dein Heimnetz verbessern kannst.
Ferner integriert Fritz mit FritzOS 8.50 eine automatische Priorisierung, die Echtzeitverbindungen wie Videoanrufe vor alle anderen Verbindungen stellt. Dadurch wird die nötige Bandbreite für Meetings und Co. freigegeben, falls andere Verbindungen die Leitung belasten. Für alle Smarthome-User:innen integriert FritzOS 8.50 vordefinierte Routinen wie beim Verlassen des Hauses. Bei selbsterstellten Routinen lassen sich künftig auch mehrere Auslöser festlegen und das Geofencing wurde verbessert.
Mit den Fritz Repeatern 3000 AX 6000 sind erstmals zwei WLAN-Verstärker unter den Update-Kandidaten. Anders als die zahlreichen Router profitieren die Gadgets unter anderem laut Winfuture jedoch nicht von neuen Funktionen. Demnach soll das Update vor allem Stabilitätsverbesserungen und Optimierungen beim Speicherbedarf liefern. Außerdem werde die Zusammenarbeit mit Amazon-Geräten und die WLAN-Stabilität beim Wechsel der Verbindungseinstellungen verbessert.

articles.title: Microsoft pushes Windows emergency updates to fix activation failures
articles.text:
Microsoft has released emergency out-of-band updates to fix Windows activation and licensing failures caused by this month's security updates.
As the company confirmed in a Wednesday service alert, this known issue affects organizations that use the Software Licensing Management Tool (SLMGR) command-line tool to automate Windows activation and licensing processes.
However, Microsoft said that enterprise customers who don't use SLMGR for licensing management and have the KMS client key installed in their image are unaffected.
"Devices that are already activated remain activated. Customers whose devices already have the appropriate KMS client key and KMS configuration, and who do not need to run the affected Slmgr.vbs commands, are not expected to be affected," the company noted.
On Friday, Microsoft released multiple emergency Windows updates to fix the bug on the following client (Windows 10 21H2/22H2 and Windows 11 23H2) and server (Windows Server 2019/2022/2025) platforms:
- Windows Server 2025: KB5136489
- Windows Server 2022: KB5136487
- Windows Server 2019 and Windows 10 Enterprise LTSC 2019: KB5136490
- Windows 11, version 23H2: KB5136483
- Windows 10, version 22H2 ESU and Windows 10 Enterprise LTSC 2021: KB5136493
For Windows Server 2025, Windows Server 2022, Windows Server 2019, and Windows 10, the out-of-band updates are available only through the Microsoft Update Catalog.
The Windows 11, version 23H2 optional OOB update is available through Windows Update and the Microsoft Update Catalog and can be installed from Settings > Windows Update > Advanced options > Optional updates to download.
"This cumulative update includes the improvements from the November 2026 Windows security update," Microsoft added. "For complete guidance and installation instructions, see the relevant KB articles."
In January, Microsoft resolved a similar issue that was causing Windows license migration failures during upgrades because impacted devices couldn't register with the Windows Activation server for digital licenses.
Last week, it also acknowledged that Windows updates released since the October Patch Tuesday are triggering SQL Server performance and stability issues and that the November 2026 Windows 11 security updates fail to install on systems with the October 2026 preview update.

La barre de son Sonos Arc Ultra Noir passe sous les 850 € chez Amazon soit une baisse d'environ 23% sur le prix habituellement constaté.
Barre de son pleine de finesse et de promesses, l’Arc Ultra est l’occasion pour Sonos de présenter une architecture audio inédite avec un woofer révolutionnaire en point d’orgue. Une formule diablement intrigante.

Points forts

- Expérience utilisateur intuitive.
- Écosystème multiroom riche.
- Possibilité d'ajouter un caisson de basses et/ou des satellites.

Malgré tout, sa connectique extrêmement dépouillée et sa gestion perfectible de la dimension Atmos la desservent face à des barres concurrentes, certes moins design et compactes, mais qui en proposent davantage pour un tarif équivalent.

articles.title: A tiny supercurrent could unlock quantum information without destroying it
articles.text:
A tiny supercurrent could unlock quantum information without destroying it
Scientists have developed a promising new method that could read quantum information with 99.85% accuracy while barely disturbing the qubit itself.
- Date:
- November 4, 2026
- Source:
- Fundação de Amparo à Pesquisa do Estado de São Paulo
- Summary:
- Researchers have proposed a breakthrough technique for reading quantum information without destroying the delicate states that make quantum computers work. By detecting an electrical signal generated by the qubit itself, their method achieved up to 99.85% accuracy in simulations and could make future quantum computers simpler and more efficient.
- Share:
One of the biggest obstacles in quantum computing is surprisingly simple to describe: how do you read information without changing or destroying it? Unlike the bits used in ordinary computers, quantum bits, or qubits, are extraordinarily sensitive to measurement. Trying to determine their state can cause that state to collapse, potentially erasing the very information scientists want to retrieve.
Researchers have now proposed a way to overcome much of this difficulty by using an unusual electrical signal produced by the qubit itself. Their approach focuses on a special type known as an "Andreev qubit," which can generate an oscillating electric supercurrent through its own quantum behavior. By monitoring this current, scientists may be able to determine the qubit's state without directly measuring it or significantly disturbing the information it contains.
The research, supported by FAPESP, was published in Physical Review B Letters. It was led by José Carlos Egues, a full professor at the São Carlos Institute of Physics at the University of São Paulo (IFSC-USP) in Brazil, and Yugui Yao of the School of Physics at the Beijing Institute of Technology in China. If experimentally confirmed, their method could simplify quantum computing by removing the need for extra qubits used in certain measurement techniques.
Why Measuring Quantum Information Is So Difficult
Conventional computers store information in bits that have one of two values, 0 or 1. These values can be checked repeatedly without changing the information. Quantum computers work differently because their qubits can exist in superpositions, meaning they can combine the states 0 and 1 in ways that are not possible with conventional bits.
This unusual ability is central to the potential power of quantum computing. However, it also creates a major vulnerability. Quantum states can be disrupted by interactions with their surroundings, including the instruments scientists use to examine them.
"In the conventional formulation of quantum mechanics, a projective measurement causes the system to assume one of the states associated with the measured quantity. Thus, if a qubit has been prepared in a certain superposition of 0 and 1, its direct measurement tends to destroy that superposition and, consequently, the information it contained," says Egues.
To minimize this problem, physicists developed techniques known as "quantum nondemolition measurements," or QND. Many of these approaches use an additional quantum system called an ancilla. Rather than measuring the original qubit directly, researchers transfer information to the ancilla and measure that auxiliary system instead.
The term "ancilla" comes from a Latin word meaning "slave" or "servant." In modern scientific usage, it describes something that performs a supporting function. Here, the ancilla acts as an intermediary, allowing researchers to obtain information while preserving the original qubit as much as possible.
Although effective, these procedures come with practical disadvantages. Scientists must prepare the auxiliary qubits, connect them to the qubits being studied, transfer information between them, and perform repeated measurements. These additional steps require time and equipment, and the complexity becomes increasingly significant as the number of qubits grows.
"Our strategy is different. Instead of transferring the information to an auxiliary qubit, we seek to obtain it from a signal produced by the qubit under study itself," says the researcher.
A Special Quantum Bit That Produces Its Own Signal
The proposed technique relies on the unusual properties of an Andreev qubit. Its name honors Soviet physicist Alexander Andreev (1939-2023), who identified a distinctive quantum process in 1964 that occurs where normal materials meet superconductors.
Superconductors are materials that can conduct electricity without electrical resistance under appropriate conditions. At the boundaries involving these materials, special quantum states known as "Andreev states" can form. In the system studied by the researchers, these states are confined to an extremely small region between two superconducting materials.
These quantum states can represent the basic values 0 and 1, along with superpositions of those values, making them suitable for storing quantum information.
"In the system under consideration, this region is a quantum dot - that is, a nanoscale structure in which electrons are spatially confined - formed in an indium arsenide [InAs] nanowire connected to superconducting materials on both sides. It's in this environment that the states characterizing the Andreev qubit are formed," Egues explains.
The key to the new approach is an electrical phenomenon called a "supercurrent." Unlike the current flowing through ordinary electrical conductors, a supercurrent moves without resistance.
The researchers found that when the Andreev qubit exists in a superposition, the supercurrent develops a component that oscillates over time. These fluctuations arise from quantum interference between the different states making up the superposition.
Crucially, the oscillations are not random. Their behavior contains information about the qubit's underlying quantum state, potentially allowing scientists to determine what that state is without directly measuring the qubit.
"It's precisely that property that we use to read the qubit. It's that supercurrent that lies at the heart of our proposal," the researcher points out.
How a Tiny Electrical Current Reveals Quantum Information
To understand how the technique works, it helps to consider how physicists describe a qubit's state mathematically.
One common representation is the "Bloch sphere," a geometric model in which every possible pure state of a single qubit corresponds to a point on the surface of a sphere. Two angles determine the location of that point.
The first angle describes how much each of the two basic states contributes to the superposition. The second describes their relative phase, which specifies how the quantum components are aligned with one another. Together, these two measurements provide the information needed to identify the qubit's state.
According to the new research, both pieces of information can be extracted from the supercurrent. Its steady component and the size of its oscillations reveal the relative contributions of the two basic states. Meanwhile, the timing of the oscillations provides information about their phase relationship.
"Our study showed that this information is encoded in the supercurrent itself. The supercurrent has a constant component and a fluctuating component. The value of the constant component and the amplitude of the oscillation reveal the proportion of each state (0 and 1) in the superposition, and the moment when that oscillation begins reveals the phase relationship between them. Thus, by measuring how the current varies over time, it's possible to reconstruct the initial state of the qubit," Egues explains.
This means the electrical current effectively carries a signature of the quantum information stored in the system. By observing how that signature changes over time, researchers could reconstruct the qubit's original state.
A Supercurrent That Oscillates Without Voltage
Another surprising feature of the proposed system is that the electrical current can oscillate without an externally applied voltage.
Ordinarily, producing an oscillating supercurrent in this type of superconducting system requires a voltage. This familiar phenomenon is called the "AC Josephson effect."
The researchers predict something different in their Andreev qubit. Here, the current's oscillations arise naturally from the qubit's own quantum evolution. No outside voltage is required to generate them.
"Our system generates a supercurrent that varies over time like an alternating current but without voltage. It's the very evolution of the qubit's state that produces that oscillation," says Egues.
This behavior is important because it transforms quantum activity occurring on an extraordinarily small scale into a detectable electrical signal. The current provides a connection between the microscopic world of quantum states and the larger physical systems scientists can measure.
That connection is what makes the proposed reading technique possible.
Detecting Quantum States With an Extremely Sensitive Sensor
The researchers envision placing the Andreev qubit inside a closed superconducting circuit, allowing its supercurrent to circulate continuously.
Next to the circuit would sit a SQUID (superconducting quantum interference device), a highly sensitive instrument capable of detecting extremely weak magnetic fields.
Whenever an electric current flows, it produces a magnetic field. Because the supercurrent in this system oscillates, the magnetic field it generates also changes over time.
The nearby SQUID could detect these tiny magnetic variations and use them to determine the behavior of the circulating current. Since the current contains information about the qubit's quantum state, the researchers could then reconstruct that state without measuring the qubit directly.
Egues compares the arrangement to two compasses that interact through a magnetic field.
"We can think of the qubit as one compass and the SQUID as another compass. The current in the circuit produces a magnetic field, and the SQUID 'senses' that field. Since the coupling between the two is very weak, the effect of the measuring instrument on the qubit tends to be very small."
The weak interaction between the sensor and the qubit is especially important. It offers a way to gather information while minimizing the disturbance that normally accompanies quantum measurements.
Reading Quantum Information With Almost No Disturbance
In quantum physics, observing a system is not necessarily a harmless process. A measuring instrument interacts with whatever it is attempting to measure, and that interaction can change the system's behavior.
This fundamental difficulty puzzled the earliest researchers studying quantum mechanics. It remains an unavoidable feature of quantum measurements today.
The proposed technique does not eliminate this effect entirely. The SQUID still interacts with the circuit, creating a small amount of feedback that can influence the qubit. However, the team's simulations suggest that this disturbance can be reduced to a level so small that it becomes effectively negligible.
"Our method doesn't eliminate the fundamental problem of quantum measurement. But it can approach the limit of a non-destructive readout and, at the same time, avoid the use of auxiliary qubits - the ancillas - employed in other non-destructive quantum measurement protocols," Egues notes.
The approach could also remove another complication found in some existing techniques. Because researchers would not need to restore the qubit to its original state after every measurement, they could make repeated observations as the state changes.
This would allow scientists to follow the qubit's quantum evolution over time, rather than obtaining information only through separate measurement and reset cycles.
Simulations Achieve Up to 99.85% Accuracy
To investigate whether the method could work outside ideal theoretical conditions, the researchers performed computer simulations designed to account for imperfections that would arise in real experiments.
These calculations included measurement noise, as well as the small amount of feedback introduced by the detection coil. The goal was to determine whether the qubit's state could still be reconstructed accurately despite these disturbances.
The results were encouraging. Depending on the number of measurements used, the simulations produced accuracies of 99.52%, 99.81%, and 99.85%.
According to the researchers, these values fall within the standard thresholds used in quantum error correction schemes, which are designed to manage errors in quantum information processing.
The findings suggest that the method could provide highly accurate quantum state reconstruction without the additional complexity of auxiliary qubits.
However, the technique has not yet been demonstrated experimentally. The results come entirely from theoretical analysis and computer simulations, so researchers still need to establish whether a physical device can achieve comparable performance.
Could This Make Quantum Computers Simpler?
Despite the lack of experimental confirmation, the researchers emphasize that their proposal does not depend on technologies that have yet to be invented.
The calculations use realistic properties drawn from existing quantum systems, and SQUID sensors are already established tools for detecting exceptionally weak magnetic fields and electric currents.
What remains to be built is the specific arrangement of components required to implement the proposed measurement technique.
"All the numbers we used are realistic. In principle, this can be achieved. In fact, we used parameters from existing systems in our calculations. What doesn't yet exist is that geometry, that setup that we proposed," he argues.
This makes the approach different from theoretical concepts that cannot be realized until scientists develop entirely new materials or manufacturing techniques. In principle, the necessary components already exist, although assembling them into the proposed configuration and demonstrating the predicted behavior remain important challenges.
The research offers two potentially significant advances.
From the standpoint of fundamental physics, it predicts that a qubit can produce an oscillating supercurrent resembling the AC Josephson effect, but without requiring an external voltage. Instead, the oscillations emerge from the qubit's own coherent quantum evolution.
From a technological perspective, the study shows how those oscillations could serve as a measurable signature of the qubit's internal state. By analyzing the electrical current, researchers could recover quantum information while causing very little disturbance to the system.
If future experiments confirm these predictions, the method could make reading Andreev qubits substantially simpler. Eliminating auxiliary qubits and repeated resets could reduce the equipment and procedures needed to retrieve quantum information.
More fundamentally, the work points toward an intriguing possibility: information hidden in the microscopic quantum world may be accessible through an electrical current produced by the quantum system itself, offering a promising new way to observe delicate quantum states without destroying them.

articles.title: NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 Achieves up to 2x Blackwell Ultra Performance in MLPerf Training v6.1 | NVIDIA Technical Blog
articles.text:
As AI agents tackle increasingly complex workflows, reducing time-to-train is critical for rapidly iterating on both models and the agents they power. MLPerf Training v6.1 marks the debut of the NVIDIA Vera Rubin architecture, and these early results demonstrate that its CUDA software stack is already highly mature. In its first appearance, the Vera Rubin NVL72 platform delivered the fastest time to train on six of the seven benchmarks, achieving up to 2x more performance than a highly optimized NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 baseline.
For the seventh benchmark, DeepSeek-V3 671B, NVIDIA captured the absolute fastest time of the round by demonstrating massive scale on a 10,240-GPU GB300 NVL72 cluster. This dual-platform approach deliberately showcases the strengths of both systems. While the GB300 results highlight the massive, reliable cluster scale NVIDIA is deploying today, Vera Rubin demonstrated its own exceptional scaling architecture by maintaining above 97% overall efficiency when scaling from 256 to 1,024 GPUs. Together, NVIDIA platforms hold the fastest time to train on every benchmark in v6.1.
NVIDIA platforms were also the only ones to submit results across all seven benchmarks, with Vera Rubin successfully completing the entire suite in its inaugural run. For developers, this breadth matters as much as any single top-line number. It proves that the performance gains inherited on day one span the entire modeling pipeline, comprehensively supporting everything from large-scale pretraining to the reinforcement learning post-training required for modern AI agents.
Comprehensive AI performance across all MLPerf training benchmarks
The simplest way to read this round is per benchmark: How much more performance does the new platform deliver per GPU on the same model?
| Model type | Benchmark | GPU Count | Vera Rubin NVL72 vs. optimized GB300 NVL72 | Submission ID (Vera Rubin / GB300) | 
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Mixture-of-Experts | DeepSeek-V3 671B | 1,024 | 2x | 6.1-0116 / 6.1-0030 | 
| Mixture-of-Experts | Qwen3.5 397B GRPO (RL) | 64 | 1.4x | 6.1-0135 / 6.1-0020 | 
| Mixture-of-Experts | gpt-oss 20B | 64 | 1.6x | 6.1-0135 / 6.1-0049 | 
| Dense | Llama 2 70B LoRA | 72 | 1.5x | 6.1-0123 / 6.1-0138 | 
| Dense | Llama 3.1 8B | 72 | 1.6x | 6.1-0073 / 6.1-0138 | 
| Diffusion | FLUX.1 | 72 | 1.5x | 6.1-0124 / 6.1-0138 | 
| Recommender | DLRMv4 | 128 | 1.4x | 6.1-0129 / 6.1-0038 |

The pattern is clear. The largest gain lands on the largest, most communication-heavy model. While the platform is consistently 1.4x to 1.6x faster across the rest of the suite, the generational advantage widens even further for the massive DeepSeek-V3 benchmark.
The suite covers natural language, image generation, recommendation, and reinforcement learning, so the gains hold across multiple modalities as well as across different model shapes and architectures.
DeepSeek-V3 671B: 2x per GPU on the hardest workload
DeepSeek-V3 671B is a 671-billion-parameter token-dropless Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model and the most demanding workload in the suite. Expert parallelism turns every iteration into a burst of all-to-all communication, so fabric efficiency shows up directly in time to train.
Vera Rubin NVL72 trained the benchmark in 4.14 minutes using 1,024 GPUs across 16 racks. GB300 NVL72 ran the identical 1,024-GPU configuration in 8.03 minutes, close to 2x per GPU, and the largest generational improvement in this round. Halving time to train roughly doubles how many experiments a team can run in a quarter, and experiment throughput is what moves model quality.
At a larger scale, GB300 NVL72 produced the fastest absolute result of the round: 1.38 minutes across 10,240 GPUs. That is one training job spread across 160 racks, each its own NVLink domain, and it shows the platform’s scale-out fabric holding up long after the job outgrows a single rack.
Post-training arrives, and Vera Rubin leads it
MLPerf Training v6.1 adds its first agentic LLM reinforcement learning post-training benchmark, Qwen 3.5 397B GRPO, reflecting a fundamental shift in AI development. Post-training has emerged as the critical differentiator for agentic accuracy, making the GRPO workload uniquely demanding. The continuous cycle of generating rollouts, scoring them, and updating weights pushes system architectures to their limits by forcing constant, massive weight migrations between inference and training engines.
Vera Rubin NVL72 achieved the fastest time for this new benchmark with a time of 10.44 minutes at 1,024 GPUs (6.1-0117), compared with 13.78 minutes for GB300 NVL72 (6.1-0031) at the same scale. The Vera Rubin platform also proved its flexibility by submitting on two different inference backends: NVIDIA NeMo RL with TensorRT-LLM at 10.44 minutes and with vLLM at 10.94 minutes (6.1-0118). Shipping two viable inference backends on a benchmark this new says as much about software maturity as it does about silicon.
Teaching these models to observe, reason, and act requires running each rollout in a simulated environment and executing tool calls, code, or API validations. Because driving these simulations is intensely CPU-bound, the NVIDIA Vera CPU is integral to the architecture, sustaining more than 22,500 concurrent RL environments across 256 CPUs in a single Vera CPU rack.
While the GPUs handle massive token generation and rapid weight updates, the Vera CPUs work in lockstep to simulate the environments, ensuring the accelerators are continuously fed with the rich feedback required to perfect agentic workflows.
NVLink, Quantum-X and Spectrum-X: Co-designed networking for high-efficiency AI scaling
Every result above is also a networking result. Modern AI training requires thousands of processors to act as one, a challenge NVIDIA solves by co-designing the internal rack domain and the external cluster fabric.
Inside the rack, Vera Rubin NVL72 connects 72 GPUs and 36 CPUs through a copper NVLink 6 spine. Delivering 3.6 TB/s per GPU and 260 TB/s per rack, this all-to-all domain keeps MoE expert dispatch off the critical path. Beyond the rack, the platform scales out via ConnectX-9 SuperNICs over Quantum-X800 InfiniBand or Spectrum-X Ethernet. To manage bursty MoE traffic, both fabrics use adaptive routing and congestion control to keep all-to-all communications hidden behind the compute layer.
This cohesive design translates directly to efficiency. On the DeepSeek-V3 benchmark, Vera Rubin NVL72 achieved above 97% scaling efficiency as it scaled from 256 to 1,024 GPUs (4 to 16 racks). GB300 NVL72 showcased the platform’s large-scale capabilities , extending to 10,240 GPUs to capture the fastest absolute result of the round.
Because the NVL72 architecture provides a consistent 72-GPU domain, developers see predictable performance jumps every generation without altering their operating model. Each cycle simply delivers more compute and bandwidth across the same consistent fabric.

See www.mlcommons.org for more information.
Continuous software optimization: Unlocking faster pretraining without hardware upgrades
Vera Rubin’s results came from the NVIDIA AI software stack that customers receive: NVIDIA NeMo Framework 26.09 for the pretraining benchmarks, NVIDIA NeMo RL for the reinforcement learning benchmark, and NVIDIA PyTorch releases for FLUX.1 and DLRMv4. The optimizations are the ones described in our MLPerf Training v6.0 round.
The stack also keeps moving after a round closes. Since v6.1 submissions were finalized, we have re-run several of the benchmarks on the same hardware and configuration with a newer software build. These are unverified results rather than MLCommons submissions, and we are sharing them because they show how continuous optimizations make NVIDIA infrastructure highly productive, durable, and fungible.

| gpt-oss 20B | 64 | 18.24 mins (6.1-0049) | 11.213 mins (6.1-0135) | 13.151 mins | 8.080 mins |

That is what a mature software stack means for customers. The infrastructure gets faster after it ships, and the improvements continue to arrive, extending the platform’s productive lifetime and revenue generating potential.
Because the CUDA platform is highly programmable, customers can unlock even more performance on their own. For example, Thinking Machines Lab developed an NVFP4 training recipe and custom kernels for its Inkling 2 Small model on GB300 NVL72, using NVFP4 for forward-pass MoE GEMMs and MXFP8 for gradients. Compared with full MXFP8 training, it sped up pretraining and fine-tuning by 8% and reinforcement learning by 20%, with minimal accuracy impact.
An ecosystem that shipped on day one
Vera Rubin’s debut in MLPerf Training v6.1 proves the architecture is built for immediate global deployment. With 80 percent of all closed-division submissions running on NVIDIA platforms across 20 partner organizations, these benchmarks represent reproducible performance across clouds and OEMs rather than isolated laboratory peaks.
Systems are already generally available across various cloud infrastructure partners, complementing a multitude of AI Factory deployments around the globe. Today, Vera Rubin leads on performance per GPU across all seven workloads, while Blackwell and Blackwell Ultra maintain the scale record. Azure’s 2,560-node, 10,240-GPU GB200 NVL72 submission tied the NVIDIA 10,240-GPU GB300 NVL72 run to claim this round’s largest clusters.
Partners are also pushing the limits of the architecture at the node level: Firmus used AI-driven kernel generation, with automated performance testing and mathematical validation, to post the fastest GB300 8-GPU result of the round, training GPT-OSS 20B in 52.90 minutes (6.1-0091) and Llama 3.1 8B in 52.40 minutes (6.1-0094). Because these platforms share a continuously optimizing CUDA software stack, developers can expect these inaugural metrics to climb steadily higher before the next MLPerf round even begins.
As the Vera Rubin software stack matures the way the Blackwell stack did, expect these initial performance advantages to continue to unlock even greater value throughout the platform’s lifecycle.
