articles.title: Nvidia presentará el 17 de noviembre sus primeros resultados sin Jensen Huang como director ejecutivo
articles.text:
Nvidia publicará el martes 17 de noviembre, después del cierre del mercado en Estados Unidos, los resultados de su tercer trimestre fiscal. Serán los primeros en 33 años sin Jensen Huang al frente: el cofundador renunció el 12 de noviembre como director ejecutivo, presidente y miembro del directorio.
La directora financiera, Colette Kress, es desde entonces la directora ejecutiva interina y mantiene su cargo anterior. El directorio busca un sucesor. La empresa informó que el informe y la conferencia con inversionistas se harán en la fecha prevista.
Los analistas consultados por Benzinga Pro, medio financiero estadounidense especializado en mercados, esperan ingresos de unos USD 109.000 millones y ganancias de USD 2,48 por acción. Nvidia había proyectado en agosto ventas de USD 108.000 millones, con un margen de error de 2%. En el trimestre anterior facturó USD 96.200 millones, según el análisis de la firma de inversión Pepperstone.
Las opciones, contratos con los que los inversionistas apuestan a la dirección de una acción, anticipan un movimiento de alrededor de 9,1% en el precio tras el informe, en cualquier sentido, según Benzinga.
Seis semanas de caídas y USD 1,8 billones menos
Las acciones de Nvidia bajaron 12,7% en la semana que terminó el 13 de noviembre y cerraron en USD 162,85. Es la sexta caída semanal consecutiva, la más larga desde octubre de 2012, según Benzinga. El precio está 31,9% por debajo del récord de USD 239,24 del 6 de octubre: unos USD 1,8 billones menos de valor de mercado.
Al menos seis firmas de análisis bajaron su recomendación sobre la acción el jueves y el viernes, entre ellas Truist, Melius Research, Oppenheimer y Bernstein. Bernstein redujo su precio objetivo de USD 400 a USD 200. HSBC recortó su calificación a “mantener”, con un objetivo de USD 170.
“El cambio de liderazgo, sin claridad sobre la sucesión, provocó una fuerte caída del valor de la acción”, escribió Frank Lee, jefe global de investigación de hardware y semiconductores de HSBC. En sentido contrario, James Demmert, director de inversiones de Main Street Research, dijo que “el camino está despejado para empezar a comprar”.
El analista de Bernstein Stacy Rasgon sostuvo que los fundamentos del negocio siguen intactos y que las cifras probablemente seguirán subiendo. Rick Schafer, de Oppenheimer, advirtió en cambio sobre una posible fuga de talento que afecte el ritmo de innovación de la empresa.
Margen, China y la proyección que los inversionistas esperan
La atención está puesta en la proyección para el trimestre siguiente. La consultora CMC Markets prevé que Nvidia anuncie ingresos cercanos a USD 125.000 millones. La firma superó el extremo alto de su propia proyección de ingresos en 8 trimestres consecutivos, según The Motley Fool.
Otro punto es el margen bruto, el porcentaje de cada dólar vendido que queda después de los costos de producción. La empresa proyectó 74% para este trimestre, frente a 75% del anterior, por el costo de la memoria de los chips. Kress advirtió que podría bajar a entre 71% y 72% en el cuarto trimestre.
China también estará en la conversación. La proyección de Nvidia excluye los ingresos de chips para centros de datos en ese país. El viernes, Bloomberg informó que una empresa china fundada por Alice Huang compró chips prohibidos instalados en un centro de datos de Shanghái.
Sobre el caso de Huang, el directorio dijo que no tiene motivos para creer que se hayan comprometido secretos de la empresa, según The Motley Fool. Nvidia presentará sus cifras el 17 de noviembre, después del cierre del mercado.

articles.title: Prise en main Honor Magic 9 Pro Max : ce détail de finition qui surclasse l’iPhone 18 Pro Max
articles.text:
Je n’aimais pas le design du Honor Magic 8 Pro. C’est comme ça. Cela doit être dit, et je sais, tous les goûts sont dans la nature, mais je préfère bien plus la proposition du nouveau Honor Magic 9 Pro Max que j’ai pu prendre en main en amont de son lancement en France.
Mieux que l’iPhone sur certains points
Oui, il est vrai, il emprunte beaucoup à l’iPhone. Jusqu’à son nom. Mais il a aussi l’intelligence de s’inspirer du niveau de finition de la marque à la pomme avec un corps unibody, comprendre d’un seul tenant entre le cadre et le dos du smartphone, plutôt réussi. Cela offre un confort premium en première prise en main que seul l’unibody peut offrir.
Il existe toutefois une différence notable, qui ne sautera pas forcément aux yeux. Les incises dans les tranches pour les antennes sont bien plus fines que la plupart des concurrents de ce Honor, y compris l’iPhone 18 Pro Max. Pour continuer sur la finesse, il faut saluer également celle exceptionnelle au niveau des bordures noires autour de l’écran. Un vrai régal. Dommage que ce bel écran quasi bord à bord soit perturbé par une pilule, nécessaire pour offrir un déverrouillage infrarouge. Là encore, toute ressemblance avec une autre marque est purement fortuite, bien sûr.
Partenariat avec Arri
Passons au module photo. Celui-ci marque déjà l’arrivée du nouveau partenariat photo de Honor avec l’apparition d’un nouveau logo Arri, du nom d’une marque de caméra très utilisée dans le cinéma hollywoodien.
Au niveau du design proprement dit, celui-ci est censé s’inspirer d’une caméra Arri justement, avec un énorme rond pour accueillir le téléobjectif arrière, le flash et le logo. Les deux autres modules profitant du reste du plateau pour se placer à droite en vertical. Pour les néophytes et amateurs de smartphone, cela s’inscrit surtout totalement dans la droite ligne des designs de téléphones chinois avec des modules volontairement visibles et protubérants.
Pour terminer le tour du propriétaire, mentionnons la présence toujours de boutons en plus de ceux consacrés au volume et au verrouillage. Nous avons toujours le bouton IA bien sûr, ainsi que le bouton déclencheur photo. Ce dernier est placé un peu trop à gauche pour son propre bien, de l’avis de plusieurs mains dans la rédaction.
L’ensemble est plutôt esthétique et réussi, avec une certaine dose de caractère. De façon tout à fait personnel, je trouve cela plus intéressant que le côté très plat et minimaliste du Honor Magic 8 Pro. Mieux vaut dans ce sens que dans l’autre pour Honor.

articles.title: Tor Updates DoS Defenses Again as Relay Attacks Continue
articles.text:
The Tor Project has released new security fixes for its core software as a distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attack continues to strain the volunteer-run relays that make up its network.
Tor 0.4.9.17, announced on November 13, patches several security issues. The project singled out one fix related to how relays’ built-in DoS protections deal with IPv6.
“This release comes in rapid response to the ongoing DDoS attack on the network, which has affected most relay operators. This is not an easy problem to address, as relays across the network are being overwhelmed by a massive flood of client circuits,” Tor developer David Goulet said in the announcement.
According to the project, more defenses are under consideration, and new versions should follow shortly. Anyone running a relay has been urged to update without delay.
The latest version comes less than three weeks after Tor 0.4.9.15, which introduced three DoS protections against what the project described as a “thunderstorm” of directory requests.
Writing to relay operators at the time, Goulet noted that a single relay could be hit with hundreds of circuits per second. He cautioned that relays would remain under heavy load for as long as the attack lasted.
Reports from relay operators suggest the latest update hasn’t ended the disruption. In a forum post on November 14, one operator said two of their relays had lost HSDir status due to attacks before the update, and that another was being targeted when 0.4.9.17 was released and installed.
Roughly ten minutes after that relay was upgraded, the attack took on a new form, according to the operator. Its traffic plunged and it kept becoming unresponsive.
“Relay unresponsiveness ultimately caused loss of HSDIR. Attack ceased immediately on loss of HSDIR,” the operator wrote.
In the operator’s view, 0.4.9.17 does not do enough to shield HSDir relays, and the attacker changes techniques while an attack is underway.
The operator also warned that the attacker could be capable of deanonymizing and tracking onion services. The Tor Project has issued no such warning in its release announcements.
Related: Firefox Vulnerability Allows Tor User Fingerprinting
Related: CryptoBandits Malware Doubles as a Backdoor, Abuses Tor
Related: Tor Exit Relays Hijacked

articles.title: Nubank agora é banco de fato • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Nubank agora é banco de fato
Antes exclusivamente digital, o roxinho tem aprovação do Banco Central para oficializar a denominação no país.
O Nubank agora pode ser chamado oficialmente de banco no Brasil. A empresa teve a aquisição do Banco Porto Real Investimentos S/A aprovada pelo Banco Central e passou a cumprir os requisitos que permitem a nomenclatura.
Na prática, a novidade não traz grandes mudanças para os clientes da instituição, mas serve como uma espécie de certificação de confiabilidade do BC. Agora, são três licenças vigentes para o Nubank, que já opera como Instituição Financeira e Corretora de Títulos e Valores Mobiliários por aqui.
Segundo o roxinho, o Brasil é seu maior mercado no mundo, e cerca de 31,5 milhões de pessoas passaram a acessar serviços financeiros pelo Nu. O banco também destacou sua atuação no atendimento ao cliente, com nove premiações consecutivas no Prêmio Reclame Aqui.
A definição de banco passa pela Resolução Conjunta nº 17, do Banco Central e do Conselho Monetário Nacional (CMN). O documento foi publicado em 2025 e dá conta da nomenclatura tanto para o nome empresarial quanto para o nome fantasia, além de marca e domínio de internet utilizado.
A principal vantagem para o Nu é a confiança que a novidade passa. Segundo Lívia Chanes, CEO do banco no Brasil e na América Latina, “confiança se constrói com transparência e respeito por quem escolhe o Nubank”. Ela afirma que a licença “reforça o compromisso” da instituição, sobretudo com o sistema financeiro nacional.
A empresa afirma que tem no país seu principal mercado, com R$ 45 bilhões investidos apenas em 2026. O Nubank também é filiado à Febraban desde março, além de ter alcançado a marca de segunda maior instituição financeira do Brasil em número de clientes – fica atrás apenas da Caixa, que é um banco público. A informação é de janeiro deste ano, quando o Nu passou da marca de 112 milhões de contas abertas.
O roxinho também destaca a economia dos clientes. Segundo comunicado publicado para celebrar a novidade, o banco afirma que foram economizados R$ 135,7 bilhões em tarifas e anuidade pelas contas cadastradas. Além do Brasil, o Nubank opera diretamente em países como México, Colômbia e Estados Unidos.

articles.title: The small African lab sounding the alarm on AI bioweapons
articles.text:
Out of curiosity, researchers at a small artificial intelligence lab in Accra, Ghana, removed the guardrails on their drug discovery AI model in 2024. They asked it to design toxins instead.
The model produced designs for 1,020 proteins and 5,000 small molecules. The researchers never made any of them in a lab, but software that predicts how poisonous a substance is scored all of them as likely toxic. Some of them resembled ricin, a deadly poison. The study was uploaded to the preprint server arXiv in May 2025.
“We were all shocked,” Darlington Akogo, founder of MinoHealth AI Labs, told Rest of World.
For Akogo, the results also raised a new question: If someone took designs like these to a company that makes DNA to order, would anyone stop them?
Across Africa, the need to regulate DNA synthesis providers is now echoing through the highest levels of government, Brenda Obuya, a senior official at Kenya’s Ministry of Information, Communications and the Digital Economy, told Rest of World.
Akogo has traveled the world warning that AI poses an existential bioweapons threat. He discussed it on the sidelines of the World Bank Group and International Monetary Fund Spring Meetings held in Washington, D.C., last year. He discussed the broader risk over dinner with Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates in 2023, whom he described as “on the fence” at the time. This year, Gates has issued numerous public warnings. “A.I. has crossed the threshold that its ability to empower a bioterrorist to kill hundreds of millions, that exists today,” he said on The Ezra Klein Show in September. The study has been discussed within Interpol, showing just how far it has reached.
“I think the fact that the Ghanaian AI lab examined this and highlighted the potential for misuse shows that African institutions are contributing to … potentially to the governance [of AI],” Adam Abdullahi, a fellow at the International Biosecurity and Biosafety Initiative for Science, told Rest of World.
LLMs have become even more capable since the study came out and the barrier for entry has lowered, Ayantola Alayande, a researcher at the Global Center on AI Governance, told Rest of World. “It wouldn’t be a surprise now to see even … [lay] users generate this sort of output via chatbots.”
Dual use
Scholars have long warned about AI’s bioweapons threat, but it is only recently that AI systems have truly outperformed Ph.D.-level biologists.
In 2022, scientists at a U.S. drug company ran a similar experiment as the MinoHealth team. They built a generative machine learning software that produced designs for possible chemical weapons.
What is different with the MinoHealth Lab study, Akogo said, is the kind of AI involved. His team used a general purpose LLM trained for biology and drug discovery.
Researchers have since gotten a number of LLMs to drop their inbuilt safeguards in a process called “jailbreaking”, and generated bioweapons advice and other kinds of hazardous content. This includes Kimi, by the Chinese company Moonshot AI; Grok; Claude; and ChatGPT, said Peter Garraghan, founder of AI security company Mindgard. All it takes is persistence and creativity with language to learn how to phrase requests to the model, he told Rest of World.
“You don’t need to be a technical expert to do jailbreaking,” he said. It took his team one day to break Kimi.
SpaceXAI, Anthropic, OpenAI, and Moonshot did not respond to a request for comment.
The latest AI models have stronger safeguards, particularly when it comes to biological misuse requests, but even these are not foolproof, according to the AI Security Institute, a U.K. government research organization.
The danger became more real this September when Anthropic reported five cases where people tried to use its AI models in ways that could support biological weapons development. Bioweapons are now the top AI misuse risk, according to Ken McCallum, director general of MI5, the U.K.’s intelligence agency. “The misuse case to which I’d attach greatest weight – is AI’s potential to change the stakes on existing or even new bioweapons,” he said.
All-in-one health AI model
When Akogo founded MinoHealth Labs in 2016, he wasn’t worried about bioweapons. Rather, he wanted to make care available to all by solving Ghana’s health worker shortage using AI.
That goal took Akogo to the edge of AI development in 2022, when his team began work on an LLM named Moremi AI. A year later, they received $149,533 from the Gates Foundation to build a foundation model that can analyze medical images for radiologists. The model would eventually process both text and images, answer medical questions, help interpret scans, and draft reports. It would also help design drugs.
The ambition is similar in scope to top Silicon Valley labs such as OpenAI and Anthropic, Leo Anthony Celi, a principal research scientist at the MIT Laboratory of Computational Physiology, told Rest of World. In October 2025, Anthropic launched Claude for Life Sciences, and this April, Open AI launched GPT-Rosalind. Both are AI tools developed to accelerate biology research and drug discovery. Investment in AI powered drug discovery reached $8.4 billion in 2025, more than double the $4.1 billion invested in 2023, according to a 2026 McKinsey report.
MinoHealth has a fraction of these resources and a 20-member team working in a modest bungalow in Accra that is the anti-thesis of Silicon Valley’s futuristic campuses.
In the early days, Akogo had sleepless nights. He worried his competitors were better funded, and had more talent. But he has since decided there is room for multiple companies working on specific use cases.
“I have a small team of extremely capable people so if that means we’re punching above our weight, I guess … it’s just more exciting,” he said.
When his team tested their model, Moremi Bio, in 2024 to see if it could be made to ignore safeguards, it took them only a few days, Akogo recalled. Few people back then knew that biology LLMs’ could have a dual purpose, so he decided to publish his findings. “To the best of our knowledge, [looking at published studies], this was the first time anyone was showing that LLMs specifically could design biological weapons,” he said.
AI models shouldn’t be able to design potential bioweapons, Abdullahi said. “The whole idea of putting guardrails is that it should never really kind of get to that stage, so to speak.”
Synthesis
Bad actors could potentially send the bioweapon designs to DNA synthesis labs to make the molecules. Although some labs screen orders for potentially toxic sequences, this process could be hacked by a malicious actor using AI, Akogo said.
In June, the heads of OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google DeepMind joined a call for U.S. lawmakers to make such checks mandatory.
Governments across Africa recognize that open-source frontier models have lowered the technical barrier to generate toxins, said Obuya from Kenya’s Ministry of Information, Communications and the Digital Economy. Cloud laboratories and AI models have created a need for regulation, she said. Intelligence agencies are setting up specialized desks to track threats at the “intersection of cyber defense and biology,” she said.
As AI design tools develop, screening must keep pace, Sandra Roy, program manager at the International Gene Synthesis Consortium, a voluntary group of nucleic acid providers, told Rest of World. They support legislation that would mandate screening across the nucleic acid supply chain, she said.
“We are also working with model developers to strengthen our ability to detect AI-designed sequences that may be engineered to evade screening, and we will keep updating our tools as the threat evolves,” she said.
AI for healthcare
Moremi Bio is currently good at a few things. For instance, it has proposed hundreds of drug candidates for diseases such as cancer, tuberculosis, and dengue. The team is now working as part of a European Union-funded consortium to develop monoclonal antibodies and diagnostics for mpox and malaria. The company is predominantly funded through sales of its AI system, Akogo said.
The promise of AI in healthcare and biology aside, Akogo continues to raise the alarm over AI risks, especially bioweapons. He believes the United Nations should set up a dedicated working group to study the risks of AI. He also suggested tighter controls over synthesis. His goal isn’t to scare people, but rather, to balance AI optimism with caution.
“I think there’s several things we can do that could limit and minimize those dangers,” he said.

articles.title: Mercedes-Benz takes on Tesla FSD with new point-to-point city driving assist
articles.text:
Mercedes-Benz is tossing its hat into the partial autonomy ring with the launch of two new features next year: hands-free highway driving and a point-to-point city navigation system. The new features will put the German automaker in competition with Tesla, which is currently leading the auto industry in the development of hands-free systems.
Mercedes-Benz takes on Tesla FSD with new point-to-point city driving assist
After pausing its Level 3 system, Mercedes-Benz is rolling out two new Level 2 driver-assistance features in 2027—starting with a California early access program next month.
Mercedes’ point-to-point driver assist feature, called MB.Drive Assist Pro, will handle most of the driving on local roads and in dense, urban traffic. Once a destination is plugged into the vehicle’s navigation, the system assists across the entire route, handling highway exits, lane changes, intersections, and traffic lights. But unlike Tesla’s Full Self-Driving, MB.Drive Assist Pro requires that drivers keep their hands on the wheel while navigating through cities.
The system is powered by 27 sensors (10 cameras, 5 radars, 12 ultrasonic sensors) and a high-performance computer capable of 254 TOPS running on the new MB.OS architecture. That computer runs on Nvidia’s Drive AV stack, blending pure AI with a deterministic “Halos” safety guardrail layer. (We got to experience the point-to-point system as a passenger during a demonstration in San Francisco last year.)
Unlike FSD, MB.Drive Assist Pro requires that drivers keep their hands on the wheel while navigating through cities.
The Hands-Free Highway Assist, meanwhile, works similarly to GM’s Super Cruise or Ford’s BlueCruise, in that drivers are able to take their hands off the steering wheel when driving on approved, controlled-access highways. The highway assist can also handle speeds of up to 85 mph, which is a big jump from Mercedes’ previous generation Drive Pilot’s 40 mph limit. It also includes Proactive Lane Change Assist, which automatically initiates lane changes to pass slower cars or follow navigation toward an exit.
Earlier this month, a number of journalists got to test out the new features in San Francisco. InsideEVs called it a “real challenger” to Tesla FSD, praising how confidently and predictably it handled double-parked trucks, construction zones, and pedestrians during a 25-minute downtown loop. The Drive noted that the system’s “confidence and fluidity” felt more assured than rival systems. And Verge contributor Tim Stevens (writing for Endgadget) said it handled jaywalkers, cyclists, and sudden U-turns “without issue” and took the stress out of city driving.
Mercedes will begin rolling out both features via an invite-only access program in California next month, ahead of a broader nationwide launch in 2027 — with highway assist arriving in the spring. Eligible vehicles include the CLA Electric, GLC Electric, GLE, GLS, and S-Class, with more vehicles to follow in 2028. While Mercedes hasn’t announced exact pricing yet, eligible owners will be able to unlock the software over the air through the automaker’s online store using one-month, one-year, or three-year subscription plans.
The launch of the new features comes after Mercedes paused development of a Level 3 system, in which drivers can take their eyes off the road, in addition to their hands off the wheel, during certain approved stretches of highway. By pivoting to hands-free highway driving and point-to-point city navigation, Mercedes is betting that its Nvidia-powered, Level 2 features will have more wide appeal — and less regulatory resistance.

articles.title: Use prompt caching with open-weight models on Amazon Bedrock | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Use prompt caching with open-weight models on Amazon Bedrock
Many generative AI applications send the same long context with every request, and prompt caching avoids processing it again each time. That context can be a system prompt, reference documents, tool definitions, or the conversation so far. Open-weight models on Amazon Bedrock can reuse it across requests, which helps reduce input costs and response latency.
Prompt caching reuses the computed state of a matching prompt prefix, so repeated context is read from cache instead of being processed again. Amazon Bedrock manages the cache for you. Depending on the model, you can use implicit caching, which works automatically, explicit caching, where you mark the reusable prefix, or both. The more context you reuse, and the more often you reuse it, the more you can save.
As with other models on Amazon Bedrock, your prompts and outputs aren’t shared with the model provider or used to train models. For more information, see Data protection in the Amazon Bedrock User Guide.
Open-weight models on Amazon Bedrock now support explicit prompt caching. In this post, we use both modes with an open-weight model through the Chat Completions API and show how to read cache usage from each response. We then apply implicit caching to an OpenCode coding agent session on the same API and close with best practices.
Prompt caching for open-weight models on Amazon Bedrock
When a request starts with the same content as an earlier one, Amazon Bedrock reads that prefix from cache and processes only the rest. Cache reads are billed at a lower rate than standard input, so the savings can grow each time a prefix is reused. Depending on the model, cache writes can be billed at a higher rate than standard input. See Amazon Bedrock pricing for the rates of each model.
Supported modes depend on the model and the API. For each model’s caching modes, minimum prefix length, and how long entries stay cached, see Models at a glance. The two modes compare as follows:
| Feature | Implicit caching | Explicit caching | 
| Request changes | None | On the Chat Completions API, prompt_cache_options with mode set to explicit, plus one or more prompt_cache_breakpoint markers | 
| What is cached | Eligible prefixes, selected automatically on a best-effort basis | Content up to and including each breakpoint | 
| Good fit | Prompts that already start with a stable prefix, such as conversations and agent loops | A fixed shared prefix with a changing question, or layered prefixes that you want to control | 
Implicit caching: Amazon Bedrock reuses eligible prefixes automatically, on a best-effort basis. In a conversation, each request resends the full context, so the previous request becomes the cached prefix of the next one (Figure 1). As the prompt caching guide recommends, put static content first and dynamic content last. Keeping the start of the prompt stable lets every later request reuse it. If an early part changes, as in turn 4 of Figure 1, the cache is rebuilt from that point.
Explicit caching: You mark the end of each reusable prefix with a cache breakpoint. You can add several breakpoints, up to the maximum that the model supports, to cache layers that change at different rates, as Figure 2 shows. Content up to each breakpoint is written to cache once and then read on later requests, and content after the last breakpoint is processed on each request. Check the model card for the minimum token count before a breakpoint, the maximum number of breakpoints, and the time to live (TTL), which resets with each cache hit.
With implicit caching, Amazon Bedrock can also write content to cache that later requests never reuse, such as a question that’s different each time. When the content after a shared prefix changes on every request, use explicit caching to limit cache writes to the shared prefix. Content after the last breakpoint is billed at the standard input rate. On models that charge more for cache writes, you don’t pay the higher write rate for content that’s never read back.
Solution overview
The following diagram shows how both examples in this post reach Amazon Bedrock through the same Chat Completions API endpoint.
- The Python application and the OpenCode coding agent send requests to the Amazon Bedrock Runtime endpoint in your Region, authenticated with a short-term Amazon Bedrock API key.
- Amazon Bedrock checks the prompt cache for a matching prefix. It reads a matching prefix from cache, and writes new cacheable content to cache.
- Amazon Bedrock sends the request to the selected open-weight model and returns the response, including the cache usage fields that the following sections show you how to read.
Prerequisites
To run the samples, you need the following:
- An AWS account with access to your selected model on Amazon Bedrock. Model availability and prompt caching support vary by AWS Region, so check the model card for the Regions that your model supports.
- AWS credentials for an AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) identity that has permission to invoke your selected model on Amazon Bedrock.
- Python 3.12 with the openai (3.26.0 or later) and aws-bedrock-token-generator (1.1.0 or later) packages.
- For the coding agent example, npm to install OpenCode 1.18.35.
Before you use a model, review its license and service terms, linked from its model card. Your use of the model is also subject to the AWS Responsible AI Policy.
Cache a product manual through the Chat Completions API
The example is a support assistant for a fictional water filter, the AnyCompany AquaPure 500. The system prompt holds a one-line instruction and the owner’s manual, which is the reusable prefix. Each request asks a different customer question.
Set up the client
The samples use the OpenAI Python SDK with the Amazon Bedrock Chat Completions endpoint. For authentication, the provide_token() function from the aws-bedrock-token-generator package turns your AWS credentials into a short-term Amazon Bedrock API key, valid for up to 12 hours. You don’t need to create or store a long-term key.
1. Create a virtual environment and install the packages:
2. Create the manual. Ours is about 4,000 tokens of Markdown. The following excerpt shows its format:
Save it as manual.md and add sections until it’s longer than the minimum prefix length on your model card. Placeholder text works, because the cache only needs an identical prefix. Keep the three sections shown, which answer the sample questions.
3. Save the following setup code as common.py in the same directory. The samples that you create next import from it.
If your model returns reasoning tokens, they count toward max_tokens. The samples set max_tokens=1024 so that short answers have room to finish.
Implicit caching
Implicit caching takes no cache controls. Put the manual in the system message and the question in the user message. Sending both as parts of one user message got no implicit cache hits. Save the following as implicit.py and run it with python implicit.py:
Verify implicit caching
Each response reports cache activity in usage.prompt_tokens_details. Figure 4 shows how to read these fields and the pattern to expect across the three calls of each sample.
In implicit mode, call 1 writes the prompt to cache. Calls 2 and 3 read the system message, with the instruction and the manual, back from cache. They also write a few tokens each, because implicit mode extends the cached prefix to cover each new question. A few tokens after the last message stay uncached on every call. This is the pattern for the first run. If you run the sample again within the TTL, every call reads from cache, and none writes.
Explicit caching
Choose explicit caching to control exactly what is cached. As Figure 4 shows, calls 2 and 3 of the implicit run each write a few tokens to cache, whereas the same calls with explicit caching write nothing. With several breakpoints, you can cache layered prefixes, such as shared instructions and tools followed by a per-customer document (Figure 2).
For explicit caching, add the following to the request:
- prompt_cache_options with mode set to explicit selects explicit mode. It’s an Amazon Bedrock request field, and the OpenAI SDK sends it through extra_body.
- prompt_cache_breakpoint on a text content part marks the end of the reusable prefix. Content up to and including that part is cached, and content after it’s processed again on every request.
Save the explicit version of the same loop as explicit.py:
Set both parts together. Explicit mode without a breakpoint caches nothing, and a breakpoint without explicit mode behaves like implicit caching. For the optional ttl field of prompt_cache_options, check the model card for supported values.
Verify explicit caching
If you run explicit.py right after implicit.py, its first call is already a cache hit. For a cold first call, add a unique first line to the system prompt, for example SYSTEM_PROMPT = f"Run ID: {uuid.uuid4()}\n" + SYSTEM_PROMPT (with import uuid at the top of explicit.py).
As the explicit bars in Figure 4 show, only the first call writes. Each repeat reads the whole prefix up to the breakpoint and writes nothing, and the question after the breakpoint makes up the uncached remainder.
Use prompt caching with the OpenCode coding agent
Coding agents resend a large, stable prefix on every step: the system prompt, tool definitions, and the conversation so far. That makes them a natural fit for implicit caching. OpenCode is an open source coding agent. It can call any Chat Completions endpoint through a custom OpenAI-compatible provider, so it can use the same Amazon Bedrock endpoint as the Python samples. Figure 5 shows the requests that OpenCode sends during one turn and which parts Amazon Bedrock reads from cache.
In one turn, OpenCode sends request 1 with its system prompt, tool definitions, and your prompt, and Amazon Bedrock writes it to cache. The model responds with a tool call, which OpenCode runs on your machine. OpenCode then sends request 2, which contains request 1 plus the tool call and its result. Amazon Bedrock reads request 1 from cache, writes only the new tail, and returns the response.
Configure OpenCode
Install OpenCode and check the version:
Next, add the following opencode.json to the root of your repository, or save it as ~/.config/opencode/opencode.json to apply it to every project. It defines a provider named bedrock that uses the OpenAI-compatible package to call the Amazon Bedrock Chat Completions endpoint:
OpenCode uses small_model for session titles, so pointing it at the same model keeps every request on a model that you’ve enabled. The provider reads its key from BEDROCK_API_KEY. Set it to a short-term Amazon Bedrock API key from provide_token(), in the virtual environment from the first example. If the key expires, run the command again to get a new one:
Confirm that OpenCode lists the model:
Verify implicit caching in a coding session
We ran a three-turn session against a small repository that holds one short Python file. Turn 1 asks for a bug review, turn 2 for a fix, and turn 3 for a short follow-up:
Replace <sessionID> with the sessionID value from the JSON output of turn 1. The opencode export <sessionID> command lists each request’s token usage: cache.read holds the cached_tokens value from Amazon Bedrock, and input holds the rest. OpenCode 1.18.35 doesn’t record cache_write_tokens for an OpenAI-compatible provider, so cache.write stays at 0.
Figure 6 shows how much of each request in the session is read from cache.
The first request processes the whole prompt, most of it the OpenCode system prompt and tool definitions, and Amazon Bedrock writes it to cache. Each later request reads everything up to the end of the previous request from cache, so only the new tail of the conversation is processed. This works with no caching configuration.
Best practices
These practices apply to any model that supports prompt caching:
- Put static content first, in both modes. Place the system prompt, tool definitions, and reference documents before content that changes, and keep them identical between requests. In explicit mode, place each breakpoint after the static content that it covers. Timestamps and request IDs belong at the end of the prompt.
- Make the prefix long enough. Prefixes that meet the minimum token count on the model card are eligible for caching.
- Confirm hits with the usage fields. Check the cache reads and writes in each response, in either mode. Across a workload, track the CacheReadInputTokenCount and CacheWriteInputTokenCount runtime metrics.
- Keep the cache warm. Steady traffic keeps a prefix cached, because the TTL resets with each hit. After an idle gap longer than the TTL, the next request writes the prefix again.
- Cache what you reuse. Savings come from cache reads, so cache content that later requests read again, especially where cache writes cost more than standard input. With cross-Region inference, expect some extra cache writes at times of high demand.
Clean up
The examples make inference calls only and create no resources in your AWS account. Cache entries expire after they go unread for the TTL. The short-term API key from provide_token() also expires on its own, and the samples never write it to disk. To clear it from your shell sooner, run unset BEDROCK_API_KEY.
To remove the local files:
1. Delete the sample directory and its Python virtual environment.
2. Delete opencode.json from your repository, or ~/.config/opencode/opencode.json if you saved it globally.
3. If you no longer need OpenCode, delete ~/.local/opt/opencode.
Conclusion
Prompt caching lets open-weight models on Amazon Bedrock reuse repeated context with little or no change to your code. In this post, implicit caching covered the support assistant and the OpenCode session with no cache settings at all. Explicit caching gave precise control with one request option and a breakpoint for each reusable layer. In every case, the usage fields on each response show what came from cache, so you can measure the benefit on your own traffic.
To get started, choose an open-weight model on Amazon Bedrock that supports prompt caching. Run the samples from this post with your own reference content, and compare the cache reads with your uncached input. The prompt caching guide covers the limits and options for each model, and the Amazon Bedrock runtime metrics let you track cache reads and writes across your applications. For questions, reach out through AWS Support or the AWS re:Post community.

articles.title: Did Canada lose its AI chip champions?
articles.text:
Last month, Toronto-founded AI chip maker Tenstorrent announced a whopping $1.5-billion USD Series E round. I say Toronto-founded because the company quietly relocated to the US in 2023 to support its fundraising and IPO goals. With over $2 billion USD in funding announced since, the move appears to have paid off.
Tenstorrent still has some 200 employees in Toronto, and hasn’t forgotten its Canadian roots. The Logic reported this week that the company has lobbied the federal government for sovereign AI contracts and funding for large-scale data centre buildouts.
Every company should be expected to make decisions in its own best interests. But Tenstorrent’s gentle tap dance back and forth across our southernmost border when it benefits them shines a light on a murky question: what makes a company Canadian?
Noting that the feds’ Buy Canadian Policy currently allows for, say, Walmart Canada, the policy wonks at The Canadian Shield Institute have argued for a revised definition in BetaKit. The think tank also recently asserted the perils of considering companies like Tenstorrent Canadian enough: “If any company, headquartered anywhere on earth, can qualify for funding because its lobbyists point to some operations here or some historic association with Canada, then economic development policy will become meaningless.”
This week, I interviewed AI Minister Evan Solomon about the federal government’s investment in Cohere. The interview will be released soon, but Tenstorrent came up. The minister said his job was to give tech companies reasons not to leave, using levers like compute, customers, and capital (i.e., why Tenstorrent said it left). But he also seemed OK with now-foreign entities continuing to hire and do business in Canada. “We want that,” he said. “They’re investing in Canadian talent.”
Successful economic development policy requires striking the tricky balance between short-term realities and long-term priorities. In the midst of Nvidia’s historic, shareholder-value-destroying self-own, it seems possible that Tenstorrent (or Untether AI or Taalas—both sold to AMD) could have been federally anointed an AI champion like Cohere had they stayed. The feds still might, but would Tenstorrent really be a sovereign selection? And if not, would it matter?
Douglas Soltys,

articles.title: VIDÉO : Recalé au contrôle antipollution, il pirate le calculateur de sa Jeep de 1994 avec deux IA et réussit son coup
articles.text:
Depuis quelques semaines, Muhammad Zulali faisait face à un problème.
Sa Jeep Cherokee de 1994 échouait au contrôle antipollution californien, obligatoire pour renouveler l’immatriculation, et chaque nouveau passage chez le technicien lui coûtait une centaine de dollars.
Plutôt que de continuer à changer des pièces au hasard, celui qui précise ne pas être mécanicien a passé près d’une semaine à faire travailler deux agents de programmation sur le calculateur moteur, d’abord Claude Code d’Anthropic, puis Codex d’OpenAI.
Il a raconté l’expérience dans une vidéo YouTube publiée le 10 novembre, qui a frôlé 1,5 million de vues en moins d’une semaine. Un succès que l’on doit également au résultat de l’expérience : la Jeep a fini par réussir son contrôle.
Une voiture trop ancienne pour les outils de diagnostic actuels
Avant que son propriétaire ne se lance dans cette expérience folle, le problème avait bien été identifié. Au palier de 25 mph (environ 40 km/h), la Jeep rejetait trop d’oxydes d’azote (NOx), des polluants qui se forment quand le moteur reçoit trop d’air par rapport au carburant.
Le propriétaire a d’abord remplacé la sonde lambda, qui mesure l’oxygène dans l’échappement, mais la voiture a alors échoué dès le palier de 15 mph (environ 24 km/h).
Pour comprendre ce qui se passait dans le moteur, il fallait interroger le calculateur, ce qui n’a rien d’évident sur un modèle de 1994. Le véhicule est antérieur à la norme OBD-II, qui permet aujourd’hui de brancher un simple lecteur sous le volant, et l’outil de diagnostic de Chrysler de l’époque est presque introuvable.
C’est pour pallier cette limite que Muhammad Zulali s’est tourné vers Claude Code. L’agent d’Anthropic a identifié le protocole de communication de la voiture, un format ancien et lent baptisé SCI.
Pour faire dialoguer le calculateur et l’ordinateur portable, une carte Arduino Nano a suffi. Ce petit circuit électronique programmable, vendu environ 3 dollars, a été installé sur une platine d’expérimentation, une plaque qui permet de relier des composants sans soudure. Le premier essai n’a rien donné, car une résistance affaiblissait trop le signal. Sur les conseils de Claude, le vidéaste l’a retirée et a obtenu sa première lecture à 1 h 30 du matin. Il ne s’agissait que de la température du liquide de refroidissement et de la tension de la batterie, mais il avait enfin l’espoir de diagnostiquer la panne au lieu de changer des pièces au hasard.
Claude a pris la main sur la pompe à carburant
Reste que les premières mesures semblaient incohérentes. D’après Claude, l’ordinateur de bord injectait 22 % d’essence en plus de la normale. Or un moteur qui reçoit davantage d’essence ne devrait pas rejeter trop de NOx, puisque ces polluants apparaissent justement quand il en manque. Pour en avoir le cœur net, Muhammad Zulali a pris la route avec son ordinateur portable sur le siège passager pendant que Claude enregistrait tout ce que la voiture transmettait. En poursuivant ses vérifications le lendemain, il a constaté que l’essence arrivait au moteur avec une pression anormalement faible.
Claude a alors proposé d’allumer lui-même la pompe à essence. Sceptique, le propriétaire l’a laissé essayer, et l’agent a fait tourner la pompe une dizaine de secondes, jusqu’à ce que le vidéaste, inquiet, lui demande d’arrêter. « C’était la première fois que Claude faisait réellement quelque chose à l’intérieur de l’ordinateur pour provoquer un changement », a-t-il expliqué. Jusque-là, l’IA s’était contentée de lire des données.
Après d’autres essais, Claude a compris que la piste était fausse. Le logiciel utilisé pour traduire les données de ce modèle, Chrysler Scanner, les interprétait à l’envers, et l’ordinateur de bord retirait en réalité de l’essence au lieu d’en ajouter.
Claude a donc copié et passé au crible le programme de l’ordinateur de bord. Il a découvert que la Jeep tournait avec une version conçue pour la Californie, qui réduisait légèrement la dose d’essence précisément dans les conditions du contrôle antipollution. Impossible pourtant d’installer une autre version, car le boîtier avait été fabriqué quatre mois avant que Chrysler ne le rende reprogrammable.
Codex, l’agent de programmation d’OpenAI, a alors trouvé un moyen de contourner l’obstacle en faisant tourner son propre code à l’intérieur de l’ordinateur de bord. Après plusieurs tentatives, la Jeep a été validée, sans que la vidéo précise exactement ce que ce code a modifié. Muhammad Zulali assure s’être contenté des branchements et de la conduite, sans mécanicien ni outil de concessionnaire.
Entre fascination et crainte
Sur Hacker News, plusieurs commentateurs ont surtout été frappés par le fait que Muhammad Zulali ait laissé Claude actionner directement la pompe à essence. Un ingénieur travaillant sur des robots quadrupèdes a expliqué que son équipe interdisait aux agents de piloter du matériel sans autorisation, notamment au moyen de fichiers d’instructions. D’autres ont rappelé qu’une consigne écrite ne suffit pas toujours. Pour une protection réelle, il faut des verrous techniques, comme un environnement isolé sans accès au matériel ou un bouton d’arrêt d’urgence physique.
La vague d’inquiétude ne s’est pas arrêtée là. Un autre utilisateur a raconté que Claude avait fait tomber l’ABS et l’antipatinage de sa voiture alors qu’elle roulait, sur un circuit qu’il présentait comme sécurisé. Selon lui, ces modèles alternent entre coups de génie et erreurs grossières en électronique automobile, il les chiffre, un peu arbitrairement, à 30 % et 70 %.
De son côté, Zulali encourage son public à refaire l’expérience. Il a publié le code et le schéma de câblage sur GitHub, tout en précisant qu’il s’agit d’un projet amateur, à utiliser à ses risques et périls.

articles.title: 450 € de rabais : la Galaxy Tab S10+ de Samsung tombe à 699 € pour le pré-Black Friday — Frandroid
articles.text:
Le 30 septembre dernier, Samsung a présenté ses nouvelles tablettes tactiles Android haut de gamme : les Galaxy Tab S12 Ultra et Galaxy Tab S12+. Mais les anciennes générations n’ont pas perdu tout leur intérêt, d’autant que les tarifs ont naturellement bien baissé depuis leur sortie. Par exemple, la Samsung Galaxy Tab S10+, dévoilée il y a deux ans, reste tout à fait recommandable, grâce à son grand écran, ses fonctionnalités Galaxy AI ou encore son prix, qui ne dépasse pas les 700 euros pendant le pré-Black Friday.
Pourquoi la Samsung Galaxy Tab S10+ vaut encore le coup
- Pour sa grande dalle Amoled de 12,4 pouces + 120 Hz
- Pour sa puce Dimensity 9300+
- Pour Galaxy AI
Lancée à 1 149,99 euros, la Samsung Galaxy Tab S10+ (Wi-Fi, 256 Go) est aujourd’hui disponible en promotion à 699,99 euros à la Fnac et chez Darty.
Si, par la suite, l’offre mentionnée dans cet article n’est plus disponible, merci de jeter un coup d’œil ci-dessous afin de dénicher d’autres offres concernant la Samsung Galaxy Tab S10 Plus. Le tableau s’actualise automatiquement.
Une tablette bien solide
Comme la nouvelle Galaxy Tab S12+, la S10+ est certifiée IP68. Cette tablette haut de gamme de 2024 est donc bien solide, ne craint pas la poussière et peut résister à une immersion dans l’eau douce jusqu’à 1,5 mètre de profondeur pendant 30 minutes. En revanche, elle n’a pas été pensée pour être emportée à la plage ou à la piscine. Cette ardoise présente par ailleurs un design élégant, avec son châssis en aluminium aux tranches plates, qui devrait offrir une bonne prise en main.
Côté écran, Samsung a opté pour une dalle Dynamic Amoled 2X de 12,4 pouces, soit une surface d’affichage bien confortable pour regarder des films et des séries. L’écran de la Galaxy Tab S12+ est un poil plus grand et mesure 12,6 pouces. Les deux dalles affichent toutefois la même définition, soit 2 800 x 1 752 pixels. La Galaxy Tab S10+ prend également en charge le format HDR10+ et bénéficie d’un taux de rafraîchissement de 120 Hz, gage d’une excellente fluidité. N’oublions pas que le S Pen, un stylet bien réactif, est bel et bien fourni.
Galaxy AI pour être plus productif
Pour animer sa Galaxy Tab S10+, Samsung a choisi une puce MediaTek, la Dimensity 9300+. Il y a deux ans, par rapport à la Galaxy Tab S9 Ultra et sa puce Snapdragon 8 Gen 2, la marque promettait 18 % de performances CPU en plus, 28 % pour la partie GPU et 14 % pour le volet NPU. Globalement, cette configuration reste aujourd’hui suffisamment solide pour assurer une navigation fluide et même faire tourner quelques jeux un peu exigeants dans de bonnes conditions. De plus, la tablette embarque évidemment Galaxy AI, la suite de fonctionnalités d’intelligence artificielle développée par le fabricant sud-coréen.
Vous pourrez ainsi profiter de l’Assistant Note, qui permet de rendre un texte manuscrit plus lisible et mieux organisé, ou encore de l’outil Traduction, qui se charge de traduire rapidement un PDF, par exemple. L’ardoise est en outre compatible avec Samsung DeX, qui transforme son interface en un environnement de travail proche de celui d’un ordinateur. Enfin, concernant son autonomie, la Galaxy Tab S10+ renferme une grosse batterie de 10 090 mAh, compatible avec la charge rapide à 45 W. Si elle fait jeu égal avec la S12+ sur la puissance de charge, cette dernière dispose toutefois d’une batterie un peu plus grande (10 600 mAh), et Samsung lui promet jusqu’à 21 heures de lecture vidéo, soit environ cinq heures de plus que la S10+. De son côté, la S10+ devrait pouvoir tenir toute une journée loin d’une prise.

articles.title: TE Connectivity at OCP Summit 2026 The Interview
articles.text:
At the 2026 OCP Global Summit, I had the chance to sit down with Brian Payne, Vice President of Product Management for the Digital Data Networks (DDN) business at TE Connectivity.
Many of our readers will know Brian from his 26 years at Dell, but he had been at TE Connectivity for about a month when we spoke. TE’s booth was built around three interconnected system-level racks, an optical interconnect rack, a sidecar power rack, and a copper IT rack, so we walked through the high-speed connectivity, the power delivery, and why TE thinks its system-level approach matters as AI infrastructure scales. We previously published a short booth tour video on STHLabs that got a surprising amount of attention, so we figured we would follow it up with the interview we did while we were there.
As always, we lightly edited this for readability.
Brian Payne and TE Connectivity at OCP
Patrick Kennedy: Brian, could you tell us a little bit about yourself?
Brian Payne: Sure. First of all, thanks. It’s great to see you again. I am vice president of product management here at TE Connectivity. I’ve got a long history in this industry. I spent 26 years at Dell.
Patrick Kennedy: Could you give us a little bit of background about TE Connectivity?
Brian Payne: TE Connectivity is a very large organization that manufactures and provides connectivity across multiple industries. But one of the most exciting things we’re doing right now is in what we call DDN, our Digital Data Networks division. We have experienced massive growth over the last three years, all building out the AI infrastructure that’s powering everything we’re doing today. It’s an exciting space to be in, with tremendous upside ahead of us.
Patrick Kennedy: As part of that, TE Connectivity is well known for its contributions to OCP.
Brian Payne: TE Connectivity has been a part of OCP since 2017, so very early days. And as you can imagine, look around us. OCP has just boomed in terms of growth. TE Connectivity is focused on power and connectivity across all domains in the AI infrastructure. We have made tremendous contributions, and there are some exciting ones we’re going to talk about today.
448G and Next-Generation Front-Panel Connectivity
Patrick Kennedy: You have some things in your hand that I think you are super excited about. Could you tell us what these are and show us a little bit?
Brian Payne: Absolutely. At TE Connectivity, we’re thinking about how we deliver power for the data center and how we connect it. With every chip innovation, more and more bandwidth is coming. How do you get that out of the compute tray, and how do you get it into the network? One of the challenges is getting to 448. There are a lot of thermal challenges and signal integrity challenges to balance, and there’s a push in the industry to find the right solution. I would say there are two competing models out there.
Patrick Kennedy: And just to be clear here, these are 3D-printed models.
Brian Payne: The reason I’ve got a 3D-printed model is that, just Monday of this week (at the October 2026 OCP Summit), in a partnership with NVIDIA and Cisco, we announced our new standard for getting to 448. That’s what I have in my hand right here. You will see that it’s a similar form factor to QSFP today. One of the things we’re trying to do is balance signal integrity, power delivery, and form factor, and not over-index on one or the other. We believe we have a winner.
When you talk about developing concepts, that’s exactly what we have here. The transceiver slides in, and we’ve got a unique way to compress it so that power delivery and signal integrity are handled separately. So our signal integrity is really, really strong. The design is also made so that, as we see the power of the transceiver escalate, we’ll be able to do cold plate liquid cooling to pull heat out of the system.
Patrick Kennedy: When you say 448G, you’re talking about the SerDes and really the per-lane communication speed.
Brian Payne: Absolutely.
Patrick Kennedy: That’s a big deal when we start talking about things like picojoules per bit, or how much power it takes to move data. But there are also a number of enabling technologies beyond USFP that you have behind us. Maybe we should start with some of the copper over here.
Copper Backplanes and Midplanes
Brian Payne: One of the huge areas of breakthrough in the industry has been copper backplane technology, and a combination of copper backplanes as well as midplanes. What we have here is an example of a midplane design, where a compute sled slides in along with power delivery. By going with this midplane design, you’re able to separate compute from GPU and then easily connect those together through the midplane. Then on the back side, we’ve got copper backplanes. In terms of an unlock for these rack-scale solutions, it is a highly technical, highly engineered solution that we have to produce in massive volumes.
TE is one of the only companies in the industry that’s able to do that. There are very few in the market, and we’re excited about that. We are focused from the chip all the way to the switch. We’ve got innovation in near-chip packaging. We’ve got innovation around optics. We’re thinking about front and back I/O connectivity and the cabling in between. We’ve got innovation and products across all of those that are being deployed today at massive scale.
Patrick Kennedy: One of the interesting things in AI deployments is just how many lanes of communication are happening in every single box in a rack. How do you make that, number one, not use too much power and not create too much heat, but then also make it reliable? I imagine that’s a lot of what TE Connectivity needs to work on.
Brian Payne: One of the things I’ve discovered, and it’s been a pleasant surprise coming into TE Connectivity, is the R&D on the front end. How do we get through the material science challenges and develop the parts necessary to unlock these massive increases in bandwidth, and then deal with all of the power that’s required to push these chips and push the data across the network?
Optics and Co-Packaged Optics
Patrick Kennedy: There are a number of technologies today focused on extending the usefulness of copper, but the next generation is really optics. I think you have a demo of that over here.
Brian Payne: The main thing I would say here is that you can go back to 10 Gigabit Ethernet, when we said the end of copper was coming, and copper is still prevalent in the industry. That being said, optics is there and solving a very, very important challenge. This is part of how we’re pathfinding and investing ahead. Earlier this year, we acquired an optics company, RAM Photonics. We’re bringing that into the product portfolio, and we’re massively investing in optics, from co-packaged optics as well as co-packaged copper, to getting the optics out of the system. So we’ve got a number of investments and new capabilities emerging to support that.
Patrick Kennedy: Folks have been talking about co-packaged optics in the industry for what feels like forever. What’s different about what’s happening today versus 10 years ago, when folks were saying, “Oh, we need co-packaged optics immediately”?
Brian Payne: I think it is the physics challenge, and how far you can route copper as we increase the number of lanes that are necessary. There is a point in time where we will have to make the pivot. I realize you could have said that 10 or 12 years ago, but it’s becoming more and more real as we face these challenges. That’s why our investment and productization are picking up in that space. But it’s not stopping our investment in copper, because copper is still the state of the art. It’s still important to deliver the outcomes our customers expect. That’s where we’ve got a dual investment.
Patrick Kennedy: One of the things you’re showing in the booth is some of the innovation around co-packaged optics, with connectors that go into the chip package so that you can service them. That was something folks didn’t know how to do even five or six years ago, and it’s a new innovation to bring co-packaged optics to the mass market and actually deploy it.
Brian Payne: When these are deployed at scale, it’s not just about getting the signal across the line. It’s about how you think about the system-level design and the operation, and what this looks like at scale. So to your point, serviceability is a critical design vector that drives innovation. That’s part of the TE approach: how do we not just get the technology working, but do it in a way that will support the massive volumes this industry is driving?
Power: The Sidecar Power Rack and Horizontal Busbar
Patrick Kennedy: This is a power shelf and a power rack. Why do we have a power rack, with racks focused on data connectivity on either side?
Brian Payne: To deliver the performance the industry is driving for, a massive amount of power is required to power the chips, and then to power the switches that connect them together. We simply don’t have the power density today to fit all of that in one rack, and that led to the innovation we see today. We’re starting to see sidecar designs like what we have here, which is a full rack of power distribution and cooling capabilities on one side.
Then on the back side, when we get around there, we’ve actually got a busbar that runs horizontally, which is unique in the industry. Nobody’s done that. We did it to solve a problem with one of our large customers, and to deliver power to the next rack, the IT rack, with the IT equipment, the compute sleds, and the switches. That’s a great example of us thinking whip to chip. How do we put together a practical solution that addresses the ever-growing thirst for more and more power?
Patrick Kennedy: One of the really interesting things there is that the density challenge is actually in the nodes, so that you can get the copper connectivity within a rack. It’s actually using power to solve a connectivity challenge. And one of the big innovations is moving that power out of the rack and figuring out how to get a lot of current back into it.
Brian Payne: Right. In this industry, we have talked about power constraints and half-full racks for years and years. We’ve talked about busbars, and none of that really took hold until the AI boom. That’s what led to the innovation where we are delivering liquid-cooled busbars that span the rack to deliver power across without having to amp up the current and the overall heat dissipation. It’s about finding that balance in power delivery, but doing it in an efficient way.
The next frontier is high voltage. We’ve got pathfinding concepts on the back side here where we’re pushing towards 800 volt. That’s what’s going to be necessary to get to a megawatt of power at the rack level. So how do we solve practically for the limitations of today, and also prepare ourselves for the future?
800V and Rack-to-Rack Power
Patrick Kennedy: One of the cool things about 800 volt is that it provides a more efficient power distribution path, which means your data center is more efficient. But there are cool things you’re doing as well. That 800 volt busbar back there has liquid cooling.
Brian Payne: Absolutely. And there are even things we can’t show you yet. Getting to 800 volt, number one, we’re thinking about how you get 800 volt all the way from the source. Every conversion has losses associated with it. So how do we bring it from the busways down into the rack, and then deliver it efficiently across the rack? To run this efficiently, liquid cooling to pull heat out is a critical element, and it’s something we’ve solved and have deployed across the industry.
Patrick Kennedy: You have another solution, which is a big, giant rack-to-rack cable. Can you tell me a little bit about that?
Brian Payne: Part of the issue is that once you get the power down to the IT equipment and you need to span multiple racks, you have to have an efficient way to get it rack to rack if a horizontal busbar isn’t the optimal choice. That’s why we’ve got prototype rack-to-rack 800 volt cables on the back of the system.
Patrick Kennedy: And that prototype is another example of how TE Connectivity is doing pathfinding with the OCP community and with customers to figure out how to solve these practical challenges.
Brian Payne: Our customer engagement starts in our customers’ data centers and in their offices, but also at places like OCP, where you can see we’re just covered up with people coming by. That inspires thought, new ideas, and future innovation. It’s super important to be a part of this community, to get those ideas in, show people what we’re thinking, and then iterate and evolve the designs going forward.
Pathfinding and Manufacturing at Scale
Patrick Kennedy: Could you give us some sense of how TE Connectivity doesn’t just make products for standards, but actually contributes to the pathfinding behind a lot of what is used in OCP?
Brian Payne: Absolutely. I’ll take power as an example. We think whip to chip. We’re one of the few, if not the only, company focused on the entire power delivery of the AI infrastructure at the AI rack. That means we see the bottlenecks before they occur, and we’re able to project ahead. The industry has the ambition to get to a megawatt of power at the rack level, and that has a lot of hard challenges. Behind us here, you’ll see some of the concepts we’re working on for how we’re going to deliver power rack to rack in the future. We get feedback on those from customers in real time, and we’re able to course correct and be ready when the industry needs us to go to full mass production.
Patrick Kennedy: I would imagine there are a bunch of steps that go into that. It starts with what problem you’re trying to solve. But then there’s also how you make something manufacturable, that you can build for a large AI data center and for an entire industry that’s really building around OCP.
Brian Payne: Everything starts with the customer. We’re partnering with the entire ecosystem, but especially the hyperscalers building out these AI data centers at a breakneck pace. The chip cycle, everything has moved faster, and we’ve got to be way ahead of where things are going: partnering, figuring out the problems they need to solve, innovating, delivering concepts, getting feedback, and continuing to iterate until we have the design the customers need.
Then that’s when we’ve got to shift to, “Oh my gosh, there are thousands of units to build to roll out in mass production.” We’ve got global manufacturing capabilities, and we’re able to rise up and produce high-quality, mass-produced parts to power the AI infrastructure we all enjoy today. TE Connectivity has a large global manufacturing footprint. We have 10 manufacturing facilities around the world, from China to Southeast Asia to North America, all focused just on the DDN business to power what’s going on in this industry.
What Is Driving TE Connectivity
Patrick Kennedy: Brian, I’ve known you for years. At the end of the day, what are the big things that are driving you?
Brian Payne: It all starts with our customers. What do they need us to do? They need us to be at the forefront of technology innovation, and they need us to be able to deliver to support their business. That means we have to be able to design high-quality products that solve the technical challenges we have. But just as important, we’ve got to be able to manufacture at scale. We’ve got that balanced investment where we can do that across power and connectivity to push the industry forward.
Patrick Kennedy: Awesome.
Final Words
A big thank you to Brian for taking the time to walk us through TE Connectivity’s booth at OCP Summit 2026. The broader theme was that AI infrastructure is no longer just a chip problem.
Getting to 448G per lane, scaling copper while preparing for co-packaged optics, and moving rack power toward 800V and the megawatt-class rack all have to work together at the system level, and then be manufactured at scale.

articles.title: Microsoft Rules Out Cyberattack in Outage, Warns of Phishing Campaign
articles.text:
Microsoft says its recent Microsoft 365 outage was not caused by a cyberattack, but warns that attackers used the disruption to send phishing emails disguised as service notifications.
The November 12 outage disrupted access to Exchange Online mailboxes and Outlook. The tech giant also identified possible effects on services such as Teams, SharePoint Online and Microsoft 365 Copilot. Organizations and government agencies in several countries reported interruptions to email and other operations.
“This was a technical issue not related to cyber or AI / agents,” Microsoft said in a statement on Friday.
The company traced the failure to an earlier network capacity upgrade, with a subsequent network change exposing the problem. Microsoft said it fixed the underlying issue and was bringing services back in stages to ensure they remained stable. The Exchange Online incident, tracked as EX1550543, was marked resolved on November 13.
Microsoft Threat Intelligence said it observed a phishing campaign exploiting the disruption. The fake emails posed as Microsoft 365 service health notices and referred to EX1550543, the actual incident identifier.
In some messages detected on November 13, recipients were falsely told that emails held during the outage would be deleted within 24 hours unless they clicked a link to restore them.
The phishing emails’ subject lines began with “Outage -” followed by a six-character code. Sender display names included organization-specific wording followed by “Outage Notification” or “Service Health.”
Microsoft identified three domains used to send the emails: moments-notice[.]com, planetmaison[.]com and newbooker[.]com. Recipient-specific SendGrid tracking links redirected to reallifeaccounting[.]com. Similar messages targeted organizations across several US sectors.
“The activity is consistent with credential phishing, although credential collection and malware delivery have not been confirmed,” Microsoft said.
The company subsequently reported that its security products were blocking the campaign.
Microsoft recommended that security teams examine suspicious emails and links, investigate user clicks, and review their Safe Links policies. It also advised organizations to verify service incidents directly through the Microsoft 365 admin center.

articles.title: NVIDIA Announces Rubin HPC — A New GPU to Accelerate Agents for Science, Engineering and Analytics
articles.text:
Announced today at SC26, NVIDIA Rubin HPC is a new GPU in the NVIDIA Vera Rubin platform designed to accelerate simulation and data processing for science, engineering and analytics workflows.
As agents help scientists and engineers explore more candidate materials, molecules and designs, they rely on simulations to test those ideas and guide their next steps. Rubin HPC will accelerate those simulations, shortening the path from exploration to scientific discovery and industrial design.
The Rubin HPC GPU features a record number of CUDA cores — more than 50,000 on a single GPU — as well as a sparse data acceleration capability that keeps those cores fed with data, and accelerates GPU-to-GPU connectivity with seventh-generation NVIDIA NVLink interconnect technology.
Scientists and engineers rely on simulation to understand complex systems before committing to experiments or physical prototypes. Working with agents, these teams can explore more candidate materials, molecules and designs. This increases demand for the GPU-accelerated simulations needed to evaluate those ideas and guide next steps.
“For agents tackling science and engineering, faster simulation means faster discovery,” said Ian Buck, vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing at NVIDIA. “Rubin HPC accelerates the simulations agents use to test ideas and guide their next steps, helping scientists and engineers explore more possibilities and bring breakthroughs closer.”
Turning Faster Computation Into Faster Discovery
Across climate models, engineering simulations, genomic analysis and financial risk, scientific computing workloads take a similar shape: an application reaches into an immense dataset, gathers a handful of scattered values, calculates a result and repeats this on an enormous scale.
To help address the challenge, Rubin HPC will offer a balanced design, scaling data movement and compute together rather than increasing compute alone.
That balance is what optimizes Rubin HPC for scientific computing. It keeps the GPU’s record number of CUDA cores supplied with data, so they spend their time computing rather than waiting. This accelerates recurring patterns of every simulation workload — from sparse matrix operations to stencil computations to sorting and reductions.
These patterns are prevalent across data analytics, science and engineering workloads, which is why a purpose-built GPU delivering the broadest acceleration can help unlock cross-industry breakthroughs.
NVIDIA CUDA-X libraries offer a growing set of optimized implementations of complex algorithms for agents to use, including those most relevant to simulation and analytics. Used together with Rubin HPC, the libraries can give agents the fastest glide path to reasoning outcomes.
And faster agent-invoked simulations mean faster feedback — shortening the loop of hypothesis, simulation and refinement, so researchers and engineers can choose next steps sooner and point lab work at the most promising candidates.
Rubin HPC is expected to be available in 2028.

articles.title: Apple is testing daily usage limits for more complex Siri AI interactions
articles.text:
Apple released betas of iOS 27.3, iPadOS 27.3, and macOS 27.3 today, and the company is using the update to test new per device daily usage limits for some Siri AI and Apple Intelligence features, according to MacRumors.
Apple is testing daily usage limits for more complex Siri AI interactions
Frequent users of some Siri AI and Apple Intelligence features will require an iCloud Plus subscription to avoid limits.
Basic Siri commands and requests will remain free and unlimited, but more advanced features that rely on cloud-based processing like generating, cleaning up, or extending images in Photos will be subjected to the daily limits. There are four categories of limited usage, MacRumors reports, including using Siri AI for “multi-step, personal context requests,” image generation and editing tools, automations in Shortcuts that “rely on Apple Foundation Cloud and Cloud Pro Models,” and third-party apps that use those same cloud models.
Apple hasn’t specified exactly how many times those features and tools can be used each day before limits are reached, but they’ll vary based on the task. The company reportedly plans to provide notifications when users are approaching their limit and have finally reached it.
Instead of having to wait until midnight each day for your usage to reset, most of Apple’s existing iCloud Plus plans (excluding the 50GB option) will include higher daily limits at their same price. The $2.99/month 200GB subscription includes 2x the usage, the $9.99/month 2TB plan includes 5x the usage, while the $29.99/month 6TB and $59.99 12TB/month options bump the usage limit to 10x and 20x, respectively. Family members sharing an iCloud Plus subscription will have a shared usage pool that’s used on a first come, first served basis.
Last week Apple updated Logic Pro with an option to “Buy More Usage” for that app’s intelligent assistant through $49.99 Intelligence Usage Packs that are expected to be added to other Apple Creator Studio apps this month, including Pixelmator Pro, Final Cut Pro, Motion, plus Pages, Keynote, and Numbers.

articles.title: AI Day Seoul Brings Together Korea’s Industry Leaders, Startups and Developer Communities
articles.text:
Over two days at COEX, more than 2,000 attendees converged for AI Day Seoul, bringing together Korea’s industry leaders, startups and developer communities advancing physical AI and AI agents.
At the plenary sessions, Deepu Talla, vice president of robotics and edge AI at NVIDIA, said Korea is “punching above its weight,” with Doosan Robotics, Hyundai Motor Group, LG Electronics and SK Group — as well as startups like Real World and Luda Robotics — using NVIDIA platforms to bring general-purpose robotics into the real world.
Jonathan Cohen, vice president of applied research at NVIDIA, showed how enterprises can build agents they own and control. Breakout sessions featured speakers from Coupang Intelligent Cloud, Doosan Robotics, LG AI Research, LG Electronics, NAVER Cloud, SK Telecom and Upstage.
“It was a genuinely enjoyable time to have candid conversations,” said Hyunho Yang, research engineer for omnimodal foundation models at SK Telecom. “Seeing the passion of fellow AI developers was a real source of inspiration for me.”
The Agentic AI 10x Bootcamp Community Day brought together Pseudo Lab, Python Korea, PyTorchKR, HAERAE, Hugging Face KREW, Graph User Group, Womxn Who Code Korea, Dnol (Datayanolja) and other developer communities. Five finalists from the Hangul Day hackathon, co-hosted with Fastcampus, built agents trained on the Korean language and culture with the OpenShell runtime. The winning team, FlyGate, received an NVIDIA DGX Spark system.
More than 500 developers also took part in full-day NVIDIA Deep Learning Institute workshops and NVIDIA Certification exams in Korean. Workshops covered deploying and optimizing AI inference at scale, building end-to-end robotics workflows with the NVIDIA Isaac platform and developing secure AI agents. Certification included the new AI Model and Application Development exam.
The Physical AI Startup Connect event included pitches from 10 NVIDIA Inception startups: AIM Intelligence, Avikus, GoLe Robotics, MOVIN, Neubility, ROAI, ROBROS, TESOLLO, TwelveLabs and XYZ. The AI for Science Forum brought together the Korea Institute of Science and Technology Information, Korean universities and NVIDIA Research.
AI Day Seoul sessions will soon be available on NVIDIA On-Demand.
